## 2026-03-26 — rev0499: Handoff-graph / receipt-edge canon pass
- Re-opened the latest archive after the kernel-shipset pass and asked what still prevented the repo from behaving like an implementable family rather than a pile of good local repos. The clearest missing layer was **handoff-graph discipline**: the repo could already say which seams matter, which journeys they compose inside, and what first repo each top seam should build, but it still lacked one explicit place to say **what artifact should move from one seam into another and what stability posture that edge relies on**.
- Fresh official Cargo and service signals all supported that move. The Cargo external-tools reference still centers stable tool integration around `cargo metadata`, `--message-format=json`, and custom subcommands, explicitly noting that `cargo metadata` is stable and versioned with explicit `--format-version`. The build-analysis goal is still prototype-stage around recorded build metadata and unstable `cargo report` commands. The March 2026 build-dir-layout testing call says the layout is internal-only but many projects still depend on unspecified details and should test their tools, tests, and release processes. Together, those signals argue that the missing value is not a new framework but a set of explicit receipt edges with stable-versus-unstable posture. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- Registry and review signals sharpened the practical edges. The January 2026 crates.io update added GitLab Trusted Publishing support, Trusted Publishing only mode, blocked risky GitHub Actions triggers, and a `pubtime` index field. The March 2026 Cargo advisory says crates.io deployed a preventative change on March 13 and audited all published crates for the incident class. The Jan/Feb 2026 Project Director update adds `cargo-capslock`, accepted vulnerability-surfacing work, and a proposed End User Group intended to aid Rust adoption and tooling innovation for industrial users. That strongly supports a local review-kit edge that imports service truth without pretending service truth is the whole decision. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/21/cve-2026-33056/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/03/25/project-director-update/
- Release and machine-readable-surface signals reinforced the same pattern. The `cargo-semver-checks` goal remains aimed at the `cargo publish` workflow and explicitly describes witness-program generation via `cargo check`, while also noting that rustdoc JSON still lacks some precise information needed for certain checks. docs.rs says hosted rustdoc JSON is programmatic but caveat-heavy: consumers must inspect `format_version`, older releases may not yet have downloads, and redirect targets may temporarily not exist. The libtest JSON goal says Cargo can benefit from programmatic test output and that shifting responsibility toward the runner enables more powerful custom runners. Those sources justify a handoff graph that preserves caveated structured facts rather than laundering them into generic “semantic tooling.” Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html ; https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/libtest-json.html
- Broader ecosystem signals kept the ranking stable while motivating the new downstream edge into navigation and readiness. The 2025 State of Rust survey still says resource usage remains a significant productivity issue, debugging remains a notable pain point, and online docs remain the preferred canonical reference even as some learning traffic appears to be moving toward LLM tooling. The March 2026 challenges post still says crate choice/trust, embedded constraints, and safety-critical maturity are real pain areas. That makes receipt-bearing defaults and readiness cards better downstream consumers of reviewed evidence than standalone portal or badge products. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/20/rust-challenges/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
- Archive decision: add `design/epic-contribution-handoff-graph-2026Q1.md`; add `meta/HANDOFF_GRAPH_PROTOCOL.md`; add `ledgers/top-band-handoff-graph-v0/README.md` and `ledgers/top-band-handoff-graph-v0/handoffs.json`; add `tools/check_handoff_graph.py`; refresh the front-door and continuity rails (`AGENTS.md`, `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/LATEST_REVISION_FILESET.md`, `meta/LLM_ARCHIVE_CONTINUITY_PROTOCOL.md`, `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`, `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`, `meta/ARCHIVE_DOCTOR_PROTOCOL.md`), plus `ledgers/README.md`, `kernels/README.md`, and the source atlas; mirror changed files under `archive/`; regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`; rerun `tools/hygiene.py`; rerun `tools/archive_doctor.py`.
- Deepening decision: keep the broad ladder intact, but add **receipt-edge discipline** as the new repo-construction layer. **Build-State Evidence** stays first overall and now also anchors the first required edge; **Package Intake + Release Boundary Review** remains the clearest urgent operator seam and now also anchors the strongest service-truth edge; **Compatibility Claims** becomes more concrete as a structured-facts handoff into release-boundary review rather than a stand-alone empire; **Feedback / Debug Acceptance Commons** deepens through explicit import of build receipts; **Safety-Critical + Institutional Readiness Commons** deepens through explicit import of review receipts; and **Adoption Navigation + Ecosystem Atlas** remains downstream of reviewed receipts rather than a free-floating recommendation layer.

## 2026-03-26 — rev0498: kernel shipsets / first-repo-shape canon / validated shipset ledger
- Re-opened the latest archive after the decision-journey pass and asked the next practical worthy-repo question: once the archive can rank seams, place them, watch them, falsify them, give them believable wedges, and say what decision journeys they compose inside, **what exact first repo should a small team actually build?** The older kernel briefs already answered pieces of that, but only in prose. The missing layer was a compact, current, machine-checkable shipset ledger.
- Cargo build analysis still strongly supports a bounded first shipset rather than a grand framework. The goal is explicitly prototype-stage, records build metadata across invocations, adds unstable `cargo report` commands for rebuild reasons and timings, keeps collection opt-in, and makes no user-facing stability guarantees during prototyping. That kept **Build-State Evidence** first and made it even clearer that the first shipset should be a careful companion, not a Cargo-core takeover. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html
- Cargo's external-tools reference still says simple integration with third-party tools happens through `cargo metadata`, `--message-format`, and custom subcommands, and that `cargo metadata` is stable and versioned when called with an explicit `--format-version`. That supported a shipset ledger that names import surfaces and repo modules explicitly rather than fantasizing about Cargo as a library. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html
- The build-dir-layout goal plus the March 2026 testing call still describe real operator pain around whole-dir locking, Rust Analyzer contention, cache reuse, and tools depending on unspecified build-dir details. That reinforced the current Build-State shipset shape: capture + diff + doctor + migration receipts, with stable-only versus unstable-enhanced posture visible. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-dir-layout.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- The January 2026 crates.io update and the Mar. 25 2026 Project Director update made the package-boundary shipset more concrete rather than broader. Trusted Publishing now supports GitLab.com, crate owners can enforce Trusted-Publishing-only mode, risky GitHub triggers are blocked, the vulnerability surfacing tab is live, and `cargo-capslock` exists for static and runtime capability analysis. That strengthened **Package Intake + Release Boundary Review** as a local-first intake-review kit with route profiles, waivers, quarantines, and drills instead of any global trust score. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/03/25/project-director-update/
- The `cargo-semver-checks` goal remains publish-workflow-shaped and still depends on more precise rustdoc information plus witness-program generation, while docs.rs rustdoc JSON stays programmatic but caveat-heavy: consumers must check `format_version`, some releases still lack downloads until rebuilds land, and redirect targets may temporarily not exist. That kept compatibility/release-boundary logic as imported truth inside shipsets rather than a magically settled substrate. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html ; https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json
- The libtest JSON goal remains another strong machine-readable signal: libtest ships with rustup, carries standard-library-class compatibility guarantees, and is being pushed toward Cargo-owned reporting. That supported the decision to keep first shipsets artifact-bearing and validator-friendly. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/libtest-json.html
- The 2025 State of Rust survey plus the March 2026 challenges note still concentrate ecosystem pain around compile/resource usage, debugging, crate-choice burden, embedded constraints, and safety-critical maturity gaps rather than one absent mega-framework. That justified keeping the shipset ledger narrow and excluding **Adoption Navigation + Ecosystem Atlas** from kernelization for now. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/20/rust-challenges/
- The 2026 goals overview says annual goals now have more time to organize and are still centered around explicit champions/resources, which favors shipsets small enough for named owners rather than vague epic programs. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/

## 2026-03-26 — rev0496: launch wedges / first-proof paths / believable entry points
- Re-opened the latest archive after the hypothesis-ledger pass and asked the next practical question: once the repo can rank worthy seams, map their homes, watch upstream drift, and name falsifiers, **how do those seams actually enter the world credibly?** The archive had enough strategy but still lacked one compact layer for first users, trigger moments, proving grounds, and anti-sprawl discipline.
- The current public Rust picture still rewards wedge-first thinking. The 2025 State of Rust survey says resource usage remains one of the main productivity limits, debugging remains a live pain point, and documentation stays the canonical learning source even as editor- and LLM-mediated learning rises. The March 2026 challenges post still points to async pain, crate-choice/trust problems, domain immaturity, and safety-critical tooling gaps rather than one missing flagship framework. Those are decision-shaped pains, which means a worthy contribution should prove itself by helping with one repeated decision quickly. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/20/rust-challenges/
- Build-State Evidence still has the clearest first wedge. Cargo build analysis is still explicitly a prototype around recorded build metadata and unstable `cargo report` subcommands, which makes a companion review wedge honest rather than redundant. The March 2026 build-dir-layout-v2 testing call also says many tools still rely on unspecified internals because Cargo features are missing, which reinforces a wedge around reviewable receipts and explicit unknowns rather than hidden archaeology. Cargo's external-tools guidance still encourages custom subcommands and CLI-driven imports. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/ ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html
- Package Intake + Release Boundary Review also has a newly concrete wedge. crates.io's January 2026 update adds a live Security tab, GitLab support for Trusted Publishing, Trusted-Publishing-only mode, and blocked risky GitHub triggers. The Jan/Feb 2026 Project Director update says `cargo-capslock` exists for static and runtime capability analysis and the vulnerability surfacing tab is live. That means the first believable wedge is not a universal trust score; it is a maintainer or reviewer carrying route, capability, and waiver receipts into publish/admission decisions. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/03/25/project-director-update/ ; https://crates.io/docs/trusted-publishing ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html
- Debug Acceptance and Safety Readiness still deepen rather than leap, but both now have clearer first-proof paths. The debugging signals still describe capability gaps across tuples, async contexts, and unsupported states, which favors session exports and tuple cards over a debugger fork. The safety-critical and Foundation signals still favor readiness-card and stewardship-heavy commons work over certification theater, and the Innovation Lab plus Foundation strategy make the host shape more believable when a wedge proves itself. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/23/rust-debugging-survey-2026/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/ ; https://rustfoundation.org/strategic-plan/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/03/welcoming-the-rust-innovation-lab/
- The enabling substrates still matter, but as imports, not empires. docs.rs rustdoc JSON remains valuable and caveat-heavy, and the 2026 goals overview still frames work as contributor-proposed and team-supported rather than automatically resourced. That supports a thin launch-wedge ledger focused on believable entry, not broad claims of inevitable execution. Sources: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/

Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/03/26/adopting-the-fls/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/FLS-up-to-date-capabilities.html

## 2026-03-23 — rev0472: reversibility map / blast-radius discipline / ratchet-versus-probe rollout grammar
- Re-opened the latest archive after the decision-rights pass and asked which practical comparative question about the strongest worthy Rust contributions was still under-specified. The sharpest missing layer was **reversibility**: not just what is important, who must agree, or where it should live, but **how safely it should begin, how expensive it is to reverse, and what kind of blast radius or ratchet it creates if the first shape is wrong**.
- Cargo's external-tools chapter and `cargo metadata` compatibility language reinforced that companion-first tooling can create real value on bounded machine-facing surfaces without immediately ratcheting Cargo-core UX or compatibility commitments. That makes core defaults more expensive to reverse than companion tools or unstable report lanes. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The Build Dir Layout v2 testing call provided a live example of blast radius: downstream tools are explicitly being asked to test because assumptions about artifact locations and integrations may be affected. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- The docs.rs default-target change provided a concrete model of a stronger rollout shape that still preserves reversibility: change the default, but retain an explicit opt-out in `Cargo.toml`. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/16/docsrs-changed-default-targets/
- `cargo fix` provided a concrete model of reviewable automation that remains defeasible and rollback-friendly because it applies compiler suggestions to source under user control rather than silently mutating project state as policy. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html
- The `cargo-semver-checks` goal provided a concrete model of a useful ratchet with escape hatch: default SemVer checking in `cargo publish` paired with an override flag analogous to `--allow-dirty`. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html
- Archive decision: add `design/epic-contribution-reversibility-map-2026Q1.md`; refresh the routing/meta canon so future portfolio passes can name advisory probes, opt-in gates, default-with-escape-hatch launches, operator boundaries, and governance ratchets explicitly; refresh the source atlas with new cards for `cargo fix` and `cargo-semver-checks`; mirror the changed canon under `archive/`; regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`; and rerun hygiene plus archive-doctor.

## 2026-03-23 — rev0470: Boundary-fit map (companion-first vs upstream, narrow upstream asks, and true substrate programs)
- Re-opened the latest archive after the distortion-risk deepening and asked which comparative question was still making the repo blur too many distinct things together. The clearest gap was **boundary fit**: the archive could say which contributions were worthy, what they should ship, what they must prove, what they should ask for, and how they could distort — but it still under-specified **where the value should actually live**. The recurring failure mode was treating “important” as shorthand for “merge it into Cargo/rustc/docs.rs”.
- Fresh primary signals aligned around a sharper split. Cargo's external-tools chapter still channels integration through bounded machine-facing surfaces (`cargo metadata`, JSON messages, custom subcommands) and tells consumers to use explicit format versions. The Cargo 1.93 and 1.94 development-cycle posts explicitly say Cargo can't be everything to everyone because of compatibility guarantees, even while showing progress on structured logging, `cargo report`, build-dir layout, custom final artifacts, and schema discussions. The Cargo plumbing goal is even more direct: experiment with a **third-party subcommand** to learn what Cargo should integrate. Those are all strong signals that many worthy bets should begin as **companion layers with narrow upstream asks**, not as merge-everything proposals. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- The opposite side of the split is equally important. Build-analysis and build-dir work are active but still evolving, which argues for companion evidence layers above narrower upstream primitives. By contrast, StableMIR / `rustc_public`, `build-std`, and Rust-for-Linux stable tooling are clearly **upstream substrate/stabilization programs**: their value is a more reliable Cargo/compiler/library contract itself, not a product wrapped around today's gaps. cargo-semver-checks adds the in-between case: strong companion checker first, maybe narrow publish-time Cargo integration later if the proof burden is paid. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/stable-mir.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/build-std.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/rfl.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html

## 2026-03-23 — rev0469: distortion-risk map / false-success discipline for worthy contributions
- Re-opened the latest archive after the renewal-burden pass and asked a narrower but more operational question: once several Rust ecosystem contributions are clearly worthy, **how do they most easily become dishonest while still looking successful?** The repo already had ranking, proof, support, and upkeep layers. What it still lacked was an explicit map for false-success patterns: unstable-surface overread, one-tuple theater, projection-becomes-canon drift, boundary collapse, scorecard corruption, and stewardship theater.
- Fresh primary signals made that question necessary rather than cosmetic. The March 20, 2026 challenges post still identifies broad recurring pain, but it is also unusually direct about summary weakness: the original version was retracted because readers felt the LLM voice bled through. The 2025 State of Rust survey still says resource usage is a major problem, debugging remains a notable pain point, and docs remain the preferred canonical reference even as editor/LLM mediation rises. Together those two sources make it harder for the archive to treat summary layers as harmless. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/20/rust-challenges/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Cargo's own docs sharpened the anti-overclaim story. `cargo metadata` is a stable/versioned JSON lane, but consumers are told to pass `--format-version` and not rely on opaque internals. The external-tools chapter routes integrations through a bounded set of machine-facing surfaces. The FAQ says human-readable output often lacks compatibility guarantees. And `cargo package` says `.cargo_vcs_info.json` is only a best-effort snapshot and does **not** verify provenance. Those are exactly the kinds of distinctions a distortion-risk note should preserve. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/faq.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- Cargo goals and related infra work reinforced different false-success patterns. The build-dir-layout goal says users often make assumptions about implementation details of `target/` and want finer-grained units, which is a warning against over-reading internals. The build-analysis goal explicitly avoids user-facing stability guarantees during prototyping. The rustc-perf improvements goal says results should be compared within a configuration, not across different configurations, which is a portable anti-Goodhart lesson for the archive. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-dir-layout.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/rustc-perf-improvements.html
- Other seam-specific signals reinforced the rest of the map. The debugging survey says stellar support must span several debugger versions across operating systems and keep working across representation changes, so one-tuple debugger demos are specifically the wrong proof shape. The `cargo-semver-checks` goal says false-positives and false-negatives are unacceptable, that over 90% of real-world false-positives trace back to cross-crate items, and that some checks need witness programs compiled with `cargo check`, which is strong evidence against syntactic overclaim. The March 2026 Cargo advisory separates crates.io mitigation posture from alternate-registry posture, which is strong evidence against boundary collapse. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/23/rust-debugging-survey-2026/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/21/cve-2026-33056/
- Comparative decision: keep **Build-State Evidence** as the strongest broad first build and now also the clearest anti-overread / anti-Goodhart first build; keep **Feedback Loop / Debuggability Acceptance** as the clearest high-value anti-one-tuple seam; keep **Adoption Navigation + Ecosystem Atlas** as the clearest projection-versus-canon seam; keep **Tooling Contract**, **Shared Spine**, **Semantic Context**, and **Compatibility Claims** as the main imported-surface and adapter-lossiness seams; keep **Package Intake Gateway** as the clearest trust-score-theater / boundary-collapse seam; and keep **Safety-Critical Readiness Commons** as the clearest stewardship-theater seam.
- Meta-hygiene decision: add a new comparative layer so future revisions stop smuggling false-success patterns into otherwise-strong recommendations. The repo now explicitly asks future worthy-contribution work to say **what weak surface is being imported**, **what false-success launch would still count as failure**, and **what artifact proves the contribution resisted distortion**.

## 2026-03-23 — rev0465: shared-spine execution blueprint for stage-0 worthy contribution work
- Re-opened the latest archive after the compounding pass and asked what practical question was still under-answered. The March 2026 challenges post still clusters pain around recurring practical taxes rather than novelty problems; just as importantly for repo hygiene, its author's note says the original version was retracted because readers felt the LLM voice bled through, even though the team still stood by the content. That is unusually direct evidence that generated prose should not silently become canonical truth. The 2025 State of Rust survey keeps resource usage high while docs remain canonical and editor/LLM mediation rises, which increases the need for bounded briefs and assistant-safe handoffs beneath later guidance layers. Cargo plumbing keeps saying the machine-facing surface is still phase-split and incomplete; build-analysis and the 1.93/1.94 Cargo cycles keep showing active motion around recorded metadata, `cargo report`, structured logging, build-dir layout, and compatibility-sensitive plugin/porcelain boundaries; docs.rs rustdoc JSON, libtest JSON, and StableMIR / `rustc_public` progress keep proving more substrate is becoming machine-usable but still version-sensitive; and current package-ingress/security posture keeps proving route/extraction boundaries need the same honesty grammar as other evidence layers.
- Archive decision: add `design/shared-spine-execution-blueprint-2026Q1.md`; add clarifying addenda to `design/portfolio-artifact-conventions-2026Q1.md` and `design/portfolio-execution-sequencing-2026Q1.md`; refresh routing/meta files so future stage-0, common-envelope, brief-versus-canon, and assistant-handoff questions route through the new note; refresh the source atlas by adding the Cargo 1.93 cycle and linking the new note from the main source cards for challenges, survey, Cargo plumbing, build-analysis, Cargo 1.94, build-dir testing, docs.rs rustdoc JSON, libtest JSON, package-ingress/security, Foundation strategy, Innovation Lab, and StableMIR / `rustc_public`; mirror the changed canon under `archive/`; regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`; and rerun hygiene plus archive-doctor.
- Stage-0 decision: keep the broad ladder intact; keep **Build-State Evidence** as the strongest broad first build; but make **Shared Spine Contract Kit** the archive's explicit answer for stage-0 glue. Its worthy shape is a thin **shared envelope + lineage receipt + compatibility gate + validator/linter + fixture corpus + bounded brief/assistant-slice family**. It should begin as a bootstrap companion protocol and fixture project with upstream liaisons. It should refuse the wrong shapes: hosted registry, universal mega-schema, Cargo replacement, or LLM memory canon. And future revisions must now say what is shared, what is seam-specific, what artifact role changed, what compatibility gates applied, and how assistant-facing slices remain weaker than canonical packs.

Cargo’s `cargo package` command makes package publication a curated boundary by rewriting the manifest, removing `[patch]`, `[replace]`, and `[workspace]`, including `Cargo.lock` by default, and verifying the packaged crate can be built. Cargo publishing remains permanent and package-oriented. crates.io’s January 2026 update added GitLab CI/CD Trusted Publishing, a Trusted-Publishing-only mode, and blocked the risky `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` GitHub triggers. Cargo’s unstable SBOM support now generates precursor JSON files for executable and linkable outputs uplifted into target or artifact directories. Rust’s 2026 flagships keep SBOM support and public/private dependencies in the active supply-chain band. cargo-dist’s `DistManifest` now exposes releases, artifacts, assets, upload files, linkage information, and GitHub artifact-attestation posture. release-plz continues to automate changelog generation, GitHub/Gitea/GitLab releases, cargo-registry publishing, and version bumps. cargo-binstall documents limited signature support, `--only-signed`, and explicit signature-skipping switches. Together those signals say the missing contribution is not another release wrapper; it is a **producer-side release-truth layer** that keeps subject, publication, artifact, signature, rebuild, inventory, and consumer-handoff truths distinct.

## 2026-03-23 — Distribution contract execution refresh (delivery/acquisition/ownership is now concrete, not just a seam)
- Cargo's current install docs still say `cargo install` manages Cargo's local installed binary set, chooses an install root through local config and environment, supports crates.io / git / path / alternate registries, and ignores packaged `Cargo.lock` unless `--locked` is used. That is strong evidence that Rust's ordinary delivery story is still a route-and-policy story rather than one universal package-management contract. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html
- Cargo config still treats installed-state tracking as a first-class local fact: `install.root` writes binaries under a chosen root and records metadata like `.crates.toml` and `.crates2.json`. That means “what this tool claims to manage” is not a side detail; it is part of the missing contract. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html
- rustup still installs into Cargo's `bin` directory by default, channel/toolchain docs still keep version/channel/host choice explicit, and the Cargo 1.90 cycle explicitly says rustup should only remove content it manages in shared paths. Taken together, those signals sharpen the archive's old intuition that shared path is not shared ownership. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/installation/index.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/concepts/channels.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/concepts/toolchains.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/
- Cargo's 1.86 cycle still highlights `cargo install-update` as plugin territory, which means initial delivery and later continuity remain separate seams in practice. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/02/27/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.86/
- cargo-dist now explicitly separates build and distribute phases, emits machine-readable manifests, and in 0.31.0 added mirror-style fallback hosting plus work to reduce partial-install risk. cargo-binstall is explicit that acquisition is a route/fallback problem, not one universal install lane. release-plz keeps producer-side release automation increasingly normal upstream. That combination strengthens the archive's earlier claim that the missing contribution is a reviewable handoff/composition layer rather than another installer. Sources: https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist ; https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md ; https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall ; https://release-plz.dev/docs/usage
- Archive decision: add [`design/distribution-contract-execution-blueprint-2026Q1.md`](./design/distribution-contract-execution-blueprint-2026Q1.md), refresh [`design/distribution-contract-2026Q1.md`](./design/distribution-contract-2026Q1.md), [`design/distribution-contract-stack.md`](./design/distribution-contract-stack.md), and [`proposals/epic-distribution-contract-stack.md`](./proposals/epic-distribution-contract-stack.md), and tighten [`INDEX.md`](./INDEX.md) / [`PRIORITIES.md`](./PRIORITIES.md) / [`STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`](./STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md) so **Distribution Contract** now has an explicit execution answer: **reference layer + report/pack command + adapter/acceptance corpus**, bounded by release-import truth, route/catalog truth, selection/fallback truth, verification truth, installed-ownership truth, and consumer-handoff truth.

## 2026-03-23 — rev0443: Cargo Artifact Contract execution blueprint
- Rust's 2026 flagships still keep Cargo plumbing under “Building blocks”, which confirms that reusable Cargo integration surfaces remain official strategic terrain rather than only downstream glue. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The accepted Cargo plumbing goal still decomposes build work into locate/read/lock/resolve/plan/execute/**stage final artifacts** and says later commands should accept earlier outputs. That keeps final-artifact staging as an explicit seam in Cargo's own mental model. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- The March 13, 2026 build-dir-layout-v2 testing call says many tools still rely on unspecified build-dir details because Cargo lacks features, while also making explicit that intermediate build artifacts and final artifacts can now be separated. That strengthens the case for a portable final-output boundary above build-dir internals. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- Nightly rustc's Cargo layout docs now say `artifact-dir` is part of Cargo's public API while `build-dir` remains internal. That is the sharpest current official signal that final-output layout is different in kind from intermediate-build layout. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/cargo/core/compiler/layout/index.html
- Cargo's unstable docs say `--artifact-dir` exists because exact filenames are otherwise awkward to determine, and those same docs tie SBOM precursor files to executable/linkable outputs uplifted into target or artifact directories. That means artifact-linked sidecars are upstream reality now, not an archive invention. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo 1.93's custom-final-artifacts discussion is the missing execution clue: Cargo is already reasoning about staged final artifacts, collision checks, selected-package uplift rules, and concurrent safety, which is exactly the seam an artifact contract should preserve. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- Cargo's external-tools docs still say the stable third-party surfaces are mainly `cargo metadata`, `--message-format=json`, and custom subcommands. That is enough to build point tools, but still too patchwork to serve as one portable final-output contract. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html
- Rust release notes now clarify that `.crate` tarballs are intermediate unless you use `cargo package`, which strengthens the archive's insistence that package outputs, copied artifacts, and other final-output classes must not be flattened together. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html
- Archive decision: add `design/cargo-artifact-contract-execution-blueprint-2026Q1.md`; refresh `design/artifact-surface-kit.md`, `proposals/epic-artifact-surface-kit.md`, `design/worthy-contribution-shortlist-2026Q1.md`, `design/ideal-rust-worthy-contributions-2026Q1.md`; update the canon/meta routing files; mirror the changed files under `archive/`; regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`; and keep future artifact revisions honest by separating **selected subject, evidence path, final artifact identity, origin/staging, sidecar attachment, and bounded consumer handoff** instead of flattening them into one “artifact list”.

## Latest addition (rev0442)
This revision is a **deepening** pass, not a new frontier promotion.

The repo's broad execution answer and ideal-Rust synthesis were already stronger:
- **Build-State Evidence** was the strongest single-project bet;
- **Feedback Loop / Debuggability Acceptance** was the clearest under-ranked missing middle;
- **Native Edge Contract** was the active specialist frontier;
- **Async Capability Commons** had just gained an execution blueprint;
- and the ideal-Rust note had already named **Safety-Critical Readiness Commons** as a worthy but program-shaped opportunity.

What the archive still lacked was a crisper answer to:
**what should that safety-critical commons contribution actually ship before it turns into one evidence pack, one vendor qualification story, or one badge system?**

The new answer is now explicit in:
- `design/safety-critical-readiness-commons-execution-blueprint-2026Q1.md`

Why this deepening was merited:
- Rust's January 2026 safety-critical writeup says the pressure in these domains is not only language semantics but process, verification, and evidence; it also recommends target-focused readiness checklists, dependency lifecycle patterns, async-runtime requirements, and treating interop as part of the safety story.
- The 2026 flagships page defines Safety-Critical Rust in terms of MC/DC, normative unsafe docs, safety-critical lints, and FLS cadence, which means the official roadmap is already about reviewable readiness surfaces rather than one feature.
- The MC/DC goal emphasizes sustainable architecture and maintenance commitment; the normative-unsafe-docs goal emphasizes authoritative guidance for real `unsafe` patterns; the Clippy goal emphasizes a durable home for 50–200 safety-relevant lints; and the FLS cadence goal emphasizes predictable spec releases for assessors.
- Ferrocene's public docs show the missing shared layer vividly: real qualification stories have explicit in-scope/out-of-scope flags, narrow qualification envelopes, and experimental targets/features that are shipped but not qualified. That is a strong signal that Rust still lacks an ecosystem-neutral readiness commons above isolated evidence and vendor documentation.

Files added or refreshed:
- New design note: `design/safety-critical-readiness-commons-execution-blueprint-2026Q1.md`
- New proposal note: `proposals/epic-safety-critical-readiness-commons.md`
- Design refresh: `design/worthy-contribution-shortlist-2026Q1.md`, `design/ideal-rust-worthy-contributions-2026Q1.md`
- Design/meta refresh: `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, `RESEARCH_LOG.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_RENEWAL_QUEUE.md`, `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`, `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`

Strategy:
- keep the broad ladder intact;
- keep **Build-State Evidence** as the strongest one-project answer;
- keep **Feedback Loop / Debuggability Acceptance** as the clearest under-ranked day-to-day missing middle;
- keep **Native Edge Contract** as the active specialist frontier;
- and make **Safety-Critical Readiness Commons execution blueprint** the canonical answer for “what should the program-shaped safety-critical contribution actually build?” rather than leaving it split across evidence, assurance, target notes, dependency lore, and interop caveats.

Hygiene:
- future safety-critical-readiness revisions should say explicitly whether they changed **critical-slice truth**, **authority truth**, **qualified-scope truth**, **target/runtime truth**, **dependency-lifecycle truth**, **interface truth**, or only **repo hygiene**;
- and do not let one target checklist, one vendor manual, one evidence stack, or one async/runtime story silently become the whole archive answer.

## 2026-03-23 — rev0437: Portfolio contribution shapes (make worthy seams choose the right kind of deliverable before overbuilding)
- Re-opened the latest archive after the source-atlas revision and asked what still felt missing once the repo could already rank seams, specify blueprints, stage the portfolio, prove pilots, keep a source atlas, and run a doctor loop. The cleanest missing layer was no longer “another worthy seam.” It was a cross-cutting answer to a different execution question: **if a Rust contribution is worthy, what kind of thing should it actually become first?** The archive had many smart ideas but no shared morphology for choosing between protocol, collector, reference layer, report command, service, corpus, checker, bridge, pilot program, or stewarded program.
- Fresh official and primary-tool signals made that shape question timely rather than decorative. Rust's March 20, 2026 challenges writeup says the recurring pain picture is not only about language features; it includes compile performance, tacit knowledge, and domain-shaped ecosystem friction. The 2025 survey says the broad problem picture is fairly stable and docs remain canonical even as editor/LLM mediation rises. The February 11, 2026 program-management update says the project now organizes work under roadmaps and application areas intended to focus industry funding, which is a direct reminder that some worthy contributions are honestly **program-shaped** rather than tool-shaped. Cargo build analysis is explicitly a collector/report-command direction, recording build metadata and introducing `cargo report` surfaces while leaving schemas unstable during prototyping. The Cargo 1.94 cycle shows that shape in motion with `cargo report rebuild`, `cargo report sessions`, structured logging, and man pages. StableMIR is explicitly a semver-governed compiler-facing API / reference-layer move meant to let tools work without compiler internals. The libtest JSON goal is explicitly about programmatic test output and shifting reporting responsibility toward Cargo and runners. crates.io's January 2026 update says the new frontend generates type-safe API client code from OpenAPI, which is a service/API shape decision rather than a local command or corpus. Together those signals made the missing contribution less “one more seam” and more “a small shared atlas for choosing the right contribution class before overbuilding.”

- Deepening decision: keep the broad ladder intact; keep **Build-State Evidence** as the strongest one-project answer; keep **Native Edge Contract** as the active specialist frontier; but make **Portfolio Contribution Shapes** the canonical answer for “what class of deliverable should this worthy seam actually become?” rather than leaving that judgment to style and instinct.

## Latest addition (rev0434)
This revision is a **deepening + hygiene** pass, not a new frontier promotion.

The repo's broad execution answer and proving-grounds layer were already stronger:
- **Build-State Evidence** was the strongest single-project bet;
- **Package Intake Gateway** was the most underappreciated operational seam;
- **Native Edge Contract** was the active specialist frontier;
- **Semantic Context Contract** was the key hidden multiplier;
- and the repo already had a shared scenario matrix for comparing serious pilots.

What the archive still lacked was a crisper answer to:
**once a pilot names a shared scenario card, what concrete representative case profile should it bind to so “tested on a real repo” stops being a fuzzy, flattering claim?**

The new answer is now explicit in:
- `design/portfolio-anchor-corpus-2026Q1.md`
- `meta/ANCHOR_CORPUS_PROTOCOL.md`
- `proofgrounds/portfolio-anchor-corpus-v0/anchors.json`
- `tools/check_anchor_corpus.py`

Why this deepening was merited:
- Rust's March 2026 challenges writeup says the pain is not one uniform beginner problem; much of it is domain-shaped and maturity-shaped.
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says the broad challenge picture is stable enough that the archive can justify more stable comparison surfaces beneath its strategic claims.
- The January 2026 program-management update says goals now sit under longer-lived roadmaps and application areas intended to focus industry funding, which increases the value of representative case profiles that say which kind of reality a pilot actually exercised.
- The rustc-perf improvements goal is explicitly about distributed benchmarking across multiple platforms and configurations, with comparison discipline that does **not** flatten incompatible runs.
- Crater exists because compiler changes should not be judged on one anecdotal repo; representative corpus matters.
- The March 2026 Build Dir Layout v2 testing call says even a crater run “won't cover everything”, which is a direct reminder that case coverage must be named rather than assumed.
- The February 2026 Rust debugging survey says debugging quality varies across debuggers and operating systems, which is another reason to stop calling one environment “representative” without saying which one.

Files added or refreshed:
- New design note: `design/portfolio-anchor-corpus-2026Q1.md`
- New meta note: `meta/ANCHOR_CORPUS_PROTOCOL.md`
- New corpus: `proofgrounds/portfolio-anchor-corpus-v0/README.md`, `proofgrounds/portfolio-anchor-corpus-v0/anchors.json`
- New tool: `tools/check_anchor_corpus.py`
- Tooling refresh: `tools/archive_doctor.py`, `tools/hygiene.py`, `meta/ARCHIVE_DOCTOR_PROTOCOL.md`, `meta/ARCHIVE_DOCTOR_LAST_RUN.json`
- Design/meta refresh: `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, `RESEARCH_LOG.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `proofgrounds/README.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`

Strategy:
- keep the broad ladder intact;
- keep **Build-State Evidence** as the strongest one-project answer;
- keep **Native Edge Contract** as the active specialist frontier;
- sharpen the proving/evaluation layer with concrete representative anchor profiles rather than inventing another #1;
- and keep anchor profiles visibly separate from scenario cards, freshness renewal, and seam-local semantics.

Hygiene:
- future representative-case revisions should say explicitly whether they changed **scenario coverage**, **anchor profile coverage**, **hold-constant rules**, **allowed variation**, or only **repo hygiene**;
- if a revision materially changes the anchor corpus, update the design note, protocol, corpus, and checker together;
- and do not let one charming private demo, one public sample repo, or one benchmark run silently become the archive's definition of “representative”.

## 2026-03-22 — rev0423: Native Edge execution blueprint (turn the active specialist frontier into a buildable reference layer)
- Re-opened the latest archive after the Adoption Navigation deepening and asked which already-ranked answer still lacked a canonical “what should this actually ship?” note. The cleanest answer was **Native Edge**: the repo already treated it as the active specialist frontier, but unlike Build-State Evidence, Semantic Context, Package Intake, Migration/Public API, and Adoption Navigation, it still had no execution blueprint making the artifact spine and anti-goals explicit.
- Fresh primary signals aligned around the same missing shape. The accepted 2025H1 seamless Rust/C++ interop goal says Rust should seriously consider adoption inside projects that must use **large, rich C++ APIs**. The 2025H2 interop problem-space map says there are **billions of lines of C++** representing enormous value and that broad rewrites are not the practical near-term answer. The July 2025 goals update says Rust should evolve toward a **first-class C++ interop story** while also stressing that different groups need different lanes. The January 2026 program-management update makes **Cross-language interop** an explicit application area and highlights live CPython collaboration topics like linker-argument splits and introducing Rust into large C codebases. The January 2026 safety-critical writeup says many teams will integrate Rust into existing C and C++ systems and carry that boundary for years. Cargo's own docs reinforce that the missing layer is still above today's ingredients: build scripts own native probing/building, `links` is one-package-per-value with metadata flowing only to immediate dependents, `target-applies-to-host` and `host-config` exist because host/target behavior is still tricky, and build-script overrides exist because some teams need structured native facts without re-running upstream probes. The major tool families remain serious but non-equivalent: CXX focuses on a safe common Rust/C++ regime, `autocxx` targets large existing C++ codebases, `bindgen` still depends on `libclang`, and Corrosion proves foreign-build handoff is real without collapsing provider and boundary choices. Together those signals say the missing contribution is not another bridge empire, but a **portable native-edge reference layer** with explicit subject, boundary, provider/link, context, handoff, and bounded consumer truth.

Cargo's March 21, 2026 advisory says the `tar`-crate vulnerability used during Cargo extraction could let a malicious crate change permissions on arbitrary directories and explicitly tells users of alternate registries to verify impact with their vendor. Cargo's package docs describe a real packaging/staging boundary: normalized manifests, default lockfile inclusion, symlink flattening, pristine extraction/build verification, and `.cargo_vcs_info.json` as best-effort rather than verified provenance. Cargo install docs describe a materially different install-intake boundary: crates.io and git installs use temporary target directories by default, packaged lockfiles are ignored unless `--locked` is passed, and config discovery starts at `$CARGO_HOME` unless `--path` is used. Source replacement docs make the “exact same source” assumption explicit, while registries docs make alternate registries and `git` vs `sparse` protocol posture explicit and note that crates.io does not accept packages depending on other registries. crates.io's January 2026 update added Trusted Publishing-only mode, the February 2026 malware-policy update says removed malicious crates will always get RustSec advisories, the 2026 flagships put public/private dependencies and SBOM support in the secure-supply-chain band, Cargo's unstable SBOM precursor gives artifact-side downstream consumers, and sandboxed build scripts remain adjacent but explicitly post-intake. Together those signals make the missing contribution less “some supply-chain tooling someday” and more “a thin package-ingress review layer with route, payload, staging, resolution, and handoff truth.”

## Latest addition (rev0418)
This revision is a **deepening** pass, not a new frontier promotion.

The repo's broad execution answer was already strong:
- **Build-State Evidence** was the strongest single-project bet;
- **Package Intake Gateway** was the most underappreciated operational seam;
- **Native Edge Contract** was the active specialist frontier;
- **Semantic Context Contract** was the key hidden multiplier.

What the archive still lacked was a crisper answer to:
**what should the strongest one-project answer actually ship in theory and practice?**

The new answer is now explicit in:
- `design/build-state-evidence-execution-blueprint-2026Q1.md`

Why this deepening was merited:
- Rust's March 2026 challenges writeup says compilation performance is a universal productivity tax rather than a niche complaint.
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says resource usage / slow compile times and storage usage remain among the biggest non-trivial productivity problems.
- The 2025 compiler-performance survey says editor latency matters greatly in practice and that more than 35% of respondents who see IDE/Cargo blocking as a big problem report the two blocking one another.
- Cargo's build-analysis and build-dir-layout work now make first-party machine-usable build evidence materially more real than before.
- The March 2026 Build Dir Layout v2 testing call says many tools still rely on unspecified build-dir details because Cargo is missing higher-level features, which is exactly the sort of situation that wants a reviewable companion layer rather than more folklore.
- Rust Analyzer's documented separate-target-dir workaround proves that some of today's practical answers explicitly trade lock avoidance for artifact duplication.
- The March 2026 Cargo extraction advisory sharpened **Package Intake Gateway** further, but it also clarified that ingress/extraction truth should stay separate from build-review truth rather than being flattened into one giant “supply-chain + builds” empire.

Files added or refreshed:
- New design note: `design/build-state-evidence-execution-blueprint-2026Q1.md`
- Design refresh: `design/worthy-contribution-shortlist-2026Q1.md`, `design/strategic-territory-map-2026Q1.md`, `proposals/epic-build-state-evidence-stack.md`
- Frontier/meta refresh: `AGENTS.md`, `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, `RESEARCH_LOG.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`, `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`

Strategy:
- keep the broad ladder intact;
- keep **Build-State Evidence** as the strongest one-project answer;
- keep **Native Edge Contract** as the active specialist frontier;
- sharpen the winner with a concrete blueprint rather than inventing another #1;
- and keep **Package Intake Gateway** visibly separate from build-state work even while its urgency rises.

Hygiene:
- future execution revisions should say explicitly whether they are **promotion**, **deepening**, **synthesis with no new promotion**, or **hygiene**;
- if a revision is mainly about the archive's current one-project winner, prefer a sharper blueprint, artifacts, and anti-goals over a fresh promotion;
- do not let one security advisory, one build-dir migration, or one editor workaround silently rewrite the entire ladder.

## 2026-03-22 — Native Edge Contract (promote the cross-language/native-adoption seam above FFI leaves, provider leaves, and foreign-build folklore)
- Re-opened the latest archive and deliberately looked for a frontier that stayed distinct from Public API, Migration Truth, Toolchain Productization, Compatibility Claims, and Polyglot Productization. The repo already had strong substrate in `design/native-edge-stack.md`, `design/ffi-boundary-kit.md`, `design/native-dependency-kit.md`, and the native-edge pilot materials, but it was still under-modeled as a stack note instead of a first-class contract.
- Fresh primary-source review kept converging on the same missing boundary. The accepted 2025H1 goal **Evaluate approaches for seamless interop between C++ and Rust** explicitly targets Rust adoption in projects that must use large, rich C++ APIs. The 2025H2 **C++/Rust Interop Problem Space Mapping** goal says there are billions of lines of C++ and that rewrites are often infeasible. The July 2025 goals update says Rust should evolve toward a **first-class C++ interop story** while also stressing that needs differ across groups. The January 2026 program-management update makes **Cross-language interop** an explicit application area for Rust and industry funding. The January 2026 safety-critical writeup says teams will carry Rust↔C/C++ boundaries for years and explicitly asks for better tooling to keep interfaces correct, auditable, and in sync. Rust 2024 now requires `unsafe extern` blocks, reinforcing that signatures themselves are a review boundary, and newer release notes keep hardening non-Rust ABI edges. Meanwhile the ecosystem tool story is real but plural: CXX carves out a safe common regime with paired code generation and static assertions; `autocxx` explicitly targets large existing C++ codebases; `bindgen` still depends on `libclang`; and Corrosion can import Rust into CMake but still leaves major binding-generation choices and integrations to user workflows. Together that made the missing contribution crisp: not another bridge, but a **portable native-edge contract**.

- Strategy: keep the broad ladder intact; keep **Public API Contract** as the release-boundary / semver seam; and promote **Native Edge Stack / Native Edge Contract** as the clearest next **cross-language / native-adoption / external-build-handoff** move.
- Hygiene: future native-edge revisions must keep **boundary truth**, **provider/link truth**, **host-vs-target/toolchain context**, **external-build handoff**, and **consumer conclusions** visibly separate instead of letting one generator, one provider lock, one CMake import, or one support/audit summary silently become the whole story.

- Fresh official signals lined up unusually well. The 2026 flagships still put **Building blocks** around rebuild-std and larger-build-system integration. The accepted `build-std` goal is explicitly about an MVP that could be stabilized, not indefinite experimentation, but Cargo’s current unstable docs still require `rust-src`, nightly Cargo, nightly rustc, and passing `-Z build-std` to all invocations. rustup still keeps toolchains, targets, profiles, components, and directory-sensitive overrides separate; rustup cross-compilation still says target stdlib install is not enough because linkers and SDKs are often also required; rustc custom-target docs still say target JSON properties are unstable and compiler versions should be pinned; sanitizer docs still strongly recommend a recompiled and instrumented standard library; the sanitizer-stabilization goal explicitly calls for shipping precompiled and instrumented standard libraries through rustup; Rust for Linux still needs stable foundations for custom std/core plus ABI-affecting, hardening, and sanitizer-related compiler options; and the end-of-2025 program-management update says CPython is surfacing a very similar cluster of needs.

## 2026-03-22 — rev0410: Defect Escalation Contract / repro-to-regression-handoff promotion
- The 2025H2 goals explicitly say stabilizing `cargo script` should make it easier to write small utilities, share examples, and create reproducible bug reports without the overhead of full Cargo projects. That makes tiny, shareable reproducers an official Rust workflow rather than repo folklore. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/
- The February 11, 2026 program-management update says `cargo script` is “fantastic for coming up with minimal bug reproducers and quick prototypes” and that a single file you can share or paste into Markdown makes a practical difference. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/11/program-management-update-2026-01/
- Forge triage already treats reproductions, missing info, MCVEs, and bisections as explicit queue state: issues can get `S-needs-repro`, `S-needs-info`, `E-needs-mcve`, `E-needs-bisection`, `S-has-mcve`, and `S-has-bisection`. That means escalation truth is already operationally real even if it is not yet portable. Source: https://forge.rust-lang.org/release/issue-triaging.html
- The rustc-dev-guide says fixes should come with regression tests and that tests derived from bug reports should be kept succinct and minimized. That means a good escalation boundary should already preserve “is this ready to become a test?” rather than stopping at issue prose. Source: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/tests/adding.html
- The 2025H2 libtest-JSON goal is explicit that users rely on programmatic test output and that reporting responsibility should shift upward toward Cargo/runners, lowering the barrier for custom runners and custom harnesses. That is a strong adjacent signal that escalation should be able to import machine-usable runner/report evidence without redefining the harness layer itself. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/libtest-json.html
- Cargo 1.94 continues the `cargo report` / build-analysis push with `cargo report rebuild` and `cargo report sessions`, which makes local evidence more likely to survive into a portable escalation packet. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The March 20, 2026 challenges post plus the 2025 survey keep debugging, resource usage, and ongoing friction visibly high, so a better repro-to-regression lane looks like real ecosystem infrastructure rather than issue-tracker polish. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/20/rust-challenges/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add `design/defect-escalation-contract-2026Q1.md`, `gaps/defect-escalation-minimal-repros-routing-and-regression-handoffs.md`, and `proposals/epic-defect-escalation-stack.md`; refresh `design/defect-escalation-stack.md`, the two ladder files, `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`; and promote **Defect Escalation Contract** so the archive now treats **observation truth + minimization-lineage truth + routing/dedup truth + regression-candidate truth + consumer-handoff truth** as a first-class missing boundary instead of letting one MCVE, one duplicate guess, or one issue template define the whole escalation story.

## 2026-03-22 — Adoption navigation contract (promote project-scoped recommendation truth into a first-class frontier)
- Re-opened the latest archive after the maintenance-reality promotion and deliberately asked which already-present seam had the strongest current-source case for promotion without duplicating the build/debug, supply-chain, delivery, compatibility, or runtime-production bands. The strongest answer was the repo's ecosystem-navigation substrate: the archive already had atlas, adoption-decision, reviewable-defaults, canonical-learning, trust, maintenance, and semantic-context notes, but it had not yet stated clearly that Rust needs a first-class **recommendation handoff boundary** above those leaves.
- Fresh official and primary-project signals lined up unusually well. Rust's March 20, 2026 challenges post explicitly names **choice paralysis** and **tacit knowledge** in ecosystem navigation, says maturity varies dramatically by domain, and says the problem is not lack of libraries so much as the expertise needed to choose among them. The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the preferred canonical reference while people increasingly learn with LLM tooling and editors with agentic support are rising. Rust's December 2025 vision work says users need help getting oriented in crates.io, says there is no clear place to get advice on a good starter set of crates, and recommends better supportive guidance from crates. docs.rs changed its default targets in October 2025, which is a reminder that recommendation canon drifts. crates.io's January 2026 development update added a Security tab, stronger Trusted Publishing controls, SLOC, and `pubtime`, which means recommendation inputs are materially stronger than they used to be. The Rust Foundation's 2026–2028 strategy explicitly couples adoption growth, sustainable maintenance, and stable infrastructure. The January 2026 maintenance writeup says maintenance is continuous and socially real, which means recommendation layers must import stewardship posture instead of confusing popularity with sustainability. Blessed.rs remains useful evidence that unofficial curation demand is real, but it is not the portable review boundary the ecosystem still lacks.

- Promotion decision: keep the broad ladder intact; keep **Build-State Evidence** as the strongest broad/buildable contribution; keep **Reviewable Lane Defaults + renewal receipts** as the immediate execution seam; but promote **Adoption Navigation Bundle**, read now as an **Adoption Navigation Contract**, as the clearest next **anti-tacit-knowledge / project-scoped recommendation** move for question records, candidate lanes, canonical references, imported evidence, local-fit checks, and bounded human/platform/CI/assistant handoffs.

The 2025 State of Rust survey still says docs are canonical while machine-mediated/support-mediated use is rising.

## 2026-03-22 — Publisher & source identity contract (promote publication / authority / route truth into a first-class frontier)
- Re-opened the latest archive after the observability promotion and deliberately asked which already-present seam had the strongest current-source case for promotion without duplicating the build/debug/tooling or runtime-production bands. The strongest answer was the repo's publisher/source identity substrate: the archive already had org-identity, trust-signals, trust-decision, package-admission, and distribution notes, but it had not yet stated clearly that publication-side identity needs its own **contract boundary** above those leaves.
- Fresh official signals lined up unusually well. The crates.io January 2026 development update says Trusted Publishing now supports GitLab CI/CD in addition to GitHub Actions, adds Trusted-Publishing-only mode, and blocks risky GitHub Actions triggers. Cargo’s publishing and owner docs are explicit that named owners and team owners are different authority classes. The registry web API says Cargo has no inherent notion of users/owners beyond registry-defined handling. Registry-authentication docs make credential-provider posture part of authenticated alternate-registry behavior. Source-replacement docs define replacement as exact-copy equivalence and say a replacement source may not contain crates absent from the original source. RFC 3243 plus the open-namespaces goal keep namespace/family control live. RFC 3052 makes it impossible to treat manifest authorship, current ownership, and user-facing identity as the same plane. `cargo package` says `.cargo_vcs_info.json` is a best-effort VCS snapshot whose provenance is not verified. Verification/mirroring work adds further pressure to keep route/source posture separate from later trust or install views.

## 2026-03-22 — Safety-critical assurance contract (promote reviewable evidence composition into a first-class frontier)
- Re-opened the latest archive after the harness-protocol promotion and deliberately asked which already-present seam had the strongest current-source case for promotion without simply duplicating the build/debug/tooling frontier. The strongest answer was the archive's existing safety-critical cluster: the repo already had safety evidence, coverage evidence, sanitizer/proof, and conformance substrate, but it had not yet stated clearly that high-assurance review needs a separate **assurance composition boundary** above those leaves.
- Fresh official signals lined up unusually well. Rust's 2026 flagship roadmap now treats **Safety-Critical Rust** as a distinct theme with explicit milestones for MC/DC coverage support, normative unsafe docs, safety-critical Clippy lints, and stable FLS cadence. The January 2026 safety-critical writeup says the pressure in these domains is process, verification, and evidence, and recommends isolating high-criticality logic into small slices. The MC/DC goal says prior support was removed for maintenance reasons, that out-of-compiler implementation is infeasible for real Rust, and that a sustainable architecture plus maintenance commitment is now the real question. The normative-unsafe-docs goal says the Nomicon is incomplete and UCG is largely abandoned, so authoritative unsafe guidance still has to be built. The Clippy goal says 50–200 safety-oriented lints may be needed and should preferably live inside community tooling. The FLS cadence goal says each FLS release should ship within six weeks of stable Rust. The standard-library contracts goal and `core::contracts` module make machine-readable contracts more real. The rustc coverage docs keep criterion, engine, and doctest caveats explicit.

- Promotion decision: keep the broad ladder intact; keep the current build/debug/tooling contracts intact; keep **Harness Protocol Contract** as the clearest current testing seam; but promote **Safety-Critical Evidence Stack / Safety-Critical Assurance Contract** as the clearest next **high-assurance / evidence-shaping** move beneath safety evidence, coverage evidence, sanitizer / verification lanes, and conformance traceability.

## 2026-03-22 — Workspace environment contract (promote environment truth into a first-class handoff layer)
- Re-opened the latest archive after the Cargo artifact and build-interop promotions and asked what high-ranked Tier-A seam was still under-modeled as a concrete frontier. The strongest answer was **Workspace Environment Stack**: the repo already had the substrate, but it had not yet stated clearly that environment truth is a separate seam from Cargo build interop or final-artifact identity.
- Fresh official signals lined up unusually well. The 2025 State of Rust survey says resource usage remains a productivity problem, online docs remain the preferred canonical reference, and editors with agentic support are rising. Cargo config is explicitly hierarchical and merges parent-directory configuration. Cargo workspace discovery also walks parent directories and changes package-selection defaults. rustup override selection and `rust-toolchain.toml` also walk the directory tree and expose channel/component/target/profile choices. Cargo 1.94 explicitly says broken parent manifests or `.cargo/config.toml` files can fail unrelated builds and says broader workspace/config discovery still needs improvement. rust-analyzer already exposes override commands, invocation strategies, extra args/env, linked-workspace behavior, and dedicated target-dir tradeoffs. Dev Containers and Nix are real realization substrates, but they are generic substrates rather than a Rust-specific review layer. The Rust Foundation’s 2026–2028 strategy couples stable infrastructure, sustainable maintenance, and adoption growth, which is exactly where environment handoff truth lives.

## 2026-03-22 — Proc-macro exit stack (turn language-motion around macros and reflection into a reviewable ecosystem transition layer)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next cross-cutting seam that was both already present in the repo and newly validated by current official Rust signals. The strongest candidate was no longer another build-only surface and not another support-only surface. It was the under-promoted seam between **today’s proc-macro burden** and **tomorrow’s declarative/reflection/language-first exit paths**.
- Fresh research made that seam much less speculative. The macro-improvements goal explicitly aims to make `macro_rules!` cover more cases that currently require proc macros, with the stated benefits of faster builds, simpler macros, and reduced dependency supply chains. The reflection-and-comptime goal explicitly says proc-macro derives have historically been hard to debug and bootstrap, and it positions reflection as a distinct path for some of the same problem families. The 2026 flagship themes now include **prototype reflection** under **Constify all the things**, which means reflection is not just a side experiment. The 2025 compiler-performance survey says some language features could remove build scripts or proc macros, calls out derive-proc-macro expansion as still not ideally incremental, and asks for tooling that could explain which proc macros are slow or expansive. Clippy/linting optimization work still treats proc-macro and expansion checking as active performance work. Cargo’s current surface (`cargo tree` proc-macro markers and `-e no-proc-macro`) is real inventory, but still not a workflow. And the Rust Reference still says proc macros run during compilation with build-script-like resource/security concerns.
- Archive decision: add `design/proc-macro-exit-stack-2026Q1.md`; add `proposals/epic-proc-macro-exit-stack.md`; refresh `design/epic-contribution-ladder-2026.md` and `design/ecosystem-priority-ladder-2026.md`; refresh frontier/meta files; mirror the changed canonical set under `archive/`; regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`; and state a new repo rule that macro/reflection revisions must keep **macro inventory/cost/debug truth**, **compile-time execution authority**, **transition-target truth**, **migration-confidence truth**, and **consumer-handoff truth** distinct.
- Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/macro-improvements.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/optimize-clippy.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html

## 2026-03-22 — Package intake gateway (deepen the supply-chain/intake band without rewriting the broad ladder)
- Re-opened the latest archive and explicitly chose **not** to do another broad ladder refresh right away. The stronger move was a stack/leaf deepening revision: identify the under-modeled seam that recent official changes made impossible to keep treating as a minor detail. The March 21, 2026 Cargo security advisory made that seam obvious. The vulnerability is about package extraction during a build, not merely build-script execution or registry moderation, and the advisory explicitly tells alternate-registry users to verify impact with their vendor. That points straight at a missing **package intake** boundary.
- Fresh primary sources aligned around the same conclusion. Cargo source replacement already distinguishes exact-copy mirrors and vendoring from private registries. Cargo registries already distinguish alternate-registry route identity, auth, protocol, and publish restrictions. `cargo package` already has a surprisingly rich local packaging/verify contract: normalized manifests, default lockfile inclusion, flattened symlinks, pristine extraction/build verification, and `.cargo_vcs_info.json` explicitly marked as best-effort rather than verified provenance. `cargo install` still has different semantics for packaged lockfiles, temporary target dirs, and config discovery. crates.io’s January 2026 update added Trusted-Publishing-only mode and `pubtime`, while the February 2026 malicious-crate policy update shifts routine malware communication toward RustSec advisories. And the sandboxed-build-scripts goal is important but clearly starts **after** package ingress. Together those signals say ideal Rust is missing an honest **route → payload → staging/extraction → lock/resolution → handoff** contract at the package-ingress layer.
- Archive decision: add `design/package-intake-gateway-2026Q1.md`; add `proposals/epic-package-intake-gateway.md`; add `gaps/package-intake-extraction-route-quarantine-and-handoff-truth.md`; refresh `design/epic-contribution-ladder-2026.md`; prepend new frontier notes to `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; refresh `AGENTS.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`, and `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`; mirror changed canonical files under `archive/`; and regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`.
- Ranking conclusion: the broad ranking is unchanged — **Build-State Evidence** first, **Adoption Navigation + reviewable defaults + receipts** second, **Debuggability** high, and **Rust inner-loop contract** still the clearest next build/debug composition move. What changed is the clarity of the supply-chain side: **Package Intake Gateway** is now the clearest under-modeled seam between **Package Admission**, **Dependency Review**, **Compile-Time Capabilities**, and **Consumer Install**. It should be treated as a newly explicit Tier A candidate, not as a new overall #1.
