- Re-opened the latest archive and asked a narrower question than in rev0393: after separating broad ranking from next public-lane candidacy, what existing frontier candidate now deserves actual promotion? The strongest answer was the archive’s already-existing **Feedback Loop Stack**, reframed here as a concrete **Rust inner-loop contract**.
- Fresh official evidence now lines up unusually well around this seam. The March 20, 2026 Rust challenges post keeps compilation performance central and treats it as a universal productivity tax. The 2025 State of Rust survey still places resource usage and debugging among the leading non-trivial productivity problems, while also saying docs remain canonical and editor/LLM mediation rises. The 2025 compiler-performance survey says more than 35% of respondents consider IDE and Cargo blocking one another to be a big problem, says full debuginfo slows builds and linking, and explicitly asks for tooling that can explain which code rebuilt and why. The Cargo build-analysis goal now names timings, rebuild reasons, CLI args, and build ids such as `CARGO_RUN_ID`, with external tooling and eventual build replay as explicit futures. The build-dir-layout goal and March 2026 testing call make Cargo ↔ rust-analyzer contention, shared-cache shape, and hidden build-dir assumptions first-class. rust-analyzer’s own docs/FAQ now make the “separate target directory avoids contention but duplicates artifacts” tradeoff explicit. And the 2026 debugging survey says strong debugging still requires multi-debugger tuple support, quality visualizers, first-class async debugging, and Rust expression evaluation. Together, those signals say ideal Rust is now missing an honest **session → build → debug → handoff** contract more concretely than before.
- Archive decision: add `design/rust-inner-loop-contract-2026Q1.md`; refresh `proposals/epic-feedback-loop-stack.md` and `gaps/developer-feedback-loops-build-debug-iteration-and-honest-session-handoffs.md`; prepend new frontier notes to `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; refresh `design/epic-contribution-ladder-2026.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`; mirror changed canonical files under `archive/`; and regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`.
- Ranking conclusion: broad ranking remains **Build-State Evidence** first, **Adoption Navigation + reviewable defaults + receipts** second, **Debuggability** high and rising; but the clearest next **bundle-shaping** move beneath the build/debug band is now **Rust inner-loop contract**, using the archive’s existing **Feedback Loop Stack** rather than inventing another adjacent seam. This does **not** change the separate next public-lane queue, where **browser + Node dual-target Wasm package overlay** still stays ahead of **raw custom Wasmtime embedder** and **durable internal library**.

## 2026-03-22 — Epic territory map + browser/Node Wasm overlay (refresh the ladder before widening the defaults corpus again)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next move that would improve the repo’s *judgment* rather than only its *surface area*. After rev0392 added the native-shell mobile default lane, the archive no longer mainly lacked another obvious missing card; it lacked a sharper answer to a different question: what is broadly most missing in Rust right now, what is most buildable as a worthy companion contribution, and which next public lane deserves promotion if widening resumes?
- Fresh official signals kept pointing toward the same ranking. Rust’s March 20, 2026 challenges post explicitly names **compilation/resource usage**, **async complexity**, and **ecosystem navigation driven by choice paralysis and tacit knowledge**, while also saying embedded and safety-critical maturity gaps remain real. The 2025 State of Rust survey still lists resource usage among the leading non-trivial problems, still keeps debugging high in the problem list, and still says online docs remain the preferred canonical reference even as editor/LLM-mediated learning rises. Cargo’s current work keeps making build-state truth more concrete (`cargo report`, build analysis, build-dir-layout reform), and the 2026 debugging survey makes missing debugger-tuple / async-debug / expression-evaluation support impossible to narrate as background noise. Together that makes the top-band answer clearer: **Build-State Evidence** remains the strongest broad/buildable epic, **Adoption Navigation + reviewable defaults** remains the strongest anti-tacit-knowledge answer, and **Debuggability** is the clearest rising cross-cutting frontier.
- The same research also sharpened the next public-lane candidate. The archive’s browser-package card already had an open watch item for **browser + Node dual-target packages**, but the omission is now easier to justify poorly than to justify well: the Rust project formally sunset the `rustwasm` organization; `wasm-pack` still exposes a real target matrix (`bundler`, `nodejs`, `web`, `deno`, etc.); `wasm-bindgen` still distinguishes browser versus Node deployment modes; `js-snippets` support is explicitly asymmetric; and Wasm Components are now on the official 2026 goals roadmap without replacing the current JS-target matrix yet. That means the next under-modeled public-lane candidate is not raw custom Wasmtime embedding and not durable internal library. It is the missing **browser + Node dual-target Wasm package overlay**.
- Archive decision: add `design/rust-ecosystem-epic-map-2026Q1.md`; add `design/browser-node-dual-target-wasm-package-overlay.md`; add `proposals/epic-browser-node-dual-target-wasm-package-overlay.md`; add `gaps/browser-node-dual-target-wasm-packages-target-contract-and-maintenance-truth.md`; refresh `design/ecosystem-priority-ladder-2026.md` and `design/epic-contribution-ladder-2026.md`; prepend matching frontier notes in `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; update `AGENTS.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`; mirror changed files under `archive/`; regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`; and keep future revisions honest by separating **broad ecosystem missingness**, **near-term buildability**, **next public-lane candidacy**, and **repo-hygiene/meta work**.

## 2026-03-22 — Native-shell mobile product default lane (turn “Rust mobile with native shells” from side-note folklore into a reviewable boring default)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next correction that would materially improve the maintained defaults corpus instead of widening it mechanically. UniFFI’s current docs now make the lane concrete enough to support a bounded default: the guide explicitly targets foreign-language bindings for Rust libraries; Swift bindings are documented as production-quality; Xcode integration is documented as real build-phase work; Kotlin/Android integration is documented as real Gradle/source integration work; Kotlin lifetime/resource behavior explicitly requires `close()` / `AutoCloseable` handling for exposed interfaces; and the motivation docs are explicit that UniFFI is **not** an end-to-end mobile packaging solution. On Android, `cargo-ndk` gives a clearer boring helper surface for Rust↔NDK builds. Together that made the missing contribution clear: not “yet another mobile framework,” but a **reviewable boring default** above the bridge/build/package reality.

## 2026-03-22 — Portable self-hosted Wasm edge host default lane (turn Wasm-host portability from folklore into a reviewable boring default)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next correction that would materially improve the maintained defaults corpus instead of widening it mechanically. The repo already had a managed worker-first edge-runtime card, but that card explicitly excluded the case where provider independence and self-hosted portability were the point. Spin now explicitly describes itself as a CNCF sandbox project for building and running event-driven Wasm-component applications across local development, self-hosted servers, Kubernetes, and hosted services. Spin docs now make `spin up` / `spin watch`, OCI registry distribution, target-environment compatibility checks, and plugin-based integrations concrete. Meanwhile Wasmtime’s `serve` subcommand still calls `wasi:http/proxy` experimental, `cargo component` still documents preview2 adaptation from `wasm32-wasip1`, and wasmCloud’s docs still flag planned scheduling/provider changes. Together that made the missing contribution clear: not another Wasm host, but a **reviewable boring default** above the moving lower layers.

## 2026-03-22 — Mobile app product default lane (turn Rust-on-mobile folklore into a bounded shell/core/store answer)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next maintained default that would correct a real gap instead of extending the now-strong web split. The missing answer turned out to be **mobile-first app productization**: the repo had a desktop app card and a polyglot component card, but still lacked a maintained answer to the recurring question “how should we ship a serious Android+iOS product with Rust in the core?”
- Fresh research kept pointing toward the same gap. Rust’s March 20, 2026 challenges post still names **choice paralysis** and **tacit knowledge** in ecosystem navigation. Tauri 2 is stable on mobile and has real capability/permission and plugin docs, but those docs still make mobile dev-server setup plus Kotlin/Swift plugin escape hatches explicit. Dioxus mobile has clearly matured, yet its current setup/bundle docs still keep Android/iOS tooling and store-signing steps visible. Slint is now serious on mobile too, including current iOS/Android safe-area and virtual-keyboard support. ## 2026-03-22 — Browser Wasm package lane (finish the public-web split with package-boundary truth)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately checked whether the repo still had one missing web card central enough to beat straightforward renewal work. It did. After adding the browser-first app card and the full-stack web-product card, the remaining recurring question was no longer “what Rust web framework?” but “what should we normalize around when the public product is a browser-consumed npm package rather than a deployable app?” The archive had named this split multiple times but had not yet turned it into a maintained card with a receipt.
- Fresh official and primary signals all pointed at the same seam. Rust’s March 20, 2026 challenges post still centers ecosystem **choice paralysis** and **tacit knowledge**; the 2025 State of Rust survey still says docs remain canonical while editor/LLM mediation rises; `wasm-pack build` still explicitly creates the JS-interoperable/npm-publication artifact set; `wasm-bindgen` still makes target-mode, browser-support, and browser-test differences explicit; and the old `rustwasm` docs now visibly say they are no longer maintained at that domain. The biggest new truth here is institutional rather than purely technical: Rust’s July 21, 2025 Inside Rust post formally sunset the `rustwasm` organization, transferred `wasm-bindgen` to a new organization, and said repos like `wasm-pack` would be archived or transferred. That means browser-package guidance now has to carry **tool-maintenance truth** inside the lane itself instead of narrating `wasm-pack` as if it still lived in the old Rust-project-owned center.
- The practical archive decision was therefore to add `design/browser-wasm-package-default-lane.md`, `proposals/epic-browser-wasm-package-default-lane.md`, `gaps/browser-wasm-package-defaults-js-glue-types-and-publication-truth.md`, `defaults/conservative-browser-wasm-package-2026Q1.md`, and `evidence/conservative-browser-wasm-package-2026Q1-renewal-2026-03-22.md`; refresh the frontier/queue/protocol files so the corpus now treats **browser-first public web app**, **full-stack Rust web product**, and **browser-consumed Wasm package** as three different maintained lanes; mirror the changed canon under `archive/`; and regenerate the manifest. The default answer is bounded and caveated: **`wasm-bindgen` + `wasm-pack build --target bundler` + explicit npm package identity + browser tests**, while keeping **raw `wasm-bindgen` + explicit package scaffolding** visible as the serious fallback if the `wasm-pack` maintenance story ever stops being good enough.

## 2026-03-22 — Installable CLI product default lane (route-aware release/distribution defaults for public binaries)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next corpus correction that would sharpen a central recurring lane rather than add another edge case. After adding the publishable-library card, the remaining gap inside the maintained defaults corpus was no longer “another app framework”, but the public-binary lane Rust is already known for: installable CLI products whose release/distribution choices change what users can actually acquire, update, and uninstall.
- Fresh research kept pointing toward the same seam. Rust’s March 20, 2026 challenges post explicitly says the ecosystem is excellent for **CLI tools** while navigation still suffers from **choice paralysis** and **tacit knowledge**. Rust’s December 2025 vision writeup says users still need help getting oriented in crates.io and finding good starter sets. Cargo’s install docs say non-`--path` installs ignore project-local config discovery, and packaged lockfiles are only used when `--locked` is passed. Cargo uninstall only removes packages installed with `cargo install`, so uninstall truth is route-specific rather than universal. Cargo package says `Cargo.lock` is included by default, warns that `--exclude-lockfile` is not for general use, emits `.cargo_vcs_info.json`, and rebuilds from a pristine extracted package. `cargo-dist` now presents a coherent plan/build/host/publish/announce model with installers, machine-readable manifests, and supply-chain hooks. `cargo-binstall` has matured into a real optional prebuilt-install route with manifest metadata and signature verification support. Cargo 1.86 still frames installed-binary update continuity as plugin territory rather than a solved built-in feature. Together those signals say ideal Rust still lacks a boring, reviewable default lane for installable binaries.

## 2026-03-22 — Publishable library default lane (manifest truth, docs.rs truth, semver gates, public API boundaries, and exact package identity)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next worthy move after the first receipt corpus. The gap was no longer “add another app lane” or “write more theory.” The corpus had become too application-shaped and still lacked a central answer for authors of reusable crates. The next correction was to add one **conservative publishable library** card plus its first readable receipt.
- Fresh official signals support that move. Rust’s March 20, 2026 challenges post still says ecosystem navigation is burdened by **choice paralysis** and **tacit knowledge**. The 2025 State of Rust survey still says **online documentation** is the preferred canonical reference while editor/LLM mediation rises. Cargo’s current docs already make `rust-version`, semver compatibility, and publication permanence first-class package truths. docs.rs documents `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`, its build model, and `cargo docs-rs` as a CI helper. The 2026 Rust goals explicitly include **public/private dependencies** and supply-chain work. crates.io’s January 2026 update exposes stronger public review surfaces including Security tab, Trusted Publishing only mode, source links, SLOC, and `pubtime`. ## Rev0378 — concrete default corpus, evaluation rubric, and first maintained cards

This revision keeps the repo on its current navigation/adoption frontier but makes one practical move down the stack: it turns **Reviewable Lane Defaults** into a **maintained corpus**.

New files:
- `design/lane-default-evaluation-framework.md`
- `design/reviewable-lane-defaults-corpus.md`
- `proposals/epic-lane-default-corpus.md`
- `gaps/concrete-reviewable-default-corpus-and-renewal-discipline.md`
- `defaults/conservative-internal-cli-2026Q1.md`
- `defaults/conservative-http-service-2026Q1.md`
- `defaults/polyglot-workspace-component-2026Q1.md`
- `meta/LANE_DEFAULT_CORPUS_PROTOCOL.md`

Research conclusion:
- The archive had already identified the missing layer between Atlas candidate space and one-off adoption briefs, but it still lacked a **current corpus of reviewable defaults**.
- The stronger move now is not another broad navigation essay but a bounded set of default cards backed by an explicit evaluation framework and renewal discipline.
- The first three defaults worth publishing are:
  1. conservative internal CLI / automation,
  2. conservative HTTP/service baseline,
  3. polyglot workspace / monorepo component.

Why these three:
- CLI is one of Rust’s strongest adoption lanes and is the easiest place to prove a reusable default honestly.
- HTTP/service is strategically important and especially prone to accidental folklore unless runtime/framework assumptions stay visible.
- Polyglot component adoption is common in practice and is where “choose a boundary framework too early” causes hidden long-term cost.

Practical repo consequence:
- future navigation/default revisions should prefer renewing or extending `defaults/` before inventing another adjacent top-band seam.
- future default-card work should use the evaluation rubric, preserve alternatives, and make escalation triggers explicit.

## 2026-03-22 — Consumer lifecycle continuity bundle (turn a top-band candidate into a real receipt-chain epic)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next move that would change the repo’s shape instead of adding another isolated stack note. After rev0373 introduced the Epic Contribution Ladder 2026, the strongest next step was to sharpen one Tier A candidate into a buildable program. Consumer Lifecycle Continuity was the best fit because the archive already had strong leaf notes for install, update continuity, distribution contract, route mobility, and release truth, but it still lacked a single document that said what the bundle itself should be.
- Fresh official Cargo/Rust signals kept pointing toward the same gap. Cargo install already defines install-root precedence, source classes, reinstall triggers, packaged-lock behavior, and config-discovery boundaries, including the fact that packaged `Cargo.lock` is ignored unless `--locked` is passed and that non-`--path` installs begin config discovery at `$CARGO_HOME/config.toml`. Cargo uninstall uses the same root-precedence model and only removes packages installed with `cargo install`, which makes ownership scope a first-class lifecycle fact. Cargo package says `--exclude-lockfile` is not for general use because some consumers expect the lockfile, including `cargo install --locked`. Cargo’s source-replacement docs say exact-copy mirrors are not patching or private registries, while cargo vendor says vendored sources are read-only and real modifications should use `[patch]` or `path`. Finally, Cargo’s 1.86 development update explicitly highlighted `cargo install-update` as a plugin and said built-in installed-binary update support is still being tracked. Together those signals say the missing contribution is a thin receipt chain for **install → update → rollback/uninstall → route change**, not a universal updater or another package-manager wrapper.
- Archive decision: add `design/consumer-lifecycle-continuity-bundle.md` and `proposals/epic-consumer-lifecycle-continuity-bundle.md`; tighten `design/epic-contribution-ladder-2026.md`; add cross-links from the install/distribution side; prepend matching frontier notes in `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; update `RESEARCH_LOG.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`; mirror the changed canonical files under `archive/`; regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`; and keep future revisions honest by separating **managed subject, current owned state, typed lifecycle mutation, route/home change, and bounded downstream handoff**.

## 2026-03-22 — Distribution-route mobility stack (reviewable home changes across registries, mirrors, vendored lanes, and local bridges)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next frontier move that would change the repo’s shape instead of adding another adjacent continuity or maintenance note. After strengthening support routing, succession continuity, fork continuity, and sunset transition, the strongest missing seam turned out to be the boundary between **knowing where a Rust subject currently lives** and **knowing how a change in that home should be represented when Cargo route classes have materially different semantics**.
- Fresh research kept pointing toward the same gap. Cargo’s registries docs make alternate registries a first-class route, let `package.publish` restrict allowed publish homes, and recent release notes say `cargo publish` will use an alternate registry by default when it is the only allowed target. Cargo’s source-replacement docs then sharpen the equivalence boundary: replacement sources must be exact copies, may not add new crates, and are not patching or private-registry divergence. Cargo’s dependency docs say crates.io packages cannot depend on code published outside crates.io, while **multiple locations** let local `git`/`path` work bridge to a registry version later. `cargo vendor` says vendored sources are read-only and directs actual modifications toward `[patch]` or local `path`, so offline/local copies and divergent local carries already have different official meanings. The January 2026 crates.io update expanded Trusted Publishing and Trusted-Publishing-only mode, making publish-home and publish-authority shifts more explicit. Together those signals say ideal Rust still lacks a compact control layer for route motion.

## 2026-03-22 — Sunset transition stack (honest support narrowing and retirement when code remains discoverable)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next frontier move that would change the repo’s shape instead of adding another adjacent governance note. After strengthening lifecycle metadata, succession continuity, fork continuity, and support routing, the strongest missing seam turned out to be the boundary between **knowing a Rust project should no longer be a normal default choice** and **knowing how that narrowing or retirement is actually represented when the registry remains a durable archive**.
- Fresh research kept pointing toward the same gap. Cargo’s publishing docs say yanks do not delete code and existing lockfiles keep working because crates.io aims to remain a permanent archive. RFC 3660 keeps deletions tightly constrained, which means many real Rust artifacts will remain discoverable even when maintainers want users to stop selecting them by default. RFC 3646 then sharpens the neighboring boundary: unreachable-owner cases should expect a different name rather than registry-mediated transfer, so sunset often borders but should not be confused with succession or continuation. The Rust Foundation’s 2026–2028 strategy and the maintenance writeup both frame maintenance as ongoing, invisible, and burnout-sensitive work, which makes support narrowing or retirement a legitimate stewardship move rather than automatic evidence of neglect. Together those signals say ideal Rust still lacks a compact control layer for honest off-ramps.

## 2026-03-22 — Deviation governance stack (turn scattered exceptions into reviewable bounded deviations)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next frontier move that would change the repo’s shape instead of adding another adjacent mechanism note. After a run of overlays, preview adoption, canary validation, baseline ratchets, incident response, and multiple waiver-carrying kits, the strongest missing seam turned out to be the boundary between **having a real exception in a Rust project** and **being able to review that exception honestly over time**.

The Edition Guide’s advanced migration docs say `cargo fix --edition` may need repeated runs, partial migration lints, or `--broken-code` carries across configurations. The nightly and unstable-features docs say preview capabilities require explicit activation and often a per-project override or pin. Cargo’s override docs show `[patch]` as a real lane for bugfix carries and unpublished upstream work, while Cargo’s config docs warn that config-local patches are usually not checked into source control and are shaped by hierarchical config merging. Source replacement then makes an even sharper distinction: mirrors/vendors must be exact copies and are not the same as patching. Cargo’s publishing docs say yanks do not fix existing lockfiles. The CI guide says latest-deps jobs may intentionally continue on error or rely on schedules/notifications that may not reach an owner. And `rust-version` docs say drift from a stated support policy creates user confusion and that multiple policies can exist in one workspace. Together those signals say Rust already has many legitimate deviation mechanisms, but still lacks a compact cross-cutting review layer for owner, scope, expiry, and exit.

## 2026-03-22 — Baseline ratchet stack (turn support-floor change into a reviewable artifact)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next seam that would change the repo’s shape instead of adding another adjacent lane. After several revisions on bootstrap, overlays, async transition, prototype elevation, defect escalation, and iteration profiles, the next missing layer turned out to be the boundary between **one specific migration run** and **the broader policy claim that a project has raised its supported Rust floor**.

Rust 1.85 stabilized Rust 2024 and the Edition Guide still presents migration as a staged workflow with repeated `cargo fix --edition` passes, multi-configuration work, and possible manual intervention. Cargo’s `rust-version` docs say changing `rust-version` is a minor incompatibility, recommend choosing and documenting a policy, warn that drift from policy creates user confusion, and explicitly allow multiple policies in one workspace. Rust 1.84 stabilized the MSRV-aware resolver, says resolver `3` can require raising your MSRV, and says 2024-edition projects get that resolver behavior by default. The resolver docs say mixed-policy workspaces are only handled heuristically, so one member can force lower dependency versions for another or version unification can still force a higher shared version. Cargo’s CI guide now treats verifying latest dependencies and verifying `rust-version` as distinct checks. ## 2026-03-22 — Iteration profile stack (turn local-loop tradeoffs into reviewable artifacts)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next frontier move that would change the repo’s shape instead of adding another adjacent tool idea. After several revisions on bootstrap, overlays, async transition, prototype elevation, and defect escalation, the next missing layer turned out to be the boundary between **diagnosing a slow or awkward Rust loop** and **choosing a reusable local iteration profile**.
- Fresh research kept pointing toward the same gap. Rust’s March 20, 2026 challenges post says compile times are a universal productivity tax and explicitly says that faster linking or hot reloading would have outsized leverage on development velocity. The 2025 compiler-performance survey says the default `dev` profile’s full debuginfo slows compilation and linking, says many users still have not tried easy build-speed mechanisms, and says Cargo is considering a lower-debuginfo default plus a built-in debugging profile. Cargo’s own profiles docs show that built-in/custom profiles, `debug = "line-tables-only"|"limited"|"full"`, config overrides, and `split-debuginfo` are already real supported levers rather than unofficial folklore. Cargo’s build-analysis goal says rebuild reasons, CLI flags, profiles, and run IDs should become machine-usable. The build-dir-layout goal plus the March 13, 2026 testing call say editor/CLI coexistence, lock contention, user-wide cache, and tool reliance on unspecified build-dir details are still live seams. rust-analyzer explicitly documents `cargo.targetDir` as a lock-avoidance tradeoff that duplicates artifacts. And the 2026 debugging survey says debugger support still varies across debugger families and operating systems and that async debugging is not yet first-class.
- Archive decision: add `design/iteration-profile-stack.md`; prepend matching frontier notes in `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `RESEARCH_LOG.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`; mirror the changed files under `archive/`; regenerate `meta/ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.md`; and keep future build/debug/workenv/bootstrap revisions honest by separating **workflow intent, evidence basis, chosen profile/config/editor realization, debug/fidelity/concurrency tradeoffs, and observed outcomes**.

## 2026-03-21 — Vector Surface lane map and ranked pilot (portable SIMD, target features, dispatch, fallbacks, and scalable vectors)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a frontier seam that was already strategically important but still too flat to resist future revisions. **Vector Surface Kit** was the clearest fit: the archive already had the gap note, design note, and epic, but it still lacked the explicit lane map and ranked pilot that would stop portable fixed-width SIMD, target-specific compile-time intrinsics, runtime multiversioning, fallback-backed abstractions, scalable-vector experiments, and downstream consumer imports from collapsing into one fake “SIMD support” verdict.
- Rust’s 2026 flagships keep **Sized Hierarchy and Scalable Vectors** active, including refined `Sized`, `const Sized`, scalable-vector RFC progress, SVE types/intrinsics in `stdarch`, and initial SME design work; the 2025H1 SVE/SME goal still says SVE is unsupported today and explicitly warns against overfitting the design to one architecture: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/arm-sve-sme.html
- `std::simd` is portable across targets but still nightly-only and still documents real semantic caveats like subnormal-`f32` flush-to-zero on some older architectures; the Rust Reference keeps `#[target_feature]` hazards explicit and also documents a materially different Wasm load-time lane: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/simd/index.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/codegen.html#the-target_feature-attribute
- Current crates already expose different present-tense vector lanes rather than one converged answer: `safe_arch` is compile-time-only via `#[cfg()]`, `multiversion` is runtime CPU-detection / multiversion dispatch, and `wide` is fallback-backed and may go scalar while keeping the math correct: https://docs.rs/safe_arch ; https://docs.rs/multiversion/latest/multiversion/ ; https://docs.rs/wide
- Added `design/vector-surface-lane-map.md` and `design/vector-surface-pilot-program.md`; refreshed `design/vector-surface-kit.md`, `gaps/vector-surfaces-simd-target-features-and-dispatch-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-vector-surface-kit.md`; updated `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and `AGENTS.md`; and added a new amnesia-resistor so future vector/scientific/media/crypto/offload revisions keep lane identity, target-feature posture, dispatch/fallback posture, alignment/layout truth, operation semantics, and evidence distinct instead of flattening them into one vector story.

- New design note: `design/tensor-surface-lane-map.md`
- Design/gap/epic refresh: `design/tensor-surface-kit.md`, `design/tensor-surface-pilot-program.md`, `design/scientific-productization-stack.md`, `design/scientific-productization-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/numerical-array-tensor-surfaces-and-interop-contracts.md`, `proposals/epic-tensor-surface-kit.md`
- Frontier/priority refresh: sharpened **Tensor Surface Kit** so the archive now treats **dense-array + matrix/linalg + runtime-tensor/device + persisted-array + interchange/attachment + adapter/consumer-import** as distinct but connected review lanes instead of one fake “tensor support” verdict
- Strategy: clarified that the worthy contribution here is not another ndarray competitor, universal array trait, or numerical mega-runtime, but a thin `cargo tensorcheck` / `tensor-pack/v0` layer whose lane catalog, shape/layout/ownership/device/storage profiles, exact-vs-copy-vs-lossy adapter reports, and bounded downstream handoffs let Rust teams compare numerical-surface claims honestly
- Hygiene: strengthened `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future tensor/scientific/model/offload/dataset revisions keep array lanes, matrix lanes, runtime-tensor lanes, persisted-array lanes, interchange lanes, and consumer-import conclusions distinct instead of flattening them into one numerical story

## 2026-03-21 — Tensor Surface lane map (dense arrays, matrices, runtime tensors, persisted arrays, interchange, and adapters)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a frontier seam that was already strategically important but still too flat to resist future revisions. **Tensor Surface Kit** was the clearest fit: the archive already had the gap note, design note, pilot, epic, and the wider Scientific Productization stack, but it still lacked the explicit lane map that would stop dense arrays, matrix vocabularies, runtime tensors, persisted multidimensional arrays, interchange structures, and adapter/import consumers from collapsing into one fake “tensor support” verdict.
- Fresh research confirmed the lane split is real rather than theoretical. `ndarray` still centers `ArrayBase`, owned arrays, views, and raw-storage vocabulary; `nalgebra` and `faer` still represent distinct matrix/linalg families; Candle and Burn keep runtime/device/autodiff posture concrete; `zarrs` keeps stored-array metadata/conformance concrete; DLPack and the Array API interchange discussion keep conversion/device/layout requirements concrete; and `argmin-math` still bridges `Vec`, `ndarray`, `nalgebra`, and `faer` rather than assuming one numerical winner.
- Archive decision: add `design/tensor-surface-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/tensor-surface-kit.md`, `design/tensor-surface-pilot-program.md`, `design/scientific-productization-stack.md`, `design/scientific-productization-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/numerical-array-tensor-surfaces-and-interop-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-tensor-surface-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and `AGENTS.md`; and add a new amnesia resistor so future tensor/scientific revisions keep lane identity separate from cross-cutting shape/layout/ownership/device/storage evidence.

## 2026-03-21 — Dataflow-surface lane-map refresh (SQL-planned, connector-programmable, custom-progress, streaming-database, source/time/state/progress, and bounded consumer imports)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next seam that was already strategically present but still too easy to flatten in later revisions. The strongest remaining case was **Dataflow Surface Kit**: the archive already had a good source/time/state/materialization substrate, but it still lacked the explicit lane map that would stop future passes from smearing SQL-planned pipelines, connector-led programmable pipelines, custom progress/replay graphs, streaming-database jobs, and bounded consumer imports into one fake “streaming support” or “real-time readiness” verdict.
- DataFusion’s current introduction page is more than a general analytics signal: it explicitly says the project aims to be the query engine of choice for databases, dataframe libraries, machine learning, and **streaming applications**, and it advertises a vectorized multithreaded **streaming execution engine** plus Substrait support. That is direct evidence that a Rust dataflow/planning substrate now exists below multiple higher-level lanes. Sources: https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/introduction.html ; https://datafusion.apache.org/blog/output/2025/11/25/datafusion-51.0.0/
- Arroyo’s concept docs made the SQL-planned lane concrete enough to deserve its own place in the map. They describe a distributed dataflow DAG, DataFusion-backed streaming SQL, explicit event-time semantics, source-produced watermarks, late-event dropping, and checkpointed state that can recover to identical results after failure. Those are not generic stream-processing vibes; they are specific source/time/state claims the archive should preserve as a named lane. Source: https://doc.arroyo.dev/concepts/
- Fluvio’s SDF docs and related Fluvio docs made a different lane equally concrete. SDF is presented as a Rust + WebAssembly platform for event-driven pipelines above Fluvio’s connectors and persistence; its window-processing docs keep watermark `grace-period`, `idleness`, and `assign-timestamp` hooks explicit; SmartModules keep in-line transform chains explicit; and the Connector Development Kit keeps build/test/publish posture explicit. That is enough to treat connector-programmable / inline-transform dataflows as a distinct lane rather than a detail of streaming SQL. Sources: https://www.fluvio.io/sdf/ ; https://www.fluvio.io/sdf/concepts/window-processing/ ; https://www.fluvio.io/docs/smartmodules/overview/ ; https://www.fluvio.io/docs/0.17.2/connectors/developers/overview/
- Timely Dataflow remained the clearest proof that the archive should not secretly reduce “dataflow” to SQL metadata. The Timely book still explicitly frames the system as one for implementing distributed streaming computation, documents probes as progress monitors over computations that may never finish, and documents capture/replay as stream interop primitives. That makes custom graph/progress/replay its own lane, not just an implementation detail hidden under other engines. Sources: https://timelydataflow.github.io/timely-dataflow/ ; https://timelydataflow.github.io/timely-dataflow/chapter_3/chapter_3_2.html ; https://timelydataflow.github.io/timely-dataflow/chapter_2/chapter_2_1.html
- RisingWave made the streaming-database / materialized-serving lane sharper than the archive had previously stated. Its architecture docs distinguish Serving, Streaming, Meta, and Compactor nodes around object storage; its key-concepts docs define sources, sinks, streaming jobs, and materialized views; and recent release notes expose live motion in watermark propagation, backfill controls, shared-source posture, and fragment-progress catalogs. That is strong evidence that materialization/progress and serving posture are distinct review lanes rather than mere outputs of ingestion logic. Sources: https://docs.risingwave.com/get-started/architecture ; https://docs.risingwave.com/reference/key-concepts ; https://docs.risingwave.com/changelog/release-notes
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still says online docs remain the canonical reference surface. For dataflow systems, that increases the value of attachable review packs rather than weakening it, because the truths that matter are otherwise split across SQL, connector manifests, runtime catalogs, checkpoint metadata, progress dashboards, and release notes. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add `design/dataflow-surface-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/dataflow-surface-kit.md`, `design/dataflow-surface-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/streaming-dataflows-sources-time-state-materialization-and-progress-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-dataflow-surface-kit.md`; prepend new frontier notes in `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; refresh `INDEX.md` and `AGENTS.md`; and strengthen `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future dataflow/event/dataset/runtime/observability revisions keep **engine-family lanes, source/sink posture, temporal semantics, state/backfill/recovery posture, materialization/progress evidence, and downstream consumer imports** distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another engine, connector marketplace, control plane, SQL dialect, or “real-time maturity” score. It is a thin `cargo dataflowcheck` / `dataflow-pack/v0` layer whose lane catalogs, source/time/state/materialization profiles, progress evidence attachments, diffs, and bounded consumer summaries let Rust teams compare dataflow claims honestly.

## 2026-03-21 — Trait-surface lane-map refresh (native dyn, opaque-return/RTN, native async non-dyn, dyn adapters, split families, and solver-sensitive coverage)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next borrowing/frontier seam that still risked being flattened. The strongest case was **Trait Surface Kit**: the archive already had the right contract language, but it still lacked the explicit lane map that would stop future revisions from smearing native dyn traits, native-but-non-dyn async traits, RTN-bound opaque returns, adapter dyn shims, split trait families, and solver-sensitive acceptance into one fake “trait support” verdict.
- Rust’s 2026 flagships now explicitly keep **return type notation**, **async fn in dyn trait**, **next-generation trait solver stabilization**, and **evolvable trait hierarchies** on the active roadmap. That is direct evidence that trait surfaces are live ecosystem infrastructure rather than compiler-team trivia. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H1 async goal is even more specific: it tracks **implementable trait aliases**, **async fn in dyn Trait**, and **Dynosaur 1.0** alongside RTN work. That means public async trait ergonomics still depend on an open mix of native language and adapter lanes. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/async.html
- The evolving-traits goal explicitly uses two concrete hierarchy-evolution cases — `Receiver` above `Deref`, and splitting `tower::Service` into a non-`Sync` supertrait plus a `Sync` subtrait — and says the design should set the stage for more general splitting. That is unusually direct evidence that trait-family evolution is part of the real contract, not just library-internal refactoring. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/evolving-traits.html
- RFC 3654 exists because methods returning opaques need reviewable bounds like `Send`, and its motivation uses Tower’s `Service` as the live ecosystem example. RFC 3185 meanwhile explicitly left dyn safety for native `async fn` traits to future work. Together they make “native trait” and “native dyn trait” visibly different lanes. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3654-return-type-notation.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3185-static-async-fn-in-trait.html
- Current docs/crate surfaces already expose the split in public. docs.rs now shows **Dyn Compatibility** on traits like `async_nats::Requester` and `embedded_hal_async::DelayNs`; `async-trait` openly says it makes async traits work with dyn traits; `dynosaur` says it creates a stand-in for `dyn Trait` for async and `-> impl Trait` methods; and `trait-variant` openly generates sendable variants with a blanket impl. Those are not edge details — they are present-tense trait lanes. Sources: https://docs.rs/async-nats/latest/async_nats/jetstream/context/traits/trait.Requester.html ; https://docs.rs/embedded-hal-async/latest/embedded_hal_async/delay/trait.DelayNs.html ; https://docs.rs/async-trait ; https://docs.rs/dynosaur/latest/dynosaur/attr.dynosaur.html ; https://docs.rs/trait-variant/latest/trait_variant/attr.make.html
- The 2025H2 in-place-initialization goal also proved to be part of the same seam: it explicitly says dyn Trait for `async fn` and `-> impl Trait` requires the callee to initialize an unknown-sized return in place. That means trait-surface truth and initialization-surface truth are coupled, but should still remain distinct archive owners. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/in-place-initialization.html
- Archive decision: add `design/trait-surface-lane-map.md` and `design/trait-surface-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/trait-surface-kit.md`, `gaps/trait-surfaces-dyn-posture-return-shapes-and-impl-truth.md`, and `proposals/epic-trait-surface-kit.md`; prepend new frontier notes in `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; refresh `INDEX.md` and `AGENTS.md`; and strengthen `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future trait/async/pointer/lending/borrowing revisions keep **ordinary static, native dyn, opaque-return obligations, native AFIT/RPITIT non-dyn posture, dyn adapters, split families, blanket/adaptation coverage, and solver-sensitive acceptance** distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another trait-helper macro, dyn badge, or universal trait metadata blob. It is a thin `cargo traitsurf` / `trait-pack/v0` layer whose lane catalog, dyn and return-shape profiles, adapter-lossiness records, family-migration notes, impl-coverage reports, and solver-watch vectors let Rust teams compare trait claims honestly.

## 2026-03-21 — Initialization Surface lane-map refresh (placement, pin timing, publication phases, internal borrowing, and teardown posture)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes keep **prototype immobile types and guaranteed destructors** under “Just Add Async” and **design alignment on in-place initialization** under “Beyond the `&`”, which is strong evidence that construction and teardown semantics are active core roadmap terrain rather than niche unsafe-crate folklore. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H2 in-place-initialization goal says the project is explicitly comparing multiple competing approaches and wants experiments with real users like the Linux kernel and Crubit before choosing a direction. That is direct evidence that Rust still needs a reviewable ecosystem layer above today’s workaround crates and below eventual language convergence. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/in-place-initialization.html
- `MaybeUninit` explicitly documents out-pointers, which is direct evidence that caller-allocated initialization is already a first-class lane rather than a hidden optimization detail. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html
- `Pin` and `Box::pin` keep “construct then pin” as a public mainstream lane, which means it should stay distinct from “pinned in place from the start”. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/pin/index.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html
- `Arc::new_cyclic` documents an allocated-but-not-fully-constructed phase in which `Weak` exists before `T` is fully placed and `upgrade` fails until construction completes. That makes cyclic bootstrap a semantically sharp lane rather than just another constructor convenience. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html
- `UniqueArc` explicitly says it is more flexible than `Arc::new_cyclic` for **fallible or async constructors**, which is strong evidence that unique-to-shared publication is a separate lane from ordinary cyclic bootstrap. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.UniqueArc.html
- `pin-init` / `pinned-init`, `pin-project`, `self_cell`, `yoke`, and `moveit` each expose distinct crate-level lanes around pinned in-place assembly, projection/destruction, self-referential or borrow-carrying setup, and C++/foreign emplacement. That strengthens the case that the missing contribution is a lane-aware artifact boundary, not one more constructor abstraction. Sources: https://docs.rs/pin-init ; https://docs.rs/pinned-init ; https://docs.rs/pin-project/latest/pin_project/attr.pin_project.html ; https://docs.rs/self_cell ; https://docs.rs/yoke/latest/yoke/struct.Yoke.html ; https://docs.rs/moveit
- Archive decision: add `design/initialization-surface-lane-map.md` and `design/initialization-surface-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/initialization-surface-kit.md`, `gaps/initialization-surfaces-in-place-construction-and-destruction-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-initialization-surface-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future initialization/borrowing/interop revisions keep **storage origin, address-stability timing, staged assembly, weak/self or borrowed-handle exposure, publication transitions, and teardown guarantees** distinct instead of flattening them into one fake init story.

## 2026-03-21 — Canonical Learning lane-map refresh (API docs, guides, executable proof, compile guidance, docs hosts, machine imports, and derived overlays should stop collapsing into one smart-docs story)
- Re-opened the archive after the async/maintenance/compatibility passes and looked for another seam that the repo already named but still had not modeled sharply enough. The strongest remaining move was to stop treating **Canonical Learning** as a general “good docs + smart consumers” theme and instead make it a **lane map**. The pattern matches earlier archive wins: the ecosystem becomes more reviewable when it preserves the actual seams between authored canon, executed proof, host assumptions, machine imports, and downstream overlays instead of narrating one smooth documentation story.
- Current Rust signals make the timing unusually good. The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the preferred canonical reference while some learning traffic appears to be shifting toward LLM/editor workflows; that same survey also says many users still find compiler error-code explanations useful, which is evidence that compile-time teaching belongs in canonical learning rather than outside it. Rust’s December 2025 vision post explicitly recommends extending crates toward **better diagnostics and guidance from crates**. docs.rs already exposes docs-host metadata/build behavior and now hosts rustdoc JSON; rustdoc documentation tests plus `#[cfg(doctest)]` make executable example lanes more explicit; mdBook keeps book-shaped testing explicit; and `trybuild` plus diagnostic attributes, rustc JSON diagnostics, and `cargo fix` prove negative-teaching, machine-readable diagnostics, and suggestion consumers are real present-tense lanes. ## 2026-03-21 — Async Commons lane-map refresh (shared substrate, runtime-shaped lanes, and environment truth should stop collapsing into one portability story)
- Re-opened the archive after the maintenance/compatibility passes and filtered for a seam that was already named but still not sharp enough to guide future revisions. The strongest surviving move was to stop treating **Async Commons** as a general portability philosophy note and instead make it a **lane map**. The reusable lesson across earlier Rust and non-Rust archives is that an ecosystem becomes more reviewable when it stops narrating one smooth neutrality story and instead preserves the exact seams that adapters, environments, and downstream consumers are actually traversing.
- Current Rust signals make the async version of that move unusually well-grounded. The March 2026 challenges writeup says async remains a major pain point and that library choice can lock users into one runtime family. The 2025H1 async flagship and July 2025 goals update say runtime choice/interoperability are central problems and that async traits plus generators/streams are meant to unblock the next generation of async libraries. The Async Book still says async Rust has compatibility constraints between runtimes and a higher maintenance burden than sync Rust. Meanwhile the actual substrate is visibly plural: `Future` lives in `std`; `futures` keeps `Spawn` / `LocalSpawn` and `futures-io` explicit; Tokio documents runtime-owned task/time/I/O surfaces plus `LocalSet`; `tokio-util::compat` proves the I/O seam is adapter-mediated; and Embassy makes embedded/no-alloc async a materially different environment lane. ## 2026-03-21 — Compatibility claims lane-map refresh (dev-host, build, release, docs, runtime, debugger, acceptance)
- The archive already had a credible **Compatibility Claims Stack**, but the current Rust signals say it was still under-modeled in one specific way: it lacked an explicit lane map for the different kinds of compatibility truth now moving independently. Rust’s target-tier policy distinguishes target support from stronger host-tool guarantees, so “supported target” is already not one thing upstream. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/target-tier-policy.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/rustc/platform-support.html
- docs.rs is also now unmistakably part of the public compatibility story. The metadata docs expose `default-target`, `targets`, and `additional-targets`, while the builds docs say `#[cfg(docsrs)]` only applies to the final rustdoc invocation and not dependencies or workspace members. Then the October 2025 docs.rs target-default change proved those docs-surface choices can drift at the ecosystem level. Sources: https://docs.rs/about/metadata ; https://docs.rs/about/builds ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/16/docsrs-changed-default-targets/
- Source-build posture also deserves a more explicit lane than the archive previously gave it. The Rust 2024 edition guide says `edition = "2024"` implies resolver `3` and a Rust-version-aware resolver, while Cargo’s resolver/MSRV docs say one workspace member’s `rust-version` can affect dependency choices for another. That means source-build compatibility can move by toolchain/MSRV lane even when the source tree is unchanged. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2024/cargo-resolver.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/resolver.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/rust-version.html
- The debugger and compiler-acceptance halves are equally plural. The Rust Reference exposes `debugger_visualizer`; the compiler dev guide documents real debugger-family differences; the 2026 debugging survey explicitly asks about debugger version / OS support, visualizers, async debugging, and expression evaluation; and the 2026 / 2025H2 goals keep next-solver, Polonius, and evolving traits live. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/debugger.html ; https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/debuginfo/intro.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/23/rust-debugging-survey-2026/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/next-solver.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/polonius.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/evolving-traits.html
- The 2025 State of Rust survey plus the March 2026 challenges writeup strengthen the ranking case: online docs remain canonical while machine consumers rise, and expert pain shifts toward domain-specific ecosystem-maturity problems rather than vanishing with experience. Compatibility-claim drift is exactly that kind of advanced-user burden. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/20/rust-challenges/
- Archive decision: add `design/compatibility-claims-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/support-envelope-kit.md`, `design/compatibility-claims-stack.md`, `design/compatibility-claims-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/compatibility-claims-platform-debugger-and-acceptance-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-compatibility-claims-stack.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add a stricter amnesia resistor so future revisions keep **dev-host, source-build, release-artifact, docs-surface, runtime-floor, debugger-tuple, acceptance-profile, and consumer-view** claims distinct instead of narrating one fake “supported” status.
