## 2026-03-21 — Repro Build lane-map refresh (package reproducibility, artifact compare, attestations, offline bundles, lifecycle)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next seam that was strategically present but still under-modeled in a way that could distort later revisions. The strongest remaining candidate was **Repro Build**: the archive already had a credible kit and a clear release-truth role, but it still lacked the explicit lane map and pilot program that would stop future revisions from flattening source-package reproducibility, final-artifact compare modes, provenance attestations, SBOM attestations, offline verification, and lifecycle posture into one fake “reproducible release” story.
- Rust 1.91 release notes now say **building a crate with `cargo package` should now be independently reproducible**. `cargo package` also still rewrites and normalizes `Cargo.toml`, includes `Cargo.lock` by default, emits `.cargo_vcs_info.json`, and verifies by extracting the `.crate` and rebuilding it. That is strong evidence that source-package reproducibility is now a first-class upstream lane rather than just a side effect of generic release hygiene. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- Cargo’s changelog says `trim-paths` now remaps all paths to `build.build-dir` and expands Windows/MSVC coverage, which is a good reminder that final-artifact equivalence still depends on active path-leakage substrate work instead of a frozen solved problem. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html
- Cargo’s unstable docs still emit SBOM precursor files for executable and linkable outputs uplifted into target or artifact directories. That makes artifact-linked inventory capture a real adjacent input lane for rebuild verification instead of a separate compliance-only story. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- dist’s introduction says users should be able to rerun the same dist invocation locally and get the same ordinary results, **not to bit-level precision**. Its supply-chain docs also keep signing, GitHub Attestation, CycloneDX SBOM output, `cargo-auditable`, and OmniBOR as distinct attachment surfaces. Together those are strong signals that the release ecosystem already knows “repeatable release build” and “strict equivalence / attached evidence” are different lanes. Sources: https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/ ; https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/supplychain-security/index.html
- GitHub’s attestation docs now make the lane split explicit enough that the archive should preserve it directly: artifact attestations establish **where and how software was built**, SBOM attestations are a separate predicate path, offline verification has its own imported-bundle workflow, and GitHub explicitly warns that attestations are **not a guarantee that an artifact is secure**. The lifecycle docs also say attestations should be deleted when the linked artifact no longer exists or should no longer be trusted. Sources: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/artifact-attestations ; https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/use-artifact-attestations ; https://docs.github.com/actions/security-for-github-actions/using-artifact-attestations/verifying-attestations-offline ; https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/manage-attestations
- Archive decision: add `design/repro-build-lane-map.md` and `design/repro-build-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/repro-build-kit.md`, `design/release-truth-stack.md`, `gaps/reproducible-build-verification-and-diffable-attestations.md`, and `proposals/epic-repro-build-kit.md`; and treat **Repro Build Kit / Release Truth Stack** as lane-mapped frontier work that must keep **source-package reproducibility, final-artifact compare modes, provenance/SBOM attestation attachments, offline-verification bundles, and lifecycle posture** distinct.
- Hygiene update: future release/repro/inventory/distribution revisions must not flatten package reproducibility, artifact equivalence, provenance, inventory attestation, offline verification, and lifecycle status into one fake “trusted release” verdict.

## 2026-03-21 — SBOM Evidence lane-map refresh (Cargo precursors, standards exports, embedded recovery, release attachments, scanner imports)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next seam that was strategically present but still under-modeled in a way that could distort later revisions. The strongest remaining candidate was **SBOM Evidence**: the archive already had a good kit + stack + pilot shape, but it still lacked the explicit lane map that would stop future revisions from flattening Cargo-native precursors, project-export standards documents, embedded binary recovery, release-attached BOMs, scanner imports, and downstream policy/support/admission conclusions into one fake “generated an SBOM” story.
- Rust’s 2026 flagship supply-chain theme explicitly names **SBOM generation** and **stabilize SBOM support**. That is strong evidence this seam now deserves first-class frontier treatment inside the archive rather than being left as plugin-level trivia. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Cargo’s unstable `sbom` docs still call the output a **pre-cursor**, emit it alongside each compiled artifact, preserve duplicate differently-compiled crates, and expose `CARGO_SBOM_PATH`. That is direct evidence that Cargo is defining a build-lane Rust-native source of truth, not a one-size-fits-all standards document. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- `cargo-cyclonedx` still represents a different source-project export lane: it generates a CycloneDX SBOM for a Cargo project by calling into Cargo, and its README explicitly warns that invoking it on untrusted projects has the same arbitrary-code risk as Cargo itself. Source: https://github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-rust-cargo/blob/main/README.md
- The CycloneDX resolver-v2 issue still says metadata-driven export can misreport some build-only dependencies as runtime dependencies and explicitly says this would be fixed with a better Cargo-emitted SBOM data source. That is direct evidence that metadata/project-export lanes and Cargo-native precursor lanes must stay separate. Source: https://github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-rust-cargo/issues/760
- `cargo-auditable` now explicitly documents a nightly mode that uses Cargo’s native SBOM precursor for more accurate recording, says the end goal is for Cargo itself to encode this information in binaries, and lists real downstream consumers and recovery/conversion tools like cargo-audit, Trivy, Grype, Syft, wasm-tools, rust-audit-info, and `auditable2cdx`. That is strong evidence that embedded/recovered binary inventory is a real lane rather than a speculative side path. Source: https://github.com/rust-secure-code/cargo-auditable
- Trivy’s current Rust docs still keep source scanning (`Cargo.lock` plus `Cargo.toml`) separate from binary scanning of cargo-auditable artifacts. cargo-dist’s changelog likewise still keeps standalone CycloneDX release attachments separate from embedded binary metadata. Those are both strong signals that scanner/import lanes and release-attachment lanes should remain distinct from build-time precursor and binary-recovery lanes. Sources: https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/coverage/language/rust/ ; https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md
- Archive decision: add `design/sbom-evidence-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/sbom-evidence-kit.md`, `design/inventory-evidence-stack.md`, `design/inventory-evidence-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/sbom-evidence-and-artifact-linked-dependency-inventory.md`, `proposals/epic-sbom-evidence-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-inventory-evidence-stack.md`; and treat **SBOM Evidence Kit** as a lane-mapped frontier that must keep **Cargo-native precursors, source-project exports, embedded binary recovery, release-attached standards documents, scanner/import views, and downstream consumer handoffs** distinct.
- Hygiene update: future SBOM/release/scanner/policy revisions must not flatten build-observed precursor truth, project-export truth, binary-recovered truth, shipped-attached standards documents, scanner/import views, and downstream verdicts into one fake inventory verdict or one universal SBOM story.

## 2026-03-20 — Build Cache lane-map refresh (Cargo-native lanes, wrapper caches, container layers, CI exchange)
- The March 13, 2026 Cargo blog post asking for testing on build-dir-layout v2 says users with Cargo 1.91 can already separate `build-dir` from `target-dir`, asks nightly users to test `-Zbuild-dir-new-layout`, and lists real failure modes in tools that infer bin paths or scrape build-dir / `OUT_DIR` details. That is strong evidence that build-cache topology is now an ecosystem-facing contract rather than a hidden Cargo implementation detail. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- The 2025H2 build-dir-layout goal still says today’s build cache is locked as a whole, that rust-analyzer contention is a concrete pain point, and that the future should include smaller lockable/cacheable units, a first-class user-wide cache, and plugin-based read/write to different cache sources. That supports a lane-aware cache map rather than another generic cache abstraction. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-dir-layout.html
- The Cargo Book’s build-cache docs now publicly distinguish `build-dir` from `target-dir` and still position `sccache` as a third-party shared-cache lane. That is direct evidence that Cargo-native cache truth and wrapper-cache truth must stay separate. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html
- rust-analyzer’s `cargo.targetDir` docs explicitly describe a private target-directory workaround that prevents locking contention at the expense of duplicating build artifacts. That is strong evidence that editor-private duplication is a real lane, not a miss. Source: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration.html
- `sccache`’s Rust docs are explicit that support is focused on cargo-shaped rustc invocations and has caveats, including proc-macros reading filesystem state. `cargo-chef` is explicit that it is for container builds, not normal local use, and that stage toolchains must match for caching to work. That supports separating compiler-wrapper and container-layer lanes from Cargo-native cache lanes. Sources: https://github.com/mozilla/sccache/blob/main/docs/Rust.md ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-chef/latest
- Archive decision: add `design/build-cache-lane-map.md` and `design/build-cache-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/build-cache-kit.md`, `gaps/userwide-build-cache.md`, and `proposals/epic-build-cache-kit.md`; and treat **Build Cache Kit** as a lane-mapped frontier that must keep **Cargo-native workspace-local state, editor-private duplication, Cargo-native user-wide intermediates, compiler-wrapper caches, container recipe/layer caching, and CI/plugin exchange** distinct.
- Hygiene update: future build-cache/build-state revisions must not flatten Cargo-native build-state reuse, wrapper-level invocation reuse, editor-private duplication, container-layer reuse, and CI/plugin exchange into one fake cache verdict or one hit-rate story.

## 2026-03-20 — Manifest Truth lane-map refresh (authored, inherited/defaulted, packaged, script/frontmatter, machine-consumer, human-projection, watch lanes)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next seam that was already strategically present but still under-modeled in a way that could distort later revisions. The strongest remaining candidate was **Manifest Truth**: the archive already had the right gap/kit/stack/pilot structure, but it still lacked the explicit lane map that would stop future revisions from flattening authored manifest text, workspace/discovery inheritance, packaged normalization, script/frontmatter subjects, machine imports, human projections, and evolving metadata work into one fake “the manifest says …” sentence.
- Cargo 1.94 still treats manifest-adjacent behavior as active infrastructure rather than frozen syntax. The current development-cycle post explicitly calls out parent-manifest and parent-config discovery hazards, notes that a stray `Cargo.toml` in a parent directory can break unrelated packages, and discusses a possible `package.workspace = false` style opt-in/out mechanism. That is strong evidence that authored file text and discovered interpretation must stay separate in the archive. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The packaged lane remains materially different from the authored lane. `cargo package` still rewrites and normalizes `Cargo.toml`, removes `[patch]`, `[replace]`, and `[workspace]`, always includes `Cargo.lock` unless excluded, emits `.cargo_vcs_info.json`, flattens symlinks, and verifies the package by rebuilding from the extracted `.crate`. That is exactly the kind of authored-vs-packaged drift the archive should model directly instead of leaving as folklore. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- Cargo’s consumer lanes are now sharp enough that they deserve first-class separation. `cargo metadata` still describes itself as machine-readable JSON whose output format may evolve and explicitly recommends pinning `--format-version`; the stable `cargo info` lane just changed in Cargo 1.94 so that, when no registry is explicitly specified, it defaults to inspecting the local package. Those are useful consumer surfaces, but they are not interchangeable and they do not see the same manifest truth. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html
- Workspace inheritance keeps widening the meaning of package-local manifest text. The workspaces reference now keeps `workspace.package`, `workspace.dependencies`, and `workspace.lints` visibly separate, and it is explicit that Cargo searches parent directories for a workspace root and that `package.workspace` can override that search. That makes an inherited/defaulted/discovered lane unavoidable. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
- Script/frontmatter is now strong enough to model as its own subject lane rather than a footnote. The cargo-script goal says Cargo and basic rustc support already exist on nightly and the remaining work is stabilization/polish, while RFCs 3502 and 3503 keep embedded manifests, defaulted fields, and disallowed-field posture explicit. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-script.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3502-cargo-script.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3503-frontmatter.html
- One smaller but useful signal is that Rust 1.93 pulled out `cargo-util-schemas` as a crate. That suggests schema extraction is becoming more explicit while final manifest semantics still live across Cargo, discovery, and consumer layers — another reason not to flatten schema availability into manifest truth itself. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html
- Archive decision: add `design/manifest-surface-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/manifest-surface-kit.md`, `design/manifest-truth-stack.md`, `design/manifest-truth-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/manifest-truth-authored-published-and-consumed.md`, and `proposals/epic-manifest-truth-stack.md`; prepend matching frontier notes in `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future manifest/repo-composition/script/publish revisions keep **authored text, inherited/defaulted meaning, packaged truth, script subjects, machine-consumer imports, human projections, and evolving watch lanes** distinct instead of collapsing them into one fake manifest verdict.


## 2026-03-20 — Filesystem Surface lane-map + pilot-program refresh (path kinds, rooted/capability resolution, canonical/display bridges, traversal, watch, staged mutation, durability, trust/privacy)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for a seam that was already strategically present but still under-modeled in a way that could distort future revisions. The strongest remaining candidate was **Filesystem Surface Kit**: the archive already had the right path/traversal/staging substrate, but it still lacked a crisp lane map separating bare-path std access, UTF-8 paths, rooted/capability-relative access, canonical-vs-display bridges, traversal, watching, staged mutation, durable replace, and trust/privacy checks.
- Current std docs make the baseline lane sharper than earlier archive text implied. The `std::fs` module now explicitly documents **TOCTOU** hazards, says metadata checks can race with other processes, recommends atomic operations such as `File::create_new`, and says keeping files open for the duration of operations helps avoid some races. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/
- The machine-path vs display-path split is still a live problem. `std::fs::canonicalize` resolves symlinks and returns canonical absolute paths, and on Windows it still emits extended-length path syntax that may be incompatible with other applications; `dunce` still exists specifically to convert Windows UNC-style results into the most compatible simpler form when possible. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.canonicalize.html ; https://docs.rs/dunce/latest/dunce/
- Rooted/capability-relative access remains a real ecosystem lane rather than theory. Nightly `std::fs::Dir` still exists as an experimental open-directory API, while `cap-std::fs::Dir` says its methods correspond to `std::fs` functions but operate relative to an open directory and even keep `canonicalize` relative because absolute paths do not interoperate well with the capability model. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Dir.html ; https://docs.rs/cap-std/latest/cap_std/fs/struct.Dir.html
- Path-kind posture is still explicitly plural. `camino` continues to frame `Utf8Path` / `Utf8PathBuf` as a deliberate UTF-8-only lane for ecosystems like Cargo that already assume UTF-8, instead of pretending `std::path::Path` is always conveniently string-like. Source: https://docs.rs/camino/latest/camino/
- Mutation/staging/durability are still visibly separate lanes. `tempfile::NamedTempFile::persist` says temp files cannot be persisted across filesystems and that neither file contents nor containing directories are synchronized when `persist` returns; `persist_noclobber` says it is not guaranteed to be atomic on all platforms. `atomic-write-file` documents a same-directory temp-file + `fsync` + replace sequence, uses directory file descriptors / `openat`-style operations on Unix to avoid remount/rename surprises, and still documents symlink-replacement plus metadata-preservation caveats. Sources: https://docs.rs/tempfile/latest/tempfile/struct.NamedTempFile.html ; https://docs.rs/atomic-write-file/latest/atomic_write_file/
- Traversal and watch semantics are still obviously plural. `walkdir` keeps symlink-following, deterministic sort, and same-filesystem boundaries explicit; `ignore::WalkBuilder` keeps `.ignore`, `.gitignore`, global gitignore, and precedence rules explicit; `notify` keeps native backends, polling fallback, editor-save differences, parent-folder deletion caveats, and large-directory caveats explicit. Sources: https://docs.rs/walkdir/latest/walkdir/struct.WalkDir.html ; https://docs.rs/ignore/latest/ignore/struct.WalkBuilder.html ; https://docs.rs/notify/latest/notify/ ; https://docs.rs/notify/latest/src/notify/lib.rs.html
- Trust/privacy checking turned out to be worth naming as its own lane. `fs-mistrust` documents why canonicalizing a final path is not enough when modifiable symlinks or ancestors can redirect meaning, and it provides checked directories for continued relative access within verified roots. Source: https://docs.rs/fs-mistrust/latest/fs_mistrust/
- `fs-err` remains a useful reminder that operation/path-rich diagnostics are part of filesystem reality too, even when no one wants to call that a separate “filesystem framework”. Source: https://docs.rs/fs-err/latest/fs_err/
- Archive decision: add `design/filesystem-surface-lane-map.md` and `design/filesystem-surface-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/filesystem-surface-kit.md`, `gaps/filesystem-surfaces-paths-traversal-and-durable-mutation-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-filesystem-surface-kit.md`; prepend a current-frontier correction in `PRIORITIES.md`; prepend a matching frontier note in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future filesystem/runtime-settings/command/security revisions keep **path kind, rooted authority, canonical-vs-display form, traversal policy, watch backend, temp staging, durability guarantees, and trust/privacy checks** distinct instead of collapsing them into one fake filesystem verdict.

## 2026-03-20 — Benchmark Evidence lane-map refresh (cargo-bench foundations, native baselines, counter lanes, runner imports, deterministic profiler lanes, hosted adapters)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next seam that would sharpen the map rather than widen it. The strongest remaining case on the performance side was **Benchmark Evidence**: the archive already had the right benchmark-native kit and a decent pilot, but it still lacked the explicit lane map that would stop future revisions from flattening cargo-bench foundations, Criterion native baselines, Divan counters, nextest imports, Iai-Callgrind profiler lanes, and hosted adapters into one fake “benchmark support” story.
- Cargo’s own docs still keep the benchmark foundation plural. `cargo bench` can use the default libtest benchmark runner, `#[bench]` remains unstable/nightly-only, and targets can disable the harness and provide their own `main`. That is direct evidence that benchmark-launch truth is already split between nightly libtest and custom-harness lanes rather than one settled built-in engine. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-bench.html
- nextest’s current benchmark docs now make the runner-import seam explicit enough to deserve its own lane in the archive: `cargo nextest bench` is experimental and supports Criterion.rs, the nightly libtest benchmark runner, and custom-harness protocol users. That is exactly the kind of imported execution truth the repo should preserve rather than narrating as ordinary native benchmark output. Source: https://nexte.st/docs/features/benchmarks/
- Criterion’s own docs and `cargo-criterion` now sharpen a baseline split that the archive should preserve directly. Criterion’s user guide still documents named baselines through `--save-baseline` and `--baseline`, while `cargo-criterion` still says it provides machine-readable JSON but does **not** currently support baselines. That makes native saved-baseline truth and JSON-export posture separate lanes, not implementation details. Sources: https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/user_guide/command_line_options.html ; https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/cargo_criterion/cargo_criterion.html
- Divan, Iai-Callgrind, and CodSpeed together make the remaining lane split impossible to ignore. Divan keeps bytes/chars/cycles/items counters explicit; Iai-Callgrind is explicit that it uses Valgrind Callgrind for extremely accurate and consistent CI-suitable measurements and can also run Cachegrind or DHAT; and CodSpeed keeps Rust compatibility layers plus `simulation`, `walltime`, and `memory` measurement modes public. Those are not different skins over one benchmark engine — they are materially different measurement and orchestration lanes. Sources: https://docs.rs/divan/latest/divan/counter/index.html ; https://docs.rs/iai-callgrind/latest/iai_callgrind/ ; https://codspeed.io/docs/benchmarks/rust ; https://codspeed.io/docs/reference/codspeed-rust/cargo-codspeed
- rustc-perf’s active multiple-collector direction also provided a useful design lesson for the archive itself: comparisons should remain within a declared configuration, not across unlike configurations by default. That maps cleanly onto the benchmark lane-map decision here. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/rustc-perf-improvements.html

## 2026-03-20 — Coverage lane-map refresh (official LLVM baseline, Cargo-native LLVM orchestration, nextest+doctest merge, external/FFI imports, Tarpaulin contrast, and future decision/MC/DC imports)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next seam that would sharpen the map rather than widen it. The strongest next move was **Coverage Evidence Kit**: the archive already had the right criterion/execution/report/gate substrate and a good ranked pilot, but it still lacked the lane map that would stop future revisions from flattening rustc/LLVM baseline coverage, `cargo-llvm-cov` orchestration, nextest+doctest merges, external/FFI imports, Tarpaulin contrast, and future decision/MC/DC imports into one fake “coverage support” story.
- Rust’s 2026 flagship roadmap now makes the timing unusually strong: **Safety-Critical Rust** explicitly includes **MC/DC coverage support**, and **Building blocks** explicitly includes **better test tooling**. The January 2026 safety-critical adoption writeup adds the governance lesson: earlier MC/DC work stalled partly because it added maintenance burden without a clear owner, and the current effort is framed around sustained shared ownership instead. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
- The rustc coverage docs still keep the official LLVM baseline lane explicit rather than magical: source-based coverage depends on `-C instrument-coverage`, the profiler runtime, raw `.profraw` files, `llvm-profdata merge`, and `llvm-cov report/show`; the official summary statistics are still function, instantiation, line, and region coverage. That is exactly why the archive should keep a named **official LLVM baseline lane** instead of narrating every percentage as the same thing. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/instrument-coverage.html
- `cargo-llvm-cov` remains the strongest Cargo-native orchestration lane above that baseline. Its README still makes several non-trivial surfaces explicit: `cargo test`, `cargo run`, and `cargo nextest`; proc-macro and UI coverage; external-test coverage; C/C++ coverage via `--include-ffi`; JSON/LCOV/Cobertura/Codecov/text/html outputs; optional branch coverage; and optional doctest coverage. That is direct evidence that **Cargo-native LLVM orchestration** is a real lane with its own review consequences rather than a transparent wrapper. Source: https://github.com/taiki-e/cargo-llvm-cov
- nextest’s current coverage docs still say coverage data from nextest must be merged with doctest data because nextest does not currently support doctests. That is a compact, decisive signal that **split execution + merge** belongs in the contract itself: one coverage result can already contain materially different execution sources whose provenance must stay visible. Source: https://nexte.st/docs/integrations/test-coverage/
- The external/native import seam is also live rather than speculative. `cargo-llvm-cov` still documents explicit support for external tests and for coverage of C/C++ code linked to Rust libraries/binaries. That means one combined report can already span Rust tests, external binaries, and linked native code, so the archive should preserve **external/FFI import** as a distinct lane instead of laundering everything into a Rust-only claim. Source: https://github.com/taiki-e/cargo-llvm-cov
- Tarpaulin remains important precisely because it is not the same engine lane as LLVM source-based coverage. Its README still presents it as a distinct Cargo coverage tool, and its 0.35.0 changelog now says delta coverage should not be reported when run-configuration changes would make the comparison meaningless. That is unusually strong evidence for a named **Tarpaulin contrast lane** and for explicit `not-comparable` posture in portable artifacts. Sources: https://github.com/xd009642/tarpaulin ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-tarpaulin/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md
- Archive decision: add `design/coverage-evidence-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/coverage-evidence-kit.md`, `design/coverage-evidence-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/coverage-evidence-and-ci-review.md`, and `proposals/epic-coverage-evidence-kit.md`; prepend matching frontier notes in `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; update `INDEX.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future coverage/safety/testing revisions keep **criterion identity, engine family, execution imports, merge/comparability truth, Rust-versus-FFI/native inclusion, and future decision/MC/DC watch posture** distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another coverage engine, hosted percentage service, or badge normalizer. It is a thin `cargo cov` / `coverage-pack/v0` layer whose lane profiles, criterion profiles, execution imports, merge reports, and bounded downstream handoffs let downstream tools compare Rust coverage claims honestly.

## 2026-03-20 — Observability lane-map refresh (tracing composition, local formatted output, `log` bridges, metrics facades, OpenTelemetry export, runtime diagnostics, and imported machine reports)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next seam that would sharpen the map rather than widen it. The strongest next move was **Observability Kit**: the archive already had the right signal/profile/report/vector substrate and an explicit productization stack, but it still lacked the lane map that would stop future revisions from flattening local `fmt` output, tracing composition, legacy `log` import, metrics recorder posture, OpenTelemetry export, Tokio-console diagnostics, and imported Cargo machine reports into one fake “observability support” story.
- Current `tracing` and `tracing-subscriber` docs keep the split unusually visible. `tracing` still defines itself as a structured, event-based diagnostics framework and still explains why traditional logs are especially hard to interpret in async systems. `tracing-subscriber` still centers on the composable `Layer` abstraction; its `fmt` lane is explicitly for formatted output, `EnvFilter` is its own filtering layer, and `reload::Layer` exists because runtime reconfiguration is a distinct surface. Sources: https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/src/tracing/lib.rs.html ; https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/latest/tracing_subscriber/layer/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/latest/tracing_subscriber/fmt/struct.Layer.html ; https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/latest/tracing_subscriber/filter/struct.EnvFilter.html ; https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/latest/tracing_subscriber/reload/struct.Layer.html
- The legacy-log seam remains real rather than historical. `tracing-log` still documents `LogTracer` as converting `log::Record`s into `tracing::Event`s, while `SubscriberInitExt` still says the `tracing-log` feature also initializes a `log` compatibility layer and can fail if a `log` logger is already set. That is direct evidence that **legacy-log import is its own lane with initialization-order and lossiness consequences**, not a silent implementation detail. Sources: https://docs.rs/tracing-log/latest/tracing_log/ ; https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/latest/tracing_subscriber/util/trait.SubscriberInitExt.html
- The metrics lane is still materially separate. `metrics` continues to describe itself as a lightweight facade abstracting over the implementation choice, and `metrics-util` still defines recorder `layers`/`Stack` separate from tracing-subscriber’s layer model. That is enough to justify preserving a distinct **metrics facade / recorder lane** instead of letting OpenTelemetry or tracing prose swallow it. Sources: https://docs.rs/metrics ; https://docs.rs/metrics-util/latest/metrics_util/layers/index.html
- OpenTelemetry’s current state made the exporter/profile lane worth sharpening now. The Rust language docs still mark traces, metrics, and logs as **Beta**; the repository still recommends OTLP exporters for production scenarios; `opentelemetry-appender-tracing` explicitly converts `tracing` events into OpenTelemetry `LogRecords` and attaches trace context; the stability proposal says complexity and lack of stability are impeding production deployments; Weaver argues for observability-by-design through semantic-convention discipline; and RustSec now marks `opentelemetry-jaeger` unmaintained. Together, those are strong signals for a visible **OpenTelemetry export / semantic-profile lane** rather than a generic “OTel enabled” box. Sources: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/rust/ ; https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-rust ; https://docs.rs/opentelemetry-appender-tracing ; https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2025/stability-proposal-announcement/ ; https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2025/otel-weaver/ ; https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2025-0123.html
- Tokio Console continues to prove that runtime diagnostics deserve their own lane. The `console-subscriber` README still describes a dedicated `Layer`, a gRPC server, runtime-specific tracing instrumentation, and an explicit `tokio_unstable` requirement. That is exactly why the archive should keep a separate **runtime-diagnostic lane** rather than quietly promoting local async-debug tooling into the general support contract. Source: https://github.com/tokio-rs/console/blob/main/console-subscriber/README.md
- Cargo 1.94 added one more adjacent signal: structured logging/reporting is now an explicit Cargo workstream. That strengthens the case for an **imported machine-report lane** inside observability productization, but only as a bounded import — not as proof that build reports and runtime telemetry are the same substrate. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- Archive decision: add `design/observability-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/observability-kit.md`, `design/observability-productization-stack.md`, `design/observability-productization-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/observability-interop-and-telemetry-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-observability-kit.md`; prepend matching frontier notes in `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; update `INDEX.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future observability/debuggability/service/support revisions keep **tracing composition, local formatted diagnostics, legacy-log import, metrics facades, OpenTelemetry export/profile posture, runtime diagnostics, and imported machine reports** distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another exporter helper, backend bootstrap crate, or one-true telemetry wrapper. It is a thin `cargo obs` / `obs-pack/v0` layer whose lane profiles, activation reports, vector reports, and bounded consumer handoffs let downstream tools compare Rust observability claims honestly.
## 2026-03-20 — Consumer Install lane-map + pilot-program refresh (source builds, prebuilt binaries, mirror fallback, CI wrappers, delegated managers, durable receipts)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next seam that would sharpen the map rather than widen it. The strongest complementary move after publish/update was **Consumer Install**: the archive already had the right leaf artifact family for install subject/catalog/plan/receipt truth, but it still lacked the explicit lane map and ranked pilot plan that would stop future revisions from flattening source builds, prebuilt downloads, mirror-aware installers, CI bootstrap wrappers, and delegated package-manager imports into one fake “install support” story.
- Current Cargo docs keep the source-build lane unusually explicit. `cargo install` says the packaged `Cargo.lock` is ignored by default unless `--locked` is used, and it says install-root tracking metadata is created by default while `--no-track` disables that file and Cargo’s concurrent-install protection. That is exactly why the archive should keep a distinct **source-build install lane** instead of narrating every install as a generic binary acquisition event. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html
- Cargo packaging docs sharpen the producer→consumer edge further: `Cargo.lock` is always included unless `--exclude-lockfile` is used, and the docs explicitly warn that the flag is not for general use because some tools may expect a lockfile, including `cargo install --locked`. That is strong evidence that the archive should preserve lockfile posture as part of install truth, not just publish truth. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- `cargo-binstall` is now explicit enough to justify a separate prebuilt lane in the archive itself. Its README says it searches linked repository releases for matching artifacts, falls back to quickinstall, then alternate targets, and only finally to `cargo install`; its signing docs separately define how signature verification works. That combination proves prebuilt install is not “Cargo install but faster,” but a distinct candidate-selection + verification lane. Sources: https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall ; https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall/blob/main/SIGNING.md
- cargo-dist 0.31.0 and `taiki-e/install-action` together sharpen two more lanes. cargo-dist’s changelog now says mirrors can fallback according to configured host order, which makes selected-source order part of install truth. install-action keeps manifest-managed installs, `cargo-binstall` fallback, `cargo install` fallback, checksum/signature posture, and even prerequisite distro package-manager setup explicit, which is direct evidence that CI/bootstrap installs are their own lane rather than transparent wrappers. Sources: https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md ; https://github.com/taiki-e/install-action
- `axoupdater` adds the downstream proof point: its README says it uses install receipts produced by cargo-dist and that those receipts contain metadata about the currently-installed version and the cargo-dist version that produced it. Meanwhile crates.io’s January 2026 update adds Trusted Publishing improvements and `pubtime`, which sharpens producer-side truth but still does not answer what any given machine installed. Together, those are strong signals that Rust needs a portable **consumer-install receipt lane** distinct from both publish truth and later update continuity. Sources: https://github.com/axodotdev/axoupdater ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Archive decision: add `design/consumer-install-lane-map.md` and `design/consumer-install-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/consumer-install-kit.md`, `gaps/consumer-install-selection-channels-mirrors-and-receipts.md`, and `proposals/epic-consumer-install-kit.md`; prepend a current-frontier correction in `PRIORITIES.md`; replace the old emerging frontier note in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` with a concrete current-frontier correction; update `INDEX.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future install/distribution/update/support revisions keep **source-build installs, prebuilt installs, mirror/host fallback, CI-wrapper installs, delegated/imported installs, and durable receipt/managed-content claims** distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another installer wrapper, package-manager shim, or download-speed optimization layer. It is a thin `cargo installproof` / `install-pack/v0` layer whose lane profiles, candidate catalogs, plan/receipt reports, and bounded handoffs let downstream tools compare Rust first-install claims honestly.

- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another ORM, migration generator, query builder bake-off, or hosted database control plane. It is a thin `cargo dbcheck` / `db-pack/v0` layer whose lane profiles, adapter reports, environment receipts, and bounded consumer handoffs let downstream tools compare Rust relational-database claims honestly.

## 2026-03-20 — Toolchain Productization lane-map refresh (stock rustup, build-std, reusable sysroot packs, custom targets, activation rules, and instrumented runtime families)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for the next seam that would sharpen the map rather than widen it. The strongest remaining case was **Toolchain Productization**: the archive already had the right stack and pilot, but it still lacked the explicit lane map that would stop future revisions from flattening stock rustup installs, local build-std rebuilds, reusable sysroot packs, compiler-pinned custom targets, activation policy, and instrumented runtime families into one fake “custom toolchain support” story.
- The official `build-std` goal now makes the missing seam unusually clear. It is explicitly about a stabilizable MVP, and its motivation keeps non-precompiled targets, non-baseline target features, ABI-changing flags, exploit mitigations, different `cfg`s, and even a blessed way to build at least `core` without Cargo for Rust-for-Linux-like users in scope. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/build-std.html
- Cargo’s current unstable docs still keep the experimental build-std lane sharp: `rust-src` is required, nightly Cargo and nightly rustc are required, and `-Z build-std` must be passed to all Cargo invocations. That is exactly why the archive should preserve a distinct **local build-std lane** instead of pretending experimental rebuilds are already portable toolchain products. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- rustup’s current docs make two other lanes explicit. The cross-compilation docs say `rustup target add` only installs the Rust standard library for a target and that other tools — particularly a linker and often an SDK — are still required; the override docs keep toolchain shorthand, `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`, directory overrides, `rust-toolchain.toml`, default toolchains, and pinned `components` / `targets` / `profile` explicit. Those are strong signals for separate **stock rustup** and **activation** lanes. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/cross-compilation.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/overrides.html
- Custom-target docs and release notes sharpened the target/sysroot side. The rustc book says target JSON properties are unstable, the schema is version-coupled, and compiler versions should always be pinned when using custom targets. Meanwhile the 1.93 release notes say rustc now searches `/lib/rustlib/<target-triple>/target.json` under the sysroot, which is a strong sign that custom-target identity and sysroot packaging/transport are becoming more coupled in practice. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/targets/custom.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html
- Cargo’s unstable `target-applies-to-host` / `host-config` docs are a particularly strong activation signal because they explicitly call the current dual behavior around `linker` / `rustflags` confusing, then add new configuration so host artifacts and target artifacts can be configured separately. That is exactly the sort of thing the archive should preserve as a distinct **host-versus-target activation lane** rather than burying under provisioning. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- The runtime-family lane is no longer hypothetical. The sanitizer-support goal says MemorySanitizer and ThreadSanitizer need a way to use precompiled and instrumented standard libraries through rustup, and the 2026 flagship page carries the same infrastructure need forward. That means **instrumented stdlib identity** is now a live ecosystem seam rather than a niche experiment. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/stabilization-of-sanitizer-support.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The end-of-2025 program update added one more adoption signal: CPython exploration is surfacing needs similar to Rust for Linux — `build-std`, platform support, sanitizer support. That is strong evidence that the missing layer here matters to large adopters beyond embedded and security niches. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/12/19/program-management-update--end-of-2025/
- Archive decision: add `design/toolchain-productization-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/toolchain-productization-stack.md`, `design/toolchain-productization-pilot-program.md`, `design/sysroot-pack-kit.md`, `gaps/toolchain-variants-sysroots-cross-builds-and-sanitizer-support-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-toolchain-productization-stack.md`; prepend a current-frontier correction in `PRIORITIES.md`; prepend a matching frontier note in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future toolchain/sysroot/sanitizer/support revisions keep stock rustup lanes, local build-std lanes, reusable sysroot packs, compiler-pinned custom targets, activation rules, runtime-family claims, and external handoffs distinct instead of collapsing them into one custom-toolchain score.

## 2026-03-20 — Update Continuity lane-map + pilot-program refresh (source-installed tools, prebuilt reinstall, receipt-driven updaters, bundle/app updaters, delegated ownership)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that was already present conceptually but still under-modeled in a way that could distort future revisions. The clearest remaining case was **update continuity**: the archive already had a good installed-subject / candidate / plan / apply / ownership substrate, but it still lacked a crisp lane map separating source-installed tools, prebuilt reinstall flows, receipt-driven updaters, bundle/app updaters, delegated-manager cases, and forensic/imported continuity.
- Current Cargo docs keep the baseline installed-tool lane sharp. `cargo install` still ignores packaged `Cargo.lock` by default unless `--locked` is used, performs system/user-level config discovery instead of local project discovery, and documents `--no-track` as disabling both install metadata and Cargo’s concurrent-install protection. The config docs also keep `.crates.toml` / `.crates2.json` explicit under the install root. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html
- The Cargo 1.86 development-cycle report is unusually direct about the missing continuity seam: it highlighted `cargo install-update` (`cargo-update`) as plugin of the cycle and said built-in support is still tracked in `#4101`. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/02/27/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.86/
- `cargo-binstall` sharpens the prebuilt reinstall lane rather than flattening it. Its README explicitly says it searches repository releases, falls back to the quickinstall host, may try alternate targets, and finally falls back to `cargo install`. That is strong evidence that candidate visibility, target matching, and final apply path are already plural. Source: https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall
- cargo-dist and `axoupdater` make a distinct receipt-driven updater lane real. cargo-dist 0.31.0 added mirror fallback for installers, while `axoupdater` explicitly says it uses install receipts produced by cargo-dist to learn the currently-installed version before checking or performing an update. Sources: https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/releases ; https://github.com/axodotdev/axoupdater
- Tauri’s updater docs make bundle/app update semantics materially different from ordinary tool refresh. The current docs keep dynamic vs static update sources, target/custom-target matching, downgrade control through `version_comparator`, and Windows `on_before_exit` hooks explicit. Source: https://v2.tauri.app/plugin/updater/
- `update-kit` and `self-replace` make the crate-level lifecycle decomposition explicit rather than weakening it: `update-kit` describes Detection -> Check -> Plan -> Apply, while `self-replace` exists because self-replace and self-uninstall remain platform-sharp, especially on Windows. Sources: https://docs.rs/update-kit/latest/update_kit/ ; https://docs.rs/self-replace/latest/self_replace/
- Cargo 1.90’s path-ownership work closes the loop by saying Rustup should only remove content it manages. That is exactly why the archive now treats ownership/uninstall as a continuity lane rather than as an afterthought. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/
- Archive decision: add `design/update-continuity-lane-map.md` and `design/update-continuity-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/update-continuity-kit.md`, `gaps/update-continuity-detection-selection-apply-rollback-and-uninstall.md`, and `proposals/epic-update-continuity-kit.md`; prepend a current-frontier correction in `PRIORITIES.md`; prepend a matching frontier note in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future update/install/support revisions keep source-installed tool lanes, prebuilt reinstall lanes, receipt-driven updater lanes, bundle/app updater lanes, delegated ownership, and rollback/uninstall conclusions distinct instead of collapsing them into one fake update verdict.

## 2026-03-20 — Publish-set lane-map refresh (source-package publication is now rich enough that package selection, authority path, checks, and receipts must stay separate)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for a move that would keep the repo cumulative after the recent async/native/Python/pointer/semantic/process/terminal/time passes. The strongest under-modeled seam was **Publish Set Kit**: the archive already had the anchor, but it still lacked the explicit lane rule and ranked pilot plan that recent frontier seams had gained.
- Cargo’s unstable-feature docs now say multi-package publishing was stabilized in Rust 1.90.0, and later note that the `pubtime` index field is stabilized in Rust 1.94.0. That is strong evidence that source publication is no longer just a single-crate upload edge case and that later index timing/receipt data is now part of the public shape. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registry-index.html
- `cargo publish` and Cargo’s changelog made the receipt lane much more concrete than older archive text implied. The publish docs describe workspace-aware selection, registry/index choice, authentication expectations, upload behavior, and client polling while waiting for index appearance; Cargo’s changelog says `cargo publish` now blocks until it sees the published package in the index and later fixed wait-for-publish for sparse registries. That means upload acceptance and index visibility are real review facts, not background trivia. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-publish.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html
- `cargo package` now gives enough payload detail to justify a sharper lane split. Its docs describe generated-versus-copied file provenance in the unstable `--message-format json` output for `--list`, explicit `Cargo.toml` normalization, packaged lockfile posture, and `.cargo_vcs_info.json` as a best-effort VCS snapshot. Release notes and changelog entries add that `cargo-package` should now be independently reproducible, `.cargo_vcs_info.json` is always included, and nonexistent `license-file` / `readme` paths are rejected during packaging. That is strong evidence that packaged payload truth is richer than a tarball hash or manifest diff. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html
- Registry-authentication and registry-index docs made the authority-path split impossible to ignore. Cargo now documents credential providers, authenticated alternative registries, sparse-index authentication, and `auth-required`; the registry-index docs also say `pubtime` is the original publish time and should not change on later status changes like `yanked`. Meanwhile the January 2026 crates.io update added GitLab Trusted Publishing, Trusted-Publishing-only mode, and blocked risky GitHub triggers. Those signals say token/credential-provider publishing, alternative-registry publishing, trusted-publishing/OIDC, and later receipt/index observation are distinct lanes rather than one generic “publish” capability. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registry-authentication.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registry-index.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- The 2025H2 `cargo-semver-checks` goal then sharpened the check/waiver lane from another angle by explicitly aiming to merge SemVer compliance into the `cargo publish` workflow with an override flag. That is exactly the kind of upstream signal that says package verification, semver checking, policy imports, waivers, and registry receipts must stay separate in this archive instead of collapsing into one publish-success bit. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html
- Archive decision: add `design/publish-set-lane-map.md` and `design/publish-set-pilot-program.md`, refresh the publish gap/kit/epic plus the frontier/root files, and strengthen the amnesia guidance so future revisions keep **selected publish subject truth, packaged payload truth, authority-path truth, check/waiver truth, upload/index/`pubtime` receipt truth, and later package-admission/release conclusions** distinct instead of flattening them into one fake publish story.

## 2026-03-20 — Time Surface lane-map + pilot-program refresh (monotonic clocks, wall clocks, civil/offset forms, zoned DST-aware values, localization, storage adapters, fake clocks)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that was already present conceptually but still under-modeled in a way that could distort future revisions. The clearest remaining case was **time surfaces**: the archive already had good clock/zone/calendar/storage/evidence language, but it still lacked a crisp lane map separating monotonic elapsed time, wall-clock capture, civil/offset forms, zoned DST-aware values, localized calendar/locale rendering, storage/migration adapters, and deterministic fake clocks.
- Current std docs keep the foundational split sharp. `Instant` is a monotonically nondecreasing opaque measurement useful only with `Duration`, but its docs also warn it is not guaranteed to be steady and that hardware/virtualization/OS bugs can violate monotonic expectations. `SystemTime` is explicitly not monotonic and is for talking to external entities like the filesystem and other processes. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.Instant.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html
- The `time` crate is still a real civil/offset/wire lane rather than a universal temporal stack. Its feature docs keep formatting, parsing, `local-offset`, and `serde-human-readable` explicit, while its `format_description` docs keep well-known standards and macro-built format descriptions visible. Sources: https://docs.rs/time/latest/time/ ; https://docs.rs/time/latest/time/format_description/index.html
- Jiff made the zoned/DST-aware lane clear enough to elevate. Its top-level docs center zone-aware values; its comparison docs explain automatic TZDB integration and contrast that with Chrono-TZ; and its platform docs explain Windows TZDB embedding plus CLDR-backed Windows-to-IANA mapping for system-zone discovery. Sources: https://docs.rs/jiff ; https://docs.rs/jiff/latest/jiff/_documentation/comparison/index.html ; https://docs.rs/jiff/latest/jiff/_documentation/platform/index.html
- Chrono and Chrono-TZ remain important precisely because they prove this seam is still plural. Chrono says timezone data is not shipped by default, while Chrono-TZ says its `TimeZone` implementations are generated by a build script using the IANA database and exposes compile-time-built zone values. Sources: https://docs.rs/chrono ; https://docs.rs/chrono-tz ; https://docs.rs/chrono-tz/latest/chrono_tz/enum.Tz.html
- Localization/rendering is a different lane from time arithmetic or zone conversion. ICU4X documents localized formatting of dates, times, and time zones, and its field-set docs keep date/time/zone combinations explicit. `jiff-icu` then proves there is already real bridge pressure between zoned temporal values and localized rendering. Sources: https://docs.rs/icu_datetime/latest/icu_datetime/ ; https://docs.rs/icu_datetime/latest/icu_datetime/fieldsets/index.html ; https://docs.rs/jiff-icu/latest/jiff_icu/
- Storage/adapter and deterministic/fake-clock lanes are real present-tense seams too. `jiff-sqlx` exists because SQL integration needs a separate boundary today, and Tokio's time docs explicitly document runtime-scoped paused/advanced clocks with caveats about auto-advance and timer processing. Sources: https://docs.rs/jiff-sqlx/latest/jiff_sqlx/ ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/time/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/time/fn.pause.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/time/fn.advance.html
- Maintenance signals are shifting as well. Dirkjan Ochtman wrote in January 2026 that they are inclined to wind down Chrono and Chrono-TZ and now feel comfortable recommending Jiff. That makes migration-aware lane discipline more valuable, not less. Source: https://dirkjan.ochtman.nl/writing/2026/01/09/reviewing-2025.html
- Archive decision: add `design/time-surface-lane-map.md` and `design/time-surface-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/time-surface-kit.md`, `gaps/time-surfaces-clocks-time-zones-and-calendrical-contracts.md`, and `proposals/epic-time-surface-kit.md`; prepend a current-frontier correction in `PRIORITIES.md`; prepend a matching frontier note in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future time/background-work/localization revisions keep monotonic, wall-clock, civil/offset, zoned, localized, storage/migration, and fake-clock claims distinct instead of collapsing them into one fake time verdict.

## 2026-03-20 — Terminal Surface lane-map + pilot-program refresh (styled output, full-screen TUI, line editing, capability probing, parser/test evidence, graphics protocols)

Sources: https://docs.rs/anstream/latest/anstream/struct.AutoStream.html ; https://docs.rs/unicode-display-width/latest/unicode_display_width/

Sources: https://docs.rs/reedline/latest/reedline/struct.Reedline.html ; https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/backend/struct.TestBackend.html ; https://docs.rs/vt100/latest/vt100/ ; https://docs.rs/ratatui-image/latest/ratatui_image/

## 2026-03-20 — Process Surface lane-map + pilot-program refresh (direct exec, shell-shaped composition, pipe topology, async lifecycle, tree control, PTY)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that was already present conceptually but still under-modeled in a way that could distort future revisions. The clearest remaining case was **process surfaces**: the archive already had good spawn/argv/stdio/supervision language, but it still lacked a crisp lane map separating direct exec, actual shell execution, shell-like but shell-free helpers, explicit pipe topology, async lifecycle/reaping, tree control, and PTY interaction.
- Current std docs still keep the baseline lane sharp. `std::process::Command` does not invoke a shell by default, warns that relative program paths combined with `current_dir` are platform-specific and unstable, and preserves explicit env/cwd/stdio configuration. Std `Child` still has no `Drop`, and docs still warn about zombie processes on Unix when exited children are not waited on. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Command.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Child.html
- `std::io::pipe`, stabilized in 1.87, is a meaningful present-tense signal: explicit pipe topology is now ordinary std substrate, with documented blocking/interleaving/EOF behavior, rather than just crate-local glue. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/fn.pipe.html
- Async child lifecycle is still visibly plural. Tokio’s current docs preserve std’s default “drop does not cancel” behavior, provide `kill_on_drop`, and only promise best-effort background reaping on Unix; `async-process` explicitly added both `reap_on_drop` and `kill_on_drop`. Sources: https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/process/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/process/struct.Command.html ; https://docs.rs/crate/async-process/2.5.0/source/CHANGELOG.md
- There is also a lesson from the past that the archive should keep visible: the older `tokio-process` crate documented the opposite drop story, where dropping the `Child` terminated the process by default because the child itself was a future. That historical swing is exactly why the archive should keep lifecycle lanes explicit rather than narrating one async-process story as timeless truth. Source: https://docs.rs/tokio-process/latest/tokio_process/
- The helper layer is plural in a semantically important way. `xshell` explicitly says it does not use the shell directly and aims for reliability/no shell injection by construction, while `duct` explicitly offers shell-like pipelines/redirection and reports non-zero exit statuses as errors by default. Those are adjacent ergonomic answers, not one subprocess lane. Sources: https://docs.rs/xshell/latest/src/xshell/lib.rs.html ; https://docs.rs/duct/latest/duct/
- Tree control and concurrent control remain separate seams. Unix `CommandExt::process_group` is now standard, `process-wrap` explicitly presents itself as a composable successor to `command-group` across std or Tokio command wrappers, and `shared_child` exists specifically because concurrent wait and kill are awkward with std `Child` due to PID-reuse race concerns. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/process/trait.CommandExt.html ; https://docs.rs/process-wrap/latest/process_wrap/ ; https://docs.rs/shared_child/latest/shared_child/
- PTY interaction is still its own first-class lane. `portable-pty` exposes a cross-platform PTY API with a separate command builder, runtime-selectable implementations, and even a serial-TTY path that cannot just spawn arbitrary commands the same way. Source: https://docs.rs/portable-pty/latest/portable_pty/
- Archive decision: add `design/process-surface-lane-map.md` and `design/process-surface-pilot-program.md`; refresh `gaps/process-surfaces-subprocesses-pipelines-and-supervision-contracts.md`, `design/process-surface-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-process-surface-kit.md`; prepend a current-frontier correction in `PRIORITIES.md`; prepend a matching frontier note in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep actual shell execution, shell-like DSLs, pipe topology, async lifecycle/reaping, tree-control wrappers, and PTY interaction distinct instead of collapsing them into one fake subprocess verdict.

## 2026-03-20 — Semantic-context authority lane map (local authoritative capture vs docs.rs cache vs derived slices vs compiler-backed watch)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose to sharpen an already-promoted frontier seam instead of widening the repo with another adjacent stack. The existing semantic-context work was strategically strong, but it still left one flattening hazard: too much of the ecosystem pressure now encourages people to say “semantic context” as if local authoritative capture, public rustdoc caches, editor slices, and compiler-backed analysis were already one interchangeable layer.
- The accepted 2025H1 Cargo plumbing goal is the clearest signal that exact local semantic capture is a first-class lane. It says `cargo metadata` can include dependency resolution but excludes feature resolution, and it names phases like `resolve features` and `plan build` explicitly. The 2025 GSoC results then report working prototypes for `resolve-features` and `plan-build`, which means the machine-facing building blocks are now concrete rather than hypothetical. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/18/gsoc-2025-results/
- The July 2025 goals update for `cargo-semver-checks` makes the cache-versus-authority split unusually explicit: docs.rs-hosted rustdoc JSON helps, but correct cross-crate work still needs recursively active dependency features and `rmeta`-based combination. docs.rs itself now hosts rustdoc JSON and warns consumers to check `format_version`, which is strong evidence that public cached semantic artifacts are real infrastructure, but not interchangeable with exact local workspace capture. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/ ; https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json
- StableMIR publication and the `rustc_public` refactoring work are strong enough signals to keep a compiler-backed watch lane, but not strong enough to erase simpler lanes yet. The StableMIR goal is explicitly about letting tool developers analyze compiled crates and dependencies without compiler internals, and the 2025 GSoC report says the refactoring/versioning work landed for the tooling ecosystem. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/stable-mir.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/18/gsoc-2025-results/
- Cargo’s 1.93 development-cycle post says schema work could improve Cargo JSON and help unlock a better `cargo fix` architecture, which makes semantic handoff to edit/fix consumers more urgent. Meanwhile the 2025 State of Rust survey says official online docs remain the preferred canonical reference even while editor/LLM workflows rise. Together, those signals argue for a lane map that keeps canonical capture, cached public artifacts, derived slices, and experimental augmentation explicitly distinct. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add `design/semantic-context-lane-map.md`; refresh `gaps/cross-crate-semantic-context-and-analysis-inputs.md`, `design/semantic-context-kit.md`, `design/semantic-context-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-semantic-context-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add an amnesia resistor so future semantic-context/edit/tooling revisions keep local authoritative capture, public cache, comparison posture, derived slices, and compiler-backed watch claims distinct instead of flattening them into one fake universal semantic index.

## 2026-03-20 — Pointer shared-ownership lane map (`Rc` vs `Arc` vs unique-to-shared vs weakless/borrowed arc families vs publication layers)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose to sharpen an existing frontier seam rather than add another adjacent kit. The Pointer Surface / Borrowing Frontier band was already strong, but it still left one flattening hazard: too much current Rust discussion treats “ergonomic ref-counting” as if it named a single semantic lane instead of a stack of related but non-equivalent ownership patterns.
- The official ergonomic-ref-counting goal is now strong enough to justify the sharpen. The 2025H2 goal says cloning friction affects async, GUI, reactive, and other high-level domains; it says the ecosystem is comparing explicit `.use` syntax with a more automatic alternative plus lints; and it explicitly cites Dioxus-style and compiler/arena-adjacent pain as part of the same pressure. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/ergonomic-rc.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Std docs confirm that even the baseline lane is not one thing. `Rc` and `Arc` each expose `ptr_eq`, `get_mut`, `make_mut`, and weak-pointer semantics that materially affect identity, uniqueness, and clone-on-write behavior. Std `UniqueArc` sharpens that further by making the uniquely-owned-to-shared construction lane explicit: weak pointers can exist before ordinary `Arc` conversion, but cannot upgrade until that conversion happens. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/struct.Rc.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.UniqueArc.html
- The crate ecology sharpens the split rather than weakening it. `triomphe` is not just “another Arc”; it removes weak refs and adds borrowed/offset/thin forms with stronger FFI/layout implications. `arc-swap` is not “an Arc variant”; it is a publication/storage layer over ref-counted pointers, optimized for read-mostly workloads, with lock-free readers, expensive writes, and explicit guard limitations. Sources: https://docs.rs/triomphe/latest/triomphe/ ; https://docs.rs/arc-swap ; https://docs.rs/arc-swap/latest/arc_swap/docs/performance/ ; https://docs.rs/arc-swap/latest/arc_swap/docs/limitations/
- Archive decision: add `design/pointer-shared-ownership-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/pointer-surface-kit.md`, `design/pointer-surface-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-pointer-surface-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add an amnesia resistor so future pointer/async revisions keep syntax ergonomics, pointer semantics, unique-to-shared construction, borrowed/layout-specialized arc forms, and publication/storage layers distinct instead of flattening them into one fake ref-counting score.

## 2026-03-20 — Python host-lane map (full-API vs `abi3` vs free-threaded vs `asyncio` bridge, with CPython-adoption adjacency)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose to sharpen an existing stack rather than invent another Python-only framework. The generic Host Package / Polyglot notes were already good, but they were still too likely to let “Python support” blur together extension ABI, wheel portability, free-threading, async bridges, and CPython-adoption work.
- The official Rust/CPython collaboration is now a strong enough signal to justify a dedicated lane map. The February 2026 program-management update says the groups are discussing thread attach/detach soundness, stdlib symbol visibility for extension modules, mixed `bin`/`lib` linker arguments, possible `asyncio` interop, and the broader challenge of introducing Rust into a large C codebase. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/11/program-management-update-2026-01/
- PyO3’s current guide still presents both native extension modules and embedding Python in Rust, which is already enough to prove this is not one lane. Its build/distribution docs say `abi3` is the limited-API route for multi-version wheels, while the free-threaded guide says the free-threaded build uses a new ABI and has no limited-API equivalent today. Sources: https://pyo3.rs/main/ ; https://pyo3.rs/main/building-and-distribution ; https://pyo3.rs/v0.28.2/free-threading ; https://pyo3.rs/v0.28.2/features
- PyO3 0.28.0 made free-threaded support opt-out rather than opt-in, which is strong evidence that free-threaded compatibility is graduating from edge experiment to product-review concern. Source: https://pyo3.rs/v0.28.2/changelog
- The async lane is real but not universal. PyO3’s async docs say the awaitable path is `asyncio`-only for now, while `pyo3-async-runtimes` exists as a separate bridge crate for Rust runtime integrations. Sources: https://pyo3.rs/v0.28.2/async-await ; https://docs.rs/crate/pyo3-async-runtimes/latest
- maturin’s distribution docs make manylinux / musllinux and cross-compilation posture first-class, while the PyO3 FAQ now says the old `extension-module` feature is deprecated and can break tests/workspaces without newer packaging flows. That means packaging/link/test handoff belongs in the lane model rather than being left as local build trivia. Sources: https://www.maturin.rs/distribution.html ; https://pyo3.rs/v0.28.2/faq
- Archive decision: add `design/python-host-lane-map.md`; refresh `design/host-package-kit.md`, `design/polyglot-productization-stack.md`, and `proposals/epic-host-package-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep full-API extension, `abi3`, free-threaded ABI, async bridge, packaging/link/test handoff, and embedding/CPython-upstream adjacency distinct instead of flattening them into one fake Python-support verdict.

## rev0321 native-edge / C++ interop lane-map refresh
- The accepted 2025H1 Rust goal **Evaluate approaches for seamless interop between C++ and Rust** is strong evidence that native adoption through rich existing C++ APIs is a first-class Rust concern, not a side quest: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/seamless-rust-cpp.html
- The 2025H2 **C++/Rust Interop Problem Space Mapping** goal says there are billions of lines of C++ representing enormous value and that external libraries solve different slices of the space today, which argues for a lane map before any “one true solution” language: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/interop-problem-map.html
- The July 2025 goals update says Rust should evolve toward a **first-class C++ interop story**, but also says different groups have materially different needs. That combination is exactly the archive pattern where distinct lanes should be preserved rather than flattened: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/
- Cargo issue #14948 says reducing user-authored build scripts matters because build scripts increase build times, bug risk, and dependency-review surface; native probing remains one of the reasons they persist. That sharpens the provider/link half of Native Edge rather than making it secondary: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/14948
- Cargo’s build-script docs still say `links` metadata is limited to one package per `links` value and metadata only flows to immediate dependents, which is a direct reminder that build-script-era native facts are real but narrow in scope: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
- The Rustonomicon still teaches FFI through C interfaces and says Rust cannot directly call into a C++ library, which keeps the archive honest about today’s baseline instead of narrating future interop aspirations as present-tense reality: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/ffi.html
- `system-deps` explicitly says native requirements can live declaratively in `Cargo.toml` so other tools can read them, while `pkg-config` explicitly says it shells out from `build.rs`; that is the provider-lane distinction in miniature: https://docs.rs/system-deps/ ; https://docs.rs/pkg-config
- CXX explicitly says it carves out a regime of commonality where Rust and C++ are semantically similar enough for a safe bridge, while `autocxx` explicitly says it targets large existing C++ codebases and layers automation over CXX-style safety. Those are adjacent lanes, not synonyms: https://cxx.rs/ ; https://google.github.io/autocxx/
- Corrosion explicitly positions itself as Cargo↔CMake integration and documents FFI binding-attachment paths, which is exactly the foreign-build handoff lane the archive should preserve separately from boundary or provider truth: https://corrosion-rs.github.io/corrosion/ ; https://corrosion-rs.github.io/corrosion/ffi_bindings.html
- Archive decision: add `design/native-edge-cpp-lane-map.md`, promote a rev0321 Native Edge frontier correction, and strengthen hygiene so future revisions stop collapsing C ABI export/import, typed safe-common bridges, large-codebase automation, provider resolution, and foreign-build/package handoff into one fake “Rust/C++ support” verdict.

## 2026-03-20 — Async Commons Kit refresh (runtime lock-in, neutral seams, watch-worthy portability truth)
- Re-opened the archive against the freshest official Rust signals instead of tunneling further into Cargo-only refinement. The strongest new cross-stack seam was **async commons**: not async reliability itself, but the lower-level shared vocabulary/capability layer that determines when async libraries and stacks are genuinely portable versus merely adapter-shaped.
- The decisive upstream signal was the Rust challenges post published on March 20, 2026. It says async remains one of the sharpest pain points, that library choice can immediately lock users into one runtime family, and that a more cohesive async ecosystem may require more fundamental async traits/functions over time. The 2025H1 async goal and the Async Book both reinforce the same gap from different angles: runtime choice/interoperability remain hard, and async still carries a higher maintenance burden plus compatibility constraints. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/20/rust-challenges/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/async.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/async-book/01_getting_started/03_state_of_async_rust.html
- The archive already had serious Async Lifecycle and Async Reliability work, but that made the missing cut clearer rather than weaker. Those stacks should not each keep re-describing runtime portability in their own language. They need one lower-level seam that preserves neutral async vocabulary, capability requirements, runtime-shaped APIs, adapter lossiness, and explicit `watch`/`defer` posture for seams still blocked on language/compiler work.
- Archive decision: add `gaps/async-commons-runtime-capabilities-traits-and-portability-contracts.md`, `design/async-commons-kit.md`, `design/async-commons-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-async-commons-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add repo-operational guardrails in `AGENTS.md` and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future async revisions do not flatten `std`/language progress, neutral futures/stream/I/O vocabulary, runtime-specific APIs, adapter costs, and downstream lifecycle/productization conclusions into one fake “runtime agnostic” story.

## 2026-03-20 — Cargo-report contradiction/arbitration refresh (same-scope competing artifacts must stay explicit)
- DelayBasin’s rev0093 materials added the strongest reusable pattern still missing from the Rust archive: **contradiction-packet / precedence-ladder / conflict-transparent-abstention** plus **arbitration witnesses, tie sets, and confusability budgets**. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/future-incompat-report.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html
