Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/sanitizer.html
- `cargo-careful` has matured into a practical middle lane: rebuilt std with debug assertions, extra UB checks, optional sanitizer integration, arbitrary system and C FFI support, and an explicit claim that it is faster and more permissive than Miri while also less exhaustive. That is strong evidence that Rust dynamic analysis is plural in ways worth preserving. Source: https://github.com/RalfJung/cargo-careful
- Miri remains uniquely valuable, but nextest’s Miri integration sharpens the archive’s missing distinction: per-test processes can make runs up to 3–4× faster, yet that runner model also loses some data-race visibility across tests sharing resources. That means execution-mode imports belong in the battery contract rather than being treated as a hidden CI detail. Sources: https://github.com/rust-lang/miri ; https://nexte.st/docs/integrations/miri/
- The retag/codegen goal and BorrowSanitizer’s February 2026 update keep widening the lane surface. Rust is not converging on one runtime-checking engine; it is gaining new native aliasing instrumentation families with their own maturity and comparability limits. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/codegen_retags.html ; https://borrowsanitizer.com/status/february_2026.html
- Rust-for-Linux is still a forcing function for stable foundations around compiler flags, custom std builds, and sanitizer integration, which keeps this problem ecosystem-level rather than app-local. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/rfl.html
- Archive decision: refresh `gaps/sanitizers-and-dynamic-analysis.md`, deepen `design/sanitizer-battery-kit.md`, add `design/sanitizer-battery-pilot-program.md`, refresh `proposals/epic-sanitizer-battery-kit.md`, prepend a current-frontier correction in `PRIORITIES.md`, prepend a matching strategic-frontier note in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep engine family, runtime/sysroot provenance, execution-import truth, capability limits, findings/waivers, and downstream assurance conclusions distinct instead of collapsing them into one fake “battery passed” story.

## 2026-03-19 — Test-execution evidence refresh (runner-native recordings now strengthen the case for a portable pack instead of weakening it)
- Rust’s 2026 flagships now explicitly list **better test tooling** under **Building blocks**. That turns test-execution evidence from a merely local devex complaint into roadmap-visible infrastructure work. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H2 libtest-JSON goal is stronger than “please add another output format”. It says libtest is Cargo’s default harness, says users rely on programmatic output, and points toward reporting shifting upward into Cargo so custom runners and custom harnesses can grow more cleanly. Cargo 1.94 still lists finishing that experiment as a live area needing owners. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/libtest-json.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- Cargo’s own docs still show why a portable boundary is needed. `cargo test` mixes libtest, rustdoc doctests, and `harness = false` custom flows, and explicitly warns that doctest execution details are not guaranteed and may change. The rustc tests book still says libtest `--format json` is unstable, and benchmarks plus custom test frameworks remain unstable/experimental. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-test.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/tests/index.html
- nextest now sharpens the seam from the other side. Its docs expose machine-readable test lists, binary lists, JUnit output, experimental libtest-like JSON, debugger/tracer hooks, and persistent run recordings with full event streams, captured outputs, and workspace metadata. Its own machine-readable docs still list first-class JSON test-run output and detected configuration as future work. That is exactly the kind of situation where the archive should prefer a portable pack above tool-native stores rather than declaring the tool-native store to be the universal answer. Sources: https://nexte.st/docs/machine-readable/ ; https://nexte.st/docs/machine-readable/junit/ ; https://nexte.st/docs/design/architecture/recording-runs/ ; https://nexte.st/docs/running/
- Cargo’s external-tools docs still say `--message-format=json` only controls Cargo and rustc output, not arbitrary tool output. That means a reviewable cross-runner execution boundary still cannot just be “whatever JSON happened to be on stdout”. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html

## 2026-03-19 — Formal-verification pilot refresh (proof/report interoperability now deserves an execution path, not just an epic)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship roadmap explicitly treats **Safety-Critical Rust** as a top-level theme and frames it in terms of evidence-oriented milestones rather than generic “safety” branding. That strengthens the case that proof artifacts need to be reviewable ecosystem infrastructure, not tool-local lore. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The safety-critical adoption writeup says that as integrity levels rise, demands on development process, verification, and evidence also rise. That makes portable proof/report artifacts strategically relevant for real adopters rather than a niche research convenience. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
- The `std` contracts goal ports safety contracts from `verify-rust-std` into the standard library and explicitly says contracts can become runtime checks when needed, can support static analysis, and provide a foundation for formal verification. That means contract/spec sources are becoming shared ecosystem inputs rather than purely local annotations. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/std-contracts.html
- `a-mir-formality` explicitly aims to help validate and prove Rust’s type safety while aligning formal models with executable semantics through MiniRust. That raises the strategic value of keeping proof intent, assumptions, and backend/model boundaries explicit. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/a-mir-formality.html
- The Verify Rust Std project now publicly lists multiple approved tools in CI — ESBMC (via GOTO-Transcoder), Flux, Kani, and VeriFast — while the Rust Foundation says ESBMC is now live in that workflow and is aiming to integrate as an alternative backend for Kani. That is strong evidence that Rust verification is plural and still widening, which increases the value of a shared report/interoperability layer. Sources: https://model-checking.github.io/verify-rust-std/tools.html ; https://rustfoundation.org/media/expanding-the-rust-formal-verification-ecosystem-welcoming-esbmc/
- The Rust Formal Methods Interest Group explicitly says it wants better tool inter-compatibility, especially for specifications. Source: https://rust-formal-methods.github.io/
- Current tool workflows differ in important ways that a shared pack must preserve rather than erase: `cargo kani` is Cargo-native and supports concrete-counterexample playback; `cargo creusot prove` splits compilation from proof search and supports replay/IDE paths; Prusti spans IDE-assisted verification and `cargo prusti`; Verus frames itself as static full-functional-correctness verification without runtime checks. Sources: https://model-checking.github.io/kani/usage.html ; https://creusot-rs.github.io/creusot/guide/ ; https://viperproject.github.io/prusti-dev/user-guide/basic.html ; https://verus-lang.github.io/verus/guide/
- Archive decision: add `design/formal-verification-pilot-program.md`, refresh `design/formal-verification-kit.md` and `proposals/epic-formal-verification-kit.md`, re-elevate Formal Verification Kit in `PRIORITIES.md`, and update `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so the next credible move is explicitly two-stage: harden proof/report interoperability first, then import that lane into the broader Safety-Critical Evidence Stack.

## 2026-03-19 — Consumer Install Kit promotion (separate first-install truth from both producer release truth and later update continuity)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next missing lower-level anchor after splitting publication, package admission, update continuity, and artifact/discovery boundaries. The clearest remaining seam was **the first install event itself**: the archive had gotten better at what producers publish and at what happens after software is already installed, but it still lacked one portable answer to “what install did the user or CI ask for, what candidates were visible, why was one chosen, what verification actually ran, what landed on disk, and what does this tool claim it manages now?”
- Cargo’s current install docs make this seam sharper than they used to. `cargo install` explicitly says packaged `Cargo.lock` is ignored unless `--locked` is passed; it documents install-root metadata tracking; and it says `--no-track` disables that metadata file plus Cargo’s concurrent-install protection. Those are already install-boundary facts rather than generic release trivia. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/faq.html
- Cargo packaging docs now reinforce the producer→install handoff rather than dissolving it: `cargo package` says `--exclude-lockfile` is not for general use because some tools expect the lockfile, including `cargo install --locked`. That makes lockfile posture a real first-install dimension rather than a side note. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- `cargo-binstall` sharpened the lane split further. Its docs describe a low-complexity alternative to source builds, expose limited/initial signature support, and document explicit policy controls like `--only-signed` and `--skip-signatures`. That means Rust already has meaningful candidate-class and verification-policy differences at install time, but still lacks one portable install record above them. Source: https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall
- cargo-dist and CI tooling then made candidate visibility and fallback order impossible to ignore. cargo-dist’s February 2026 release added mirror-aware fallback ordering, while `taiki-e/install-action` exposes fallback choices between `cargo-binstall` and `cargo install`. That is exactly the kind of ecosystem signal the archive should read as “install boundary missing,” not just “more helper tools exist.” Sources: https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md ; https://github.com/taiki-e/install-action
- `axoupdater` provided another useful clue: it already has an install-receipt concept in its public library surface. That is evidence that install receipts are real and useful, but still too tool-local to serve as a Rust-wide contract. Source: https://docs.rs/axoupdater/latest/axoupdater/
- crates.io’s January 2026 update and Rust’s 2026 flagships strengthened the timing. Publish-side truth is getting better through Trusted Publishing controls and `pubtime`, and Cargo supply-chain work is still active through public/private dependencies and SBOM support. The more trustworthy producer-side evidence becomes, the more valuable it is to preserve the package → release → install handoff honestly on the consumer side. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Archive decision: refresh `gaps/consumer-install-selection-channels-mirrors-and-receipts.md`; add `design/consumer-install-kit.md` and `proposals/epic-consumer-install-kit.md`; refresh `design/distribution-contract-stack.md`, `design/distribution-contract-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-distribution-contract-stack.md` so Distribution Contract becomes explicitly stack-level above a leaf install boundary; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and `AGENTS.md`; and strengthen `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future passes keep install subject, visible candidates, policy/plan, receipt/mutation, managed-content claims, and later update/support/policy conclusions distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another installer wrapper, package-manager shim, or self-update helper. It is a thin `cargo installproof` / `install-pack/v0` layer above ordinary install lanes and below **Distribution Contract Stack** and **Update Continuity Kit**.

## 2026-03-19 — Update Continuity Kit promotion (separate ongoing update / rollback / uninstall truth from first-install receipts)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked specifically for a structural seam that the recent publish/install/distribution work had made more obvious rather than less. The clearest missing boundary was **consumer-side update continuity**: the archive had gotten much better at source publication, release truth, install selection, and install receipts, but still lacked one portable answer to “what installation did this machine start from, what candidates were considered, what plan was chosen, what changed, and who owns the result now?”
- Cargo’s own docs now make this seam much sharper than it used to be. `cargo install` documents concrete reinstall triggers, says packaged `Cargo.lock` is ignored by default unless `--locked` is used, says the command operates at system/user level rather than project level, and says Cargo tracks installed packages in metadata under the install root. Those are already lifecycle-bearing facts rather than one-shot download trivia. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html
- The Cargo 1.86 development-cycle report is unusually explicit that Rust still lacks a first-class built-in update path for installed binaries: it highlighted `cargo install-update` as the plugin of the cycle and said built-in support is being tracked in `#4101`. That is exactly the kind of ecosystem signal the archive should treat as “boundary missing,” not merely “use this plugin.” Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/02/27/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.86/
- `cargo-binstall` makes the composition problem concrete rather than hypothetical. Its docs say it falls back across GitHub-style releases, quickinstall, and `cargo install`; it tells users to upgrade `cargo-binstall` by rerunning `cargo binstall cargo-binstall`; and it explicitly points to `cargo-update` for updating all tools. That means Rust already has plural update lanes for CLI tools, but no shared continuity artifact above them. Sources: https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-update/latest/source/README.md
- cargo-dist and `axoupdater` sharpened the producer-to-consumer lifecycle bridge further. The cargo-dist site says the tool is now covering plan/build/host/publish/announce, while the February 2026 cargo-dist release added mirror-aware fallback and explicitly mentioned reducing the risk of interrupted installation leading to a partial installation; `axoupdater` now has explicit updater-process / install-receipt concepts in its library surface. That is exactly the point where first-install receipts stop being enough. Sources: https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/ ; https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/releases ; https://docs.rs/axoupdater/latest/axoupdater/
- Tauri’s updater docs make the app side equally concrete: updater sources can be dynamic or static, downgrades are explicit rather than impossible, target matching is explicit, permissions gate updater commands, and Windows has a before-exit hook because install semantics there are operationally different. That is strong evidence that update continuity is already a real product concern in Rust apps rather than a CLI-only afterthought. Sources: https://v2.tauri.app/plugin/updater/ ; https://docs.rs/tauri-plugin-updater/
- The ecosystem is also starting to name the lifecycle pieces directly. `update-kit` explicitly describes a Detection -> Check -> Plan -> Apply pipeline, while `self-replace` exists because self-replace and self-uninstall semantics are platform-sharp. This is exactly the pattern the archive should respond to by promoting a reusable continuity boundary rather than another crate wishlist fragment. Sources: https://docs.rs/update-kit/latest/update_kit/ ; https://docs.rs/self-replace/latest/self_replace/
- Cargo 1.90 provided the ownership-pressure proof: Cargo/rustup path work says Rustup should only remove content it manages. That means uninstall and cleanup scope can no longer be treated as a casual side note of installation. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/update-continuity-detection-selection-apply-rollback-and-uninstall.md`, `design/update-continuity-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-update-continuity-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Update Continuity Kit** becomes an explicit lower-level anchor; refresh `design/distribution-contract-stack.md`, `design/cli-productization-stack.md`, and `design/client-productization-stack.md` so first-install receipts stop half-owning ongoing lifecycle change; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep current install truth, candidate/comparator truth, chosen plan truth, apply/rollback truth, ownership/uninstall scope, and downstream support/policy/product conclusions distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another self-update crate, release-feed parser, installer rerun wrapper, or fake “latest” badge. It is a thin `cargo update-continuity` / `update-pack/v0` layer above **Distribution Contract** and below broader CLI/client/extension/operator/support consumers.

## 2026-03-19 — Reflection Transition Stack refresh (prototype reflection, Bevy pressure, lane honesty)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose a non-Cargo-heavy move to rebalance the repo. The strongest next step was not another new crate category, but a sharper frontier promotion for **Reflection Transition Stack** because live Rust roadmap signals and live userland lanes now line up unusually well.
- The critical upstream shift is that Rust’s 2026 flagship themes now explicitly include **prototype reflection**, while the 2025H2 reflection-and-comptime goal says proc-macro derives have historically been hard to debug and bootstrap and positions compile-time reflection as a real future lane rather than a thought experiment.
- The strongest new practical evidence came from the August 2025 program-management update: Bevy and gamedev users raised reflection as a major pain point, the writeup explains why `derive(Reflect)`-style workflows are difficult to write and debug, and it calls out orphan-rule limitations for standard-library and foreign types. That turns “reflection transition” from an abstract language-design note into a concrete ecosystem migration problem.
- The userland picture still remains genuinely plural rather than converged: `bevy_reflect` is a runtime metadata + registry lane; `facet` is an associated-const shape lane; `valuable` plus `tracing` is a visit-only/object-safe observability lane; and `serde_reflection` is a schema/format tracing lane. Those are not just four crates in the same category. They are four different semantic families that need to stay distinct in any serious archive design.
- Archive decision: refresh the reflection-transition gap/design/pilot/epic docs, promote the seam into the current frontier-correction band in `PRIORITIES.md`, strengthen the corresponding frontier section in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and add a small repo-operational guardrail so future passes cite both roadmap motion and at least two different live reflection-lane families before claiming the seam has moved.

## 2026-03-19 — FuzzPack refresh (engine plurality, regression imports, execution-envelope truth, replay/diff handoff)
- The Rust Fuzz Book still says `cargo-fuzz` is the recommended tool for fuzz testing Rust code, while the current `cargo-fuzz` docs make the lane boundaries explicit: it is a `libFuzzer`-based Cargo subcommand with workspace posture plus `fmt`, `tmin`, `cmin`, and `coverage` commands. That is strong evidence that Rust already has serious fuzzing workflow surface area, but not yet one portable review boundary above it. Sources: https://rust-fuzz.github.io/book/cargo-fuzz.html ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-fuzz/latest/source/README.md
- The Rust Fuzz Book guide also shows that feature forwarding and `--cfg fuzzing` are part of ordinary fuzzing reality. That means build/runtime assumptions belong inside the evidence model rather than in shell history. Source: https://rust-fuzz.github.io/book/cargo-fuzz/guide.html
- `honggfuzz` remains a real alternative lane and documents both conditional-compilation support and persistent-fuzzing material. That strengthens the archive’s claim that the missing layer is above engines, not another engine-specific wrapper. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/honggfuzz/latest
- `proptest` already has persisted-failure machinery, with a default file-persistence lane under `std` and no persistence under `no_std`. That is unusually clear evidence that Rust already has durable generative-regression truth that is not reducible to byte corpora. Sources: https://docs.rs/proptest/latest/proptest/test_runner/struct.Config.html ; https://docs.rs/proptest/latest/proptest/test_runner/enum.FileFailurePersistence.html
- `test-fuzz` shows another important bridge: it records target arguments during `cargo test` to generate a fuzzing corpus and then implements a fuzz harness as an additional test. That means Rust’s ordinary testing and fuzzing worlds already overlap in practice. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/test-fuzz/latest
- `LibAFL` is now powerful evidence that Rust fuzzing is widening in backend/runtime scope rather than collapsing to one lane: the project emphasizes structured-input adaptability and scaling across cores/machines, and its recent release moved to Rust 2024 while adding binary-only ASan-in-Rust and improved snapshot/QEMU support. Sources: https://github.com/AFLplusplus/LibAFL ; https://github.com/AFLplusplus/LibAFL/releases
- Archive decision: substantially deepen `gaps/fuzzing-orchestration.md`, `design/fuzzpack-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-fuzzpack-kit.md`; elevate **FuzzPack Kit** in `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` as the most under-modeled execution-evidence lane inside the broader Testing Contract Stack; and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep target profile truth, corpus/crash/regression truth, shrink/minimization truth, execution-envelope truth, and downstream conclusions distinct instead of flattening everything into one fake “we fuzz this crate” story.

## 2026-03-19 — Package Admission Stack refresh (publish-review synthesis above Publish Set + API + inventory + trust + policy)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the next high-leverage move after adding **Publish Set Kit**. The strongest follow-on was not another lower-level leaf, but the higher publish-review boundary that the archive already wanted: **Package Admission Stack** needed to stop treating package selection/payload/receipts as implicit background and instead import them explicitly from Publish Set.
- Cargo’s own docs now make this synthesis more credible than before. `cargo package` documents manifest normalization, packaged `Cargo.lock`, inclusion of `.cargo_vcs_info.json`, and an unstable machine-readable `--message-format json` for `--list`; it also says the VCS snapshot is only best-effort and not verified provenance. That is a direct sign that package payload truth exists, but still needs a higher review layer. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- `cargo publish` documents workspace-aware package selection, `--workspace`, `--exclude`, registry targeting, `--dry-run`, `--no-verify`, and polling for the package to appear in the index. That means package admission is increasingly about explicit publication-path facts rather than just a terminal success line. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-publish.html
- Cargo’s unstable docs already expose `public-dependency` and `sbom`, which means public-contract and inventory-relevant package facts are becoming machine-facing Cargo seams rather than purely third-party conventions. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- The 2025H2 `cargo-semver-checks` goal explicitly targets integration into the `cargo publish` workflow, including an override when maintainers intentionally proceed. That is a strong upstream sign that publish-time review and waivers are part of the likely ecosystem path. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html
- Rust’s 2026 flagships keep Cargo SBOM support active, and crates.io’s January 2026 update added Security-tab advisory views, GitLab Trusted Publishing, Trusted-Publishing-only mode, blocked risky triggers, and `pubtime`. That combination makes package-side review more evidence-rich than before without yet giving the ecosystem one honest admission bundle. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/package-admission-publish-review-evidence-waivers-and-handoffs.md`; refresh `design/package-admission-stack.md`, `design/package-admission-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-package-admission-stack.md` so Publish Set is now an explicit imported layer; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future passes do not collapse publish-set truth, chosen graph, exposure/semver evidence, inventory evidence, trust inputs, policy decisions, and later release/install/support conclusions into one fake “safe publish” story.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another release bot, secure-publish wrapper, registry risk score, or one umbrella release platform. It is a thin `cargo package-admission` / `package-admission-pack/v0` layer that imports `publish-pack/v0`, `api-pack/v0`, inventory evidence, trust signals, and policy decisions to make Rust package publication reviewable.

## 2026-03-19 — Publish Set Kit (source-package publication subject, payload, checks, authority path, and registry receipt truth)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a lower-level release/registry seam that multiple neighboring stacks were already importing informally without yet having its own explicit anchor. The strongest missing seam was **source-package publication truth**: not “how do we automate releases,” but “what exact package or workspace set was actually published, with what payload, under what checks, through which authority path, and with what receipt?”
- Cargo’s own docs now make this seam more real than it used to be. The unstable-features chapter says **multi-package publishing was stabilized in Rust 1.90.0**, which means publication is no longer just a single-package path. `cargo publish` documents workspace-aware package selection, `--workspace`, `--exclude`, registry selection, `--dry-run`, `--no-verify`, upload, and polling for index appearance. `cargo package` documents workspace-aware packaging, registry-aware packaging assumptions for inter-dependent crates, and an unstable machine-readable `--message-format json` for `--list`. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-publish.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- The manifest/workspace layer also now clearly shapes publication rather than merely feeding it. Manifest docs make `include`, `exclude`, and `publish` explicit publication controls, and workspace docs show `workspace.package` can inherit `version`, `publish`, `include`, and `exclude`. That is strong evidence that a publish boundary must preserve both selected-package truth and packaged-payload truth instead of pretending the authored manifest and the published tarball are the same object. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
- Publish-time checking is broadening in exactly the way the archive should care about. The 2025H2 `cargo-semver-checks` goal explicitly says the Cargo team wants SemVer compliance integrated into the `cargo publish` workflow, which means publication is becoming more than packaging-plus-upload and needs a check/waiver layer of its own. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update sharpened the producer-side receipt story: GitLab Trusted Publishing support, Trusted-Publishing-only mode, blocked risky GitHub triggers, and `pubtime` in the index all make authority-path and index-visibility facts more important and more machine-relevant than they were before. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/publish-sets-package-selection-contents-verification-and-registry-receipts.md`, `design/publish-set-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-publish-set-kit.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; tighten nearby boundaries in `design/release-pipeline-kit.md`, `design/release-truth-stack.md`, and `design/publisher-source-identity-stack.md`; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future passes do not collapse selected publish subject, packaged payload truth, check/waiver posture, authority/registry-path posture, upload/index receipts, and downstream release/library/package-admission conclusions into one fake “published successfully” story.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another release bot, registry dashboard, trusted-publishing badge, or version-bump helper. It is a thin `cargo publish-set` / `publish-pack/v0` layer above Cargo packaging and upload, with ranked pilots that start at single-package crates.io publication and only later widen into workspace publish sets, trusted-publishing authority imports, semver-check attachment, and release/package-admission handoffs.

## 2026-03-19 — Discovery Boundary Kit (invocation subject + manifest walk + workspace attachment + config-discovery provenance + consumer import truth)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a lower-level seam that several existing notes kept importing implicitly without giving it its own clear contract. The strongest missing anchor was **discovery truth** itself: the archive repeatedly needed to say what Cargo discovered, from where, and why before repo governance, package selection, build plans, script posture, or workspace environment discussions could stay honest.
- Cargo’s configuration reference says config discovery is hierarchical through the current directory, parent directories, and `$CARGO_HOME`. That means discovery is already a merge-provenance problem rather than only a manifest-path convenience. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html
- Cargo’s workspace and manifest references say Cargo searches parent directories for a `[workspace]` root, allows `package.workspace` to override that search, and makes default package selection depend on whether invocation happened at a member or at the workspace root. That means workspace attachment and package-selection surprises start with discovery posture. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html
- `cargo locate-project` makes the multi-step nature explicit: it searches upward for a `Cargo.toml`, and the workspace root is then found by traversing further upward or by using `package.workspace`. `cargo build` and `cargo metadata` also still default to searching for `Cargo.toml` in the current directory or parent directories, and command-level cwd changes affect config discovery too. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-locate-project.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-build.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html
- Cargo’s 1.94 development-cycle note says broken or nightly-only parent `Cargo.toml` or `.cargo/config.toml` files can break unrelated projects, discusses possible explicit opt-out controls such as `package.workspace = false`, and says cargo-script is starting with workspace auto-discovery disabled. That is a direct upstream sign that discovery is not a solved footnote. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The accepted Cargo plumbing goal begins with **Locate project** and **Read the manifests for a workspace**, while the 1.90 development-cycle report says the `cargo-plumbing` prototype still had to re-read manifests within commands because Cargo’s Rust APIs were not yet exposing enough structure. That combination strongly suggests discovery should become a thinner portable boundary rather than a detail repeatedly reimplemented in later layers. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/discovery-boundaries-manifest-workspace-config-and-explicit-attachment.md`, `design/discovery-boundary-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-discovery-boundary-kit.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md`; and tighten nearby ownership so Discovery Boundary owns invocation/manifests/workspace-attachment/config-discovery/consumer-import truth while Workspace Governance, Repo Composition, Build Interop, ScriptKit, and Workspace Environment import it rather than re-own it.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another workspace manager, config wrapper, repo-root detector, or editor-specific discovery adapter. It is a thin `cargo discoverbound` / `discovery-pack/v0` layer that makes Cargo discovery reviewable before later governance/build/environment conclusions are drawn.

## 2026-03-19 — Starter Pack Kit refresh (the missing contribution is now clearly a contract above real bootstrap diversity, not another generator)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam where the repo already had good conceptual coverage but still needed a sharper practical theory-of-execution. The strongest candidate was **Starter Pack Kit**: the archive already knew recommendation and bootstrapping were separate, but it still needed a clearer answer to the real-world fact that Rust starters are now produced through **multiple non-equivalent renderers and domain bootstrappers**.
- Rust’s December 2025 vision writeup explicitly says users need help navigating crates.io and that they do not have a clear place to get advice on a good “starter set” of crates. That means the archive should not stop at atlas/adoption prose when the next question is “what repo do we actually start from?” Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/19/what-do-people-love-about-rust/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the preferred canonical reference while LLM/editor workflows are rising. That strengthens the case for starter artifacts that are machine-usable without making assistant output the new canon. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Cargo’s own docs keep `cargo new` intentionally simple, while Cargo’s changelog/release notes say `cargo new` / `cargo init` now automatically inherit workspace fields. That means starter repos are increasingly where workspace governance begins, even though Cargo is not trying to become a full starter-repo system. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-new.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html
- `cargo-generate` remains strong proof that template-driven bootstrapping is real, and its docs still direct users toward a GitHub topic for template discovery. At the same time, Tauri’s `create-tauri-app`, Dioxus’s `dx new`, Cargo Lambda’s `cargo lambda new`, and Espressif’s `esp-generate` make the plurality of bootstrap lanes impossible to ignore. That is strong evidence the missing layer is **above** generators, not another generator. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-generate/latest ; https://cargo-generate.github.io/cargo-generate/ ; https://cargo-generate.github.io/cargo-generate/templates/index.html ; https://v2.tauri.app/start/create-project/ ; https://dioxuslabs.com/learn/0.7/tutorial/new_app/ ; https://www.cargo-lambda.info/commands/new.html ; https://docs.espressif.com/projects/rust/book/getting-started/tooling/esp-generate.html
- Rust’s 2026 flagship roadmap explicitly includes public/private dependencies and SBOM support. That makes starter repos more strategic because supply-chain posture is often encoded at repository creation time rather than only later in CI or release automation. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Archive decision: refresh `gaps/starter-repos-template-provenance-and-freshness.md`, `design/starter-pack-kit.md`, `design/starter-pack-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-starter-pack-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so Starter Pack becomes a sharper frontier execution bridge; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future passes keep imported recommendation truth, render-plan/adapter truth, rendered ownership, overlays, freshness, and derived outputs distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another template engine, framework quickstart wrapper, or giant repo generator. It is a thin `cargo starter` / `starter-pack/v0` layer with explicit `starter-render-plan/v0` and `starter-render-report/v0` artifacts above both direct and delegated renderers.

## 2026-03-19 — Artifact Surface Kit promotion (Cargo’s final-output surface is becoming more public, but the reusable contract above it is still missing)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a lower-level anchor already implied by Build Extension, Tooling Contract, Release Truth, Distribution, Inventory, and recent Host Package work. The strongest missing seam was **final Cargo-facing artifact truth**: too many downstream lanes still reconstruct it from target-dir archaeology, JSON streams, or release-tool manifests.
- The March 2026 build-dir-layout-v2 testing call says the build-dir layout is internal-only but many projects still rely on unspecified details because the right Cargo features are missing. Cargo’s own docs now separately model final outputs in `target-dir` and intermediate state in `build-dir`, while the compiler-layout docs treat `artifact-dir` as public API and `build-dir` as internal. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/ ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/cargo/core/compiler/layout/index.html
- Cargo’s unstable `--artifact-dir` docs explicitly say exact final filenames are otherwise awkward and require JSON parsing; Cargo’s external-tools surface still mainly provides stable package metadata plus per-build JSON messages; and Cargo 1.93’s custom-final-artifacts discussion says Cargo-mediated uplift with collision checks is the right direction instead of direct build-script writes. That is strong evidence for a thin final-output contract above today’s ingredients. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- Cargo’s unstable SBOM precursor support now emits precursor files next to executable/linkable outputs, including uplift into target/artifact directories, which makes artifact-linked sidecars a real upstream concept. Meanwhile `cargo-dist` already keeps a machine-readable manifest for release/distribution work, proving downstream demand without replacing Cargo-native artifact truth. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html ; https://docs.rs/cargo-dist-schema/latest/cargo_dist_schema/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-dist/latest
- Archive decision: add `gaps/final-artifact-surface-identity-selection-outputs-and-handoffs.md`, `design/artifact-surface-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-artifact-surface-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Artifact Surface Kit** becomes an explicit frontier seam; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep selected-subject truth, final-artifact truth, sidecar truth, release truth, and installed-state truth distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another target-dir scraper, JSON helper, release wrapper, or installer manifest. It is a thin `cargo artifacts` / `artifact-pack/v0` layer above **Cargo final outputs + bounded uplift imports + explicit downstream handoffs**.

## 2026-03-19 — Host Package Kit (promote foreign-consumer package truth as a reusable anchor above Rust’s Python/Node/mobile/component lanes)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for the strongest missing **proposal-layer anchor** that was already doing real work across multiple stack notes. The best buried winner was **Host Package Kit**: Polyglot Productization, Extension Productization, and browser/package-adjacent Web Productization all depend on foreign-consumer package truth, but the archive still lacked a direct epic for the lower-level anchor itself.
- Rust’s 2026 flagship slate explicitly includes **Wasm Components**, which is a direct signal that packaging/runtime surfaces for code consumed outside ordinary Cargo-only contexts are strategically important. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The Rust/component-model docs now say native `wasm32-wasip2` support is first-class, while the `cargo-component` repository says plain Cargo already covers simple WASI-only lanes but custom-WIT workflows still need `cargo-component` and remain experimental. That is exactly the kind of lane plurality a host-package contract should preserve rather than flatten. Sources: https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org/language-support/rust.html ; https://github.com/bytecodealliance/cargo-component
- maturin is now explicit about the breadth of its host-package lane: it builds and publishes crates with PyO3, cffi, UniFFI bindings, and Rust binaries as Python packages, and its distribution guide makes cross-compilation plus `manylinux` / `musllinux` posture first-class packaging concerns. That is strong evidence that the missing layer is above wheel helpers rather than inside one more wheel helper. Sources: https://github.com/PyO3/maturin ; https://www.maturin.rs/distribution.html
- Node-API’s docs say the API is ABI stable across Node versions and independent from the underlying JavaScript runtime. That is a real host-package guarantee, but it belongs to the Node-API boundary itself rather than every library or runtime assumption surrounding an addon. That is exactly the kind of package/runtime truth the archive should make reviewable. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/n-api.html
- UniFFI’s design-principles and interface docs are explicit that exposed interfaces must be `Send + Sync` and that borrowed-return-style foreign contracts should not leak across the boundary. That is not just FFI trivia; it is foreign-consumer runtime/lifetime truth that belongs in a package artifact. Sources: https://mozilla.github.io/uniffi-rs/latest/internals/design_principles.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/uniffi-rs/0.27/udl/interfaces.html
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the preferred canonical reference while some learning traffic appears to be shifting toward LLM tooling. For host packages, that strengthens rather than weakens the case for small machine-readable package/support artifacts that keep docs, install facts, and runtime constraints aligned. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: refresh `gaps/polyglot-host-packages-runtime-and-support-contracts.md` and `design/host-package-kit.md`; add `proposals/epic-host-package-kit.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so the archive treats **Host Package Kit** as an explicit reusable anchor inside Polyglot, Extension, and package-adjacent Web work; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future passes prefer promoting reusable lower-level anchors before inventing another adjacent stack and keep foreign package truth, imported boundary truth, runtime constraints, install receipts, and downstream conclusions distinct.

## 2026-03-19 — Native Edge Stack (promote the adoption boundary above FFI review, provider locks, and external-build handoff)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a high-leverage move that was already strongly implied by canon but still missing its own clean proposal layer. The strongest buried winner was the **Native Edge Stack**: the archive already had FFI Boundary, Native Dependency, and a ranked pilot program, but it still lacked the thin stack note and explicit epic that would stop future passes from treating native adoption as two adjacent kits plus folklore.
- The accepted Rust goal **Evaluate approaches for seamless interop between C++ and Rust** explicitly frames the problem as enabling Rust adoption in projects that must make serious use of large, rich C++ APIs. That is stronger than “interop is nice to have”; it is a direct adoption signal. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/seamless-rust-cpp.html
- The proposed **C++/Rust Interop Problem Space Mapping** effort sharpens the strategic picture: there are billions of lines of C++ representing enormous value, rewrites are often infeasible, and current external libraries solve the space in different ways that require significant investment from end users. That is exactly the signal the archive should read as “portable boundary above non-equivalent lanes,” not “pick the winner.” Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-project-goals/blob/main/src/2025h2/interop-problem-map.md
- The July 2025 project-goals update says the language team established that Rust should evolve toward a **first-class C++ interop story**, while also noting that any two groups are likely to have different specific needs. That combination matters: first-class importance without false convergence. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/
- Cargo’s roadmap issue to **reduce the need for users to write build scripts** says build scripts hurt build times, raise bug risk, and enlarge dependency-review scope; it also explicitly asks whether the work can help `-sys` crates / FFI. That strengthens the case that native-edge evidence should become a structured companion layer rather than remain build-script folklore. Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/14948
- The sandboxed build-script goal sharpens the same point from the governance side: build scripts are being examined for determinism and least privilege, and native probing is one of the hardest reasons arbitrary build behavior remains. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/sandboxed-build-script.html
- Cargo’s build-script reference shows that `links` is useful but limited: at most one package per `links` value, build-script mediation, and metadata only for immediate dependents. That is enough to prove the native-identity problem is real, but not enough to serve as the portable adoption boundary by itself. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
- The current tool families remain clearly plural. `system-deps` says system-library requirements can be declared in `Cargo.toml` metadata; `pkg-config` shells out to the system utility from build scripts; CXX defines a safe common regime for Rust/C++; and `autocxx` explicitly targets large existing C++ codebases by combining automation with CXX-style safety. Those are good ingredients, but they do not by themselves define one reviewable subject. Sources: https://docs.rs/system-deps/ ; https://docs.rs/pkg-config ; https://cxx.rs/ ; https://google.github.io/autocxx/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says organizations continue to hire Rust developers, suggesting growing structural presence in companies and codebases. That makes mixed-language adoption infrastructure more leveraged than a hobby-only lens would suggest. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/native-edge-adoption-boundaries-provider-locks-and-build-handoffs.md`, `design/native-edge-stack.md`, and `proposals/epic-native-edge-stack.md`; refresh `design/native-edge-pilot-program.md`, `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add a native-edge amnesia resistor so future revisions do not collapse boundary truth, provider/link truth, host/target/toolchain context, external-build handoff, and downstream conclusions into one fake “interop readiness” story.

## 2026-03-19 — Dataflow Surface Kit (portable source/sink, event-time, checkpoint/state, materialization, and progress truth above Rust’s newly-plural streaming/dataflow lanes)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a strategically important seam that was becoming real in practice without yet having one clean portable boundary in canon. The strongest missing seam was **dataflow surface truth**: not just “Rust has some streaming tools,” but “Rust now has enough serious and non-equivalent streaming/dataflow lanes that the missing contribution is the contract layer above them.”
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online documentation remains the canonical reference surface. For dataflow systems, that makes machine-readable review bundles more valuable, not less, because the facts that matter are scattered across SQL, connectors, checkpoint metadata, catalogs, dashboards, and release notes.
  https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- DataFusion now explicitly says it aims to be the query engine of choice for databases, dataframe libraries, machine learning, and **streaming applications**, and its 51.0.0 release notes underline the project’s active evolution. That is enough to treat it as a real substrate for Rust-side streaming/dataflow work rather than a batch-only side ingredient.
  https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/introduction.html
  https://datafusion.apache.org/blog/2025/11/25/datafusion-51.0.0/
- Arroyo makes the streaming-SQL/runtime lane concrete in exactly the way the archive should care about: it is a distributed stream-processing engine written in Rust; its docs make event time, watermarks, windows, stateful processing, and remote checkpointing first-class; its SQL layer is built on DataFusion; and its documented releases surface exactly-once source/sink lanes.
  https://www.arroyo.dev/
  https://doc.arroyo.dev/concepts/
  https://doc.arroyo.dev/releases/v0.5.0/
- Fluvio + Stateful Dataflows make a different but equally important lane concrete: Fluvio documents itself as a programmable streaming platform written in Rust, while SDF documents Rust+WebAssembly dataflows with watermarks, grace periods, idleness, and stateful window processing; SmartModules and connector docs make transform and connector deployment first-class shareable artifacts.
  https://docs.rs/fluvio/latest/fluvio/
  https://www.fluvio.io/sdf/
  https://www.fluvio.io/sdf/concepts/window-processing/
  https://www.fluvio.io/docs/smartmodules/overview/
  https://www.fluvio.io/docs/0.17.2/connectors/developers/overview/
  https://fluvio.io/docs/0.14.1/hub/use-the-hub/
- Timely Dataflow remains the strongest “custom dataflow computation” signal because it explicitly treats distributed streaming computation, probes/progress, and capture/replay as first-class. That matters because it prevents the archive from secretly reducing “dataflow” to “streaming SQL metadata.”
  https://timelydataflow.github.io/timely-dataflow/
  https://timelydataflow.github.io/timely-dataflow/chapter_3/chapter_3_2.html
  https://timelydataflow.github.io/timely-dataflow/chapter_4/chapter_4_4.html

## 2026-03-19 — Workflow Productization Stack (durable work needs one boring boundary above runtime, history, and release truth)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a move that would add a real synthesis rather than another adjacent kit. **Workflow Productization Stack** won because the archive already had a strong Background Work Kit, but the ecosystem now clearly spans several non-equivalent workflow lanes and still lacks the higher product boundary above them.
- The 2024 State of Rust survey still says Rust is especially popular for server backends, web/networking services, and cloud technologies. That matters here because background jobs, schedules, and durable workflows in those domains often become user-visible or support-visible product behavior, not merely internal plumbing. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/13/2024-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still says online docs remain the canonical reference surface. That raises the value of machine-readable workflow-product artifacts over README prose and dashboard archaeology. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- `apalis` now makes the lower lane concrete: distributed backends, concurrency/parallelism, worker monitoring, graceful shutdown, persisted cron jobs, and an optional Web UI are all first-class documented features. That is strong evidence that Rust already has real workflow-product ingredients rather than only toy queues. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/apalis/latest
- `apalis-workflow` sharpened the “why now” case: it explicitly documents durable and resumable workflows, distributed execution, sequential and DAG workflow forms, and backend support on top of the broader apalis worker substrate. Source: https://docs.rs/apalis-workflow/latest/apalis_workflow/
- `fang` and `sqlxmq` made the non-equivalence even clearer. `fang` documents scheduled tasks, periodic/CRON tasks, unique tasks, and retries with custom backoff; `sqlxmq` documents transactional send/completion/checkpointing, future scheduling, reliable delivery, and consistent database-plus-job backup/restore semantics. These are not just different APIs; they are different product postures. Sources: https://docs.rs/fang/ ; https://docs.rs/sqlxmq/latest/sqlxmq/
- The Restate Rust SDK made the higher stack boundary unavoidable. Its docs expose durable handlers, Services/Virtual Objects/Workflows, durable timers, durable promises, and journal-backed retries that eliminate manual retry logic. The Restate architecture docs then make the mechanics explicit: invocations, steps, state updates, timers, and promises all commit log-first; retries resume from journal state; duplicate client calls with the same idempotency key resolve to the same invocation. Sources: https://docs.rs/restate-sdk/latest/restate_sdk/ ; https://docs.rs/restate-sdk/latest/restate_sdk/context/trait.ContextTimers.html ; https://docs.rs/restate-sdk/latest/restate_sdk/context/trait.ContextClient.html ; https://docs.restate.dev/references/architecture
- Temporal provided the outside-in forcing function. Temporal’s own writing says workflow/activity workers are long-lived and must be extremely reliable, and its glossary says the Rust Core SDK centralizes complex concurrency-management and state-machine logic for several language SDKs. That is direct evidence that workflow products need better review boundaries than ordinary job helpers. Sources: https://temporal.io/blog/why-rust-powers-core-sdk ; https://docs.temporal.io/glossary
- External prior art also helped discipline the move. DBOS now openly productizes exactly-once event processing, scheduled jobs, reliable queues, durable workflows, and built-in observability. Even without a Rust SDK today, it sharpened the conclusion that “workflow productization” is a real category the Rust archive should model honestly rather than burying inside generic service or event work. Source: https://docs.dbos.dev/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/workflow-products-jobs-schedules-journals-and-support-contracts.md`, `design/workflow-productization-stack.md`, `design/workflow-productization-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-workflow-productization-stack.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Workflow Productization Stack** becomes an explicit frontier seam; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions do not flatten declared work truth, runtime activation, history/recovery evidence, release lineage, and downstream support/release/incident conclusions into one fake “workflow reliability” story.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another queue crate, scheduler helper, workflow UI, hosted orchestration platform, or universal workflow DSL. It is a thin `cargo workflow-product` / `workflow-product-pack/v0` layer above **Background Work + Runtime Settings + Observability + Release Truth + Support Envelope**, with Service / Agent / Event / Identity as importing consumers.

## 2026-03-19 — Operator productization stack (CRDs, RBAC, webhook/admin surfaces, install/update truth, and runtime evidence need one boring boundary)
- Kubernetes still defines operators as software extensions built around custom resources and control loops. That matters because Rust’s operator story is no longer hypothetical; it is playing against a stable upstream product model rather than inventing one from scratch. Source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/operator/
- `kube` now explicitly packages a Rust Kubernetes client, controller runtime, custom-resource derive, and related tooling. The kube-rs controller docs also now span admission, testing, observability, security, scaling, and availability, which is strong evidence that Rust has a real operator lane rather than only an API client story. Sources: https://docs.rs/kube/latest/kube/ ; https://kube.rs/controllers/admission/ ; https://kube.rs/controllers/testing/ ; https://kube.rs/controllers/observability/ ; https://kube.rs/controllers/security/ ; https://kube.rs/controllers/availability/
- The kube-rs testing docs are especially clarifying: they are honest that there is no `envtest` equivalent in Rust so far, and show that full integration/e2e testing requires real cluster machinery or substantial API-server mocking. That sharpens the missing contribution: Rust needs more portable operator-product evidence, not just more hidden cluster folklore. Source: https://kube.rs/controllers/testing/
- `kube-derive` and `KubeSchema` now make typed CRDs and CEL-validation-aware schema generation part of the Rust lane instead of pure YAML drift. This raises the value of an explicit boundary that keeps schema/validation truth separate from runtime/install/support truth. Sources: https://docs.rs/kube-derive/latest/kube_derive/derive.CustomResource.html ; https://docs.rs/kube/latest/kube/derive.KubeSchema.html
- Stackable’s current operator docs show what a real product family has to publish: supported product versions, monitoring posture, shared CRDs, secret/certificate operators, listener operators, and release notes. That is powerful evidence that operator productization is already happening in practice, but still without a portable ecosystem-level contract. Sources: https://docs.stackable.tech/home/stable/operators/ ; https://github.com/stackabletech/operator-rs
- The comparison with Go sharpened the seam further. `controller-runtime` explicitly treats managers, controllers, reconcilers, clients/caches, schemes, webhooks, logging/metrics, and testing (`envtest`) as one coherent mainstream lane. Rust has serious ingredients, but not yet the shared product boundary above them. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime
- Archive decision: add `gaps/operator-products-crds-rbac-webhooks-status-and-support-contracts.md`, `design/operator-productization-stack.md`, `design/operator-productization-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-operator-productization-stack.md`; refresh `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so the archive now treats **Operator Productization Stack** as a real frontier band above Schema Contract + Runtime Capability + Service Surface + Observability + Distribution Contract + Support Envelope.

## 2026-03-19 — Geospatial Productization Stack (promote the product boundary above Rust’s now-plural geospatial ecosystem)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a move that would add a genuinely new domain seam rather than another Cargo-adjacent refinement. **Geospatial Productization Stack** won because the archive already had a strong Geospatial Surface Kit, and current geospatial ecosystem signals now say the missing problem is the product boundary above spatial semantics rather than another geometry crate, format wrapper, or renderer.
- GeoRust is explicitly an ecosystem of geospatial tools and libraries written in Rust, which is a strong signal that the archive should treat geospatial work as a real frontier band rather than a niche side alley. Source: https://georust.org/
- GeoArrow and GeoParquet together sharpen the “why now” case. GeoArrow explicitly defines a geospatial Arrow-compatible format/specification and Rust implementation, while GeoParquet is now an incubating OGC standard with a current v1.1.0 release. That means cloud-native columnar geospatial publication is no longer just project-local convention. Sources: https://geoarrow.org/ ; https://docs.rs/geoarrow/ ; https://geoparquet.org/ ; https://geoparquet.org/releases/v1.1.0/
- STAC and PMTiles make the product-boundary argument even stronger because they pull publication and discovery out of pure library space. STAC is now an OGC Community Standard and Rust has live `stac`, `stac-client`, and rustac lanes, while PMTiles is an explicit single-file tile/archive publication format with live Rust crates. Those are exactly the kinds of signals that say Rust geospatial products now span catalog/discovery and tiled distribution rather than only geometry processing. Sources: https://docs.ogc.org/cs/25-004/25-004.html ; https://docs.rs/stac/ ; https://docs.rs/stac-client/ ; https://stac-utils.github.io/rustac/ ; https://docs.protomaps.com/pmtiles/ ; https://crates.io/crates/pmtiles
- The client/runtime side is now real as well. `maplibre-rs` explicitly documents a portable WebGPU-based map renderer for web/mobile/desktop, while GeoPolars explicitly says it uses GeoArrow as its core memory model and is still a prototype. That is exactly the maturity pattern the archive should care about: real lanes, but uneven readiness and no honest shared product boundary yet. Sources: https://docs.rs/maplibre/ ; https://maplibre.org/maplibre-rs/docs/book/introduction.html ; https://geopolars.org/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/geospatial-products-datasets-catalogs-tiles-and-support-contracts.md`, `design/geospatial-productization-stack.md`, `design/geospatial-productization-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-geospatial-productization-stack.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Geospatial Productization Stack** becomes an explicit frontier seam; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions do not flatten spatial semantics, dataset/catalog/archive publication, runtime activation, importing client/search/service lanes, and downstream support/release conclusions into one fake “geospatial support” story.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another GIS engine, map renderer, STAC server, or dataframe wrapper. It is a thin `cargo geo-product` / `geo-product-pack/v0` layer above **Geospatial Surface + Dataset Surface + Runtime Settings + Support Envelope**, with Client/Interactive/Search/Protocol/Service lanes importing it.

## 2026-03-18 — Firmware productization promotion (embedded Rust now has enough real runtime/tooling plurality to justify an explicit product boundary)
- `embedded-hal` 1.0 plus its companion crates make the layer boundary clearer, not blurrier: platform-agnostic traits remain central, but async and nb execution-model companions confirm that the HAL layer is not the whole firmware product contract. Sources: https://docs.rs/embedded-hal/ ; https://blog.rust-embedded.org/embedded-hal-v1/
- Runtime plurality is now too concrete to hand-wave away. Embassy explicitly presents async and energy-efficient embedded execution as a first-class path, RTIC presents a hardware-accelerated real-time concurrency model, and Hubris presents a memory-isolated operating environment with restartable tasks and offline dumps. That is exactly the pattern where the next worthy contribution is a portable boundary above runtimes rather than a winner-take-all framework pitch. Sources: https://embassy.dev/book/ ; https://github.com/rtic-rs/rtic ; https://hubris.oxide.computer/
- The host↔device tooling substrate is real but still uneven. `probe-rs run` says it should be the preferred path where applicable and can flash/start/log through RTT and `defmt`; the probe-rs VS Code debugger is still documented as pre-production/Alpha; and the `probe-run` deprecation note still calls out the lack of a replacement for the older `--json` structured-log output. That is strong evidence for a durable evidence/report layer above tools rather than more tool-specific glue. Sources: https://probe.rs/docs/tools/probe-rs/ ; https://probe.rs/docs/tools/debugger/ ; https://ferrous-systems.com/blog/probe-run-deprecation/
- Vendor-backed maturity is now clearer too. Espressif’s `esp-hal` 1.0 announcement calls it the first vendor-backed Rust SDK, exposes both async and blocking modes, ships `esp-generate`, and points users to a curated book; the ESP logging docs explicitly recommend pairing `defmt` with `probe-rs` for best results. Sources: https://developer.espressif.com/blog/2025/10/esp-hal-1/ ; https://docs.espressif.com/projects/rust/book/application-development/logging.html
- The active `build-std` goal and the Embedonomicon’s SoC-support guide still underline that target/sysroot/linker/docs/flash-algorithm truth is part of the embedded reality. That keeps the proposal honest: the missing layer is not a framework replacement, but a product boundary that imports build and target truth instead of hiding it. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/build-std.html ; https://docs.rust-embedded.org/embedonomicon/soc-support.html
- Archive decision: add [`proposals/epic-firmware-productization-stack.md`](./proposals/epic-firmware-productization-stack.md), refresh the firmware stack and pilot docs, refresh [`INDEX.md`](./INDEX.md), [`PRIORITIES.md`](./PRIORITIES.md), and [`STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`](./STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md) so **Firmware Productization Stack** now has an explicit proposal layer, and strengthen repo/archival resistors so future revisions keep board/run truth, target activation, footprint truth, runtime-evidence channels, and shipped/support conclusions distinct.

## 2026-03-18 — Data Productization Stack proposal layer (query truth, schema boundaries, migration choreography, runtime activation, and supportable stateful data products)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for frontier seams that already had a stack note and a ranked pilot but still lacked the explicit proposal-layer file. **Data Productization Stack** was the strongest fit: it is already ranked in the frontier, already has a clean ownership model, and was one of the last high-leverage stack notes still missing its direct epic anchor.
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still says online documentation is the preferred canonical reference while resource usage and debugging remain major productivity problems. That increases the value of machine-usable, reviewable data-plane artifacts over README folklore and operator memory. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- SQLx makes the query/docs boundary concrete rather than hypothetical. SQLx documents compile-time checked queries without a DSL, and its FAQ says docs.rs cannot access your database, so projects using query macros need a prepared `.sqlx` directory and `SQLX_OFFLINE=true` during docs.rs builds. That is exactly the kind of evidence lane a stack-level product boundary should preserve rather than hide. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/sqlx/latest/source/FAQ.md ; https://github.com/launchbadge/sqlx/blob/main/FAQ.md
- Diesel, SeaORM, and refinery show that Rust data truth is already plural rather than converged. Diesel’s `print-schema` connects to the database, queries tables/columns, and generates Rust `table!` invocations; SeaORM’s current migration docs support migrations plus an entity-first workflow; and refinery explicitly supports embedded or CLI-driven SQL migrations across multiple databases. Those are non-equivalent but legitimate lanes. Sources: https://diesel.rs/guides/schema-in-depth/ ; https://www.sea-ql.org/SeaORM/docs/migration/setting-up-migration/ ; https://docs.rs/refinery/
- Testcontainers for Rust strengthens the test-environment side of the stack because it explicitly targets integration/smoke tests, container-based dependency lifecycles, and readiness/wait strategies. That makes ephemeral database evidence a first-class review lane rather than a local-dev afterthought. Sources: https://rust.testcontainers.org/ ; https://rust.testcontainers.org/quickstart/testcontainers/ ; https://rust.testcontainers.org/features/wait_strategies/
- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-data-productization-stack.md`; refresh `design/data-productization-stack.md` and `design/data-productization-pilot-program.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Data Productization Stack** becomes an explicit proposal-layer candidate; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep checked-query truth, live database truth, public schema truth, migration choreography, runtime activation, and downstream conclusions distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another ORM winner, query DSL, migration generator, or hosted control plane. It is a thin `cargo data-product` / `data-product-pack/v0` layer above **Database Contract + Schema Contract + Migration Truth + Runtime Settings + Support Envelope**.

## 2026-03-18 — Local-First Productization Stack proposal layer (product-boundary truth above replica engines, sync/plumbing, client shells, runtime activation, and recovery)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that was already strategically strong, already had a gap + stack design + pilot program, but still lacked its explicit proposal-layer anchor. **Local-First Productization Stack** was the clearest fit: the archive already had a real frontier case, but without the epic layer it was still too easy for future passes to keep adding adjacent CRDT or app-shell leaves instead of promoting the shared product boundary.
- The local-first essay still gives the clearest product standard: software should work offline, sync across devices, and improve ownership, privacy, longevity, and user control. That makes the real bar product behavior rather than merely “uses CRDTs somewhere.” Source: https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/
- Automerge’s current docs are unusually explicit about the seam. The “hello” page frames Automerge as a library for building collaborative local-first apps; the concepts/tutorial docs split apps into documents and repositories; the repository docs say the CRDT + sync protocol still leave a lot of plumbing to do in an application; and the storage docs say a repo without a `StorageAdapter` is transient across restart. That is strong evidence that Rust’s missing problem is no longer raw mergeable data structures but the product boundary above storage/network/runtime choices. Sources: https://automerge.org/docs/hello/ ; https://automerge.org/docs/tutorial/concepts/ ; https://automerge.org/docs/reference/repositories/ ; https://automerge.org/docs/reference/repositories/storage/
- The Rust-side lanes are also clearly plural rather than converged. `automerge_repo` exposes repo handles, peer-doc state, and background orchestration; Yrs is a high-performance Rust port of Yjs while its `Awareness` docs explicitly define awareness as non-persistent state like cursors and status; Loro’s docs say the project wants better DevTools for local-first apps, Loro 1.0 says its storage format is stable, the new Loro Protocol ships matching Rust client/server implementations, and Loro Mirror exists because CRDT↔UI glue is repetitive and easy to get wrong. Sources: https://docs.rs/automerge_repo ; https://docs.rs/yrs/latest/yrs/ ; https://docs.rs/yrs/latest/yrs/sync/awareness/struct.Awareness.html ; https://loro.dev/docs ; https://loro.dev/blog/v1.0 ; https://loro.dev/blog/loro-protocol ; https://loro.dev/blog/loro-mirror
- The typed mapping and app-shell layers sharpen the same point from above. `autosurgeon` gives Automerge a serde-like Rust mapping story; `lorosurgeon` does the same for Loro; and Tauri 2 positions Rust-backed apps as cross-platform across desktop and mobile from one codebase. That makes it even less plausible that one engine or one app shell should define the whole support story. Sources: https://docs.rs/autosurgeon ; https://docs.rs/lorosurgeon ; https://v2.tauri.app/
- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-local-first-productization-stack.md`, refresh `design/local-first-productization-stack.md` and `design/local-first-productization-pilot-program.md`, update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Local-First Productization Stack** becomes an explicit proposal-layer candidate, and tighten `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep durable replica truth, ephemeral awareness/presence truth, client/relay/runtime-role truth, recovery/export posture, and downstream conclusions distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another CRDT engine, relay backend, full-stack sync framework, or Tauri-plus-sync starter. It is a thin `cargo local-product` / `local-first-product-pack/v0` layer above **Replica Surface + Client App Surface + Event/Service Surface + Runtime Settings + Identity Surface + Support Envelope**.
