## 2026-03-18 — Scientific Productization Stack proposal layer (array/storage truth, backend/device activation, model/runtime attachments, and support above Rust scientific ecosystems)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that already had strong strategic weight, a stack note, and a pilot program but still lacked its direct proposal-layer anchor. **Scientific Productization Stack** was the clearest fit: the archive already had the component kits and the ranked rollout, but it still lacked the explicit epic that would turn it from “important frontier” into “concrete contribution candidate.”
- Rust’s current offload work now makes this seam more timely, not less. The 2025H1 GPU-offload goal explicitly frames the intended direction as combining batching, autodiff, and offloading, with the hope of state-of-the-art libraries like `faer` and more non-Rust libraries using Rust as their backend. The December 2025 goals update then says work was spent enabling offload in CI to enable `std::offload` on nightly. That is exactly the kind of signal that says backend/device truth is becoming product-surface reality rather than remaining benchmark-side lore. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/GPU-Offload.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/05/project-goals-2025-december-update/
- The ecosystem evidence is now clearly plural rather than hypothetical. `faer` explicitly focuses on high-performance linear algebra; `zarrs` explicitly focuses on multidimensional-array storage and metadata; Apache Arrow is a native Rust cross-language in-memory data platform; Polars explicitly builds a Rust dataframe lane on Arrow’s memory model; and `object_store` explicitly says the same binary can run across multiple clouds and local test environments via runtime configuration changes. That combination is a strong sign that the missing contribution is above the ingredients rather than another ingredient. Sources: https://docs.rs/faer/latest/faer/ ; https://docs.rs/zarrs/latest/zarrs/ ; https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/ ; https://docs.pola.rs/api/rust/dev/polars/ ; https://docs.rs/object_store/latest/object_store/
- The model/runtime side is equally non-converged. Burn presents itself as a comprehensive dynamic deep-learning framework with flexibility, compute efficiency, and portability goals; Candle presents itself as a minimalist ML framework focused on performance and GPU support; `ort` is a Rust binding for ONNX Runtime; and `tract` is intentionally tiny, self-contained, and portable for TensorFlow/ONNX inference. That is the pattern the archive should read as “needs a productization layer above the runtimes,” not “pick the winner.” Sources: https://docs.rs/burn/latest/burn/ ; https://github.com/huggingface/candle ; https://docs.rs/ort/latest/ort/ ; https://docs.rs/tract-core/latest/tract_core/
- Interchange prior art makes the case stronger because it shows what coordination looks like without convergence theater. `dlpackrs` frames DLPack as the standard in-memory, mostly hardware-agnostic tensor format recognized by major deep-learning and array-processing frameworks, while the 2024 Array API release explicitly frames interoperability and consistent semantics as the point. Rust should learn from that rather than trying to skip straight to a giant “one scientific framework” answer. Sources: https://docs.rs/dlpackrs/latest/dlpackrs/ ; https://data-apis.org/blog/array_api_v2024_release/
- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-scientific-productization-stack.md`; refresh `design/scientific-productization-stack.md` and `design/scientific-productization-pilot-program.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Scientific Productization Stack** becomes an explicit proposal-layer candidate; strengthen `AGENTS.md` so future passes prefer promoting already-designed stacks before inventing adjacent kits; and strengthen `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future scientific-productization revisions keep imported interchange prior art, activation truth, and downstream conclusions distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** a Rust NumPy clone, one universal array trait, one magical GPU stack, or a model-runtime winner pitch. It is a thin `cargo science-product` / `scientific-product-pack/v0` layer above **Tensor Surface + Dataset Surface + Offload Surface + Model Surface + Runtime Settings + Support Envelope**.

## 2026-03-18 — Borrowing Frontier Stack proposal layer (trait truth, pointer truth, lending truth, init/teardown truth, and migration horizon above the moving language frontier)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that already had strategic weight, gap coverage, and a ranked pilot but still lacked its direct proposal-layer anchor. **Borrowing Frontier Stack** was the clearest fit: the archive already had the stack note, the pilot, and the four lower-level kit families, but it still lacked the explicit epic that would turn it from “important frontier” into “concrete contribution candidate.”
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes explicitly keep **Beyond the `&`** and **Unblocking dormant traits** active, with milestones around field projections, reborrow traits, in-place initialization, the next-generation trait solver, and the Sized hierarchy. That is strong evidence that pointer/reference semantics, lending patterns, trait-family evolution, and construction/destruction posture are still a live ecosystem frontier rather than archive archaeology. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H2 reborrow-traits goal sharpens the point: user-space types still cannot get true autoreborrowing today; the project wants to remove `Pin` special-casing, enable Rust-for-Linux custom reborrowable reference types, and explicitly names users of the `reborrow` crate as a migration population. That is exactly the kind of “language motion plus workaround ecology” situation where the archive should add a comparison/migration layer instead of another pseudo-final crate pitch. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/autoreborrow-traits.html ; https://docs.rs/reborrow/latest/reborrow/
- The 2025H2 field-projections and in-place-initialization goals make the stack boundary even more justified. Field projections explicitly frames smart pointers, modified references, and custom pointer types as design pressure. In-place initialization explicitly says the ecosystem already has multiple approaches that the language wants to evaluate and learn from rather than leaving the space permanently fragmented. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/field-projections.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/in-place-initialization.html
- The current crate ecosystem is now mature enough that the archive should treat it as durable evidence rather than temporary noise. `lending-iterator` explicitly presents fully generic lending iterators in stable Rust; `dynosaur` explicitly targets dynamic dispatch for traits using `async fn` and `-> impl Trait`; `pin-project` focuses on safe pin projection; `pinned-init`, `pin-init`, and `moveit` each cover real in-place-init / pinned-construction territory; and `ouroboros` plus `self_cell` keep self-referential setup alive in different ways. That is exactly the pattern where the worthy contribution is a portable review/migration layer above the crates rather than a winner-take-all crate. Sources: https://docs.rs/lending-iterator/latest/lending_iterator/ ; https://docs.rs/dynosaur ; https://docs.rs/pin-project ; https://docs.rs/pinned-init ; https://docs.rs/pin-init ; https://docs.rs/moveit/latest/moveit/ ; https://docs.rs/ouroboros ; https://docs.rs/self_cell
- RFC 3519 and RFC 3621 keep the pointer/receiver side concrete: custom receiver types are part of the language-adjacent plan, and derive-smart-pointer is explicitly about getting custom smart pointers to participate in trait objects and receiver positions without pretending the whole underlying trait machinery is ready for broad stable exposure. RFC 2996 keeps the lending/async side concrete: `AsyncIterator` is real, but the ergonomic/object-safe story remains incomplete. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3519-arbitrary-self-types-v2.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3621-derive-smart-pointer.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2996-async-iterator.html
- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-borrowing-frontier-stack.md`; refresh `design/borrowing-frontier-stack.md` and `design/borrowing-frontier-pilot-program.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Borrowing Frontier Stack** becomes an explicit proposal-layer candidate; and strengthen `AGENTS.md` plus `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions do not flatten roadmap motion, userland workaround crates, stable-vs-nightly posture, migration horizon, and downstream conclusions into one fake “borrowing ergonomics solved” story.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** a universal smart-pointer trait, one true lending iterator or stream facade, or a constructor macro empire. It is a thin `cargo borrowfront` / `borrowing-frontier-pack/v0` layer above **Trait Surface + Pointer Surface + Lending Surface + Initialization Surface**.

## 2026-03-18 — Extension Productization Stack proposal layer (host/plugin surface truth, runtime-kind and capability truth, package/install/update truth, and support above Rust extension ecosystems)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that already had real strategic weight but still lacked its direct proposal-layer anchor. **Extension Productization Stack** was the clearest fit: the archive already had a strong gap note, stack design, and ranked pilot program, but it still lacked the explicit epic that would turn it from “important frontier” into “concrete contribution candidate.”
- Rust’s 2026 flagship slate explicitly includes **Wasm Components**, which keeps typed extension/runtime lanes inside the language/toolchain frontier rather than leaving them as niche host-specific experiments. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The current component-model guidance makes the transition boundary sharper, not fuzzier. The Rust/component-model docs now say native `wasm32-wasip2` support is first-class and older `cargo-component`-centric workflows are being deprecated for the simple path, while the `cargo-component` repository itself explicitly says plain `cargo` + `wasm32-wasip2` already works for WASI-only lanes but custom-WIT lanes still need `cargo-component`. That is exactly the kind of runtime-lane plurality the archive should preserve instead of flattening into “Wasm extension support.” Sources: https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org/language-support/rust.html ; https://github.com/bytecodealliance/cargo-component
- The host ecosystems are now clearly serious and clearly non-equivalent. Zed extensions are Git repositories with `extension.toml`, can provide languages/debuggers/themes/snippets/slash commands/MCP servers, and run under an explicit user-restrictable capability system. Nushell plugins are separately installed executables speaking a versioned `nu-plugin` protocol, and the docs explicitly warn that host updates require plugin updates. Tauri plugins are package families made of a Cargo crate plus optional NPM / Android / iOS packages, and its plugin-permission docs explicitly say potentially dangerous commands/scopes are blocked by default until enabled in capabilities configuration. Extism treats the plugin system itself as a host-defined interface, gives plug-ins a manifest carrying runtime constraints, and exposes host functions/runtime embedding as first-class concepts. Sources: https://zed.dev/docs/extensions/developing-extensions ; https://zed.dev/docs/extensions/capabilities ; https://www.nushell.sh/book/plugins.html ; https://v2.tauri.app/develop/plugins/ ; https://v2.tauri.app/plugin/os-info/ ; https://extism.org/docs/concepts/manifest/ ; https://extism.org/docs/concepts/runtime-apis/ ; https://extism.org/docs/concepts/host-functions/

The 2025H2 interop problem-space goal says the near term is not rewriting a significant fraction of active C++, but cooperating across language communities on the real issues mixed-language systems hit. The Rust safety-critical writeup then sharpens the practical pressure: many teams will integrate Rust into existing C and C++ systems and carry that boundary for years, and guidance/tooling to keep interfaces correct, auditable, and in sync would help. Sources: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-project-goals/blob/main/src/2025h2/interop-problem-map.md ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/

PyO3 now directly recommends `maturin`, and maturin’s distribution docs make wheel portability, manylinux/musllinux compliance, platform tags, and even optional separate debug-info files part of what gets shipped. Node-API’s docs say the ABI stability promise belongs to the Node-API boundary itself. UniFFI explicitly targets Kotlin and Swift in its getting-started path, and its design principles require exposed objects to be `Sync` and `Send` and reject returning borrowed data across the foreign boundary. Sources: https://pyo3.rs/main/getting-started ; https://www.maturin.rs/distribution.html ; https://nodejs.org/api/n-api.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/uniffi-rs/latest/Getting_started.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/uniffi-rs/latest/internals/design_principles.html

The WebAssembly Component Model says components can work together regardless of source language using portable binaries plus WIT and a standardized ABI, while also making clear that publishing/distribution are handled by registries and tools outside the core model. ## 2026-03-18 — Reflection Transition Stack proposal layer (lane comparison and migration above proc-macro burden, runtime reflection, inspect-only lanes, and future core reflection)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that had already earned strategic attention but was still missing its direct proposal-layer anchor. **Reflection Transition Stack** was the clearest fit: the archive already had a strong stack design and ranked pilot program, but it still lacked the explicit epic that would turn it from “important frontier” into “concrete contribution candidate.”
- Rust's 2026 flagship goals explicitly include **prototype reflection**, which makes reflection a live language-adjacent frontier rather than a niche crate-level curiosity. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The reflection-and-comptime goal is unusually direct about the transition problem. It proposes compile-time reflection, says proc-macro derives have historically been hard to debug and bootstrap from scratch, and explicitly says crates like `bevy_reflect` and `facet` would still exist afterwards with different goals and methods. That is strong evidence that the missing contribution is not another reflection crate, but the migration/comparison boundary above multiple lanes. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html
- The macro-improvements goal sharpens the same seam from another direction: reducing proc-macro demand is explicitly valuable for build speed, simplicity, and dependency-chain reduction. The 2025 compiler-performance survey then says stabilizing language features could remove some proc macros or build scripts. Together, those signals make current macro burden part of the reflection story rather than a side note. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/macro-improvements.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- The ecosystem evidence is now strong enough that “reflection” plainly means several different things. `bevy_reflect` presents itself as a general-purpose runtime reflection system with dynamic interaction and type metadata; `facet` exposes a `SHAPE` associated const with layout/field/attribute information; `valuable` explicitly scopes itself to object-safe value inspection and `tracing`'s support for it remains opt-in and experimental; and `serde_reflection` explicitly traces serialization structure into format descriptions rather than claiming universal type reflection. Those are serious lanes, but not interchangeable ones. Sources: https://docs.rs/bevy_reflect/latest/bevy_reflect/ ; https://docs.rs/facet/latest/facet/ ; https://docs.rs/valuable/latest/valuable/ ; https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/field/index.html ; https://docs.rs/serde-reflection/latest/serde_reflection/

## 2026-03-18 — Dependency Review Stack (dependency intake and upgrade review above advisories, effect audit, capability analysis, and artifact linkage)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that would add a real new review boundary rather than another adjacent leaf tool. The archive already had strong **Trust Decision**, **Dependency Control**, **Runtime Capability**, and **SBOM / inventory** work, but it still lacked the composition layer for the moment teams actually feel: should we add, upgrade, or ship this dependency set?
- The crates.io January 2026 development update makes the timing unusually good. crates.io now has a Security tab for RustSec advisories, expanded Trusted Publishing support including GitLab CI/CD and Trusted Publishing-only mode, blocked risky GitHub Actions triggers, and a new `pubtime` field in index entries. That means the ecosystem is finally emitting better intake-time trust and freshness facts, but not yet one review boundary above them. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- The February 2026 malicious-crate policy update says routine malware removals will always get a RustSec advisory rather than a blog post. That is a subtle but important shift: the durable signal is moving toward advisories and away from ambient announcement noise, which raises the value of local diffable dependency-review artifacts. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/13/crates.io-malicious-crate-update/
- Cargo Vet remains the strongest practical review-import signal. Its docs say the tool is designed to minimize friction, share audit work, import external audit sets, and choose the smallest review path when possible; the performing-audits docs also make explicit that `cargo vet suggest` is attack-surface-reduction-oriented rather than merely a bookkeeping aid. That supports a stack that imports vetting rather than trying to replace it. Sources: https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/how-it-works.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/performing-audits.html
- The 2026 Cargo Scan paper is the clearest new forcing function. It says 69.2% of flagged effects can be judged locally, median auditing burden can fall to 0.2% of lines of code relative to whole-crate review, 3.5K of the top 10K crates can be automatically classified as safe, and most effects are concentrated in roughly 3% of crates. That is unusually strong evidence that Rust dependency review should now import **dangerous-code review** explicitly instead of staying at the advisory/publisher layer. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06466v1
- Runtime authority review is also no longer hypothetical. The Rust Foundation security update says crate-scanning pilots are underway and a Rust-focused Capslock implementation exists; `cargo-capslock` already exists; and FOSDEM 2026 material explicitly frames Rust capability analysis as a path to generated seccomp profiles that prevent updates from silently opening new attack vectors. That makes capability posture a real import lane for dependency review rather than a speculative tangent. Sources: https://rustfoundation.org/media/strengthening-rust-security-with-alpha-omega-a-progress-update/ ; https://github.com/ksuzuki/cargo-capslock ; https://fosdem.org/2026/schedule/event/QGCFDA-using_capslock_analysis_to_develop_seccomp_filters_for_rust_and_other_services/
- `cargo-auditable` closes the loop on artifact linkage: it embeds dependency-tree JSON into compiled executables and says the end goal is Cargo-native binary embedding. That means the missing boundary is now the stack that keeps package review, capability review, and built-artifact linkage separate but connected. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-auditable/latest
- Archive decision: add `gaps/dependency-review-effect-capability-and-intake-truth.md`, add `design/dependency-review-stack.md`, add `design/dependency-review-pilot-program.md`, add `proposals/epic-dependency-review-stack.md`, refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep subject identity, imported trust/effect/capability/artifact evidence, and consumer verdicts distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another registry score, malware dashboard, universal allowlist, or `cargo vet` successor. It is a thin `cargo dep-review` / `dependency-review-pack/v0` layer above **Trust Decision + effect-audit imports + Runtime Capability + artifact-linked inventory**.

## 2026-03-18 — Feedback Loop Stack (session-shaped build/debug iteration continuity above Cargo reports, rust-analyzer coexistence, and debugger evidence)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately avoided adding another leaf tool. The archive already had a strong **Build-State Evidence Stack** and a strong **Debuggability Stack**, but it still lacked the composition layer for the thing users actually feel every day: the developer loop from a change or intent, through build evidence, into debugging evidence, and out into issue/support/assistant consumers.
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still says resource usage (slow compile times and storage usage) remains one of the main non-trivial productivity problems, says debugging remains a major problem, and says online docs remain the canonical reference while LLM/tool usage rises. That is unusually strong evidence that the missing contribution is not just a performance fix or just a debugger improvement; it is the boundary that keeps loop evidence importable and canonical-friendly. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The 2025 compiler-performance survey sharpens the exact seam: build pain varies by workflow, more than 35% of users say IDE and Cargo blocking one another is a big problem, and the default dev-profile debug info materially increases disk usage and slows compilation/linking. That means build performance and debugging are entangled in practice even when the ecosystem discusses them separately. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- Cargo’s build-analysis goal is the strongest enabling signal. It explicitly aims to record metadata across invocations, associate it with `CARGO_RUN_ID`, explain rebuilds, and eventually unlock build replay for debugging and CI reproducibility. The missing contribution is now the review layer above those raw records rather than more handcrafted log parsers. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html
- Cargo’s build-dir-layout goal and the March 2026 build-dir-layout-v2 call for testing make the loop boundary even more concrete: Cargo is trying to reduce lock contention with rust-analyzer, enable smaller self-contained units and shared caches, and it publicly says many projects still rely on unspecified build-dir details because Cargo lacks some missing features. That is unusually direct support for a session/handoff layer that stays honest about internal-vs-stable boundaries. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-dir-layout.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- The 2026 debugging survey makes the second half of the seam explicit: Rust still needs stronger multi-debugger, multi-OS, async-aware debugging, high-quality visualizers, and Rust expression evaluation, and maintaining that support across debugger versions and std-layout changes remains hard. That argues for keeping debugger tuple truth and runtime-side inspection truth linked to the same loop session without pretending parity already exists. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/23/rust-debugging-survey-2026/
- Cargo 1.94’s development-cycle report now gives the right posture for the worthy-contribution claim: `cargo report rebuild`, `cargo report sessions`, and improved timing support are landing, but Cargo also reiterates that it cannot be everything to everyone and that plugins matter. ## 2026-03-17 — Async Reliability Stack proposal-layer promotion (shutdown truth, replay posture, and deterministic exploration continuity)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a frontier seam that already had a strong stack design plus pilot program but still lacked the stack-level epic and a stack-level gap statement. **Async Reliability Stack** was the clearest fit: the archive already had Async Lifecycle, Replay, and DST lanes, but still lacked the explicit proposal-layer artifact that would make them one buildable ecosystem contribution instead of three adjacent notes.
- The 2025H1 async flagship explicitly says async Rust is a multi-year parity effort and calls out runtime choice, runtime interoperability, cancellation sharp edges, and reliability as active ecosystem pain. Rust’s 2026 flagships keep **Just Add Async** active with milestones for return type notation, `async fn in dyn trait`, immobile types / guaranteed destructors, and ergonomic ref-counting. Together, that means async reliability is still live ecosystem infrastructure, not legacy cleanup. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/async.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The May 2025 project-goals update says the Async Book recently added chapters on concurrency primitives, structured concurrency, and pinning, while the current Async Book still says async Rust has runtime compatibility constraints and a higher maintenance burden than sync Rust. That strongly supports a proposal shaped around structured lifecycle evidence rather than log-driven folklore. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/06/20/may-project-goals-update/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/async-book/01_getting_started/03_state_of_async_rust.html
- Tokio’s own shutdown guidance now makes an important lifecycle boundary concrete: it recommends `CancellationToken` for shutdown signaling, `CancellationToken::child_token` documents one-way propagation from parent to child, and `TaskTracker::wait` guarantees that once the tracker is closed and empty all tracked tasks have exited and their future destructors have finished. That is strong evidence that Rust now has real shutdown/lifecycle primitives, but still lacks a portable evidence layer above them. Sources: https://tokio.rs/tokio/topics/shutdown ; https://docs.rs/tokio-util/latest/tokio_util/sync/struct.CancellationToken.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio-util/latest/tokio_util/task/task_tracker/struct.TaskTracker.html
- The exploration side is also clearly ripe for composition rather than replacement: Loom permutes valid concurrent executions with state reduction; Shuttle explicitly trades exhaustive soundness for larger-scale randomized testing; Turmoil provides deterministic execution for distributed systems with seeded network hardship; and MadSim describes itself as a deterministic simulator for distributed systems. Those are serious but non-equivalent lanes, which makes a shared contract layer more appropriate than an attempt to bless one winner. Sources: https://docs.rs/loom/latest/loom/ ; https://docs.rs/shuttle/latest/shuttle/ ; https://docs.rs/turmoil/latest/turmoil/ ; https://docs.rs/madsim/latest/madsim/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still lists resource usage and debugging among the main productivity problems. That matters here because async failures often surface as hangs, leaked tasks, shutdown races, and timing-sensitive bugs that are expensive to explain after the fact. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/async-reliability-lifecycle-replay-simulation-and-consumer-handoffs.md`; add `proposals/epic-async-reliability-stack.md`; deepen `design/async-reliability-stack.md`; refresh `design/async-reliability-pilot-program.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so **Async Reliability Stack** becomes an explicit proposal-layer candidate; repair the stale `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` revision label; and strengthen `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep runtime/lifecycle truth, replay truth, exploration truth, and consumer imports distinct.
- Strategy conclusion: the worthy contribution here is **not** another runtime wrapper, deterministic scheduler, simulator bake-off, or async dashboard. It is a thin `cargo asyncdoctor` / `async-reliability-pack/v0` layer above **Async Lifecycle + Replay + DST**, with explicit artifacts for lifecycle policy, failure capture, replay posture, exploration semantics, and bounded downstream handoffs.

- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately looked for a seam that already had strong leaf-level execution but still lacked the stack-level proposal that would make it a buildable ecosystem contribution. **Canonical Learning Stack** was the clearest fit: the archive already had DocProof, Compile Guidance, and a shared consumer pilot, but still lacked the explicit stack-level rollout and epic.
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online documentation remains the preferred canonical reference, notes that some learning traffic appears to be shifting toward LLM tooling, and separately says editors with agentic support are on the rise. - Rust’s 2025 vision work explicitly recommends extending crates toward **better diagnostics and guidance from crates**. That is a strong upstream signal that compile-time teaching belongs in the same strategic band as executable docs and guides rather than being treated as an isolated diagnostics curiosity. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/19/what-do-people-love-about-rust/
- docs.rs already provides two key machine-usable ingredients: crates can declare docs-build posture through `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`, and docs.rs documents host-specific build behavior such as nightly builds, `docsrs` cfg / `DOCS_RS`, cross-compilation posture, and CI-facing advice for catching docs.rs-specific failures. Sources: https://docs.rs/about/metadata ; https://docs.rs/about/builds

- rustdoc’s docs book already treats documentation examples as executable tests and supports `compile_fail`, `no_run`, and edition-tagged doctests; Rust 1.94 also added `#[cfg(doctest)]`. Together these signals strengthen the idea that documentation surfaces already have a real test/subject boundary. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/write-documentation/documentation-tests.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html

## 2026-03-17 — Lint Governance Stack promotion (policy locks, baseline drift, and fix/application continuity)
- Re-read the latest archive and found that **Lint Governance Stack** was already being treated as a real frontier seam, already had a stack note and a pilot program, and already had strong leaf-level proposals under Lint Baseline, Compile Guidance, Edit Workflow, and Policy — but still lacked the stack-level epic that would turn those pieces into one reviewable ecosystem contribution.
- Rust’s 2026 flagship slate explicitly includes **safety-critical lints in Clippy**. That raises the strategic value of lint posture from convenience or style into assurance-adjacent ecosystem work and strengthens the case for keeping curated lint subsets, evidence, and higher-stakes consumer handoffs explicit. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Cargo now provides stable manifest/workspace lint configuration through `[lints]` and `[workspace.lints]`, with workspace lint inheritance respected as of 1.74. That means selected lint posture is now first-class project metadata rather than only command-line or CI folklore. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-lints-section ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
- Cargo’s unstable docs now include `[lints.cargo]`, which is exactly the kind of signal the archive should react to: Cargo-native warning families are moving toward the same policy plane rather than staying forever outside lint governance. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html#lintscargo
- Cargo 1.94’s changelog says Cargo added the `report` subcommand and renamed the old future-incompat reporting command to `cargo report future-incompatibilities`; the current docs say `cargo report` is the report surface and `future-incompat` is the currently supported report family. That is enough official substrate to justify a stack-level import lane above raw console text. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-report.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/future-incompat-report.html
- rustc’s lint model already includes `allow`, `expect`, `warn`, `force-warn`, `deny`, and `forbid`, plus precedence rules across attributes and CLI flags. That makes it harder to justify any proposal that pretends lint policy is just one scalar warning threshold or one CI bit. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/lints/levels.html
- Clippy’s current configuration docs still say `clippy.toml` is unstable and may be deprecated in the future, which makes exported profile locks and visible governance artifacts more important than hidden tool-local config state. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/clippy/configuration.html
- The Edition Guide says `cargo fix` can only work with a single configuration at a time and may require multiple passes across targets or feature combinations. Cargo’s docs and release notes also make auto-fix flows more visible, including suggestions to use `cargo fix` or `cargo clippy --fix` when warnings are auto-fixable. Together these signals make the missing contribution feel like **fix handoff and application receipts**, not a bigger autofix button. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/editions/advanced-migrations.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html
- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-lint-governance-stack.md`; deepen `design/lint-governance-stack.md`; refresh `design/lint-governance-pilot-program.md` and `gaps/lint-profiles-baselines-and-fixpacks.md`; update priorities/frontier so **Lint Governance Stack** has an explicit proposal-layer candidate; and strengthen the archive’s amnesia resistors so future lint-governance revisions keep authored guidance, selected policy, observed findings, fix/application receipts, and consumer verdicts explicit.
- Stack stance: the worthy contribution here is now explicit — a thin `cargo lint-governance` / `lint-governance-pack/v0` composition layer above **Compile Guidance + Lint Baseline + Edit Workflow + Policy**. The archive should now prefer profile locks, baseline drift, Cargo-side import notes, fixpack/apply-receipt separation, and bounded release/safety/policy handoffs over another Clippy preset, lint dashboard, or stealth codemod story.

## 2026-03-17 — Publisher & Source Identity Stack proposal-layer promotion (authority/claim/source separation, best-effort provenance humility, and bounded downstream handoffs)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for a seam that was already strategically strong, already had both a stack design and pilot program, but still lacked a concrete stack-level proposal file. **Publisher & Source Identity Stack** was the clearest gap: the archive already had Org Identity & Registry UX plus a ranked pilot rollout, but it still lacked the explicit epic that would turn those ingredients into one buildable contribution instead of a good cluster of notes.
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update makes the authority side materially stronger than it was even a few revisions ago: Trusted Publishing now supports GitLab CI/CD, crate owners can require Trusted-Publishing-only mode, and risky GitHub Actions triggers are blocked. That means publish authority is increasingly issuer-backed and configuration-shaped rather than just “who has a token”. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Cargo’s docs are already explicit that authority itself has internal structure. The publishing docs say the owner of a crate is the only person allowed to publish new versions, but can designate additional owners; they also distinguish **named owners** from **team owners**, with different powers over owner-set mutation. That is strong evidence that a future stack should report authority posture, not flatten it into one generic “owned by” field. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-owner.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registry-web-api.html
- The source side is equally strong. Cargo’s registry-authentication docs say authenticated alternate registries require a credential provider to avoid unknowingly storing unencrypted credentials on disk, while the registries and source-replacement docs keep alternate registries and replacement sources as distinct mechanisms. Source replacement is defined in terms of exact-copy equivalence, not “another registry with roughly similar content”. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registry-authentication.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registries.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/source-replacement.html
- The claim/provenance side also sharpened. RFC 3243 and the open-namespaces project goal make namespace control an active Cargo/compiler/crates.io seam, while RFC 3052 made `package.authors` optional and moved crates.io/docs.rs UI toward current owners. Meanwhile `cargo package` includes `.cargo_vcs_info.json` but explicitly says the package provenance is not verified and the tarball is not guaranteed to match that VCS information. Together, those changes make it much harder to honestly collapse authorship, ownership, publish authority, namespace control, repository linkage, and package provenance into one package-identity field. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3243-packages-as-optional-namespaces.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/open-namespaces.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3052-optional-authors-field.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- Archive decision: add `gaps/publisher-source-identity-authority-claims-and-source-posture-continuity.md`; add `proposals/epic-publisher-source-identity-stack.md`; deepen `design/publisher-source-identity-stack.md`; refresh `design/publisher-source-identity-pilot-program.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so the seam now has an explicit proposal-layer candidate; and strengthen `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep owners, authors, trusted-publisher subjects, source posture, family claims, and downstream trust/install conclusions in an explicit import relationship.

## 2026-03-17 — Test Execution Evidence Stack proposal-layer promotion (harness/run boundary, runner-semantic imports, and bounded attachment continuity)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for a stack that was already strategically strong, already had a synthesis design plus pilot program, but still lacked a concrete proposal-layer file. **Test Execution Evidence Stack** was the clearest gap: the archive already had Harness Protocol, Test Run Evidence, Config Set, and a ranked pilot order, but it still lacked the stack-level epic that would turn those ingredients into one buildable contribution instead of a cluster of good notes.
- RFC 3558 is stronger than “please stabilize JSON”. It explicitly aims to stabilize **programmatic output for libtest**, says Cargo should be able to provide better UX on top of that output, and calls for a future Cargo proposal so **custom test harnesses can opt into the same protocol**. It also evaluates the design against ignored tests, parallel execution, benches, and discovery. That makes the missing contribution look like a shared execution contract above runners and harnesses rather than another point-format adapter. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3558-libtest-json.html
- The Testing Team RFC says Rust’s automated testing experience spans **Cargo, libtest, rustdoc doctests, CI, IDEs, and custom tools**, and that there was no single team focused on the testing picture holistically. That reinforces the archive’s thesis that the next contribution should be a contract between actors rather than one more runner or formatter. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3455-t-test.html
- Cargo 1.94 still lists **Finish the libtest json output experiment** among project goals in need of owners, which is a strong sign that the seam is still live. Cargo’s unstable-features docs also keep the stability boundary explicit for nightly-only interfaces, which means any archive proposal has to model import posture honestly instead of pretending the underlying plumbing is already final. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/ ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo’s docs still expose why testing truth cannot be flattened casually: `cargo test` says doctest execution details are **not guaranteed and may change in the future**; `cargo bench` says Cargo always passes `--bench` whether the harness is libtest or custom, `harness = false` enables a custom `main`, and `#[bench]` remains nightly-only. Together those details argue for explicit harness/adapter semantics rather than letting run reports quietly redefine doctest and benchmark behavior. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-test.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-bench.html
- nextest now strengthens the runner-semantic side of the stack rather than weakening it. Its current design docs say that when recording is enabled it persists the **full event stream**, captured outputs, and workspace metadata for every run, while the running docs emphasize stable **binary IDs**, package-selection compatibility with `cargo test`, and configurable termination behavior. That is exactly the kind of runner-native truth the archive should import rather than hide behind one normalized verdict. Sources: https://nexte.st/docs/design/architecture/recording-runs/ ; https://nexte.st/docs/running/
- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-test-execution-evidence-stack.md`; deepen `design/test-execution-evidence-stack.md`; update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so the seam now has an explicit proposal-layer candidate; and strengthen `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions keep harness truth, runner-native recordings, raw outputs, config ids, and downstream conclusions in an explicit import relationship.

## 2026-03-17 — Safety-Critical Evidence Stack proposal-layer promotion (authority, criterion honesty, dynamic-analysis truth, and bounded qualification handoffs)
- Re-read the latest archive and looked for a stack that was already strategically strong, already had a synthesis design plus pilot program, but still lacked a concrete proposal-layer file. **Safety-Critical Evidence Stack** was the clearest gap: it was already a frontier-ranked band and already imported by Conformance Traceability, but it still lacked the stack-level epic that would make it a buildable ecosystem contribution instead of only a strong note.
- Rust’s 2026 flagship roadmap now makes this seam unusually explicit: **Safety-Critical Rust** is defined in terms of MC/DC coverage support, normative `unsafe` documentation, safety-critical lints in Clippy, and FLS release cadence. That is already an evidence roadmap, not just a general aspiration. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The January 2026 safety-critical adoption writeup says the real pressure in these domains is process, verification, and evidence, and that teams are strongly incentivized to isolate the highest-criticality logic into the smallest surface area possible. That makes a slice-oriented evidence stack more plausible than a whole-product certification fantasy. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
- The MC/DC goal says MC/DC is required by standards such as DO-178C, ISO 26262, and IEC 61508, and that implementing it outside the compiler is infeasible because macro expansion makes a post-expansion source model unrealistic. That strengthens the case for a shared artifact layer above compiler-integrated evidence rather than another external report wrapper. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/mcdc-coverage-support.html
- The normative-unsafe-docs goal says the present unsafe-documentation story is not yet authoritative enough for rigorous safety cases, while the safety-critical Clippy goal says the likely lint surface is on the order of 50 to 200 lints over one to two years. Together, those signals make **authority + lint posture + waiver visibility** look like first-class stack concerns rather than details to leave in prose or CI glue. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/safe-unsafe-for-safety-critical.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/safety-critical-lints-in-clippy.html
- The FLS and contracts lanes also make this seam more operational than before: Rust already published the first rust-lang-owned FLS release, now wants a stable release cadence, and the standard-library contracts effort plus `core::contracts` show executable contract surfaces are no longer purely aspirational. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/spec-fls-publish.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/stabilize-fls-releases.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/std-contracts.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/contracts/index.html
- rustc’s official source-based coverage docs and the unstable sanitizer book already expose enough engine/criterion/target caveats that the missing contribution is no longer “find some evidence source”. It is the attachable review boundary that keeps criterion truth, target/runtime provenance, capability blind spots, and proof assumptions honest together. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/instrument-coverage.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/sanitizer.html

## 2026-03-17 — SDK Productization Stack (SDK family truth above source contracts, generators, and release/support)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose a new seam **above** the existing Schema Contract, Service/Protocol, Identity, Runtime Settings, Library Productization, Release Truth, and Support work. The archive already had strong producer-side and crate-side pieces; what it lacked was the thin layer for **API products consumed as Rust SDKs**.
- The 2024 State of Rust survey says Rust is especially popular for server backends, web/networking services, and cloud technologies. That matters because these are exactly the places where teams increasingly need supported client libraries, CLIs, and mocks rather than only service implementations. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/13/2024-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the preferred canonical reference, hints that some questions are shifting toward LLM tooling, and notes that editors with agentic support are rising. That is a strong signal that SDK product truth should be machine-readable and bounded rather than living only in README prose and example code. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The OpenAPI lane is now too real to ignore. `utoipa` positions itself as Rust’s code-first OpenAPI path, `progenitor` generates opinionated Rust clients from OpenAPI 3.0.x, and OpenAPI Generator keeps a Rust client lane with multiple runtime templates and middleware/configuration options. Those are strong ingredients, but they still do not define a portable SDK product boundary. Sources: https://docs.rs/utoipa ; https://docs.rs/progenitor ; https://openapi-generator.tech/docs/generators/rust/
- The gRPC/descriptor lane is also mature enough that the missing contribution is no longer another client runtime. `tonic` says codegen is generally the intended way to use its client/server surface, which means Rust already has a normal generated-client workflow here too. ## 2026-03-17 — Workspace Environment Stack (workspace subject + environment intent + realization truth + bounded handoff)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose a new seam **above** the existing Tooling Contract, Toolchain Productization, Native Dependency, Runtime Settings, and Credentials work. The archive already had strong lower-layer pieces; what it lacked was the thin environment handoff layer joining them into a contributor-facing and machine-consumable contract.
- The 2025 State of Rust survey now makes the machine-consumption angle impossible to ignore: online documentation remains the preferred canonical reference, people increasingly learn with LLM tooling in the loop, and editors with agentic support are on the rise. That is a strong signal that workspace setup truth needs bounded machine-readable handoff instead of living only in README prose and shell snippets. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The same survey still keeps resource usage and debugging among important productivity problems. That is a reminder that developer-loop reality and local setup remain ecosystem pain, not mere onboarding trivia. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Cargo’s current config model and workflow direction reinforce the seam. Cargo config is hierarchical across parent directories up to `$CARGO_HOME`; rustup overrides and `rust-toolchain.toml` are also discovered by directory walk; and Cargo 1.94 is actively discussing workspace/configuration discovery because stray parent manifests or `.cargo/config.toml` files can poison unrelated builds. That means workspace environment identity is already partly a discovery problem. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/overrides.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- rust-analyzer’s configuration surface shows the editor reality clearly: override commands, extra env, features, targets, build-script invocation strategy, and linked-workspace behavior all materially affect how a workspace is interpreted. That is strong evidence that a shared handoff layer is missing between build truth and editor truth. Source: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration.html
- Dev Containers and Nix prove that reproducible realization substrates already exist, but they are generic. The missing Rust contribution is the reviewable layer above them that can preserve workspace subject, toolchain/native/settings/credential imports, and bounded human/editor/CI/agent handoffs without forcing one substrate to win. Sources: https://containers.dev/implementors/spec/ ; https://nix.dev/concepts/flakes.html
- The Rust Foundation’s 2026–2028 strategy makes Stable Infrastructure, Sustainable Maintenance, and Adoption & Innovation simultaneous priorities. A good workspace-environment contract lives exactly at that overlap by reducing maintainer re-explanation, contributor setup drift, and machine-consumption ambiguity. Source: https://rustfoundation.org/strategic-plan/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/workspace-environments-onboarding-and-agent-safe-dev-contracts.md`, `design/workspace-environment-stack.md`, and `proposals/epic-workspace-environment-stack.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add an amnesia resistor so later revisions keep workspace subject, declared intent, realization substrate, secret posture, observed state, and handoff authority distinct.

## 2026-03-17 — Tooling Contract epic refresh (Cargo discovery + scope + plan + evidence + honest adapters)
- Re-read the latest archive and promoted the **Tooling Contract Stack** from a strong synthesis seam into an explicit epic candidate. The archive already had the stack and ranked pilots; the missing move was a proposal layer saying this should be built as its own ecosystem contribution.
- Rust’s 2026 flagships put **integrate Cargo into larger build systems** and **prototype cargo plumbing commands** inside the active “Building blocks” agenda. That makes machine-facing Cargo contracts feel strategic rather than niche tooling polish. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Cargo’s accepted plumbing goal is unusually direct about the missing layer: it says today’s plumbing is limited or deprecated, `cargo metadata` excludes feature resolution, and `--build-plan` was not a durable answer, while also framing the build as explicit phases from project discovery through final-artifact staging. That is a strong argument for a thin contract layer above current surfaces instead of more scraping of Cargo internals. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- Cargo’s stable external-tools docs still center on only three general-purpose lanes — `cargo metadata`, `--message-format=json`, and custom subcommands — and the metadata docs explicitly recommend passing `--format-version` to stay forward-compatible. Useful, yes; but it is still not one coherent discovery → scope → plan → execute contract story. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html
- Cargo’s build-cache and unstable docs sharpen the missing seam further: final artifacts and intermediate build artifacts are now documented separately; the build-dir layout is explicitly internal and subject to change; `build.build-dir` was stabilized in 1.91; `--build-plan` was removed in 1.93; and build analysis/report commands are still experimental imports. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo 1.94 is almost a direct justification for the stack: plugins matter because Cargo cannot be everything to everyone; active work continues on build-dir layout, target-dir locking, structured logging, and workspace/config discovery; and cargo plumbing commands remain a named focus area without progress yet. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- rust-analyzer’s `cargo.targetDir` setting exists specifically to avoid lock contention from rust-analyzer’s own Cargo activity, at the cost of duplicated build artifacts. That is exactly the sort of editor/build-tool reality the archive should expose as bounded adapter posture rather than hide inside private configuration folklore. Source: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration
- The March 2026 call for testing the build-dir-v2 layout says the build-dir is internal-only **but many projects need to rely on unspecified details due to missing features within Cargo**. That is about as direct a demand signal for a tooling-contract layer as the ecosystem is likely to get. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-tooling-contract-stack.md`, deepen `design/tooling-contract-stack.md` and `design/tooling-contract-pilot-program.md`, update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and treat the **Tooling Contract Stack** as an explicit epic candidate so future revisions prefer **discovery-boundary truth + selected-scope truth + graph/plan truth + imported-evidence posture + bounded adapter/handoff summaries** over another Cargo wrapper, BSP-only bridge, or target-dir folklore layer.

## 2026-03-17 — Compiler Extensibility epic proposal (make compiler-attached tools reviewable companions, not just clever demos)

- The `rustc_public` motion matters because it changes the seam from fantasy to plausible product surface. The 2025H1 StableMIR goal explicitly framed the work as enabling analyzers, linters, dev environments, and other tools across Rust versions, and the July 2025 update says the crate was renamed to `rustc_public` and moved toward publication infrastructure and an MCP. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/stable-mir.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/

- The strongest concrete proving ground is still `cargo-semver-checks`. It is close enough to mainstream utility to target Cargo integration, but its own goal page documents the hard realities — cross-crate visibility, type precision, and witness-generation support — and also records the lesson from `semverver`: depending on compiler-internal APIs is not a sustainable ecosystem strategy. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html

- The 2026 flagship framing makes this seam broader than SemVer alone. Supply-chain/public-API work, safety-critical lints in Clippy, and Cargo plumbing are all strategic priorities, which implies the ecosystem needs a better contract layer for compiler-attached tools and not merely one more special-purpose analyzer. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html

- Cargo’s own direction still reinforces the companion-tool posture: plugins matter because Cargo cannot be everything to everyone. That is strong evidence that the right archive move is a thin reviewable `cargo toolcontract` / `tool-pack` layer, not a demand that every successful lane be merged upstream before it can count as real ecosystem infrastructure. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/

- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-compiler-extensibility-stack.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and `RESEARCH_LOG.md`; lightly deepen the compiler-extensibility design and pilot docs with proposal links; and add a new amnesia resistor so future revisions do not confuse current companion-tool contracts with possible future Cargo/rustc integration.

## 2026-03-17 — Compiler Extensibility Stack (compiler-attached tools as products with declared attachment lanes and consumer handoffs)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose to add a **synthesis layer** above MIR Analysis, Lint Governance, Compile Guidance, and Conformance Traceability instead of inventing another isolated analyzer or build wrapper. The missing leverage is not one more tool; it is the contract layer that makes compiler-attached tools portable and reviewable.
- Rust’s current vision work is unusually direct here: it recommends doubling down on extensibility beyond the earliest compilation stages and names Stable MIR and build-std as examples. That makes compiler-extensibility an ecosystem direction, not just a private tooling hobby. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/19/what-do-people-love-about-rust/
- The StableMIR goal says publishing compiler-facing crates should let analyzers, linters, dev environments, and other tools work without depending directly on compiler internals; and the July 2025 project-goals update says `stable_mir` had already become `rustc_public` and was moving toward publication infrastructure. That is a strong signal that the missing work is now the **tool contract layer above the export surface**, not merely the export surface itself. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/stable-mir.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/
- The `cargo-semver-checks` goal provides the clearest practical lesson. It is important enough to be considered for Cargo integration, but it still needs better cross-crate visibility, type precision, and witness-generation support; and the same page explicitly says the older `semverver` path became unsustainable because it depended on compiler-internal APIs. That is almost a perfect statement of why Rust needs reviewable compiler-extensibility contracts. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes broaden the demand further: safety-critical lints in Clippy, prototype reflection, build-std, and cargo plumbing are all active goals. Cargo’s 1.94 development notes also reiterate that Cargo cannot be everything to everyone and that plugins matter. Together, those signals argue for a companion stack for compiler-attached tools rather than a fantasy where every useful lane becomes core Cargo immediately. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- Archive decision: add `gaps/compiler-extensibility-analysis-lints-and-reviewable-tool-contracts.md`, `design/compiler-extensibility-stack.md`, and `design/compiler-extensibility-pilot-program.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add an amnesia resistor so later revisions keep attachment lane, analysis scope, capability/stability posture, emitted artifacts, and downstream consumer conclusions distinct.

## 2026-03-17 — Keystone Stewardship Stack (criticality, institutional backing, continuity, and obligations above ordinary crate metadata)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose a **strategic institutional seam** rather than one more crate-local productization note. The archive already had strong layers for maintenance reality, trust, release, and support. What it still lacked was an explicit way to describe when a Rust project has become keystone infrastructure and what stewardship posture follows from that.
- The Rust Foundation’s 2026–2028 strategy makes **Stable Infrastructure** and **Sustainable Maintenance** core pillars. That is strong evidence that continuity for key Rust projects is no longer just social nicety or volunteer heroics; it is now ecosystem strategy. Source: https://rustfoundation.org/strategic-plan/
- The Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund is explicitly about **consistent, transparent, long-term support**, alignment with high-impact priorities, visibility into how funding is used, and creating conditions for long-term maintainer roles and continuity. That means Rust now has real downstream programs that could consume keystone-stewardship evidence if the ecosystem could express it well. Source: https://rustfoundation.org/media/announcing-the-rust-foundation-maintainers-fund/
- The Rust Innovation Lab exists because many Rust projects have matured into **critical pieces of global software infrastructure** and increasingly need **neutral, community-led governance and reliable institutional backing**. That is practically a statement that some Rust projects now need a boundary above ordinary crate metadata and release pages. Source: https://rustfoundation.org/media/rust-foundation-launches-rust-innovation-lab-with-rustls-as-inaugural-project/
- The Rustls / Innovation Lab framing is especially clarifying because it states concrete keystone criteria: the Foundation wants to support projects that **provide foundational infrastructure**, have **clear industry traction and operational need**, and are driven by **deeply committed maintainers who need space to build**. That is exactly the sort of explicit keystone review vocabulary the archive was missing. Source: https://rustfoundation.org/media/rustls-shortlisted-for-two-2025-openuk-awards/
- Official Rust writing on maintenance makes the human part of this seam concrete: maintenance includes triage, CI failures, documentation, security incidents, review, refactoring, and contributor unblocking, and that work is multiplicative rather than merely janitorial. Keystone projects need a way to represent that continuity work explicitly instead of leaving it hidden behind popularity or “everyone knows this crate matters.” Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/12/what-is-maintenance-anyway/
- crates.io’s 2026 development update adds stronger Trusted Publishing controls and SLOC visibility, while the 2025 State of Rust survey says docs remain canonical and maintainer support remains a live concern. Together those are good inputs, but they still do not answer the keystone question: which projects need stronger institutional support, and what obligations or continuity posture follow when they receive it? Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/keystone-projects-critical-infrastructure-and-institutional-stewardship-contracts.md`, `design/keystone-stewardship-stack.md`, `design/keystone-stewardship-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-keystone-stewardship-stack.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `RESEARCH_LOG.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add an amnesia resistor so later revisions keep criticality, institutional support, continuity risk, obligations, and consumer conclusions distinct.

## 2026-03-17 — Runtime Capability pilot program (declared authority, inferred authority, generated enforcement, enacted enforcement)
- Re-read the latest archive and chose to **turn an already-strong kit into an execution seam** rather than add another adjacent security note. The archive already had Runtime Capability as a worthy idea; the missing leverage was the ranked pilot layer that can keep declaration, inference, generation, enforcement, and observed behavior distinct.
- The Rust Foundation’s 2025 security update says Alpha-Omega funding is supporting a Rust-focused implementation of Capslock, and the January 2026 Project Director update says the capability analyzer now has a functioning prototype. That is strong evidence that capability analysis is becoming real Rust ecosystem infrastructure rather than a speculative side project. Sources: https://rustfoundation.org/media/strengthening-rust-security-with-alpha-omega-a-progress-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/09/project-director-update/
- The `cargo-capslock` repository describes itself as an in-development experimental tool for analysing Rust projects and determining which Capslock capabilities they require. FOSDEM 2026 material goes one step further and explicitly frames the Rust output as a basis for generating seccomp profiles for services. That combination makes the archive’s missing honesty rule obvious: **generated policy is not deployed policy**. Sources: https://github.com/rustfoundation/cargo-capslock ; https://fosdem.org/2026/schedule/event/QGCFDA-using_capslock_analysis_to_develop_seccomp_filters_for_rust_and_other_services/
- `cap-std`, Wasmtime/WASI, and Tauri already expose materially different capability models with real consumers. That means a good runtime-capability contribution should be an attachable review contract above those systems, not one universal permissions language pretending they are identical. Sources: https://docs.rs/cap-std/latest/cap_std/ ; https://docs.wasmtime.dev/security.html ; https://v2.tauri.app/security/capabilities/
- Archive decision: add `design/runtime-capability-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/runtime-capability-kit.md`, `proposals/epic-runtime-capability-kit.md`, `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `RESEARCH_LOG.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add an amnesia resistor so later revisions keep declaration, inference, generation, enforcement, and observed behavior visibly separate.

- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately chose to **flesh out the new frontier seam into an epic proposal** instead of adding another adjacent substrate kit. That is strong support for adoption briefs that are freshness-aware, bounded, and able to survive machine consumption without losing caveats. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- crates.io’s January 2026 update says crate pages now show a Security tab, GitLab-backed Trusted Publishing, and SLOC metrics. docs.rs changed its default targets in October 2025 to reflect platform-support reality. - Cargo’s 1.94 development note again says Cargo cannot be everything to everyone and that plugins matter, while the Rust Foundation’s 2026–2028 strategy explicitly pairs responsible adoption growth with sustainable support for maintainers and stable, secure infrastructure. That combination is exactly why the archive should treat adoption decisions as a **thin companion layer** importing trust and maintenance reality, not as a hidden recommender that ignores them. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/ ; https://rustfoundation.org/media/annual-report-strategy-2025/

## 2026-03-16 — Toolchain Productization Stack (toolchain variants as products instead of local state)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately promoted an **already-emerging seam** into an explicit stack instead of adding another adjacent `build-std`, cross-compilation, or firmware note.
- The official signals now line up unusually well: the `build-std` goal is explicitly about an MVP that could be stabilized, while Cargo’s current unstable docs still say `-Z build-std` is early-stage, requires nightly plus `rust-src`, and must be passed to all Cargo invocations. That combination is exactly the “strong need, weak portable contract” pattern the archive should care about. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/build-std.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- rustup’s own model reinforces the gap. Toolchains, components, targets, profiles, and directory overrides are separate surfaces; cross-compilation docs say target stdlib installation is not enough because linkers or SDKs are often still required; and custom-target docs explicitly warn that target JSON is unstable and should be pinned to a compiler version. That means “which toolchain did we use?” is already more than a channel string. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/concepts/toolchains.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/concepts/components.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/cross-compilation.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/overrides.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/targets/custom.html
- The sanitizer lane makes the missing boundary impossible to ignore. The sanitizer-support goal says stabilizing MSan/TSan needs infrastructure to provide **precompiled and instrumented standard libraries**, while the 2026 flagships page carries that work forward. The current sanitizer docs still recommend rebuilding std for important lanes such as CFI. That turns stdlib profile identity into ecosystem-grade product surface instead of hidden local setup. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/stabilization-of-sanitizer-support.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/sanitizer.html
- Rust for Linux and adjacent adopters make the demand broader than sanitizers. The Rust-for-Linux tooling goal explicitly calls out unstable compiler options for target optimizations, hardening, and sanitizer integration plus the need for a custom std build; and the end-of-2025 program update says CPython exploration is surfacing a similar cluster of needs: `build-std`, platform support, sanitizer support, and arbitrary self types. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/rfl.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/12/19/program-management-update--end-of-2025/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/toolchain-variants-sysroots-cross-builds-and-sanitizer-support-contracts.md`, `design/toolchain-productization-stack.md`, and `proposals/epic-toolchain-productization-stack.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add a sharper amnesia resistor so later revisions keep provisioning truth, stdlib/profile truth, activation/reuse truth, and runtime-analysis truth distinct.

## 2026-03-17 — Event Productization Stack (event truth + replay truth + support truth above broker/client folklore)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately promoted a seam **above** the existing Event Surface Kit instead of adding another broker-specific comparison, schema-registry tangent, or replay-daemon note.
- AsyncAPI 3.1.0 explicitly frames the AsyncAPI document as a **communication contract between senders and receivers**, while CloudEvents explicitly exists to describe event data in a common way and improve consistency, accessibility, and portability. That is strong evidence that message-driven systems already have standards-side product-boundary language. Sources: https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/reference/specification/latest ; https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/concepts/asyncapi-document ; https://cloudevents.io/ ; https://github.com/cloudevents/spec
- The Rust-side ingredient set is clearly heterogeneous now: `async-nats` exposes JetStream, key-value store, object store, and service API examples and deprecates the old synchronous client; `rdkafka` exposes async producer/consumer roles plus exactly-once semantics via idempotent and transactional producers with read-committed consumers, while still warning that the APIs are under active development; `lapin` carries runtime and TLS-backend diversity; and `zenoh` mixes pub/sub with query/reply, storage, and computation while explicitly saying the configuration surface is unstable. That is exactly the archive pattern of “strong ingredients, weak shared product boundary.” Sources: https://docs.rs/async-nats/latest/async_nats/ ; https://docs.rs/rdkafka/latest/rdkafka/ ; https://docs.rs/lapin/latest/lapin/ ; https://docs.rs/zenoh/latest/zenoh/ ; https://docs.rs/zenoh/latest/zenoh/struct.Config.html
- The Rust CloudEvents SDK further reinforces the point: it implements the CloudEvents spec for Rust, but explicitly says the project is WIP and all APIs are unstable, while its current spec-support table includes HTTP/JSON/Kafka/NATS lanes and missing AMQP/MQTT/webhook support. That is a strong reason to design the productization layer above the crate rather than pretending the crate already solved the product boundary. Source: https://github.com/cloudevents/sdk-rust
- `sea-streamer` and `testcontainers` make the local/test lane concrete enough to design around: SeaStreamer explicitly aims for backend-agnostic real-time stream processors with Kafka/Redpanda and Redis backends plus stdio/unix-pipe-friendly testing, while `testcontainers` / `testcontainers-modules` already make ephemeral infrastructure and community-maintained broker modules practical in Rust tests. That means event-product evidence can plausibly be checked and attached rather than remaining prose. Sources: https://docs.rs/sea-streamer ; https://docs.rs/testcontainers/latest/testcontainers/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/testcontainers-modules/latest

- Zed’s extension docs make the current host reality concrete: extensions are Git repositories with `extension.toml`, procedural code is written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, the extension surface already includes languages/debuggers/snippets/slash commands/MCP servers, and users can explicitly restrict granted extension capabilities such as `process:exec`. - Tauri’s current plugin/security story now spans real productization layers: plugins are Cargo crates with optional NPM/Android/iOS packages, can hook lifecycle and expose commands, permissions and capabilities determine what commands and scopes are granted, and the updater plugin docs say potentially dangerous commands/scopes are blocked by default until enabled in capabilities configuration. Sources: https://v2.tauri.app/develop/plugins/ ; https://v2.tauri.app/security/permissions/ ; https://v2.tauri.app/security/capabilities/ ; https://v2.tauri.app/plugin/updater/ ; https://v2.tauri.app/blog/tauri-20/
- Extism reinforces the same seam from another angle: a plug-in system is a host-defined interface, the manifest describes the plugin and runtime constraints, host functions are the explicit way to grant deeper capabilities, and the runtime is itself a Rust crate with a C API used by multiple SDKs. Sources: https://extism.org/docs/concepts/plug-in-system/ ; https://extism.org/docs/concepts/manifest/ ; https://extism.org/docs/concepts/host-functions/ ; https://extism.org/docs/concepts/runtime-apis/

- The Rust CLI book itself still reads like evidence that serious tools need more than argument parsing: it explicitly treats **stdout vs stderr**, black-box testing, and packaging/distribution as core CLI design concerns. That is strong support for a stack that keeps command truth, runtime/output truth, and install/support truth separate. Sources: https://rust-cli.github.io/book/tutorial/output.html ; https://rust-cli.github.io/book/tutorial/testing.html ; https://rust-cli.github.io/book/tutorial/packaging.html
- The acquisition/distribution layer is now clearly real in practice: `cargo-dist` explicitly describes plan/build/host/publish/announce flows and machine-readable manifests for shippable binaries, while `cargo-binstall` explicitly offers a prebuilt-binary path with fallback search behavior ending in `cargo install`. Those are ecosystem ingredients, but they are still not one reviewable consumer-side tool contract. Sources: https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist ; https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall
- Terminal/runtime semantics are also already too substantive to leave implicit: `crossterm` owns cross-platform terminal actions and flush control; Ratatui owns buffered terminal drawing, viewport/buffer state, and restore/setup helpers; and `anstream` owns stream-sensitive color policy with env-based and Windows-console behavior. Together they say the missing move is not “yet another TUI abstraction” but a product layer above command, terminal, config, and install realities. Sources: https://docs.rs/crossterm/latest/crossterm/ ; https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/struct.Terminal.html ; https://docs.rs/anstream/latest/anstream/struct.AutoStream.html
- Archive decision: add `gaps/cli-tools-terminal-apps-and-cargo-subcommand-productization-contracts.md`, `design/cli-productization-stack.md`, `design/cli-productization-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-cli-productization-stack.md`; update `PRIORITIES.md` and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so the archive treats **Command Surface + Terminal Surface + Runtime Settings + Distribution Contract + Support Envelope** as an explicit ranked seam; and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep command truth, terminal truth, runtime truth, install truth, and support truth distinct.
