## 2026-03-16 — Firmware productization refresh (embedded Rust now needs a boring contract/evidence layer above traits and board templates)
- The 2024 State of Rust survey says embedded use is gaining traction while debugging and resource friction remain real and documentation remains a relative strength. That combination usually means the next missing thing is a supportable contract/evidence layer rather than a new core framework. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/13/2024-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- `embedded-hal` 1.0 now states its scope unusually clearly: it is a foundation for platform-agnostic drivers, it is not tied to one execution model, and functionality beyond that scope should use the target platform directly. That is a strong signal that the missing standardization pressure is above the trait layer rather than inside it. Source: https://github.com/rust-embedded/embedded-hal
- The host↔device workflow substrate is now real: `probe-rs` spans flashing/debugging/RTT/`defmt`, `embedded-test` provides a libtest-compatible on-device runner that reads tests from the ELF and resets the device per test, Embassy explicitly presents async embedded development as a first-class path, and `esp-hal` reached a 1.0 release in October 2025 as the first vendor-backed Rust SDK for embedded devices. Those are strong ingredients, but still not a shared product/support layer. Sources: https://probe.rs/ ; https://github.com/probe-rs/embedded-test ; https://embassy.dev/ ; https://developer.espressif.com/blog/2025/10/esp-hal-1/ ; https://developer.espressif.com/blog/2025/02/rust-esp-hal-beta/
- The Embedonomicon's SoC-support guide and the active `build-std` goal both underline that target enablement still depends on documentation, register descriptions, flash algorithms, and target/sysroot work. Meanwhile the 2024 CCS embedded-Rust study found inadequate software support, poorly organized docs, and tool/build diversity pain. That makes a **Firmware Productization Stack** more plausible than another board template, runner wrapper, or framework bake-off. Sources: https://docs.rust-embedded.org/embedonomicon/soc-support.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/build-std.html ; https://arxiv.org/html/2311.05063v2
- Tool churn remains a useful signal. The `probe-run` deprecation note says migration to `probe-rs` is straightforward, but it also explicitly notes the lack of a replacement for the older `--json` structured-log output. That is exactly the sort of missing portable evidence lane the archive should care about. Source: https://ferrous-systems.com/blog/probe-run-deprecation/

## 2026-03-16 — Scientific Productization Stack (array/storage/backend/model truth above scientific-fragmentation theater)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately promoted the next seam *above* recent tensor work instead of adding another adjacent array, model, or offload note.
- The Rust project’s scientific-computing / offloading goal explicitly says scientific computing, HPC, and ML users expect high-performance autodifferentiation and easier GPU use, and it names a future with state-of-the-art libraries like `faer` plus more Rust backends. - The current ingredient set is real but heterogeneous: Burn positions itself as both a tensor library and deep learning framework for numerical computing, inference, and training; Candle exposes core tensor/device/storage structures; `faer` is a pure-Rust linear-algebra library focused on portability, correctness, and performance; `zarrs` gives Rust a multidimensional-array storage lane; `ort` targets hardware-accelerated ONNX inference/training; and `tract` targets tiny portable TensorFlow/ONNX inference. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/burn/latest ; https://docs.rs/candle-core/latest/candle_core/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/faer/latest ; https://docs.rs/crate/zarrs/latest ; https://docs.rs/crate/ort/latest ; https://docs.rs/tract-core/latest/tract_core/
- The external interop lesson is also clear: the 2024 Array API release frames interoperability and consistent array behavior as the point, while DLPack exists specifically as a stable in-memory tensor-exchange structure across frameworks and hardware. Sources: https://data-apis.org/blog/array_api_v2024_release/ ; https://dmlc.github.io/dlpack/latest/

## 2026-03-16 — Tensor Surface Kit (shape/layout/device/interchange truth above numerical-library fragmentation)
- Re-read the latest archive and deliberately rebalanced toward an underrepresented scientific/numerical seam after several Cargo-heavy and productization-heavy revisions.
- `ndarray` already exposes a serious n-dimensional array vocabulary with `ArrayBase`, read-only views, and raw-storage traits. That is direct evidence that shape/layout/view semantics are already first-class Rust surface concerns rather than internal implementation details. Sources: https://docs.rs/ndarray/latest/ndarray/struct.ArrayBase.html ; https://docs.rs/ndarray/latest/ndarray/type.ArrayView.html ; https://docs.rs/ndarray/latest/ndarray/trait.RawData.html
- `nalgebra` explicitly distinguishes statically and dynamically sized matrices and uses column-major storage, while `faer` exposes owned and borrowed matrix vocabulary types (`Mat`, `MatRef`, `MatMut`). That is strong evidence that the Rust numerical ecosystem already has multiple legitimate dense-array/matrix families with materially different public semantics. Sources: https://www.nalgebra.rs/docs/user_guide/vectors_and_matrices/ ; https://docs.rs/nalgebra/latest/nalgebra/base/type.Matrix3.html ; https://docs.rs/faer/latest/faer/ ; https://docs.rs/faer/latest/faer/mat/index.html
- Candle and Burn both make tensor/runtime concepts explicit, but in different ways: Candle centers `Tensor`, `Shape`, `Layout`, and `Device`, while Burn centers backend/device/autodiff/tensor metadata and now has Burn Store for cross-framework tensor/model storage. That argues for a shared contract layer above runtimes rather than a runtime-winner story. Sources: https://docs.rs/candle-core/latest/candle_core/struct.Tensor.html ; https://docs.rs/candle-core/latest/candle_core/shape/index.html ; https://docs.rs/candle-core/latest/candle_core/layout/index.html ; https://docs.rs/burn/latest/burn/tensor/index.html ; https://docs.rs/burn/latest/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/burn/tensor/backend/index.html ; https://docs.rs/burn-store
- `argmin-math` already supports `Vec`, `ndarray`, `nalgebra`, and `faer`, which is excellent prior art for the claim that Rust numerical users already need multi-family interop without choosing one universal tensor type. Source: https://docs.rs/argmin-math/
- DLPack explicitly exists to provide a stable in-memory tensor exchange structure across frameworks and hardware backends, and Rust already has `dlpark` as a safe versioned wrapper/trait layer. That is direct evidence that exchange/adapter truth is now part of the real ecosystem surface. Sources: https://dmlc.github.io/dlpack/latest/ ; https://dmlc.github.io/dlpack/latest/c_api.html ; https://docs.rs/dlpark/latest/dlpark/versioned/index.html ; https://docs.rs/dlpark/latest/dlpark/traits/index.html
- `zarrs` demonstrates that Rust already has a serious multidimensional-array storage lane with metadata validation, while Arrow’s docs remain a good boundary reminder that table/columnar truth is adjacent but not the same as general tensor truth. Sources: https://docs.rs/zarrs/latest/zarrs/ ; https://docs.rs/zarrs/latest/zarrs/array/struct.Array.html ; https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html ; https://docs.rs/arrow-array/latest/arrow_array/struct.RecordBatch.html
- Archive decision: add `gaps/numerical-array-tensor-surfaces-and-interop-contracts.md`, `design/tensor-surface-kit.md`, `design/tensor-surface-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-tensor-surface-kit.md`; add Tensor Surface Kit to `PRIORITIES.md` as a Tier 1/2 candidate; and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep shape/dtype truth, layout/view truth, ownership/device/autodiff truth, interchange/storage truth, and adapter outcomes distinct.

## 2026-03-16 — Client Productization Stack (boring productization for real Rust apps)
- Recent archive revisions leaned heavily Cargo/build/publication oriented, and the archive’s own hygiene rules now explicitly warn against letting too many revisions in a row stay Cargo-heavy. This revision deliberately rebalances toward an underrepresented deployment domain: real desktop/mobile/embedded applications.
- Tauri 2 is stable and explicitly positions itself as a framework for building tiny, fast binaries across major desktop and mobile platforms, with Rust/Swift/Kotlin integration when needed. Its capabilities system makes permissions and webview/window security boundaries explicit, which is exactly the kind of app-surface truth a portable contract stack should preserve. Sources: https://v2.tauri.app/blog/tauri-20/ ; https://v2.tauri.app/security/capabilities/
- Dioxus now documents platform-specific setup for desktop, iOS, and Android, plus explicit desktop/mobile deployment guidance and says easier native-app distribution is a top priority. Slint explicitly positions itself across embedded, desktop, and mobile. Together, those are strong signals that “Rust apps” are real enough now that the missing problem is productization quality above the frameworks, not whether a Rust GUI/mobile story exists at all. Sources: https://dioxuslabs.com/learn/0.7/getting_started/ ; https://dioxuslabs.com/learn/0.7/tutorial/deploy/ ; https://docs.slint.dev/latest/docs/slint/
- AccessKit now presents itself as accessibility infrastructure for UI toolkits and explicitly lists multiple Rust integrations, including egui, Slint, Bevy, and Xilem. That is a strong signal that the ecosystem has a plausible shared a11y substrate and should stop treating accessibility as only framework-local glue or visual-testing fallout. Source: https://accesskit.dev/
- The mobile/client glue layer is still visibly fragmented: `cargo-mobile2` says it was created as a base for Tauri mobile support, can only promise maintenance for that single use case, and cannot broadly support non-Tauri uses. That is exactly the sort of ecosystem warning that argues for a portable contract/report layer instead of another one-framework wrapper. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-mobile2/latest
- Localization is also increasingly a real client/product surface rather than a nice-to-have: Project Fluent remains an expressive message system, ICU4X explicitly targets client-side and resource-constrained environments, and `i18n-embed` exists to embed localization assets into Rust binaries/libraries for runtime use. That argues for preserving locale/catalog/fallback/runtime-data truth as its own lane rather than burying it in app templates or framework-specific docs. Sources: https://projectfluent.org/ ; https://projectfluent.org/fluent/guide/ ; https://github.com/unicode-org/icu4x ; https://docs.rs/i18n-embed
- The OpenFeature Rust SDK is mature enough on providers, targeting, hooks, logging, named clients, shutdown, and extensibility to make rollout/channel work a plausible *later* client-productization consumer, but its eventing gap is also a healthy reminder not to over-promise v0. Source: https://openfeature.dev/docs/reference/sdks/server/rust/
- Support truth is moving under real users too: the rustdoc `doc_cfg` goal says readers currently have to read source to know item availability, and docs.rs changed its default targets to better reflect the current Rust ecosystem. ## 2026-03-16 — Tooling Contract Stack (Cargo discovery/plan/execute contracts for external tools)
- Rust’s 2026 roadmap explicitly puts **integrate Cargo into larger build systems** and **prototype cargo plumbing commands** in the active “Building blocks” flagship. That is strong evidence that machine-facing Cargo contracts are strategic Rust infrastructure, not just editor glue or enterprise-local build plumbing. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Cargo’s accepted plumbing goal says the current programmatic surfaces are still too porcelain-oriented: `cargo metadata` excludes feature resolution, older plumbing commands are deprecated or underpowered, `--build-plan` was not a durable answer, and the build can be decomposed into phases from project discovery through final-artifact staging. That is a direct signal that ideal Rust is missing a better reviewable contract layer for external tools. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- Cargo’s stable external-tools docs still center on only three general-purpose lanes — `cargo metadata`, `--message-format=json`, and custom subcommands — and they explicitly note that JSON build messages cannot control arbitrary output from other tools. That is useful, but it is not yet a coherent discovery→plan→execute story for IDEs, CI, wrappers, or outer build systems. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html
- Cargo’s build-cache docs now publicly separate **final artifacts** in `target-dir` from **intermediate build artifacts** in `build-dir`, while also saying the build-dir layout is internal and subject to change. The March 2026 build-dir-v2 call for testing sharpens the pain: many projects still rely on unspecified build-dir details because Cargo lacks the right features. That is exactly the kind of ecosystem signal that justifies a contract stack rather than another scraper. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- Cargo’s build-analysis experiment now emits JSONL session logs with rebuild reasons and report commands, but it is opt-in and explicitly not yet a user-facing stability promise. That strengthens the archive’s preferred shape: import Cargo-native report evidence where it exists, but keep discovery roots, graph/plan truth, live execution, and report-derived conclusions distinct. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo 1.94 reiterates that plugins matter because Cargo cannot be everything to everyone. That makes a plugin-first Tooling Contract Stack more plausible than waiting for Cargo itself to solve every external-tool need. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- Archive decision: add `design/tooling-contract-stack.md` and `design/tooling-contract-pilot-program.md`; update `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` and `PRIORITIES.md` so the archive treats **Repo Composition + Build Interop + Build-State Evidence** as one explicit machine-facing seam; promote **Build Interop Kit** to **Tier 0/1**; and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep discovery roots, package selection, planned graph, execution events, report imports, and downstream consumer conclusions distinct.

## 2026-03-16 — Service productization stack (boring production service contracts)
- The 2024 State of Rust survey says Rust is especially popular for **server backends, web and networking services, and cloud technologies**, that Rust-at-work usage keeps rising, and that companies are using it because it helps them build relatively correct and bug-free software. That is strong evidence that the ecosystem’s missing seam is no longer “can Rust serve HTTP?” but “how do teams make services reviewable, supportable, and operable without one giant platform framework?” Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/13/2024-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The same 2024 survey says slow compilation, debugging support, high disk usage, async struggles, slow/resource-intensive tooling, and IDE/interoperability pain remain material constraints. The 2025 survey keeps resource usage and debugging in the problem set and says online documentation remains the preferred canonical reference. Together that is a strong argument for a service-productization layer that treats **route truth + settings truth + runtime evidence + support/docs truth** as first-class artifacts instead of README prose and framework folklore. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/13/2024-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The 2026 flagship themes keep **Just Add Async** active, which means service/runtime ergonomics are still evolving rather than settled. In parallel, the rustdoc `doc_cfg` goal says readers still need to read source code today to know item availability, and the docs.rs target-default change shows docs/support targets are moving under real ecosystems. That means a credible service story must keep **behavior truth, runtime truth, and support/docs truth** distinct instead of assuming docs.rs output or one CI job proves support. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/rustdoc-doc-cfg.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/16/docsrs-changed-default-targets/
- Cargo 1.94 is another enabling signal: Cargo is pushing more structured reporting and still wrestling with workspace/config discovery, which makes an artifact-first, plugin-friendly service-productization layer more plausible now than it was when the archive first sketched service/config/obs/background ideas separately. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- Archive decision: add `design/service-productization-stack.md` and `design/service-productization-pilot-program.md`, update `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` and `PRIORITIES.md` so the archive treats **Service Surface + Runtime Settings + Observability + Async Reliability + Background Work + Support Envelope** as one ranked execution band, and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions do not flatten service contracts, config, telemetry, lifecycle, jobs, support truth, and downstream consumers into one fake production-readiness story.

## 2026-03-09 — Lint Governance Stack promotion (profile locks, baseline debt, and fixpack/apply handoff)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship roadmap explicitly includes establishing **safety-critical lints in Clippy**. That is strong evidence lint posture is now an assurance-facing ecosystem concern rather than only style or pedagogy. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Cargo’s manifest and workspace references now document stable `[lints]` and `[workspace.lints]` configuration, with explicit inheritance through `[lints] workspace = true`. That means selected lint posture and inheritance are now reviewable manifest facts instead of only `RUSTFLAGS` or crate attributes. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-lints-section ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
- Cargo’s unstable features now include `[lints.cargo]`, which means Cargo-native warning families are moving toward the same configuration plane rather than staying forever outside it. That strengthens the case for a shared governance boundary above engines and below verdicts. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html#lintscargo
- `cargo report` currently exposes future-incompatibility reports as a first-class report family, and Cargo’s future-incompat report docs are explicit that these are machine-usable package-scoped warnings about code that may be rejected by a future Rust version. That is strong evidence Cargo-side warning/report lanes already need an import path into broader lint/migration governance. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-report.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/future-incompat-report.html
- `cargo fix` is valuable but still not a sufficient governance layer: the Edition Guide says it can only work with a single configuration at a time and often needs multiple passes over features, targets, or packages, while the Cargo 1.90 development report says the current architecture is slow, only handles a subset of lints, and makes selective/interactive fixing difficult. That is strong evidence ideal Rust needs a clear handoff between suggested fixes and governed edit waves. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/editions/advanced-migrations.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/ ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html

## 2026-03-09 — Reflection Transition Stack promotion (macro burden, runtime reflection, and future compile-time reflection)
- Rust's 2026 flagship themes explicitly include **prototype reflection** under **Constify all the things**. That is strong evidence that reflection is no longer just an ecosystem side experiment; it is now an active language-adjacent frontier whose downstream effects are worth designing for early. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H2 reflection-and-comptime goal proposes a `const fn`-based compile-time reflection scheme, explicitly says proc-macro derives have historically been hard to debug and bootstrap from scratch, and says crates like `bevy_reflect` and `facet` would still exist afterwards but with different goals and methods. That sharpened the repo's missing seam from “one more reflection kit” to “a transition layer that can compare and migrate multiple reflection lanes honestly.” Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html
- The 2025H1 macro-improvements goal explicitly aims to make many macro use cases possible in `macro_rules!`, with the stated benefits of faster builds, simpler macros, and smaller dependency supply chains. That is strong evidence that today's proc-macro burden belongs in the same frontier conversation as future reflection rather than living in a separate tooling silo. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/macro-improvements.html
- The 2025 compiler-performance survey says stabilizing language features could remove the need for some build scripts or proc macros and speed up compilation across the ecosystem. That makes macro-removal and reflection/comptime substitution a build-performance issue as well as a metaprogramming issue. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- The current library landscape is heterogeneous in exactly the way the archive should care about: `bevy_reflect` offers general-purpose runtime reflection with dynamic interaction and runtime type metadata; `facet` exposes a `SHAPE` associated const with layout, field, doc-comment, and attribute metadata; `valuable` offers object-safe value inspection with `tracing` integration; and `serde_reflection` extracts version-controllable format descriptions. Together they show the ecosystem already has several legitimate but non-equivalent introspection lanes. Sources: https://docs.rs/bevy_reflect/latest/bevy_reflect/ ; https://docs.rs/facet/latest/facet/ ; https://docs.rs/valuable/latest/valuable/ ; https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/field/ ; https://docs.rs/serde-reflection/latest/serde_reflection/
- Archive decision: add `design/reflection-transition-stack.md` and `design/reflection-transition-pilot-program.md`; refresh `design/reflection-surface-kit.md`, `design/macro-workflow-kit.md`, `design/const-surface-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-reflection-surface-kit.md`; update priorities/frontier so **Reflection Transition Stack** becomes an explicit near-frontier seam and **Reflection Surface Kit** is promoted to **Tier 0/1**; and strengthen the archive's amnesia resistors so future revisions keep proc-macro burden, runtime reflection, compile-time reflection, registry semantics, and downstream adapter claims distinct.

## 2026-03-09 — Inventory Evidence Stack promotion (Cargo precursor truth, artifact linkage, and package→release→install continuity)
- Rust's 2026 flagships explicitly keep **SBOM generation** inside the active supply-chain agenda, which is strong evidence that dependency inventory is now an ecosystem-core seam rather than a compliance afterthought. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Cargo's unstable `sbom` support emits precursor files alongside compiled artifacts, exposes `CARGO_SBOM_PATH`, and allows duplicate crate entries when compiled differently. That means Cargo is surfacing build-lane inventory facts, but not yet claiming one universal package/release/install inventory truth. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- The Cargo SBOM tracking issue says the remaining work includes demonstrating end-to-end generation of an industry-standard SBOM from the precursor while explicitly keeping non-Rust dependencies out of scope for the precursor itself. That sharpened the repo's missing seam from “another exporter” to “a continuity layer above precursor and below downstream consumers.” Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/16565
- RFC 3553 is explicit that Cargo should emit a Cargo-specific precursor and let external tools project it into formats like SPDX or CycloneDX. That is strong evidence that format export should stay a projection layer, not the root of truth. Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3553
- `cargo package` rewrites and normalizes the published manifest and always includes `Cargo.lock` unless excluded, while `cargo install` ignores the packaged lockfile by default unless `--locked` is passed. That made the package→install divergence more central to the archive's inventory framing. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html
- `cargo-auditable` remains especially useful here because it proves binary-recovered dependency evidence is practical while also warning that SBOMs are not supply-chain verdicts. That strengthened the archive's decision to keep inventory evidence separate from trust and policy. Source: https://github.com/rust-secure-code/cargo-auditable

- The PubGrub-in-Cargo goal explicitly says the work is groundwork for better MSRV support, CVE-aware resolution, and a richer ecosystem of Cargo extensions. That is strong evidence that dependency resolution is becoming an extension seam rather than a black box whose only durable output is a lockfile. - Cargo’s unstable docs still expose `minimal-versions`, `direct-minimal-versions`, and `msrv-policy`, which are not random flags but named alternative objectives that teams already use to validate lower bounds and resolution posture. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo 1.93 documents publish-time-aware “time traveling dependency resolution” and ongoing exploration of `minimumReleaseAge`. That is exactly the kind of policy-sensitive objective that deserves an attachable strategy artifact instead of living in one CI command or maintainer notebook. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/

## 2026-03-09 — Manifest Truth Stack promotion (authored, packaged, frontmatter, and consumer-import truth)
- Cargo 1.94 makes manifest behavior look more strategic than cosmetic: TOML 1.1 compatibility, `cargo-cargofmt`, and workspace/config discovery are all active concerns. That is strong evidence that Cargo manifests remain a live boundary rather than a solved file format. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- `cargo package` explicitly rewrites and normalizes the published `Cargo.toml`, removes `[patch]`, `[replace]`, and `[workspace]`, and includes `Cargo.lock` by default. That means authored-manifest truth and packaged-manifest truth are already materially different artifacts, but the ecosystem still lacks a first-class semantic diff/report layer. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html
- RFC 3416 argues that feature descriptions, visibility, and deprecation metadata belong in Cargo manifests, and Cargo’s current planning still tracks visibility/deprecation follow-ons. That is strong evidence that the manifest is becoming more consumer-facing and review-sensitive rather than less important over time. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3416-feature-metadata.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The cargo-script/frontmatter RFCs widen the seam further by allowing embedded manifests in `.rs` files with explicit defaulting and field restrictions. That means manifest truth now spans both ordinary packages and lightweight script lanes. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3502-cargo-script.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3503-frontmatter.html
- Cargo’s external-tools docs say `cargo metadata` is the stable, versioned machine-readable interface, and `cargo info` provides an official human-readable consumer surface. Those are useful anchor points, but they still do not cover authored-vs-packaged diffs, frontmatter/defaulting truth, or consumer-lossiness across lanes. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-info.html

## 2026-03-09 — Publisher / source identity stack promotion (claims, authority, source truth, consumer handoff)
- crates.io’s Jan 2026 development update strengthened publish-authority signals directly on the registry side: the Security tab is now visible on crate pages, Trusted Publishing now supports GitLab CI/CD in addition to GitHub Actions, and crate owners can require Trusted Publishing only. That means publisher identity is becoming more issuer-backed and less purely token-backed. https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Cargo’s registry-authentication docs now explicitly require configured credential providers for authenticated registries, while the registries and source-replacement docs keep alternate registries and exact-copy replacements semantically distinct. That is strong evidence that source identity needs to be modeled explicitly instead of being flattened into one vague “custom registry” or “mirror” idea. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registry-authentication.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registries.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/source-replacement.html
- RFC 3243 remains the accepted optional-namespaces design, and the 2025H2 open-namespaces goal says Cargo/compiler work is partially implemented while crates.io work still needs coordination. That makes namespace control an active seam, but not one mature enough to carry all org/publisher/source use cases by itself. https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3243-packages-as-optional-namespaces.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/open-namespaces.html
- The Feb 2026 Internals survey threads are unusually useful here because they explicitly try to reduce circular debate and separate organizational-ownership, alternative-identifier, and registry-namespace design spaces. That supports a stack design that can stay useful even if the final namespace choice changes. https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/survey-of-organizational-ownership-and-registry-namespace-designs-for-cargo-and-crates-io/24027 ; https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/child-thread-survey-of-organizational-ownership-designs-for-cargo-and-crates-io/24028 ; https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/child-thread-survey-of-registry-namespace-designs-for-cargo-and-crates-io/24030
- Archive decision: refresh `gaps/org-ownership-and-registry-ux.md`, rewrite `design/org-identity-registry-ux-kit.md` around `cargo source` + `cargo publisher` plus `source-report/v0` / `publisher-report/v0` / `claim-report/v0`, add `design/publisher-source-identity-stack.md` and `design/publisher-source-identity-pilot-program.md`, refresh `proposals/epic-org-identity-registry-ux-kit.md`, and update priorities/frontier so publisher/source identity is now an explicit seam adjacent to Trust, Package Admission, and Distribution rather than a loose Tier-1 UX footnote.

## 2026-03-09 — Distribution Contract Stack promotion (consumer-side channel, fallback, and install receipts)
- Cargo’s install docs are still one of the clearest signals that consumer acquisition remains under-specified. `cargo install` manages locally installed binaries, can install from multiple sources, and by default ignores a packaged `Cargo.lock` unless `--locked` is used. That means “installed from crates.io” can already imply materially different dependency choices from what the publisher last built, which is exactly why the archive should stop flattening source-build installs and prebuilt installs into one outcome. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html
- The Rust book still frames `cargo install` as a convenience flow rather than a replacement for system packages. That is subtle but important evidence that Rust’s install/distribution story is natively multi-channel rather than secretly meant to collapse into one canonical mechanism. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch14-04-installing-binaries.html
- `cargo-binstall` is now mature enough to prove the prebuilt path is real, but its own docs still say unsupported crates may need explicit metadata and that signature support is initial/limited. That combination is strong evidence that the missing contribution is no longer “make binaries possible” but “make acquisition receipts, fallback behavior, and verification posture reviewable”. Sources: https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall/blob/main/README.md ; https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall/blob/main/SIGNING.md
- `cargo-dist` has crossed the threshold from nice release helper to genuine producer-side distribution substrate: it emits machine-readable manifests, installers, package-manager publishing hooks, and as of 0.31 adds mirror-capable `simple` hosting with ordered fallback. That sharpens the missing seam: producer-side release truth is converging, but consumer-side selection and installed-state truth still have no common receipt. Sources: https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist ; https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md
- crates.io’s January 2026 update strengthens publish-side truth with Security-tab advisory views, Trusted Publishing controls, blocked risky triggers, and `pubtime`, while Rust’s 2026 flagship themes keep supply-chain work active through public/private dependencies and SBOM support. Together, those are strong reasons to preserve package → release → install handoffs honestly instead of letting “published” silently stand in for “what users got”. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Archive decision: add `design/distribution-contract-stack.md`, `design/distribution-contract-pilot-program.md`, `proposals/epic-distribution-contract-kit.md`, and `gaps/consumer-install-selection-channels-mirrors-and-receipts.md`; refresh `design/release-pipeline-kit.md`, `design/signed-binaries-kit.md`, and `gaps/release-engineering-and-distribution-contract.md`; update `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` and `PRIORITIES.md` so the archive treats consumer-side acquisition as a first-class seam; and add a matching amnesia resistor so future revisions keep release truth, visible candidates, selection/fallback, verification posture, installed-state truth, and downstream support/incident conclusions separate.

## 2026-03-09 — Package-admission stack promotion (publish-side graph/exposure/inventory/trust/policy handoff)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes keep supply-chain work unusually concrete by explicitly naming **public/private dependencies** and **SBOM generation** as active milestones. That is a strong signal that package-admission review is not just a downstream-enterprise concern; it is part of the mainstream Cargo/crates.io direction. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The accepted public/private-dependencies goal is explicit that the feature is meant to help users catch accidental exposure of implementation details and help tooling identify what constitutes an API. That strengthens the archive’s decision to treat package admission as a coupled graph-plus-public-contract problem rather than a pure inventory or policy problem. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/pub-priv.html
- Cargo’s 1.94 development-cycle update still lists public/private dependencies as open work and keeps the Cargo SBOM Fragment work in planning. That is good evidence that the upstream substrate is real but the orchestration boundary is still missing. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- Cargo’s 1.93 development-cycle update says Cargo now supports package publish time in registry summaries and exposes time-traveling dependency resolution as an exploration path. That is exactly the sort of publish-side freshness/cooldown and archaeology input the archive should treat as package-admission evidence rather than burying in resolver lore. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- Cargo’s unstable feature surface now includes `public-dependency`, `sbom`, and `lockfile-publish-time`, which means package-admission-relevant seams are increasingly machine-facing and therefore more amenable to attachable artifacts. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- crates.io’s January 2026 update is the strongest registry-side signal: crate pages now have a Security tab, Trusted Publishing supports GitLab CI/CD, crate owners can require Trusted Publishing only, risky GitHub triggers are blocked, and `pubtime` is now in index entries. That makes it harder to justify leaving package-admission truth scattered across registry pages, CI settings, and local policy glue. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- crates.io’s February 2026 malicious-crate policy change says routine malicious-crate removals will always produce RustSec advisories while blog-post escalation is reserved for materially used or exploited crates. That supports keeping advisory imports as first-class trust/policy inputs instead of ambient blog scraping. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/13/crates.io-malicious-crate-update/
- Cargo’s publishing docs still frame publication as a durable, review-worthy act and recommend thinking through the full release process. That is another good reason to give package publication its own linked admission bundle before it gets swallowed by broader release orchestration. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html
- Archive decision: add [`design/package-admission-stack.md`](./design/package-admission-stack.md) and [`design/package-admission-pilot-program.md`](./design/package-admission-pilot-program.md), tighten [`STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`](./STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md) and [`PRIORITIES.md`](./PRIORITIES.md) so the archive treats **Dependency Control + Public API + SBOM Evidence + Trust Signals + Policy** as one explicit package-side execution band, and add an amnesia resistor requiring future package-admission revisions to keep graph truth, exposure truth, inventory truth, trust inputs, decision truth, and package-to-release handoff distinct.

## 2026-03-09 — Borrowing Frontier Stack refresh (trait truth + pointer truth + lending truth + initialization truth)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes now make the coupling explicit: **Beyond the `&`** keeps field projections, reborrow traits, and in-place initialization active, while **Unblocking dormant traits** keeps next-solver stabilization and the Sized hierarchy active. That is stronger evidence than the archive had previously encoded that pointer/reference semantics, trait evolution, lending patterns, and construction/destruction posture now form one frontier neighborhood rather than scattered language-adjacent curiosities. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H2 reborrow-traits goal is especially important because it says userland still cannot achieve **true reborrowing**, wants to remove `Pin` reborrow special-casing from `rustc`, and wants Rust-for-Linux custom reference experiments to move onto a core solution. That means the right ecosystem contribution is not to pretend crates can finish the language, but to publish honest reviewable surfaces around where they currently fall short. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/autoreborrow-traits.html
- The 2025H2 pin-ergonomics goal makes the same seam more concrete: pinned borrowing syntax, patterns, coercions, and receiver ergonomics are all still being designed, which means pointer and trait surfaces cannot be treated as settled folklore. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/pin-ergonomics.html
- The 2025H2 in-place-initialization goal says the ecosystem already has multiple competing crate-level approaches (including `pin-init`, C++ interop lanes, and kernel-facing patterns) and that the language now wants to learn from those experiments instead of leaving them forever fragmented. That is strong evidence that Initialization Surface should be tied into the same frontier story rather than left as a separate constructor note. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/in-place-initialization.html
- The 2025H2 Polonius goal explicitly motivates the improved borrow checker in part by future patterns such as lending iterators, which makes Lending Surface look less like an isolated async-library idea and more like one face of the same borrowing frontier. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/polonius.html
- RFC 3519 says user-defined smart pointers remain second-class citizens today and motivates `Receiver` partly from foreign-language and systems use cases that cannot honestly claim `&T` semantics. That strengthens the archive’s decision that future pointer/trait work must keep foreign-semantic honesty and receiver posture explicit rather than flattening everything into “smart pointers like references”. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3519-arbitrary-self-types-v2.html
- Archive decision: add `design/borrowing-frontier-stack.md` and `design/borrowing-frontier-pilot-program.md`, update `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` and `PRIORITIES.md` so **Trait Surface Kit + Pointer Surface Kit + Lending Surface Kit + Initialization Surface Kit** are treated as a shared **Borrowing Frontier Stack**, and strengthen archive memory aids so future revisions keep trait-family semantics, pointer/reference semantics, lending/sequence semantics, and initialization/destruction semantics distinct instead of flattening them into one fake “borrowing support” story.

## 2026-03-09 — Harness Protocol Kit (testing contract layer above run evidence)

- The Testing Team RFC is a strong signal that Rust’s testing problem is organizationally and technically cross-cutting: it explicitly says the automated testing experience spans `cargo test`, libtest, rustdoc doctests, CI, IDEs, and external tools, and asks what underlying needs sit beneath nextest and the proliferation of external frameworks. That argues for a shared contract layer, not only a better runner or output mode: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3455-t-test.html
- The libtest JSON RFC is stronger than “please stabilize JSON”. It explicitly wants Cargo `test`/`bench` UX on top of programmatic output, expects a future Cargo RFC so custom harnesses can opt into the protocol, and evaluates the design against benches, doctests, parameterization, markers, locations, and metrics. That is the clearest current evidence that a **Harness Protocol Kit** is a distinct seam rather than just more detail inside Test Run Evidence: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3558-libtest-json.html
- Cargo’s `bench` docs make the stable-vs-nightly split especially clear: `cargo bench` can drive either libtest or a custom harness, but `#[bench]` remains unstable/nightly-only. This means stable benchmarking already depends on ecosystem harnesses and conventions, which strengthens the case for a portable harness contract instead of another benchmark-only tool: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-bench.html
- Cargo’s `test` docs say doctest execution details are not guaranteed and may change, which is exactly why doctest posture should be declared as a capability/adapter boundary instead of being smuggled in as a hidden assumption inside run reports: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-test.html
- Cargo 1.94 still lists finishing the libtest JSON experiment as work needing owners, so this seam is still live. Archive decision: add **Harness Protocol Kit** (`cargo harness` + `harness-capability-report/v0` + `harness-discovery-report/v0` + `harness-adapter-report/v0` + `harness-pack/v0`), add a ranked pilot program, refresh the existing testing stack so harness capability/discovery sits upstream of run/result evidence, and strengthen archive memory aids so later revisions do not collapse harness truth, run truth, benchmark metrics, and doctest posture into one fake universal testing story.

## 2026-03-09 — Trust Decision Stack refresh (issuer-aware trust evidence, policy handoff, thin views)
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update says crate pages now expose a Security tab for RustSec advisories, GitLab CI/CD support for Trusted Publishing, Trusted Publishing-only mode, blocked risky GitHub Actions triggers, and a new `pubtime` field in index entries. That is unusually strong evidence that the registry now emits multiple trust-relevant facts, but still lacks one portable evidence/report layer that can feed review, policy, and registry/search UX coherently. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- The crates.io malicious-crate notification update says the team will usually publish RustSec advisories rather than a blog post for every malware removal unless there is evidence of real-world usage or exploitation. That is healthy, but it increases the value of local attachable trust artifacts and diffable reports instead of ambient incident-post awareness. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/13/crates.io-malicious-crate-update/
- Cargo’s publishing reference remains explicit that a publish is permanent, versions cannot be overwritten, and code cannot be deleted. That keeps package-release and release-candidate trust review high-leverage: the decision point is real, durable, and not easily reversible. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html
- Cargo Vet’s docs make the trust side of the stack much more operational than the archive had encoded. The tool already models imported audits, built-in `safe-to-run` / `safe-to-deploy` criteria, subtree-sensitive policies, violations, and audit-backlog reduction. That is direct evidence that ideal Rust does not need another scanner first; it needs a portable trust substrate and a cleaner handoff into policy. Sources: https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/how-it-works.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/audit-criteria.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/specifying-policies.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/performing-audits.html
- Rust’s 2026 flagships keep supply-chain work active through public/private dependency and SBOM milestones, which means trust/policy/inventory composition is still part of the near-term agenda rather than an afterthought. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Archive decision: add `design/trust-decision-stack.md` and `design/trust-signals-pilot-program.md`, refresh `design/trust-signals-kit.md` and `proposals/epic-trust-signals-kit.md`, clarify the explicit **Trust Decision Stack** in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, tighten `PRIORITIES.md` so Trust Signals now advances through a ranked evidence-first pilot program, and remove the confusing `trust-policy/v0` overlap so Policy Kit remains the owner of verdicts, waivers, and decision reports.

## 2026-03-09 — Conformance Traceability Stack refresh (spec text, acceptance reality, assurance imports)
- RFC 3355, the rust-lang-owned FLS publication work, and the FLS-upkeep goal make Rust’s specification trajectory much more operational than the archive had been treating it. The missing problem is no longer whether Rust should have specification text, but how that text becomes attachable evidence without collapsing into compiler-internal harnesses or prose-only process. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3355-rust-spec.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/spec-fls-publish.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/FLS-up-to-date-capabilities.html

That is strong evidence that conformance artifacts now have real downstream assurance consumers rather than being only language-team nice-to-haves. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/mcdc-coverage-support.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/safe-unsafe-for-safety-critical.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/safety-critical-lints-in-clippy.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/stabilize-fls-releases.html
- The experimental language-specification goal and the a-mir-formality integration direction make another missing seam explicit: ideal Rust needs to preserve stable text, experimental text, executable vectors, and compiler-lane acceptance reality as related but non-identical truths. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/experimental-language-specification.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reference-expansion.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/a-mir-formality.html
- The std-contract goal strengthens the same picture from the assurance side: Rust is increasingly able to publish programmatic contracts and verification-oriented semantics, but those consumers still need a shared conformance subject rather than bespoke restatements of language truth. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/std-contracts.html
- Archive decision: add `design/conformance-traceability-stack.md` and `design/spec-conformance-pilot-program.md`, refresh `design/spec-conformance-kit.md` and `proposals/epic-spec-conformance-kit.md`, promote Spec Conformance Kit from Tier 1 to Tier 0/1 in `PRIORITIES.md`, and add a new emerging seam to `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so the archive now treats **Spec Conformance + Acceptance Surface + Safety-Critical Evidence** as one traceability band instead of scattered adjacent ideas.

## 2026-03-09 — Migration Truth Stack frontier refresh (upgrade choreography, destination semantics, archaeology)
- The Edition Guide’s advanced migration path still treats edition upgrades as staged, configuration-sensitive work rather than one command. That remains strong evidence that Rust migrations need explicit source/destination/program truth instead of command-transcript folklore. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/editions/advanced-migrations.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html

That sharply supports the archive’s insistence on separating mechanical edit output from intended destination semantics. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/20/Rust-1.85.0/
- Cargo’s 1.90 development report and the 2025 GSoC results both say the current `cargo fix` architecture is slow, incomplete, and awkward for selective/interactive use. That is direct evidence that a worthy contribution here should live above whichever edit architecture wins, not pretend to replace the whole problem with one better fixer. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/18/gsoc-2025-results/
- Cargo’s `rust-version` docs say workspaces can have multiple Rust-version policies and that verification can get complicated, while rustup already makes committed toolchain selection and overrides explicit. That means toolchain/MSRV migrations are a real orchestration seam, not just a manifest edit or one CI job. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/rust-version.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/overrides.html
- Rust’s 2026 flagship supply-chain work still includes public/private dependencies, and the 2025H2 `cargo-semver-checks` goal says publish-path semver checking still needs better provenance/type-sensitive reasoning. docs.rs now hosts rustdoc JSON. Together these make migration packs much more valuable because API/docs/support evidence increasingly has machine-usable downstream consumers. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/pub-priv.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html ; https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json
- Archive decision: add `design/migration-truth-stack.md` and `design/migration-pilot-program.md`, refresh `design/migration-kit.md` and `proposals/epic-migration-kit.md`, and promote migration from a worthy standalone idea into a ranked frontier orchestration seam. The next credible move is a five-lane pilot program: edition transition truth first, workspace toolchain / `rust-version` truth second, dependency-upgrade + API/MSRV truth third, docs/support/downstream truth fourth, and release/archaeology / migration-diff truth fifth.

## 2026-03-08 — Dependency-control stack refresh (selection truth, feature truth, policy handoffs)
- Cargo’s current direction makes dependency selection policy much more real than the archive had encoded. The 2026 flagships still keep **Secure your supply chain** active with public/private dependencies as an explicit milestone, which means dependency-boundary truth remains part of upstream Rust’s near-term agenda rather than a niche tooling wish. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The public/private dependencies goal is especially clarifying because its motivation is not just security theater: it is about helping users catch accidental implementation-detail exposure and helping tooling identify what constitutes an API. That means chosen dependency edges and API-boundary consumers are now connected by design, not merely by downstream convention. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/pub-priv.html
- Cargo 1.93 adds another important signal: dependency-resolution summaries are gaining publish-time information and Cargo is explicitly exploring “time traveling dependency resolution”. That makes selection policy visible in a new way; ideal Rust should be able to export which graph was chosen under which time or upgrade assumptions instead of hiding that in command history and lockfile churn. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- Cargo’s unstable docs now expose both `resolver.feature-unification` and `public-dependency`, while the resolver docs remain explicit that workspace builds unify dependency features across selected packages and that separate invocations may be required to avoid that. This is strong evidence that feature posture and chosen-graph posture should be reviewed together more often than the archive had been doing. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/resolver.html
- The PubGrub-in-Cargo goal and the November 2025 cargo-semver-checks update sharpen the same seam from different directions: richer resolver infrastructure should enable better error messages, MSRV support, and cargo extensions, while semver tooling still says getting dependency features right has many Cargo-specific edge cases. That is a strong argument for a shared dependency-control substrate rather than separate per-tool re-derivation. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/pubgrub-in-cargo.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/16/Project-Goals-2025-November-Update.md/

## 2026-03-08 — Async reliability stack (shutdown truth, replay truth, deterministic-simulation truth)
- The 2025H1 async flagship still describes async as a multi-year parity effort and is unusually explicit that runtime choice, runtime interoperability, cancellation sharp edges, and reliability remain core pain points. That is strong evidence that the missing contribution is still ecosystem structure, not just one more runtime helper: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/async.html
- The 2026 flagship themes keep **Just Add Async** active with milestones around return type notation, `async fn in dyn Trait`, immobile types / guaranteed destructors, and ergonomic ref-counting. That means the language is still unblocking async, so the archive should emphasize portable contracts and pilot discipline rather than pretend the async story has already settled: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The May 2025 project-goals update says the Async Book gained chapters on concurrency primitives, structured concurrency, and pinning, while the Async Book itself still says async Rust has compatibility constraints and a higher maintenance burden. Together those signals say the ecosystem now has enough shared vocabulary to standardize around lifecycle/replay/simulation seams, but not enough maturity to flatten them into one fake abstraction: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/06/20/may-project-goals-update/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/async-book/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/async-book/01_getting_started/03_state_of_async_rust.html
- Tokio’s official graceful-shutdown guidance is another strong clue: it normalizes `CancellationToken` and `TaskTracker` for telling tasks to stop and waiting for them to finish. That means the next worthy contribution is not inventing graceful shutdown from scratch; it is exporting portable lifecycle truth and then connecting it cleanly to replay and deterministic-simulation consumers: https://tokio.rs/tokio/topics/shutdown ; https://docs.rs/tokio-util/latest/tokio_util/task/task_tracker/struct.TaskTracker.html
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says resource usage remains high among notable productivity problems and debugging remains a notable problem, while docs remain the preferred canonical reference. That is exactly the environment where a reviewable async reliability layer matters: people need better artifacts for shutdown failures, hangs, and timing-sensitive behavior without replacing the canonical docs/runtime guidance story: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add `design/async-reliability-stack.md` and `design/async-reliability-pilot-program.md`, refresh async/replay/DST docs so they route through one ranked stack, update `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` and `PRIORITIES.md` so the archive treats **Async Lifecycle + Replay + DST** as a shared execution band, and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep lifecycle, replay, and exploration truths separate.

## 2026-03-08 — Test execution evidence stack (run truth, config ids, attachable consumers)
- The Rust project is now unusually explicit that machine-readable test output is a real ecosystem seam. The libtest JSON goal says libtest is Cargo’s default harness, that people had come to rely on programmatic output, and that Cargo wants this partly to support better summaries, smarter execution, and lower-friction custom-runner experiments like `cargo nextest` and `libtest-mimic`: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/libtest-json.html
- Cargo 1.94 still lists finishing libtest JSON among the focus areas needing owners, which means the seam is alive and strategically relevant rather than already solved: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- nextest already looks like infrastructure, not just a nicer runner. Its docs expose machine-readable test and binary lists, JUnit output, experimental libtest-like JSON run output, stable run ids and binary ids, and explicit future work toward richer newline-delimited JSON. That means the missing contribution is less “invent a better runner” and more “define one portable result boundary that runners can publish into honestly”: https://nexte.st/docs/machine-readable/ ; https://nexte.st/docs/glossary/
- Execution semantics are now part of the truth, not an implementation footnote. nextest’s Miri integration says process-per-test can make Miri runs 3–4× faster, while also losing visibility into races between tests sharing resources. `cargo-llvm-cov` already exports multiple machine-readable formats, and `cargo-mutants` already writes structured run directories (`mutants.json`, `outcomes.json`, diff/log refs) that other programs can read while the run is in progress. Together that says specialized testing tools now need a shared execution substrate, not another console-only integration layer. Sources: https://nexte.st/docs/integrations/miri/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-llvm-cov/latest/source/README.md ; https://mutants.rs/mutants-out.html ; https://mutants.rs/list.html
- Archive decision: add `gaps/test-run-machine-readable-and-reviewable-results.md`, `design/test-run-evidence-kit.md`, `design/test-execution-evidence-stack.md`, `design/test-execution-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-test-run-evidence-kit.md`; promote **Test Run Evidence Kit** in `PRIORITIES.md`; add **Test Execution Evidence Stack** to `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep test inventory, run profiles, specialized attachments, flake observations, and downstream conclusions distinct instead of flattening them into one vague testing scorecard.

## 2026-03-08 — Safety-critical evidence stack (authority, criterion, runtime, proof)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship roadmap is unusually explicit that Safety-Critical Rust is not one vague aspiration but a bundle of concrete evidence seams: MC/DC coverage support, normative `unsafe` documentation, safety-critical lints in Clippy, and FLS release cadence. That makes the archive’s earlier safety materials look under-synthesized rather than over-ambitious: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The safety-critical adoption writeup makes the execution lesson very clear: as criticality rises, process, verification, and evidence costs rise too, and teams are strongly incentivized to isolate the highest-criticality logic into the smallest surface area possible. That is a strong argument for scoped pilot lanes and against any fake “certified crate” story: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
- The upstream safety work is now rich enough that the missing contribution is orchestration and evidence discipline, not raw ambition. The MC/DC goal says compiler-integrated support is the viable path and that the old implementation was removed for maintenance reasons; the normative-unsafe-docs goal says current authoritative documentation is insufficient for rigorous safety cases; the Clippy goal says a substantial lint volume is expected; and the FLS goals say spec upkeep and cadence are becoming operational commitments. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/mcdc-coverage-support.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/safe-unsafe-for-safety-critical.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/safety-critical-lints-in-clippy.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/FLS-up-to-date-capabilities.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/stabilize-fls-releases.html
- The right archive move is therefore not another standalone kit. It is to treat **Safety Evidence Kit + Coverage Evidence Kit + Sanitizer Battery Kit + Formal Verification Kit** as one shared **Safety-Critical Evidence Stack**, then add a ranked pilot program so the archive starts with unsafe-heavy library review and only later widens toward proof-augmented modules and certification-facing release candidates.
- Archive decision: add `design/safety-critical-evidence-stack.md` and `design/safety-critical-pilot-program.md`, refresh the safety/coverage/sanitizer/verification design layer plus the safety epic, update the frontier and priorities to name the stack explicitly, and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep authority classes, coverage criteria, runtime/proof lanes, waiver budgets, and consumer claims distinct.

## 2026-03-08 — Wasm component execution refresh (native Cargo transition, bridge lane, composition truth)
- Rust’s 2026 flagships explicitly include **Wasm Components**, which is already enough to justify treating this as more than a side topic. The missing question is what kind of contribution composes with that push instead of duplicating it: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The official component-model Rust guide is now more interesting than the archive’s earlier wording captured. It says Rust has first-class component targets, shows native `cargo build --target wasm32-wasip2`, says `cargo-component` is being deprecated as native tooling can be used directly, and yet also says custom-WIT bindings still require `wit-bindgen`. That is not a settled ecosystem; it is a transition state that especially benefits from reviewable contract layers: https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org/language-support/building-a-simple-component/rust.html
- `cargo component` is therefore not “obsolete”; it is transitional and still materially important. Its README still calls it experimental, still documents adapter-based preview1→preview2 flows, still says the upstream `wasm32-wasip2` target is not a complete replacement for all workflows, still offers `cargo component publish` for Warg registries, and still requires a rust-analyzer check-command override in some cases. That means the archive should preserve native-Cargo and `cargo-component` lanes separately instead of pretending one has already won: https://github.com/bytecodealliance/cargo-component
- `wkg` / `wasm-pkg-tools` sharpen the registry side in the same direction. Their docs describe shared config intended for use by other language-specific tooling, support for OCI and Warg registries, and a standardized `wkg.lock`. That makes package and publication identity much more real than a build-log-only workflow: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-pkg-common/0.13.0
- Archive decision: add `design/wasm-component-pilot-program.md`, refresh the Wasm-component design/epic/gap docs around transition-aware execution, update the frontier and priorities so this area now has a ranked rollout (native Cargo export → `cargo-component` bridge → composition/host requirements → registry/package identity → downstream consumer imports), and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep identity layers and lane differences distinct.

## 2026-03-08 — ScriptKit promotion (single-file package truth, ranked pilots, explicit consumer imports)
- cargo-script is now a 2026 flagship, which means single-file packages are no longer just ecosystem folklore or a third-party convenience story. The archive should treat this as real upstream motion worth composing with: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Cargo’s unstable-features docs are now unusually concrete about single-file packages: they are selected through `--manifest-path`, can embed frontmatter, infer `package.name` and `package.edition`, forbid several workspace/build-script-style fields, place their default target dir under `$CARGO_HOME/target/<hash>`, and store the lockfile in `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. That is strong evidence that the missing contribution is shifting from “can Cargo run this?” to “can humans and tools review the lane honestly?” https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- The January 2026 program-management update sharpens the use case: cargo-script is explicitly framed as great for minimal bug reproducers and quick prototypes, and it shows the direct `cargo file.rs` / shebang posture. That means one-file packages now touch support, debugging, and issue-routing workflows rather than staying a niche scripting topic: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/11/program-management-update-2026-01/
- The remaining gaps are largely import/consumer discipline. The December 2025 goals update still listed rustdoc handling of frontmatter in doctests as a blocker; Cargo 1.94 says cargo-script starts with workspace auto-discovery disabled amid broader workspace/config discovery problems; rust-analyzer still has an open shebang-support issue; and Cargo still has open UX questions around suppressing Cargo noise on no-change script runs. Together, that says the next worthy contribution is not a new runner but a **script-truth layer** with honest partial-support reports. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/05/project-goals-2025-december-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/ ; https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/issues/15318 ; https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/16388
- Archive decision: add `design/scriptkit-pilot-program.md`, refresh the ScriptKit gap/design/epic docs around subject identity + frontmatter/default truth + lock/cache/discovery posture + consumer-import reports, promote ScriptKit in `PRIORITIES.md`, add a frontier note that one-file package truth is now a first-class emerging seam, and add an amnesia resistor so future revisions keep standalone-vs-workspace, inferred-vs-explicit fields, import lossiness, and policy posture distinct.

## 2026-03-08 — Build-state evidence execution refresh (shared stack, ranked pilots, grounded diagnosis)
- The archive already ranked the **Build-State Evidence Stack** highly, but it still lacked the execution layer that would turn that ranking into a real contribution plan. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/

That means any serious contribution must keep layout/locking/reuse truth separate from diagnosis or optimization claims. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-dir-layout.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/ ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html

Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/relink-dont-rebuild.html
- The user-pain side remains strong enough to justify promotion. The 2025 State of Rust survey still lists resource usage, especially slow compile times and storage usage, among the biggest productivity problems; the 2025 compiler-performance survey also says users want better explanations of slow builds and mentions editor latency and rust-analyzer performance as blockers. That makes a ranked pilot order centered on everyday developer pain more credible than jumping straight to remote-cache architecture or giant dashboards. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- Archive decision: add `design/build-state-evidence-stack.md` and `design/build-state-evidence-pilot-program.md`, refresh Build Cache / Change Impact / Build Doctor around the shared stack, update the frontier/priorities so build-state work now advances through a ranked pilot program, and add a new amnesia resistor requiring lane profile, imported evidence, reuse/block distinctions, impact truth, diagnosis scope, and scorecards to remain separate.

## 2026-03-08 — Repo Composition Stack (workspace discovery, default-members truth, config-layer visibility)
- Cargo’s configuration docs are unusually explicit that `.cargo/config.toml` files are probed hierarchically through parent directories up to `$CARGO_HOME`. That means discovery root and config-layer visibility are real behavior, not just debugging trivia: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html
- Cargo’s workspaces docs make package-selection posture first-class via `default-members`, clarify root-package vs virtual-workspace behavior, and keep `package.workspace`, `workspace.package`, `workspace.dependencies`, `workspace.lints`, and `workspace.metadata` in one place. That is strong evidence that repo composition is broader than nested-workspace explanation alone: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
- Cargo’s changelog/release notes say `cargo metadata` now includes `workspace_default_members`, and that `cargo new` / `cargo init` automatically inherit workspace fields. That means package-selection and workspace-scaffolding truth are now more machine-visible and ecosystem-facing than when the archive first added Workspace Governance Kit: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html
- Cargo 1.93 resumed active `-Zconfig-include` work, including richer include forms and optional-include direction. That is a strong signal that config layering is getting more expressive and therefore more deserving of explanation/diff tooling: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- Cargo 1.94 explicitly calls out workspace/config discovery as a design problem because broken or nightly-only parent `Cargo.toml` / `.cargo/config.toml` files can interfere with unrelated workspaces, and it discusses opt-out ideas around workspace auto-discovery. That makes discovery-boundary diagnostics a first-class near-term need rather than a niche ergonomics bug: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The accepted Cargo plumbing goal remains the deeper substrate signal: Cargo’s current machine-facing surface is still too porcelain-oriented, `cargo metadata` excludes feature resolution, and build work naturally splits into discovery / workspace-read / lock / resolve-features / plan / execute / stage phases. That makes a repo-composition stack a plausible companion layer rather than an arbitrary abstraction: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- Archive decision: add a new synthesis layer around the existing Workspace Governance Kit + Config Set Kit + Build Interop Kit, centered on **repo composition truth** rather than a new mega-kit; promote it in the frontier and add a ranked pilot program that starts with workspace truth and discovery diagnostics before widening to cross-tool consumers.

- The 2025H2 reborrow-traits goal says userland still cannot achieve **true reborrowing**, and specifically wants users of crates like `reborrow` to be able to move to a core solution. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/autoreborrow-traits.html
- The 2025H2 pin-ergonomics goal says async and generators depend on pinning, but pinning still has notoriously poor ergonomics. - RFC 2996 makes the case for a shared `AsyncIterator` trait and explicitly frames it as the async analogue of `Iterator`, while also showing why the current `poll_next` / object-safety story is still incomplete. RTN and async-closures work make returned-future bounds and borrowing callbacks more expressible, but they do not eliminate the need for honest adapter semantics. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2996-async-iterator.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3654-return-type-notation.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3668-async-closures.html

- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online documentation remains the preferred canonical reference, while the learning and editor/tooling data hint that more questions are moving into LLM tooling and agentic/editor workflows. - Cargo’s 1.90 development-cycle report says the current `cargo fix` architecture can be slow, only applies a subset of lints, and is hard to make selective or interactive because it runs in a special `rustc`-proxy mode with a cross-process lock. - The GSoC 2025 `cargo-fixit` writeup says moving control to the top-level program makes it easier to coordinate what fixes get applied, removes the locking bottleneck, and opens the door to interactive selection. That directly supports making candidate selection / apply / verify first-class archive artifacts: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/18/gsoc-2025-results/
- Cargo’s 1.93 development-cycle report says the structured-logging schema discussion matters partly because unifying that schema with Cargo JSON output could unblock a new, faster, more flexible `cargo fix` architecture. That is strong evidence that edit-governance artifacts should be designed to compose with Cargo’s broader machine-facing report work rather than living as one-off editor glue: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- The Cargo Book and Edition Guide together show why edit governance must preserve phase and incompleteness truth: `cargo fix` applies `rustc` suggestions automatically, but edition migration can require target-by-target / feature-by-feature runs, partial migration, `--broken-code`, and manual macro or doctest follow-up. That means candidate discovery, selection, application, and verification are different truths: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/editions/advanced-migrations.html
- docs.rs now hosts rustdoc JSON with explicit `format_version` handling, and the StableMIR goal explicitly aims to let tool developers build analysis and development tools on a stable interface. That strengthens the archive’s view that canonical machine-usable context should sit underneath edit producers rather than inside them: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/stable-mir.html
- rust-analyzer’s docs show that assist quality and analysis behavior depend on configuration such as borrow-checking term-search assists and whether build scripts are run for precise analysis. That is further evidence that editor-originated edits need explicit context/provenance rather than being treated as universally valid facts: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration ; https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/other_editors.html
- Archive decision: add `design/edit-governance-pilot-program.md`, strengthen the Semantic Context / Edit Workflow connection, and make the next credible move a ranked rollout (compiler suggestions → Cargo fix / edition waves → rust-analyzer assist export → assistant proposals under manual review → CI consumers) instead of another opaque autofix or direct assistant patch lane.
