- Cargo Vet’s intro also says projects can share audits, record relative audits between versions, and defer pre-existing gaps via exceptions ratcheted down over time. That is strong evidence that the missing contribution is not a replacement audit engine, but a common explanation-and-waiver boundary over imported evidence and local decisions. https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/
- cargo-deny’s config docs say checks can be filtered to the targets you actually build for; its advisories docs cover security and unmaintained-crate signals; its bans docs cover explicit crate bans and duplicate-version handling; its license docs expose SPDX-oriented allowlists, exceptions, and clarification records; and its CLI docs expose check-specific exit-code bits for advisories, bans, licenses, and sources. That is strong evidence that the ecosystem already has rich policy ingredients, but still lacks a shared artifact that preserves inputs, rules, reasons, and decision outcomes together. https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/cfg.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/advisories/index.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/bans/index.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/licenses/cfg.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/cli/check.html
- The `cargo-audit` docs say it audits dependencies against RustSec advisories and can also scan binaries with `cargo audit bin`, while the `rustsec` crate docs say the library audits `Cargo.lock` files and also includes binary-scanning and OSV-export support. That is good evidence that policy increasingly needs to reason about both workspace-time and artifact-linked evidence, but still has no standard decision pack for doing so. https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-audit/latest ; https://docs.rs/rustsec/latest/rustsec/
- Archive decision: rewrite **Policy Kit** as a first-class **Tier 0/1 steering-shortlist substrate** centered on `policy-subject/v0` + `policy-input-catalog/v0` + `policy-rule-catalog/v0` + `policy-waiver/v0` + `policy-decision-report/v0` + `policy-diff-report/v0` + `policy-pack/v0`, explicitly bounded against Trust Signals Kit, Lifecycle Ledger Kit, SBOM Evidence Kit, Incident Kit, and registry-native UI. The key design move is to treat policy as a reviewable decision layer over imported evidence rather than as one more scanner or one fake ecosystem-wide score.

## 2026-03-07 — Sanitizer Battery Kit rewrite (analysis lanes, runtime provenance, diffable findings)
- Rust’s 2025H2 sanitizer goal explicitly aims to stabilize MemorySanitizer and ThreadSanitizer for Tier 1 targets and to provide sanitizer-instrumented standard libraries through rustup, which is strong evidence that Rust is moving from “expert nightly hack” to real distributed sanitizer workflows. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/stabilization-of-sanitizer-support.html
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes keep sanitizers inside the mainstream story for specialized build scenarios. That is further evidence that the archive should treat dynamic analysis as infrastructure rather than as a niche appendix to safety. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The unstable-book sanitizer docs still show substantial lane divergence: support varies by engine and target, some flows require `--target` and `-Zbuild-std`, CFI requires LTO, and cross-language CFI needs matching clang-side normalization flags. That is strong evidence that “engine selected” and “runtime/instrumentation provenance” must be separate artifacts. https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/sanitizer.html
- The rustc exploit-mitigations chapter documents a broader hardening surface including safe stack and shadow call stack, which means the missing contribution is not just a nicer ASan wrapper but a substrate for heterogeneous runtime-checking and mitigation lanes. https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/exploit-mitigations.html
- Miri’s README says it defaults to deterministic execution and host isolation, approximates Rust UB under the current compiler, and has limited support for platform APIs and native FFI. That is clear evidence that execution semantics and visibility bounds must be explicit metadata rather than folklore. https://github.com/rust-lang/miri
- `nextest`’s Miri integration says process-per-test execution can make Miri 3–4× faster but loses visibility into races between tests sharing a resource. That is an unusually crisp example of why runner semantics belong in the artifact family. https://nexte.st/docs/integrations/miri/
- `cargo-careful` documents a distinct middle lane: std with debug assertions, extra UB checks, optional sanitizer integration, and support for arbitrary system/C FFI calls. That justifies modeling lane families rather than pretending Miri and native execution differ only by speed. https://github.com/RalfJung/cargo-careful
- The retag/codegen goal and BorrowSanitizer’s February 2026 update together show a credible future lane for native aliasing instrumentation with improving diagnostics and LLVM integration. That is strong evidence that the archive should leave explicit room for future engines instead of freezing the design around today’s sanitizers. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/codegen_retags.html ; https://borrowsanitizer.com/status/february_2026.html
- Archive decision: rewrite and promote **Sanitizer Battery Kit** as a **Tier 0/1** candidate centered on `sanitize-subject/v0` + `sanitize-lane-profile/v0` + `sanitize-runtime-profile/v0` + `sanitize-capability-profile/v0` + `sanitize-observation-report/v0` + `sanitize-finding-report/v0` + `sanitize-waiver/v0` + `sanitize-diff-report/v0` + `sanitize-pack/v0`, explicitly bounded against Safety Evidence Kit, Replay Kit, FFI Boundary Kit, Sysroot Pack Kit, and Compile-Time Capabilities Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Reflection Surface Kit (type-shape metadata, value access, registry truth)
- The 2025H2 reflection-and-comptime goal is unusually direct that ecosystem innovation is hindered when new general-purpose crates must convince everyone else to adopt their traits and derives; it names serialization, logging/tracing, and game-engine state inspection as motivating examples, and proposes compile-time reflection specifically to reduce that lock-in. That is strong evidence that the missing contribution is not another local reflection crate, but a reusable boundary over reflection acquisition and exposure: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html
- The same goal explicitly says crates like `bevy_reflect` and `facet` would still exist even if reflection lands in core, but with different goals and methods for exposing reflection information. That is a crucial archive-design signal: a worthy contribution should help compare reflection lanes honestly, not pretend one future feature erases today's library ecosystems: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html
- Rust's 2026 flagship themes include **prototype reflection** under **Constify all the things**, which is further evidence that reflection is becoming a strategic library-design frontier rather than only a niche experimental topic: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- `bevy_reflect` describes itself as a general-purpose runtime reflection solution that allows dynamic interaction with values, runtime type metadata, and reflected serialization/deserialization, while also noting that missing language features impose limitations. That is strong evidence that the ecosystem already needs a way to state which reflection powers are actually present instead of overloading a crate name: https://docs.rs/bevy_reflect/latest/bevy_reflect/
- `bevy_reflect`'s `TypeRegistry` and feature flags show that registration/discovery is already an operational surface, not an implementation detail: `register_derived_types` depends on auto-registration support, and the inventory-backed path is explicitly not supported on all platforms. That justifies giving registry/discovery its own artifact instead of hiding it under generic “reflection support”: https://docs.rs/bevy_reflect/latest/bevy_reflect/struct.TypeRegistry.html ; https://docs.rs/crate/bevy_reflect/0.17.3/source/Cargo.toml.orig
- `facet` says it provides reflection via a `SHAPE` associated const with layout, field, doc-comment, and attribute details, and its `Shape` model includes type ids, declaration ids, layout, vtables, generic parameters, docs, and caveats about identifier stability. That is unusually strong evidence that exposed shape metadata deserves to be modeled separately from value access or registration: https://docs.rs/facet/latest/facet/ ; https://docs.rs/facet/latest/facet/struct.Shape.html
- `valuable` says it provides object-safe value inspection, and `tracing` explicitly exposes experimental `valuable` support because its default `Value` model is intentionally minimalist. That is exactly the kind of split the archive should preserve: object-safe inspection of structured values is valuable, but it is not the same thing as general-purpose mutable runtime reflection: https://docs.rs/valuable/latest/valuable/ ; https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/field/
- `serde_reflection` extracts format descriptions from Serde containers, explicitly says those descriptions can be checked into version control to prevent unintended format drift, and supports code generation and dynamic translation. That is strong evidence that schema-tracing reflection is a real lane in its own right rather than a footnote under serialization: https://docs.rs/serde-reflection/latest/serde_reflection/
- `inventory` provides distributed typed registration with no central list and explicitly says iteration order is not guaranteed. That is another reason the archive should separate registry semantics from reflection shape and access claims: https://docs.rs/inventory/latest/inventory/
- Archive decision: add **Reflection Surface Kit** as a Tier 1 candidate centered on `reflection-subject/v0` + `reflection-acquisition-profile/v0` + `reflection-shape-profile/v0` + `reflection-value-access-profile/v0` + `reflection-registry-profile/v0` + `reflection-adapter-profile/v0` + `reflection-check-report/v0` + `reflection-diff-report/v0` + `reflect-pack/v0`, explicitly bounded against Const Surface Kit, Macro Workflow Kit, Encoding Surface Kit, Semantic Context Kit, and Override Surface Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Change Impact Kit (change slices, rebuild scope, relink opportunity truth)
- The 2025H2 **Relink don’t Rebuild** goal is explicit that Rust should avoid rebuilding reverse dependencies when a crate’s public interface has not changed, and it names concrete cases like comments, formatting, impl-item reordering, and adding `dbg!` to a non-inlinable function. That is strong evidence that the missing ecosystem contribution is not another generic perf tip list, but a reusable boundary over change classification and downstream action scope: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/relink-dont-rebuild.html
- Cargo’s unstable build-analysis docs say `-Zbuild-analysis` records and persists build metrics on disk and exposes `cargo report rebuilds` specifically to report why crates were rebuilt. That means rebuild explanation is now an emerging machine-facing Cargo seam rather than only a debugging trick: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo’s FAQ still says after-the-fact rebuild debugging has historically been weak and that users often have to inspect `CARGO_LOG=cargo::core::compiler::fingerprint=info` output and “connect some dots” themselves. That is direct support for a higher-level portable report layer: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/faq.html
- Cargo’s fingerprint docs say freshness today depends on fingerprints, mtimes, dep-info anchors, and only partial environment capture, while explicitly noting that stronger tracking would require much more complete filesystem/environment/network observation. That is strong evidence that observed rebuild behavior and semantically required rebuild scope must remain separate truths: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/cargo/core/compiler/fingerprint/index.html
- rustc’s incremental-compilation guide says naive change detection creates false positives and explains the red-green algorithm as the way to distinguish potentially affected queries from actually changed results. That is the deeper conceptual precedent for a Change Impact Kit: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/queries/incremental-compilation-in-detail.html
- Cargo’s build-script docs say that if a build script emits no `rerun-if-*` instructions, Cargo conservatively reruns it for broad package changes, and even explicit tracking currently relies on mtime-based checks. That is concrete evidence that compile-time invalidation belongs in the impact story instead of being hand-waved as ordinary source churn: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
- Archive decision: add **Change Impact Kit** as a Tier 0/1 candidate focused on `impact-subject/v0` + `change-slice/v0` + `impact-lane-profile/v0` + `impact-classification-report/v0` + `rebuild-scope-report/v0` + `relink-opportunity-report/v0` + `impact-diff-report/v0` + `impact-pack/v0`, explicitly bounded against Build Cache Kit, Build Doctor Kit, Public API Kit, Compile-Time Capabilities Kit, and Semantic Context Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Build Cache Kit rewrite (build-state topology, lock clarity, reuse truth)
- The 2025h2 Cargo goal for **Rework Cargo Build Dir Layout** says the current build cache is not easily broken into smaller units, so Cargo locks the entire build cache; it explicitly calls out contention with tools like rust-analyzer, and says the future should include fine-grained caching/locking plus a first-class user-wide cache. That is strong evidence that the missing contribution is not just one more cache backend but a reviewable build-state model: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-dir-layout.html
- The Cargo 1.93 development-cycle update says Cargo is exploring a finer-grained locking scheme on top of the build-dir layout work and explains the split between an intermediate-artifact build dir and a final-artifact dir. That is direct support for separating topology and lock scope instead of talking about one monolithic `target/` cache: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- The Cargo Book now documents both `target-dir` and `build-dir`, and distinguishes final build artifacts from intermediate build artifacts. That is a major sign that build-state topology is becoming a public-facing concept rather than a purely internal implementation detail: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html
- rust-analyzer documents `cargo.targetDir` as a rust-analyzer-specific target directory that avoids locking contention at the cost of duplicated build artifacts. That is unusually crisp evidence that the ecosystem is currently paying for missing shared semantics by duplicating state: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration
- The user-wide build cache goal frames cross-workspace reuse, reduced disk usage, and more precise cross-job caching as strategic requirements. That supports promoting Build Cache Kit from “nice wrapper around sccache” to a real Tier 0/1 substrate candidate: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/user-wide-cache.html
- Priority update: promoted Build Cache Kit from Tier 1 to Tier 0/1 and rewrote it around `build-state-subject`, `build-layout-report`, `build-lock-report`, `cache-entry-report`, `reuse-verdict-report`, `cache-retention-policy`, `cache-exchange-profile`, and `build-state-pack` so the archive models Cargo’s emerging build-state topology directly instead of treating cache behavior as an opaque side effect.
- Hygiene update: future build-cache proposals must keep layout, lock scope, entry identity, reuse verdicts, and retention/exchange policy distinct so the archive does not collapse “blocked on a lock”, “rebuilt”, “duplicated by editor policy”, and “garbage-collected” into one fake cache story.

- The Rust 1.85 / Rust 2024 release post says `cargo fix` can automate many necessary edition changes, but still points users to staged migration/testing guidance. - `rustc` already emits structured JSON diagnostics with suggestion applicability metadata, which is exactly the sort of candidate-edit evidence a shared edit kit should preserve instead of flattening into one applied patch: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/rustc/json.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/rustfix/diagnostics/index.html

That is strong evidence that the missing contribution is not another single refactor helper but a reviewable interchange across heterogeneous edit producers: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/ ; https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration ; https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/other_editors.html ; https://rust-analyzer.github.io/thisweek/2020/07/06/changelog-32.html ; https://rust-analyzer.github.io/thisweek/2021/03/15/changelog-68.html ; https://rust-analyzer.github.io/thisweek/2024/12/16/changelog-264.html

## 2026-03-07 — Safety Evidence Kit deepening (reviewable safety cases, contract traceability, criterion-aware evidence)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship roadmap explicitly names **Safety-Critical Rust** and lists four key milestones: MC/DC coverage support, normative unsafe documentation, safety-critical lints in Clippy, and stabilizing the FLS release cadence. That is direct evidence that safety cases are no longer a peripheral out-of-tree concern; they are becoming part of Rust’s upstream ecosystem direction: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The proposed 2026 goal **Normative Documentation for Sound `unsafe` Rust** says Rust’s current unsafe documentation has gaps, notes that the Rustonomicon is incomplete and the Unsafe Code Guidelines reference is largely abandoned, and argues that safety-critical projects need authoritative documentation to build rigorous safety cases. It also proposes a concrete pattern-catalog workflow over real unsafe-heavy codebases such as `iceoryx2`. That is strong evidence that a worthy archive proposal should model unsafe-contract traceability, not just unsafe counts: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/safe-unsafe-for-safety-critical.html
- The proposed 2026 goal **Implement and Maintain MC/DC Coverage Support** says MC/DC is required by standards like DO-178C, ISO 26262, and IEC 61508, that it is different from ordinary branch coverage, and that doing this outside the compiler is infeasible for real Rust because macro expansion makes valid post-expansion source reconstruction unrealistic. That is unusually strong support for making coverage-criterion identity a first-class artifact in any Rust safety-case design: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/mcdc-coverage-support.html
- The accepted 2025H1 goal **Instrument the Rust standard library with safety contracts** and the current `core::contracts` docs show that upstream Rust is actively growing machine-readable contract hooks (`#[requires]`, `#[ensures]`) rather than leaving all safety preconditions as prose forever. That is direct evidence that contracts should be treated as attachable evidence inputs, not just comments: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/std-contracts.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/contracts/index.html
- The accepted 2025H1 goal **Unsafe Fields** exists specifically because safety invariants carried by fields are otherwise hard to denote and hard to evaluate. That is strong evidence that the archive should keep “where obligations live” distinct from “how they are justified”: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/unsafe-fields.html
- The FLS is now under rust-lang infrastructure and defines conformance requirements for tools, while the follow-on upkeep goal says the project needs capability and cadence to keep it updated for stakeholders. That is exactly the sort of normative/spec substrate a safety-case layer should point at instead of copying into bespoke binders: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/spec-fls-publish.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/FLS-up-to-date-capabilities.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/fls/general.html
- Clippy already exposes lint groups, configurable lint levels, Cargo.toml integration, and MSRV-sensitive configuration. That means Rust already has meaningful lint-policy building blocks; the missing piece is the safety-case layer that records which lints mattered, what severity/waiver posture applied, and how that fed the review outcome: https://doc.rust-lang.org/clippy/configuration.html ; https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy
- The rustc coverage docs already define stable instrumentation-based coverage flows, but those flows are criterion-agnostic unless the report artifact names exactly what was measured. That is direct evidence that “coverage passed” is too weak for serious safety review: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/rustc/instrument-coverage.html
- Archive decision: substantially deepen the existing **Safety Evidence Kit** around `safety-subject/v0` + `unsafe-surface-report/v0` + `safety-contract-report/v0` + `safety-lint-report/v0` + `coverage-criterion-report/v0` + `verification-claim-report/v0` + `safety-case-report/v0` + `safety-pack/v0`, explicitly bounded against Coverage Evidence Kit, Formal Verification Kit, Sanitizer Battery Kit, Spec Conformance Kit, and Trust Signals Kit instead of treating safety review as one generic pile of “unsafe + audits + proofs”.

## 2026-03-07 — SBOM Evidence Kit (scope-aware inventory, artifact linkage, format projections)
- Rust’s official 2026 goals include **stabilizing Cargo SBOM precursor**, and the 2026 flagship supply-chain theme explicitly includes **SBOM generation** alongside public/private dependencies and breaking-change detection. That is direct evidence that inventory is no longer just a third-party compliance sidecar; it is now part of upstream Rust’s ecosystem direction: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Cargo’s unstable `sbom` docs say precursor files are emitted alongside executable and linkable outputs, include dependencies / target / features / compiler identity, may include the same crate multiple times when compiled differently, and expose `CARGO_SBOM_PATH` for downstream tooling. That is unusually strong support for modeling capture provenance, duplicated compile instances, and build-to-postprocess handoff as first-class facts: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo’s new `sbom` tracking issue says remaining work includes demonstrating end-to-end SBOM generation in an industry-standard format using the precursor data source, while explicitly scoping non-Rust dependencies out of the precursor feature. That is strong evidence that a good archive proposal should separate Rust-native inventory truth from later format projection and completeness claims: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/16565
- RFC 3553 explicitly positions Cargo’s output as a Cargo-specific SBOM emitted beside artifacts and then transformed by external tooling into standards like SPDX or CycloneDX. That is exactly the architecture the archive should sharpen instead of pretending one export format is the source of truth: https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3553
- The CycloneDX Cargo plugin proves real demand for standard-format export, but its own issue tracker says current `cargo metadata`-based inputs can misreport some build-only dependencies as runtime dependencies under resolver v2. That is direct evidence that scope classification and capture-lane provenance must remain explicit instead of getting flattened inside the exported BOM: https://github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-rust-cargo/blob/main/README.md ; https://github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-rust-cargo/issues/760
- Cargo’s long-standing metadata bug on workspace-level feature resolution is another reminder that “what metadata reported” and “what was actually built” are not always identical. A worthy design should keep those truths distinguishable rather than silently collapsing them: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/7754
- `cargo-auditable` proves a second valuable lane: shipped binaries can carry a compact dependency list that downstream tools can recover and convert, and the project says this embedded data is designed not to break reproducible builds. But it also explicitly warns that SBOMs do not by themselves prevent supply-chain attacks or explain the impact of a malicious dependency. That is exactly why inventory should be modeled as evidence input, not as trust or incident verdict: https://github.com/rust-secure-code/cargo-auditable
- Archive decision: add a new **SBOM Evidence Kit** centered on `inventory-subject/v0` + `inventory-capture-report/v0` + `inventory-graph/v0` + `artifact-inventory-report/v0` + `inventory-projection-report/v0` + `inventory-diff-report/v0` + `inventory-pack/v0`, explicitly bounded against Trust Signals Kit, Policy Kit, Release Pipeline Kit, Repro Build Kit, and Incident Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Public API Kit deepening (cross-crate provenance, witness evidence, publish-admission posture)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes explicitly frame supply-chain progress around control over public API dependencies, breaking-change detection, and SBOM generation. That is direct evidence that API-boundary evidence is no longer just library-maintainer hygiene; it is now part of Rust’s official ecosystem direction: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The public/private-dependencies goal says the feature should let users tell Rustc and Cargo what dependencies are private, help users catch unexpected exposure of implementation details, and help tooling better identify what constitutes an API. - The `cargo-semver-checks` goal says the desired end state is SemVer checking in the `cargo publish` workflow with an override flag, calls out cross-crate items and type-sensitive checking as the major remaining blockers, and says more than 90% of real-world false-positives trace back to cross-crate items. That is strong evidence that the missing layer is not “more lints somewhere,” but a real release-admission artifact that can preserve provenance, reason codes, and unsupported lanes honestly: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-semver-checks.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html
- The 2025 GSoC witness-generation writeup says the way forward for type-sensitive SemVer checking is to generate witness programs and ask the compiler whether they still compile, instead of trying to reimplement Rust’s type checker in `cargo-semver-checks`. That is exactly the sort of evidence lane the archive should model explicitly rather than hiding it inside one generic semver result: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/18/gsoc-2025-results/
- Cargo’s 1.94 development-cycle report shows continued movement toward structured logging, `cargo report *`, and low-level plumbing commands. That does not solve API evolution by itself, but it does strengthen the strategic case for a portable `api-pack`/report boundary that composes with Cargo-native reporting rather than fighting it: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/

## 2026-03-07 — Trust Signals Kit deepening (issuer-aware evidence, policy evaluation, freshness, diffable trust posture)
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update says crate pages now have a Security tab for RustSec advisories, GitLab CI/CD support for Trusted Publishing, Trusted Publishing only mode, blocked risky GitHub triggers, and a new `pubtime` field in index entries. That is unusually strong evidence that the registry already has multiple trust-relevant facts, but still lacks one shared evidence/report layer that can feed Cargo, CI, and registry/search UX coherently: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Cargo Vet’s “How it Works” page says the system is built to minimize friction, lazily import audits from trusted organizations, and keep audit metadata in-tree so approvals fall to code owners of a `supply-chain/` directory. That is direct evidence that Rust already has one serious human-review trust signal with explicit issuers and trust roots: https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/how-it-works.html
- Cargo Vet’s audit-criteria docs make the multi-dimensional story even clearer: built-in `safe-to-run` and `safe-to-deploy` exist, but projects can also define custom criteria like `crypto-reviewed`. That is strong evidence that a good trust substrate must preserve issuer + criteria semantics rather than flattening all audits into one yes/no badge: https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/audit-criteria.html
- crates.io’s February 2026 malicious-crate notification update says most malware removals will be communicated through RustSec advisories unless there is evidence of real-world usage or exploitation. - The Cargo manifest reference still documents a dormant `maintenance` badge vocabulary that crates.io no longer uses directly, and RFC 1824 already established that crates.io search/ranking legitimately consumes recommendation signals. Together those are strong evidence that the ecosystem wants recommendation-time inputs, but still lacks the right evidence boundary to keep them explainable: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/1824-crates.io-default-ranking.html
- Community discussions about crate reliability/verification keep resurfacing, which is another sign that the demand for trust signaling is durable; the missing part is a neutral artifact substrate that avoids collapsing into one opaque score: https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/adding-a-reliability-rating-system-to-crates-io/23567

## 2026-03-07 — Lifecycle Ledger Kit deepening (support windows, successor truth, handoff consent, maintenance visibility)
- The Rust Foundation Maintainer Fund design work says maintenance labor is often invisible, that maintainers are frequently volunteers, and that the project wants better ways both to support that work and to publicize it. That is direct evidence that lifecycle/maintenance state needs a real artifact channel rather than being buried in issue trackers or assumed from commit activity: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/12/what-is-maintenance-anyway/
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update says crate pages now have a Security tab for RustSec advisories and that Trusted Publishing and other security UX are continuing to improve. That is strong evidence that the registry is already becoming a richer dependency-selection surface, and therefore lifecycle/support metadata has a realistic place to land if it gets a good contract: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- crates.io’s February 2026 malicious-crate notification update says most malware removals will now be communicated through RustSec advisories unless there is evidence of real-world usage or exploitation. That is healthy for security signal quality, but it also sharpens the design boundary: ordinary deprecation, support-window, successor, and maintainer-help facts should not keep overloading security channels: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/13/crates.io-malicious-crate-update/
- The Cargo manifest reference still defines a `[badges].maintenance` vocabulary, while explicitly noting that crates.io no longer uses badges directly. That is unusually clear evidence of a partially abandoned lifecycle metadata seam that should be replaced by a better registry- and tool-consumable artifact family instead of ignored: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html
- RFC 3537 explicitly calls out “version maintenance status on crates.io” as missing context, especially when an older line may still be supported even if it is not the newest release. That is a strong signal that lifecycle artifacts must model **version-line support windows**, not only whole-crate health: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3537-msrv-resolver.html
- crates.io policy says ownership transfer requires explicit current-owner approval, which is strong evidence that maintainer-help / handoff intent must remain an explicit artifact and must not be inferred from inactivity or forum rumor: https://crates.io/policies
- `cargo-unmaintained` exists because users clearly want lifecycle signals badly enough to consume heuristic ones, but its docs also show the limits of that approach and even quantify partial recall against RustSec’s unmaintained advisories. That is exactly the sort of “demand is real, source-of-truth is weak” pattern that justifies a Lifecycle Ledger substrate: https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-unmaintained/1.9.0
- Archive decision: substantially deepen the existing **Lifecycle Ledger Kit** around `lifecycle-intent/v0` + `support-window-map/v0` + `successor-map/v0` + `handoff-consent/v0` + `maintenance-report/v0` + `lifecycle-report/v0` + `lifecycle-diff-report/v0` + `lifecycle-pack/v0`, explicitly bounded against Trust Signals Kit, Incident Kit, Policy Kit, Migration Kit, and registry-identity work rather than another crate-health scoreboard or automatic transfer policy.

## 2026-03-07 — Debugger Experience Kit deepening (capability matrices, visualizer packs, async-runtime adapters, repro truth)
- The compiler team’s 2026 debugging survey is unusually concrete about what “stellar debugging” would mean for Rust: support for several debugger versions across GDB/LLDB/CDB on multiple operating systems, high-quality visualizers, first-class `async` debugging, and Rust-expression evaluation. It also says Rust is not there yet and that debugger quality varies across debuggers/OSes and can regress as debuggers or std internals change. That is direct evidence that Rust needs a portable capability-and-regression layer rather than more one-off setup notes: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/23/rust-debugging-survey-2026/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still lists debugging among the leading non-trivial productivity problems, even after build/resource usage remains the largest pain. That is strong evidence the debugging seam is still strategically important enough to justify a serious ecosystem artifact layer, not just better blog posts or IDE tips: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The Rust compiler development guide says the toolchain already ships `rust-lldb`, `rust-gdb`, and `rust-windbg.cmd` support scripts that preload Rust visualizers; it also explains that visualizers reconstruct useful synthetic children, that `#![debugger_visualizer]` currently works for GDB and Natvis, that LLDB remains a different and unresolved lane, and that visualizer performance can become painfully important in debugger GUIs. That is direct evidence that debugger support should be modeled as tuple-specific capability + visualizer coverage + performance truth instead of one fake universal debugging badge: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/debuginfo/debugger-visualizers.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/debugger.html
- `console-subscriber` and `tokio-console` show that async debugging already uses a real instrumentation/consumer split: runtime-emitted tracing data, an explicit wire format, a CLI consumer, version requirements, and instrumentation prerequisites such as Tokio tracing support and `tokio_unstable`. That is excellent evidence that Rust needs an explicit `async-debug-profile` / adapter artifact rather than pretending async debugging is automatically part of native debugger support: https://docs.rs/console-subscriber/latest/console_subscriber/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/tokio-console/latest
- Archive decision: substantially deepen the existing **Debugger Experience Kit** around `debug-profile/v0` + `debug-capability-report/v0` + `viz-pack/v0` + `async-debug-profile/v0` + `expr-eval-profile/v0` + `debug-battery-report/v0` + `debug-pack/v0`, explicitly bounded against Diagnostic Surface Kit, Replay Kit, Synchronization Surface Kit, and Terminal Surface Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Build Doctor Kit (workflow-aware build diagnosis, bottleneck classification, actionable suggestions)
- The 2025 Rust compiler performance survey says long compile times still materially limit productivity, and around 45% of respondents who are no longer using Rust cite long compile times as at least one reason. The survey then identifies the most painful workflows as incremental rebuilds, editor/IDE type-check latency, and clean/CI builds. That is strong evidence that any worthy build-performance contribution must start from explicit workflow selection rather than one fake universal “fast build” story: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- The same survey says `cargo check` / `cargo build` cache non-sharing is a real pain point, around 33% of users find waiting for inline editor diagnostics a big blocker, more than 35% see IDE/Cargo blocking one another as a big problem, and very few users use profiling tools because the existing surfaces are hard to interpret. That is direct evidence that Rust does not merely need more raw numbers; it needs a reviewable interpretation layer over those numbers: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- The survey explicitly says long-term tooling should help answer questions like which code had to be recompiled after a source change, which proc-macros take longest, and what actionable suggestions follow. That is unusually direct support for a Build Doctor-style diagnosis/report layer above raw telemetry: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- The proposed Cargo build-analysis goal is now explicit about the raw data it wants to collect across invocations — timings, rebuild reasons, CLI arguments, and later richer insights and actionable suggestions. That is strong evidence that Cargo itself is growing the observation substrate a diagnosis kit would need, but is not yet the portable diagnosis artifact itself: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html
- The Cargo 1.94 development-cycle report says structured logging work added `cargo report rebuild`, `cargo report sessions`, and more timing support. That is concrete proof the ecosystem now has real report plumbing worth converging on, rather than another excuse to invent bespoke ad hoc logging: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The official Cargo book now has an “Optimizing Build Performance” chapter that recommends reducing dev debuginfo, optionally using Cranelift, trying the parallel frontend, switching linkers, resolving features for the whole workspace, and pruning unused dependencies/features — while repeatedly emphasizing trade-offs and workflow-specific measurement. That is excellent evidence that the missing contribution is not more prose alone, but a portable way to connect observed bottlenecks to specific, tradeoff-aware suggestions: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/cargo/guide/build-performance.html
- That guidance chapter is itself tracked as an explicit Cargo issue, which is another sign that build-performance guidance is becoming a maintained product surface rather than scattered community folklore: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/16119
- Accepted/proposed Cargo goals around user-wide build cache, build-dir relayout, and reduced locking show that cache reuse, target-dir structure, and editor/build contention are ecosystem seams in their own right. That means a build doctor layer should classify cache and lock pathologies explicitly instead of flattening them into generic “slow compiler” complaints: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/user-wide-cache.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-dir-layout.html

## 2026-03-07 — Cryptography Surface Kit (algorithm families, providers, secret handling, side-channel/audit/compliance posture)
- `rustls`’s `CryptoProvider` docs now explicitly say the crate ships with two built-in providers: `aws_lc_rs::default_provider` behind the default-enabled `aws_lc_rs` feature and `ring::default_provider` behind the optional `ring` feature. The same docs also say there is an implicit process-default provider used by `ClientConfig::builder()` and `ServerConfig::builder()`. That is direct evidence that provider choice is already a first-class public support seam in Rust cryptography rather than an invisible implementation detail: https://docs.rs/rustls/latest/rustls/crypto/struct.CryptoProvider.html
- `rustls`’s FIPS manual says users must enable the `fips` crate feature, use the FIPS `CryptoProvider`, and validate the FIPS status of `ClientConfig`/`ServerConfig` at run time. It also points at certificate-specific coverage details for the underlying module. That is unusually strong evidence that compliance claims need explicit artifacts rather than README-level branding: https://docs.rs/rustls/latest/rustls/manual/_06_fips/index.html
- `aws-lc-rs` explicitly presents itself as a `ring`-compatible library backed by AWS-LC, says non-FIPS builds need a C/C++ compiler but not CMake or bindgen, says FIPS builds require CMake and Go (and sometimes bindgen), documents mutually exclusive `fips` and `non-fips` features, and says it currently does not support `#![no_std]`. That is direct evidence that backend/build/compliance posture is a public contract surface, not a hidden implementation note: https://docs.rs/aws-lc-rs/latest/aws_lc_rs/
- `ring` 0.17.14’s docs explicitly expose target-sensitive feature flags like `less-safe-getrandom-custom-or-rdrand`, `less-safe-getrandom-espidf`, and `wasm32_unknown_unknown_js`, and document that some of those features relax what counts as a secure RNG on specific targets. That is strong evidence that target/backend truth and randomness dependencies belong in the crypto surface rather than being buried inside platform notes: https://docs.rs/ring/latest/ring/
- The RustCrypto `crypto` facade crate explicitly exists because RustCrypto’s trait crates are independently versioned and often interdependent, and it provides one place to pull compatible versions of traits like `aead`, `digest`, `elliptic-curve`, `password-hash`, and `signature`. That is concrete evidence that trait-family compatibility is already a real ecosystem seam worth artifacting: https://docs.rs/crate/crypto/latest
- RustCrypto trait crates already expose generic cryptography lanes directly: `digest` describes generic hash-function traits, `signature` describes generic object-safe APIs for digital signatures, and `aead` describes a generic high-level interface for authenticated encryption. That is evidence that the ecosystem already wants algorithm-family artifacts above concrete implementations: https://docs.rs/crate/digest/latest ; https://docs.rs/crate/signature/latest ; https://docs.rs/crate/aead/latest
- Secret handling is visibly split across real public surfaces: `secrecy` says it wraps values to make secret access explicit and tries to limit accidental copying/logging while zeroizing on drop, but also warns that serde-based input paths may still make extra copies; `zeroize` says it provides portable zeroing guarantees using stable Rust primitives rather than broader memory-hardening claims. That is strong motivation for a separate key-material profile instead of a fake “secrets safe” checkbox: https://docs.rs/secrecy/latest/secrecy/ ; https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/
- `subtle` explicitly frames itself as a best-effort constant-time utility crate and warns that side-channel resistance is a property of the deployed system, not software alone. Concrete algorithm crates can be even sharper: `p256` says it is designed around constant-time formulas and the `subtle` crate, but also warns that it has not been independently audited and that generated assembly has not been thoroughly assessed for constant-time behavior on common CPU architectures. That is direct evidence that side-channel and audit posture need first-class artifacts: https://docs.rs/subtle/latest/subtle/ ; https://docs.rs/p256/latest/p256/
- The `signature` crate’s `Error` type is deliberately opaque to avoid side-channel leakage that could help recover private keys or forge signatures, yet it allows `std`-feature source errors for external signers like HSMs or KMS providers. The `RandomizedDigestSigner` trait also takes a `CryptoRngCore`. Together that is concrete evidence that Rust already spans local-key, remote-signer, and randomness-dependent cryptographic lanes that need explicit review objects: https://docs.rs/signature/latest/signature/struct.Error.html ; https://docs.rs/signature/latest/signature/trait.RandomizedDigestSigner.html
- `password-hash` explicitly models the PHC string format as a parsed structure with algorithm id, version, params, salt, and hash output, while `password_auth` says it uses the best available enabled password hashing algorithm, typically Argon2. That is strong evidence that password-hash interchange and “best available algorithm” policy belong in the cryptography surface rather than being left to helper-crate defaults: https://docs.rs/password-hash/latest/password_hash/struct.PasswordHash.html ; https://docs.rs/password-auth/latest/password_auth/fn.generate_hash.html
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still says resource usage remains a major productivity problem and that complexity concerns persist. That strengthens the case for a contract layer that can honestly distinguish pure-Rust trait-generic lanes, FFI/provider-heavy compliance lanes, and minimal secret-handling helpers instead of pretending one stack fits every cryptographic workload: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add **Cryptography Surface Kit** as a Tier 1 proposal focused on `crypto-surface/v0` + `algorithm-family-profile/v0` + `provider-backend-profile/v0` + `key-material-profile/v0` + `sidechannel-audit-profile/v0` + `compliance-certification-profile/v0` + `crypto-adapter-profile/v0` + `crypto-vector-set/v0` + `crypto-check-report/v0` + `crypto-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Randomness Surface Kit, Protocol Surface Kit, Identity Surface Kit, Encoding Surface Kit, and Validity Surface Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Randomness Surface Kit (entropy sources, seeding, reproducibility, crypto-strength posture, target/backend truth)
- `rand` 0.10’s module docs now explicitly publish several distinct randomness lanes: `SysRng` as a stateless OS-randomness interface, `ThreadRng` as a periodically seeded thread-local generator, `StdRng` and `SmallRng` as non-portable standard choices, and named portable generators like ChaCha and Xoshiro. That is strong evidence that the Rust ecosystem already has multiple honest randomness stories rather than one boring default: https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/rngs/
- `rand_core` 0.10 says the release is intended to be the last significant breakage before 1.0, renames `RngCore` / `TryRngCore` to `Rng` / `TryRng`, adds `SeedableRng::{fork, try_fork}`, and removes the `getrandom` dependency plus `OsRng`-related items from the core crate. That is direct evidence that trait boundaries, entropy acquisition, and fork semantics are currently live ecosystem seams: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md
- `getrandom` 0.4 explicitly presents itself as the low-level system-entropy crate, roughly tracks std target support, and documents WebAssembly caveats for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, multiple opt-in backends, custom backends, an unsupported backend, and warnings that incorrect backend configuration may yield vulnerable or always-panicking applications. That is unusually direct evidence that target/backend truth needs first-class artifacts: https://docs.rs/getrandom
- `ThreadRng` explicitly says it is not automatically reseeded on `fork` and recommends an explicit reseed in child processes. It also says stronger in-memory-state protections are not promised. That is direct evidence that fork/reseed posture belongs in the public support surface rather than in folklore: https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/rngs/struct.ThreadRng.html
- `StdRng` and `SmallRng` both explicitly document non-portability, while `rand_chacha` explicitly documents deterministic portable ChaCha generators with testing against reference vectors and secure-use guidance around seeding. That split is strong motivation for separate reproducibility and crypto-strength artifacts: https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/rngs/struct.StdRng.html ; https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/rngs/struct.SmallRng.html ; https://docs.rs/rand_chacha
- `fastrand` and `oorandom` remain valuable counter-evidence against any attempt to flatten the ecosystem: `fastrand` explicitly uses Wyrand and says it is not cryptographically secure, while `oorandom` explicitly sells simplicity, `no_std`, compile-time economy, and a stable API rather than the larger `rand` ecosystem. That is good evidence that lightweight/simple lanes should be modeled explicitly rather than treated as inferior accidents: https://docs.rs/fastrand ; https://docs.rs/crate/oorandom/latest
- `rand_seeder` explicitly positions itself as a portable and reproducible way to seed any `SeedableRng` from any hashable value. That is concrete evidence that seed-derivation and user-facing reproducibility are already real ecosystem needs, not merely internal helper details: https://docs.rs/rand_seeder/latest/rand_seeder/struct.Seeder.html
- Crypto-facing traits already consume RNG posture directly: the `signature` crate’s `RandomizedSigner` requires a `CryptoRngCore`, and `rand_core`’s `TryCryptoRng` docs explicitly say the trait is meant to aid review while not guaranteeing suitability by itself. That is strong evidence that Rust lacks a shared vocabulary for “crypto-capable randomness” above raw marker traits: https://docs.rs/signature/latest/signature/trait.RandomizedSigner.html ; https://docs.rs/rand_core/latest/rand_core/trait.TryCryptoRng.html
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still says resource usage is a major productivity problem and concerns about complexity persist. That strengthens the case for a contract layer that can honestly distinguish broad, feature-rich randomness stacks from simpler/lighter lanes instead of pretending one stack fits all workloads: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add **Randomness Surface Kit** as a Tier 1 proposal focused on `randomness-surface/v0` + `entropy-source-profile/v0` + `rng-semantics-profile/v0` + `seed-repro-profile/v0` + `crypto-strength-profile/v0` + `target-backend-profile/v0` + `randomness-adapter-profile/v0` + `randomness-vector-set/v0` + `randomness-check-report/v0` + `randomness-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Runtime Capability Kit, Time Surface Kit, FuzzPack / Replay / DST, Encoding Surface Kit, and higher-level crypto/protocol kits.

## 2026-03-07 — Terminal Surface Kit (capabilities, render/input posture, Unicode layout, and terminal evidence)
- Ratatui’s `Terminal` docs and backend guide explicitly say Ratatui abstracts over multiple backends, while real applications still use the backend directly for terminal properties, raw mode, alternate screen, and keyboard/mouse/window events; that is strong evidence that backend choice alone is not enough to describe the public terminal contract: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/struct.Terminal.html ; https://ratatui.rs/concepts/backends/
- `crossterm` explicitly presents itself as a cross-platform terminal manipulation library for text-based interfaces and documents alternate screen, raw mode, styling, keyboard/mouse/resize events, focus events, and bracketed paste; that is concrete evidence that a serious terminal surface needs capability and input artifacts rather than a generic “CLI supports terminal output” claim: https://docs.rs/crossterm ; https://docs.rs/crossterm/latest/crossterm/event/index.html
- `termwiz` documents both capability probing and semantic escape parsing/encoding, which is strong evidence that terminal capability posture and escape semantics are already their own first-class lane in Rust rather than a hidden implementation detail: https://docs.rs/termwiz ; https://docs.rs/termwiz/latest/termwiz/caps/index.html ; https://docs.rs/termwiz/latest/termwiz/escape/index.html
- `anstream` explicitly documents auto-detecting color support, respecting `NO_COLOR` / `CLICOLOR`, and falling back to Windows console APIs when virtual terminal processing is unavailable; that is excellent evidence that color/style support is a real portability contract rather than a cosmetic toggle: https://docs.rs/anstream/latest/anstream/struct.AutoStream.html
- Unicode layout is visibly split into multiple real lanes already: `unicode-width` computes displayed width according to Unicode width rules, `unicode-segmentation` exposes grapheme-cluster boundaries according to UAX #29, and `unicode-display-width` computes display width over grapheme clusters; this is direct motivation for keeping width policy and grapheme policy separate in the archive: https://docs.rs/unicode-width ; https://docs.rs/unicode-segmentation ; https://docs.rs/unicode-display-width
- `reedline` explicitly positions itself as a modern Rust line editor with Unicode support and documents bracketed-paste behavior that changes multiline paste semantics, which is strong evidence that interactive input semantics deserve first-class terminal artifacts rather than disappearing into examples: https://docs.rs/reedline ; https://docs.rs/reedline/latest/reedline/struct.Reedline.html
- Ratatui’s `TestBackend` and the `vt100` parser together show that terminal behavior is already testable through both buffer-level and terminal-parser-level evidence lanes, which supports the repo’s push toward explicit `terminal-vector-set` and `terminal-check-report` artifacts instead of screenshot-only confidence: https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/backend/struct.TestBackend.html ; https://docs.rs/vt100/latest/vt100/
- `ratatui-image` explicitly targets multiple terminal graphics protocols across Sixel, Kitty, and iTerm2, which is concrete evidence that richer terminal media/protocol claims are already real ecosystem territory and should be modeled explicitly rather than hidden behind a vague “advanced TUI” label: https://docs.rs/ratatui-image

## 2026-03-07 — Process Surface Kit (spawn model, argv/env/cwd truth, stdio topology, supervision, PTY behavior, subprocess evidence)
- Std `Command` says arguments are passed literally rather than through a shell, warns that `cmd.exe` and `.bat` files on Windows use non-standard decoding that can make malicious input dangerous, and documents that combining a relative program path with `current_dir` is platform-specific and unstable. That is strong evidence that spawn model and argv/cwd posture are first-class review objects, not incidental details: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Command.html
- Std `Child` explicitly has no `Drop`, says that dropped child handles leave processes running, and warns that terminated-but-unwaited children can remain as zombies on Unix. That is direct evidence that subprocess cleanup in Rust is an explicit contract surface, not a mere implementation detail: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Child.html
- Std `wait` and `wait_with_output` close stdin before waiting to help avoid deadlock, while `try_wait` explicitly does not try to drop stdin. That is strong evidence that stdio topology and waiting semantics should be published together rather than inferred from helper choice: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Child.html
- Std `Stdio` and `std::io::pipe` now make parent/child pipe wiring an explicit standard-library lane rather than only a crate-level trick. That is good evidence that pipe topology deserves first-class artifacts: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Stdio.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/fn.pipe.html
- Unix `CommandExt` exposes `process_group` and `setsid`, and its docs explicitly note that process groups determine which processes receive signals. That is direct evidence that lone-child control and process-tree/signal semantics are separate review objects: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/process/trait.CommandExt.html
- Tokio’s process docs preserve the standard library’s default “drop does not imply cancellation” behavior, add `kill_on_drop`, and only promise best-effort background reaping on Unix. Tokio’s `Child::kill` also differs from std by killing and then waiting. That is concrete evidence that “async process support” is not a single semantic lane: https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/process/struct.Command.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/process/struct.Child.html
- Tokio’s signal docs say signal handling is generally tricky and should be used with great care. That is useful evidence that signal/shutdown strategy should be recorded explicitly instead of hidden behind runtime branding: https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/signal/index.html
- `async-process` explicitly documents a background reaper thread and contrasts itself with std’s leaked-resource behavior when a running `Child` is dropped. That is strong evidence that reaping/cleanup policy is a real ecosystem seam: https://docs.rs/async-process
- `duct` explicitly positions itself as a library for running child processes and building pipelines, while `xshell` explicitly says it re-implements parts of shell scripting in Rust instead of using the shell directly. Those are good signals that shelling-out and pipeline ergonomics are durable demand lanes with different semantics: https://docs.rs/duct ; https://docs.rs/xshell
- `portable-pty` documents a cross-platform PTY API and a command builder intentionally similar to `std::process::Command`; its `CommandBuilder` also exposes controlling-terminal posture. That is direct evidence that PTY execution is a separate first-class lane, not just a stdio option: https://docs.rs/portable-pty ; https://docs.rs/portable-pty/latest/portable_pty/cmdbuilder/struct.CommandBuilder.html
- `command-group` and `process-wrap` both exist because process-group/session/job-object semantics are not boringly solved by std alone; `process-wrap` explicitly describes itself as a more flexible, composable successor to `command-group`. Sources: https://docs.rs/command-group ; https://docs.rs/process-wrap
- `shared_child` exists because std `Child` requires `&mut self` for `wait` and `kill`, and its docs explain the associated Unix `waitpid` / PID-reuse race. That is strong evidence that concurrent wait/kill and shared-child control are substantive semantics, not niche API trivia: https://docs.rs/shared_child
- `signal-hook` explicitly frames signals as their own handling layer and recommends iterator/adaptor patterns. That reinforces that signal posture belongs in the published process surface rather than in ad hoc examples: https://docs.rs/signal-hook
- Archive decision: add **Process Surface Kit** as a Tier 1 proposal focused on `process-surface/v0` + `spawn-model-profile/v0` + `argv-env-cwd-profile/v0` + `stdio-topology-profile/v0` + `supervision-termination-profile/v0` + `tty-pty-profile/v0` + `process-adapter-profile/v0` + `process-vector-set/v0` + `process-check-report/v0` + `process-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Command Surface Kit, Runtime Capability Kit, Background Work Kit, Filesystem Surface Kit, and Async Lifecycle Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Filesystem Surface Kit (path posture, rooted resolution, traversal/watch policy, temp staging, durability evidence)
- Std `fs` now explicitly documents TOCTOU hazards, warns that metadata checks can race with later use, recommends atomic operations like `File::create_new`, and says keeping files open for the duration of operations helps avoid check-then-use bugs. That is strong evidence that filesystem semantics in Rust are already more than a pile of helper functions: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/
- Nightly `std::fs::Dir` is especially telling because its docs say that on supported systems it acquires a directory handle/file descriptor so descendant opens can avoid some TOCTOU errors when the directory itself moves, while on other systems it falls back to absolute-path storage with no TOCTOU guarantees. That is unusually direct evidence that Rust is still searching for a better reviewable directory/rooted-filesystem lane: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Dir.html
- Std `canonicalize` returns the canonical absolute path with symlinks resolved, and on Windows it converts to extended-length path syntax that may be awkward for joining or for interop with other applications. That is strong evidence that machine-resolved path identity and human-/tool-facing path rendering must remain separate review objects: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.canonicalize.html
- Std `rename` documents that it does not work across mount points and that overwrite behavior differs by platform and object kind. That is concrete evidence that “rename means atomic safe replace” is not a portable filesystem story on its own: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.rename.html
- Std `read_dir` says new errors may appear after iterator construction and that entry order is platform/filesystem dependent unless callers sort explicitly. That is direct evidence that recursive traversal/determinism is a public semantic choice, not an implementation detail: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/fn.read_dir.html
- `cap-std` explicitly de-emphasizes a process-wide current working directory and global filesystem namespace, instead passing `Dir` capabilities around; its `Dir` docs also say capability-mode `canonicalize` returns a relative path because absolute paths do not interoperate well with the capability model. That is strong evidence that bare global paths, rooted resolution, and canonical-path reporting should remain separate lanes in the archive. Sources: https://docs.rs/cap-std ; https://docs.rs/cap-std/latest/cap_std/fs/struct.Dir.html
- `cap-std-ext` adds `RootDir` with `RESOLVE_IN_ROOT` semantics. That is further evidence that rooted-resolution policy is becoming an explicit ecosystem seam rather than only an implementation trick: https://docs.rs/cap-std-ext
- `camino` documents UTF-8-only path types as a deliberate tradeoff over std’s more general `Path` / `OsStr` model. That is concrete evidence that path encoding assumptions should be published explicitly rather than inferred from API ergonomics: https://docs.rs/camino
- `tempfile` documents cleanup-on-drop, `persist`, `persist_noclobber`, and child-process-oriented `TempPath`; it also says persistence cannot cross filesystems, that `persist` does not imply file+directory sync, and that `persist_noclobber` is not guaranteed atomic on all platforms. That is exactly the kind of staging/durability truth most public APIs still fail to publish cleanly. Sources: https://docs.rs/tempfile ; https://docs.rs/tempfile/latest/tempfile/struct.NamedTempFile.html
- `atomic-write-file` exists specifically because direct truncating writes can leave a file in a broken intermediate state if a process is interrupted. That is strong evidence that staged replace versus direct write is a first-class semantic boundary, not a minor implementation note: https://docs.rs/atomic-write-file
- `notify` explicitly says watcher implementations use the best available platform backend but also provide a polling implementation that should work anywhere, and its watch docs say rename/remove behavior may be unexpected on some platforms. That is strong evidence that filesystem watch support needs backend and caveat artifacts instead of one fake universal watch claim: https://docs.rs/notify
- `walkdir` and `ignore` together show how much policy a recursive walk already carries: symlink following defaults, loop handling, deterministic sorting, file-descriptor limits, `.gitignore` / `.ignore` / hidden-file handling, and same-filesystem options are all public semantic choices. Sources: https://docs.rs/walkdir ; https://docs.rs/ignore/latest/ignore/struct.WalkBuilder.html
- `fs-err` advertises itself as a drop-in `std::fs` replacement with better operation/path context on errors, while `dunce` exists because std canonical paths on Windows are often not the human-facing form users actually want. Those are good ecosystem signals that operation/path reporting is part of the filesystem surface, not just error-style polish. Sources: https://crates.io/crates/fs-err ; https://docs.rs/dunce
- Archive decision: add **Filesystem Surface Kit** as a Tier 1 proposal focused on `fs-surface/v0` + `path-kind-profile/v0` + `resolution-traversal-profile/v0` + `mutation-durability-profile/v0` + `temp-staging-profile/v0` + `walk-watch-profile/v0` + `fs-adapter-profile/v0` + `fs-vector-set/v0` + `fs-check-report/v0` + `fs-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Runtime Capability Kit, Command Surface Kit, Build Interop Kit, Airgap Kit, and Runtime Settings Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Time Surface Kit (clock kinds, timezone/DST truth, calendar/localization posture, storage interop, deterministic-test evidence)
- Std’s `Instant` docs make the clock split explicit: `Instant` is an opaque monotonically nondecreasing measurement, but the docs also warn that hardware, virtualization, or operating-system bugs can violate monotonic expectations and that some APIs saturate to zero rather than panicking. That is direct evidence that elapsed-time APIs and wall-clock APIs should remain separate review objects: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.Instant.html
- Std’s `SystemTime` docs are equally direct that wall-clock time is **not monotonic** and can go backward. That is strong evidence that “timestamp support” and “timeout/latency clock support” must not be flattened together: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html
- Chrono’s docs still center `Utc`, `Local`, and `FixedOffset`, and explicitly say you often want to normalize parsed textual datetimes into `FixedOffset` because it stores the most information without depending on the system environment. That is concrete evidence that Chrono’s public surface remains strongly offset-centric even when local/UTC helpers exist: https://docs.rs/chrono
- The `time` crate’s public docs center `OffsetDateTime`, `PrimitiveDateTime`, `UtcOffset`, feature-gated parsing/formatting, and compile-time `format_description!`. That is good evidence that `time` occupies a different lane: a cleaner, largely offset-oriented surface with strong format-description tooling rather than a built-in IANA-zone / localized-calendar story. Sources: https://docs.rs/time ; https://docs.rs/time/latest/time/format_description/index.html ; https://docs.rs/time/latest/time/macros/macro.format_description.html
- Jiff’s docs explicitly advertise automatic IANA Time Zone Database integration, DST-aware arithmetic, and a separation between timestamps, civil values, and zoned values. That is strong evidence that the ecosystem now has a first-class zone-aware / civil-aware lane rather than just “offset datetimes with helpers”. Sources: https://docs.rs/jiff ; https://docs.rs/jiff/latest/jiff/tz/struct.TimeZone.html ; https://docs.rs/jiff/latest/jiff/_documentation/comparison/index.html
- Jiff’s platform docs are especially valuable because they make host-zone discovery concrete: on Windows it maps the system zone to IANA identifiers via CLDR, while on Unix it inspects `/etc/localtime` or TZif data. That is exactly the sort of host-dependent truth most public APIs still fail to publish: https://docs.rs/jiff/latest/jiff/_documentation/platform/index.html
- ICU4X’s datetime docs explicitly provide localized formatting of dates, times, and time zones, and `AnyCalendar` provides runtime-selectable calendars. That is concrete evidence that user-facing temporal rendering in Rust is already a distinct lane from protocol-formatting or offset math: https://docs.rs/icu_datetime/latest/icu_datetime/ ; https://docs.rs/icu/latest/icu/calendar/enum.AnyCalendar.html
- `jiff-icu` and `jiff-sqlx` now exist as real crates. That is strong ecosystem evidence that cross-lane temporal adapters (localization/calendar bridges and database bridges) are no longer hypothetical; they are already needed enough to publish separately: https://crates.io/crates/jiff-icu ; https://crates.io/crates/jiff-sqlx
- Dirkjan Ochtman’s 2026 maintenance review says they are inclined to wind down Chrono and Chrono-TZ in coming months and now feel comfortable recommending Jiff. That is not an official Rust-project decision, but it is still an important ecosystem-maintenance signal that the temporal stack is in motion and that migration/interoperability artifacts are becoming more valuable, not less: https://dirkjan.ochtman.nl/writing/2026/01/09/reviewing-2025.html
- Archive decision: add **Time Surface Kit** as a shortlist / Tier 0/1 proposal focused on `time-surface/v0` + `clock-kind-profile/v0` + `civil-zone-profile/v0` + `calendar-locale-profile/v0` + `time-storage-profile/v0` + `time-adapter-profile/v0` + `time-vector-set/v0` + `time-check-report/v0` + `time-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Runtime Capability Kit, Background Work Kit, Localization Surface Kit, Dataset Surface Kit, and Replay Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Allocation Surface Kit (allocators, arenas, OOM posture, reset/drop truth, stable/nightly interop)
- Std’s `Allocator` trait still documents itself as a nightly-only experimental API, even though it already defines allocate / grow / shrink / deallocate semantics over arbitrary `Layout`s. That is direct evidence that allocator-generic Rust is real but still not a boring stable baseline: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/alloc/trait.Allocator.html
- Std’s allocation docs still distinguish the process-global allocator lane from the experimental generic allocator lane, which is good evidence that “global allocator” and “allocator-generic resource” should remain separate review objects: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/alloc/index.html
- Std `Vec`, `Box`, `HashSet`, `LinkedList`, and related types already expose `new_in` / `try_*_in`-style constructors on nightly under `allocator_api`. That is strong evidence that allocator-aware containers and pointers are not speculative; they are real public surfaces waiting for better ecosystem articulation. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/std/collections/struct.HashSet.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/collections/linked_list/struct.LinkedList.html
- `allocator-api2` explicitly describes itself as a mirror of Rust’s allocator API and says that when `allocator_api` is stable it will become a 1.0 re-export from `core` / `alloc` / `std`. That is unusually direct evidence that the ecosystem already needs a stable bridge lane now: https://docs.rs/allocator-api2
- `hashbrown` advertises allocator support through its `allocator-api2` feature, which is concrete proof that major collection crates already treat custom allocator interop as real public API rather than niche experimentation: https://docs.rs/hashbrown
- `bumpalo` explicitly says it can use `allocator-api2` on stable Rust and also documents reset semantics that mass-deallocate arena contents without running `Drop`; that is direct evidence that region-style allocation and normal allocator-generic containers are related but not semantically identical lanes. Sources: https://docs.rs/bumpalo ; https://docs.rs/bumpalo/latest/struct.Bump.html
- `typed-arena` still describes a fast but limited arena where objects are destroyed all at once when the arena is destroyed and individual objects are not deallocated independently. That is strong evidence that bulk-teardown and per-object-free semantics must remain visibly distinct: https://docs.rs/typed-arena/
- `mimalloc` remains a drop-in global allocator wrapper using `#[global_allocator]`, which is useful evidence that process-global override lanes still matter even as allocator-generic and arena lanes evolve: https://docs.rs/mimalloc
- Externally Implementable Items explicitly names the global allocator among the built-in override points Rust wants to make more like ordinary library features. That is a good strategic signal that allocator/provider seams are moving deeper into explicit ecosystem design territory rather than staying compiler magic forever: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/eii.html
- The 2025 State of Rust survey results say resource usage remains a productivity problem. That supports treating memory-resource clarity as ecosystem substrate work rather than only a low-level optimization hobby: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add **Allocation Surface Kit** as a Tier 1 proposal focused on `allocation-surface/v0` + `memory-resource-profile/v0` + `container-allocation-profile/v0` + `region-lifetime-profile/v0` + `oom-failure-profile/v0` + `allocation-adapter-profile/v0` + `allocation-vector-set/v0` + `allocation-check-report/v0` + `allocation-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Override Surface Kit, Initialization Surface Kit, Pointer Surface Kit, Footprint Kit, and Validity Surface Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Atomic Surface Kit (ordering contracts, progress/reclamation truth, and target-atomic posture)
- Std’s atomic docs now explicitly say Rust atomics follow the C++20 atomics rules (without consume), that data races are UB, and that mixed-size conflicting atomic accesses are also UB; they also make the public distinction that atomics may be lock-free without being wait-free. That is unusually direct evidence that ordering and progress claims are real public surface area, not implementation trivia: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/atomic/index.html
- The same std docs also make the portability story concrete: some targets lack some widths, some Arm targets have only load/store without full CAS, and maximally portable code needs to be careful about width assumptions. That supports treating target atomic capability as a first-class review object rather than burying it in cfgs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/atomic/index.html
- The Rust Reference exposes `target_has_atomic` as the machine-readable primitive for width/CAS capability. The missing layer is not a new low-level cfg, but a reusable artifact family above it: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#target_has_atomic
- `portable-atomic` is strong evidence that the ecosystem already needs multiple atomic portability lanes. Its docs advertise portable atomic integer types, 128-bit atomics, atomic floats, load/store or CAS support on targets where std lacks them, and fallback implementations including global-lock and critical-section-based behavior. That is exactly the kind of public truth most crates still do not expose in a reviewable form: https://docs.rs/portable-atomic/latest/portable_atomic/
- `crossbeam-epoch` is strong evidence that reclamation is part of the atomic surface. Its docs explain that removed lock-free nodes cannot be destructed until no thread can still be referencing them, and that epoch-based reclamation plus pin/unpin participation is the mechanism. That supports treating remove-vs-destroy timing and participation requirements as first-class contract material: https://docs.rs/crossbeam-epoch/latest/crossbeam_epoch/
- `arc-swap` is equally strong evidence that not all atomic surfaces are low-level integer or pointer cells. Its docs explicitly frame `ArcSwap` as “making `Arc` itself atomic” and optimize for read-mostly scenarios. That supports a distinct snapshot/publication lane inside the broader atomic surface family: https://docs.rs/arc-swap/latest/arc_swap/
- Loom remains one of the clearest proofs that atomic/shared-state evidence needs adversarial exploration, not just ordinary unit tests. Its docs say it permutes possible concurrent executions under the C11 memory model and uses state reduction to manage the explosion. That supports making Loom/model evidence a first-class atomic-check lane instead of a nice-to-have footnote: https://docs.rs/loom/latest/loom/
- The Rust-for-Linux smart-pointer RFC explicitly says kernel use-cases raise atomic memory-model issues because the kernel uses the Linux Kernel Memory Model rather than the usual C++ model. That is direct evidence that any future atomic-surface contract must not overfit to one universal userland memory-model story: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3621-derive-smart-pointer.html
- Rust’s 2026 safety-critical research says ecosystem support thins out in higher-criticality environments and explicitly names atomics among the building blocks teams want in evidence-friendly stacks. That supports ranking atomic-surface work as an ecosystem-substrate problem, not just a niche lock-free-library concern: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
