## 2026-03-07 — Override Surface Kit (provider slots, install lifecycle, scoped defaults, distributed registration, reset/test-isolation evidence)
- Externally Implementable Items is an active project-goal effort intended to make `#[panic_handler]`, global allocator, and similar features more like ordinary library features instead of compiler built-ins. That is strong evidence that override points are moving into explicit ecosystem design space rather than remaining compiler magic forever. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/eii.html
- The Rust Reference says `#[panic_handler]` defines panic behavior and must be unique in the dependency graph, while the attributes reference lists `global_allocator` as a runtime attribute. Std allocation docs add that `#[global_allocator]` can only be used once in a crate or its recursive dependencies. That is direct evidence that Rust already has first-class graph-wide override slots. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/panic.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/alloc/index.html
- `std::panic::set_hook` replaces the current panic hook, and `update_hook` atomically combines taking and setting the hook so a wrapper can do something and then execute the old handler. That is direct evidence that replacement versus composition semantics are part of the public contract. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.set_hook.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.update_hook.html
- `std::alloc::set_alloc_error_hook` documents a default hook and separate replacement path, which is useful evidence that allocator-slot semantics and allocation-failure-hook semantics are distinct override families rather than one generic “allocator config” concept. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/std/alloc/fn.set_alloc_error_hook.html
- `log::set_logger` may only be called once in the lifetime of a program, and log events before the call completes are ignored. That is direct evidence that install timing and one-shot process-global ownership are first-class semantics. Source: https://docs.rs/log/latest/log/fn.set_logger.html
- `tracing::subscriber::set_global_default` can only be set once, acts as a fallback when no thread-local subscriber has been set, and `tracing` separately exposes scoped/thread-local default APIs. That is direct evidence that global default, scoped default, and fallback-chain semantics are public behavior, not implementation detail. Sources: https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/subscriber/fn.set_global_default.html ; https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/subscriber/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/dispatcher/fn.with_default.html
- `inventory` provides typed distributed plugin registration from anywhere in linked code, while `linkme` gathers distributed slices into linker-collected sections contributed from anywhere in the dependency graph. That is direct evidence that Rust already has real collect-many discovery surfaces that are neither normal globals nor ordinary plugin hosts. Sources: https://docs.rs/inventory ; https://docs.rs/linkme ; https://docs.rs/linkme/latest/linkme/struct.DistributedSlice.html
- Archive decision: add **Override Surface Kit** as a Tier 1 proposal focused on `override-surface/v0` + `provider-slot-profile/v0` + `install-lifecycle-profile/v0` + `scope-multiplicity-profile/v0` + `registry-discovery-profile/v0` + `override-adapter-profile/v0` + `override-vector-set/v0` + `override-check-report/v0` + `override-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Runtime Capability Kit, Compile-Time Capabilities Kit, Plugin Surface Kit, Compile Guidance Kit, and Interop Commons Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Synchronization Surface Kit (fairness, backpressure, lag/retention, shutdown/cancellation, interleaving evidence)
- Rust’s 2026 flagships explicitly say that patterns that work in sync Rust should work in async Rust. That is direct evidence that the seam between blocking and async coordination remains active design territory rather than settled background detail. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H1 goals framed async parity work as part of making Rust easier to use for network systems, while also improving `Pin` ergonomics and preparing async/sync generators. That is strong evidence that the ecosystem is still unblocking core async-library shapes rather than merely polishing finished abstractions. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/index.html
- The 2026 safety-critical vision work says async is not “just a language feature”: it pulls in runtime choices, scheduling assumptions, and quality/process artifacts, and it explicitly recommends defining requirements for safety-case-friendly async runtimes. That is unusually direct evidence that synchronization/runtime semantics need to be explainable and reviewable. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
- Tokio’s `sync` docs say message passing is the most common form of synchronization in Tokio programs, while Tokio’s mutex docs say the ordinary std `Mutex` is often preferred in async code unless the guard must be held across `.await`. That is direct evidence that “async primitive” versus “blocking primitive” is not a naming detail but a semantic support surface that users must navigate. Sources: https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/struct.Mutex.html
- Std and Tokio already publish materially different coordination semantics: std `mpsc::channel` is infinitely buffered while `sync_channel` is bounded (with rendezvous possible at capacity 0); Tokio `mpsc` makes bounded backpressure explicit and also offers an unbounded sender usable from both sync and async code; `watch` only retains the latest value; `broadcast` delivers each value to all receivers; `Notify` carries no data; `Semaphore` models permits rather than ownership of one protected value. That is concrete evidence that Rust needs honest coordination-surface vocabulary above individual crate docs. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/mpsc/ ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/mpsc/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/watch/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/broadcast/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/struct.Notify.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/struct.Semaphore.html
- Fairness and lock semantics are already nontrivial and user-visible: std mutexes have poisoning semantics; `parking_lot` advertises smaller/faster/more-flexible synchronization and exposes fair unlock behavior; Tokio’s `Mutex` is FIFO/fair; Tokio’s `RwLock` is fair / write-preferring to avoid writer starvation. That is strong evidence that lock selection is about semantics and review posture, not just microbenchmark taste. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/poison/struct.Mutex.html ; https://docs.rs/parking_lot ; https://docs.rs/parking_lot/latest/parking_lot/type.Mutex.html ; https://docs.rs/parking_lot/latest/parking_lot/type.FairMutex.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/struct.Mutex.html ; https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/struct.RwLock.html
- Verification already has meaningful point tools: `loom` explores many valid concurrent executions under the C11 memory model, while `shuttle` explicitly trades soundness for scale via randomized concurrency testing. That is direct evidence that the missing layer is not “invent schedule testing”, but “attach reviewable concurrency evidence to declared synchronization surfaces”. Sources: https://docs.rs/loom/latest/loom/ ; https://docs.rs/shuttle/latest/shuttle/
- The old async status-quo stories remain relevant evidence that users get confused by which lock/channel family to use and why ecosystem divergence feels semantically costly. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/wg-async/vision/submitted_stories/status_quo/alan_thinks_he_needs_async_locks.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/wg-async/vision/submitted_stories/status_quo/alan_builds_a_task_scheduler.html
- Archive decision: add **Synchronization Surface Kit** as a shortlist / Tier 0/1 proposal focused on `sync-surface/v0` + `lock-profile/v0` + `channel-profile/v0` + `signal-permit-profile/v0` + `shutdown-cancel-profile/v0` + `sync-adapter-profile/v0` + `sync-vector-set/v0` + `sync-check-report/v0` + `sync-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Async Lifecycle Kit, Replay Kit, Trait Surface Kit, Interop Commons Kit, Formal Verification Kit, and Validity Surface Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Validity Surface Kit (invalid values, niche/layout assumptions, ingress checks, attachable validity evidence)
- The `std` contracts goal explicitly says safety contracts define preconditions, postconditions, and invariants, and that contract attributes should be convertible into runtime checks and exposed to external tools. That is direct evidence that Rust is moving toward machine-readable safety/validity surfaces, not just prose. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/std-contracts.html
- The unsafe-fields goal exists because Rust currently lacks mechanisms for denoting fields that carry library safety invariants, and says that without such a mechanism one must check all places where invariants might be violated, even safe code. That is direct evidence that library invariants need a first-class review surface. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/unsafe-fields.html
- The comprehensive niche-checks goal says invalid values should ideally be checked at load-time or on function entry, motivates this with unsafe Rust and FFI, and explicitly notes that Miri cannot call extern functions or execute mixed-language binaries. That is unusually direct evidence for a missing ecosystem artifact layer around validity at boundaries. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/comprehensive-niche-checks.html
- The sanitizer stabilization goal says unsafe Rust and foreign code in mixed-language binaries do not enjoy the same memory/thread-safety guarantees, and that sanitizer support therefore needs to improve. That is strong evidence that validity bugs remain boundary-sensitive in real production systems. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/stabilization-of-sanitizer-support.html
- Rust’s 2026 flagships explicitly elevate Safety-Critical Rust, including tooling, specifications, and evidence. That makes validity claims and invalid-value checks look less like niche unsafe lore and more like ecosystem substrate. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- `MaybeUninit` docs state that the compiler assumes values are properly initialized according to their type requirements and give references as an example of types that must always be aligned and non-null. That is a useful anchor for why “invalid on creation” and “invalid on use” must not be conflated. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html
- The Reference’s UB page and the niche-checks goal together are strong evidence that invalid-value production is a first-class correctness boundary in Rust, not just a downstream crash symptom. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/comprehensive-niche-checks.html
- `zerocopy` already exposes `KnownLayout`, `FromBytes`, `TryFromBytes`, and `IntoBytes`, while `bytemuck` exposes `Pod`, `Zeroable`, and `CheckedBitPattern`. That is concrete evidence that the ecosystem already needs structured vocabulary for layout validity, zero validity, and checked bit patterns, but does not yet share one boundary artifact family above them. Sources: https://docs.rs/zerocopy ; https://docs.rs/bytemuck
- `abi_stable` documents load-time checking of expected type layout for dynamic libraries, while `safer_ffi` explicitly frames itself as a way to write and generate safer FFI. That is good evidence that validity and boundary checking already matter outside pure-Rust byte parsing. Sources: https://docs.rs/abi_stable ; https://docs.rs/safer_ffi
- Archive decision: add **Validity Surface Kit** as a shortlist / Tier 0/1 proposal focused on `validity-surface/v0` + `niche-profile/v0` + `layout-validity-profile/v0` + `boundary-ingress-profile/v0` + `unsafe-invariant-profile/v0` + `validity-adapter-profile/v0` + `validity-vector-set/v0` + `validity-check-report/v0` + `validity-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Sanitizer Battery Kit, Safety Evidence Kit, FFI Boundary Kit, Pointer Surface Kit, Trait Surface Kit, and Formal Verification Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Trait Surface Kit (dyn posture, return-shape guarantees, impl coverage, attachable trait-family evidence)
- Rust’s 2026 flagships explicitly target stabilizing return type notation, async fn in dyn trait, the next-generation trait solver, and evolvable trait hierarchies. That is unusually direct evidence that trait surfaces are now an active ecosystem seam rather than a mostly-settled language background detail. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The evolving-traits goal is specifically about unblocking changes like `Deref: Receiver` and splitting `tower::Service` into a non-`Sync` supertrait plus a `Sync` subtrait, while also paving the way for more general splitting of traits into supertraits. That is direct evidence that trait-family evolution needs better published contracts than prose and migration folklore. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/evolving-traits.html
- The next-solver goal says the new solver is intended to replace the existing type-system components responsible for proving trait bounds and normalizing associated types, fixing long-standing unsoundnesses and enabling future type-system improvements. That is strong evidence that trait reasoning and trait-surface guarantees remain implementation-sensitive enough to deserve explicit vectors and reports. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/next-solver.html
- RFC 3654 defines return type notation specifically so users can add bounds such as `Send` to the futures returned by `async fn` in traits and by `-> impl Trait` methods, and it generalizes beyond async. That is direct proof that return-shape guarantees are part of the public trait surface, not hidden implementation detail. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3654-return-type-notation.html
- RFC 3185 stabilized `async fn` in traits but explicitly says such traits are not dyn safe today and describes their desugaring through anonymous associated types / GAT-like machinery. That is strong evidence that a trait’s method list alone is not enough to communicate its real dispatch posture. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3185-static-async-fn-in-trait.html
- The 2025H1 async goal says AFIT in public traits needs RTN and implementable trait aliases to unblock real use cases like Tower 1.0, and it treats `dynosaur` as a practical path for dynamic dispatch. That is direct evidence that real ecosystem trait surfaces already require adapters, migration paths, and explicit return-bound stories. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/async.html
- The July 2025 project-goals update says `dynosaur` was developed as a proc macro to support `async fn` together with `dyn Trait`, and frames async traits/streams as blockers for the next generation of async libraries. That is strong evidence that the ecosystem is carrying nontrivial trait-surface workaround layers today. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/
- `async-trait` explicitly presents itself as the macro that makes `async fn` in traits work with dyn traits, while `dynosaur` presents itself as dynamic dispatch for traits using async fn or `-> impl Trait` while preserving static dispatch otherwise. That is concrete evidence that “trait support” already splits across multiple adaptation strategies with different semantics. Sources: https://docs.rs/async-trait ; https://docs.rs/dynosaur
- `tower-service` documents `Service` as the foundation for Tower and describes it as a simple but powerful asynchronous function-like abstraction. That is a useful reminder that one trait surface can become broad ecosystem substrate, so split-family evolution and attached evidence matter. Source: https://docs.rs/tower-service
- Archive decision: add **Trait Surface Kit** as a shortlist / Tier 0/1 proposal focused on `trait-surface/v0` + `trait-semantics-profile/v0` + `dyn-dispatch-profile/v0` + `return-shape-profile/v0` + `impl-coverage-profile/v0` + `trait-adapter-profile/v0` + `trait-vector-set/v0` + `trait-check-report/v0` + `trait-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Interop Commons Kit, Pointer Surface Kit, Lending Surface Kit, Compile Guidance Kit, and Public API Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Pointer Surface Kit (smart-pointer semantics, projection/reborrow truth, receiver posture, attachable pointer evidence)
- Rust’s 2025H2 flagship theme is “Beyond the `&`”, explicitly aimed at making user-defined smart pointers as ergonomic as built-in references, and it names field projections, reborrow traits, and pin ergonomics as part of that lane. That is strong evidence that custom pointer semantics are now a first-class ecosystem seam, not a niche unsafe trick. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/28/project-goals-2025h2/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/pin-ergonomics.html
- The 2026 flagships continue that direction: “Beyond the `&`” keeps field projections, reborrow traits, and in-place initialization on the roadmap, while “Just Add Async” includes ergonomic ref-counting. That is direct evidence that Rust is opening new space for pointer-like library abstractions on multiple fronts at once. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- RFC 3519 says user-defined smart pointers are still second-class citizens today, motivates arbitrary self types partly from Rust-for-Linux and foreign-language semantics, and explicitly shows a custom C++-reference-style wrapper that should allow method calls without claiming ordinary Rust-reference behavior. That is unusually direct evidence for the missing archive seam: custom pointer surfaces need explicit semantics, not just more syntax. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs//3519-arbitrary-self-types-v2.html
- RFC 3621 exists to let custom smart pointers work with trait objects, which is strong evidence that method receivers alone are not enough; dyn/receiver posture is part of the ecosystem contract. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3621-derive-smart-pointer.html
- The field-projections goal says modified references and custom pointer types often conceptually support indexing into subfields even when `Deref` is not the right model. That is strong evidence that projection semantics deserve first-class artifacts instead of being buried in per-crate prose. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/field-projections.html
- The reborrow-traits goal explicitly says Rust-for-Linux should be enabled to experiment with custom reborrowable reference types and that users of the `reborrow` crate and similar should be able to move to a core solution. That is direct evidence that reborrow behavior is a real ecosystem seam, not just compiler implementation detail. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/autoreborrow-traits.html
- Rust-for-Linux’s stable-tooling progress notes mention stabilizing `CoercePointee` derive to support the kernel’s use of smart pointers for intrusive linked lists, and the earlier stable-build blockers explicitly called out the need for custom `Arc` receivers and dyn coercions. That is good proof that production systems users already need this seam. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/rfl.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/rfl_stable.html
- Std docs already show materially different pointer semantics across `Rc`, `Arc`, and `Pin`: `Rc` gives shared ownership with clone and clone-on-write paths, `Arc` gives shared ownership with thread-safe refcounting, and `Pin<Ptr>` is about preventing movement or invalidation at a location. That is enough ecosystem diversity to justify a common review layer above trait names alone. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/ ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/struct.Rc.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/pin/index.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/pin/struct.Pin.html
- The provenance RFC makes clear that pointer behavior depends on provenance, not only address. That is a useful warning that pointer abstractions should publish their guarantees and raw invariants honestly instead of collapsing semantics into marketing labels like “reference-like”. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3559-rust-has-provenance.html
- Archive decision: add **Pointer Surface Kit** as a shortlist / Tier 0/1 proposal focused on `pointer-surface/v0` + `pointer-semantics-profile/v0` + `projection-reborrow-profile/v0` + `receiver-dispatch-profile/v0` + `pointer-adapter-profile/v0` + `pointer-vector-set/v0` + `pointer-check-report/v0` + `pointer-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Lending Surface Kit, FFI Boundary Kit, Safety Evidence Kit, and Interop Commons Kit.

## 2026-03-07 — Interop Commons Kit (shared building blocks, adapter profiles, conformance vectors, attachable interop evidence)
- The Rust vision work explicitly says part of helping users navigate crates.io is enabling smoother interop, potentially via key interop traits or by blessing standard building blocks like the `http` crate; it also notes current coherence rules make incremental ecosystem interop traits difficult to introduce. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/19/what-do-people-love-about-rust/
- The 2025 async project-goal updates say progress toward the next generation of async libraries has been blocked on stable solutions for async traits and streams. That is direct evidence that some of Rust's missing ecosystem work is interop substrate, not another framework. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/04/08/Project-Goals-2025-March-Update/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still reports resource usage as a major productivity problem and notes ongoing concern around developer/maintainer support and complexity. That argues for smaller shared seams and reusable adapters rather than proliferating whole new stacks. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The `http` crate explicitly describes itself as a general-purpose library of common HTTP types and says it is intended as the “standard library” for HTTP clients and servers without dictating implementation. That is a strong precedent for the kind of neutral common layer this archive should take seriously. Sources: https://docs.rs/http ; https://docs.rs/http/latest/src/http/lib.rs.html
- Tower says `Service` and `Layer` are important integration points and keeps them in separate crates with breaking changes made rarely; `tower-http` says its middleware uses `http` and `http-body` abstractions and is compatible with libraries/frameworks such as Hyper, Tonic, and Warp. That is direct evidence that stable interop seams can unlock large amounts of reusable ecosystem behavior. Sources: https://docs.rs/tower ; https://docs.rs/tower/latest/tower/trait.Service.html ; https://docs.rs/tower-http
- `axum` says using `tower::Service` lets it share middleware with Hyper or Tonic, while `tonic` exposes Tower-based service/layer integration and middleware attachment. That is concrete proof that shared interop seams already pay off in production-grade crates. Sources: https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/ ; https://docs.rs/tonic/latest/tonic/service/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tonic/latest/tonic/transport/server/struct.Server.html
- Archive decision: add **Interop Commons Kit** as a shortlist / Tier 0/1 proposal focused on `interop-seam/v0` + `shared-building-block/v0` + `adapter-profile/v0` + `conformance-vector-set/v0` + optional `adoption-profile/v0` + `interop-check-report/v0` + `commons-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Ecosystem Atlas Kit, Build Interop Kit, Schema Contract Kit, and the domain-specific surface kits.

## 2026-03-07 — Runtime Capability Kit (least-privilege runtime authority, delegation, sandbox posture, checked denial evidence)
- `cap-std` explicitly says capability-based APIs represent access to external resources as values passed around the program, and spotlights `Dir` and `Pool` as core filesystem/network authority types. That is strong evidence that Rust already has a serious library-level capability substrate rather than only framework-specific ACLs. Source: https://docs.rs/cap-std/latest/cap_std/
- `ambient-authority` explicitly says APIs using ambient authority should include an `AmbientAuthority` argument, and that the returned token indicates the user explicitly opted into ambient authority. That is a strong signal that the ecosystem already has a vocabulary for distinguishing delegated capability from ambient access. Source: https://docs.rs/ambient-authority/latest/src/ambient_authority/lib.rs.html
- Wasmtime’s security docs explicitly say WASI filesystem access follows a capability-based security model, and Wasmtime’s WASI 0.2 host implementation is explicitly built primarily on `tokio` and `cap-std`. That is strong evidence that capability-oriented runtime authority is part of mainstream Rust/Wasm embedding rather than a side project. Sources: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/security.html ; https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime_wasi/p2/index.html
- Tauri v2 explicitly says capabilities define which permissions are granted or denied for which windows or webviews, and its permissions model explicitly describes permissions as explicit command privileges with attachable scopes. That is strong evidence that real Rust app frameworks are already converging on explicit runtime-authority surfaces even if they are not portable across stacks yet. Sources: https://v2.tauri.app/security/capabilities/ ; https://v2.tauri.app/security/permissions/
- `rustix` explicitly positions itself as safe Rust bindings to POSIX/Unix/Linux/Winsock-like syscalls with memory safety, I/O safety, and provenance. That is useful evidence that least-privilege/runtime-authority design can connect cleanly down into lower-level systems APIs rather than stopping at app-framework config. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/latest
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update added a Security tab, expanded trusted publishing support, and highlighted security posture work; its February 2026 malware-notification update also makes clear that malicious impersonation crates continue to appear. That is a useful reminder that supply-chain hygiene is necessary but not sufficient; reducing runtime blast radius is a distinct ecosystem need. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/13/crates.io-malicious-crate-update/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says resource usage is still among the most common productivity problems, notes ongoing complexity concerns, and shows a slight uptick in worries about developer and maintainer support. That is a strong signal to prefer convergent, evidence-friendly substrates over another wave of one-off frameworks or bespoke security DSLs. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Rust’s 2026 safety-critical vision work says the ecosystem support thins out fast beyond prototyping, that teams need evidence-friendly software stacks and runtime/process artifacts, and that async/runtime choices become qualification questions. That is strong evidence that a portable runtime-authority/evidence layer would matter beyond desktop or Wasm niches. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
- Archive decision: add **Runtime Capability Kit** as a Tier 0/1 proposal focused on `runtime-capability-surface/v0` + `authority-profile/v0` + `scope-profile/v0` + `delegation-map/v0` + optional `sandbox-profile/v0` + `cap-check-report/v0` + `cap-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Compile-Time Capabilities Kit, Policy Kit, Plugin Surface Kit, Client App Surface Kit, Wasm Component Kit, and Service/Protocol surface kits.

## 2026-03-06 — Geospatial Surface Kit (geometry families, CRS/projection truth, format/runtime support, checked spatial evidence)
- GeoRust is explicitly an ecosystem of geospatial tools and libraries written in Rust. That is a strong signal that the archive should treat geospatial support as a real ecosystem frontier, not a niche side alley. Source: https://georust.org/
- `geo` explicitly provides planar geospatial geometries and algorithms, including DE-9IM/topological operations, multiple distance models, and support for projecting and converting between coordinate reference systems using PROJ. That is direct evidence that geometry semantics and CRS/projection posture are already separate and review-worthy support surfaces. Source: https://docs.rs/geo/
- `geo-types` explicitly defines geometric types for the GeoRust ecosystem and positions itself as the compatibility layer crate authors use when they want interoperability with other GeoRust crates. That is strong evidence that Rust geospatial support already has a shared type substrate but still lacks a higher-level support contract. Source: https://docs.rs/geo-types/
- `geozero` explicitly defines an API for reading geospatial data formats without an intermediate representation and advertises zero-copy reading and writing across WKT/WKB, GeoJSON, MVT, GDAL, and other formats. That is a strong signal that support truth is no longer just about one in-memory geometry model. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/geozero/latest
- `geoarrow` explicitly describes itself as a complete, safe, native Rust implementation of GeoArrow, and the GeoArrow specification explicitly defines Arrow extension-type metadata so CRS and related type-level metadata can propagate. That is strong evidence that Rust geospatial support already includes a serious columnar/interchange lane whose support truth deserves explicit artifacts. Sources: https://docs.rs/geoarrow/ ; https://geoarrow.org/
- `proj` explicitly provides coordinate transformation via bindings to PROJ v9.6 and is explicit that it will either use a pre-existing libproj or build from source with `bundled_proj`. That is useful evidence that bundled-vs-system native behavior is part of the real support contract. Source: https://docs.rs/proj/
- `gdal` explicitly provides safe, idiomatic Rust bindings for GDAL’s raster/vector capabilities, but it is also explicit that builds assume a compatible GDAL installation and that authoritative docs remain upstream GDAL documentation. That is strong evidence that runtime/native-driver truth is a first-class part of the Rust geospatial story. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/gdal/latest
- `flatgeobuf` explicitly describes itself as a performant binary encoding for geographic data based on FlatBuffers. That is useful evidence that high-performance geospatial interchange is already a real Rust lane rather than a purely academic possibility. Source: https://docs.rs/flatgeobuf/
- Archive decision: add **Geospatial Surface Kit** as a Tier 1/2 proposal focused on `geo-surface/v0` + `geometry-catalog/v0` + `crs-profile/v0` + `geo-format-catalog/v0` + optional `geo-runtime-profile/v0` + `geo-check-report/v0` + `geo-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Dataset Surface Kit, Service Surface Kit, Client App Surface Kit, Media Surface Kit, Support Envelope Kit, and format-specific crates.

## 2026-03-06 — Replica Surface Kit (replicated documents, sync profiles, history/merge posture, storage truth, convergence evidence)
- `automerge` explicitly positions itself as a library for collaborative local-first applications, with a sync protocol and efficient binary storage format, and its “Welcome” docs emphasize offline local copies, later synchronization, automatic merges, and history/branching. That is strong evidence that Rust already has a real local-first substrate rather than a purely academic one. Sources: https://automerge.org/automerge/automerge/index.html ; https://automerge.org/docs/hello/
- Automerge’s repository docs explicitly say the core JSON-like CRDT and sync protocol still leave a lot of application plumbing, and repo-based apps must choose storage and network adapters. That is a direct signal that the missing layer is no longer the bare sync algorithm but the reviewable support boundary above adapters, formats, and transports. Source: https://automerge.org/docs/reference/repositories/
- Yrs is already a high-performance Rust port of Yjs whose docs expose shared types, update events, undo/redo, past revisions, and awareness/y-sync support. That is strong evidence that Rust local-first/collaboration stacks already have real operational surfaces beyond “a text CRDT.” Source: https://docs.rs/yrs/latest/yrs/
- `yrs-lmdb` is explicitly a persistence layer for storing Yrs documents on LMDB, and `yrs-kvstore` generalizes the pattern to persistent key-value stores. That is useful evidence that durability/recovery adapters are already part of the real support story. Sources: https://docs.rs/yrs-lmdb/latest/yrs_lmdb/ ; https://docs.rs/yrs-kvstore/latest/yrs_kvstore/
- Loro’s docs explicitly frame syncing/offline collaboration as difficult, position Loro as local-first state management with better DevTools, and show document import/export, time travel, version control, and peer-id-aware synchronization. That is strong evidence that the missing contribution should be a support/evidence layer above those parts rather than another CRDT core. Sources: https://loro.dev/docs ; https://loro.dev/docs/tutorial/loro_doc
- Loro 1.0 now claims a stable data format, version control features, and support across Rust, JS/WASM, and Swift. That is a strong signal that cross-runtime compatibility and long-lived format promises are now review-worthy support surfaces. Source: https://loro.dev/blog/v1.0
- Loro’s own docs also explicitly say some applications requiring strong consistency should consider alternatives. ## 2026-03-06 — Migration Kit (reviewable source→destination change programs)
- The Edition Guide already defines migration as an ordered workflow: update dependencies, run `cargo fix --edition`, update the `edition` field, and then build/test. That is strong evidence the missing contribution is orchestration and durable review state, not just syntax rewriting. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/editions/transitioning-an-existing-project-to-a-new-edition.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/20/Rust-1.85.0/
- The advanced migrations guide explicitly says some changes must still be handled manually or with a custom tool built on `rustfix`, which shows the real migration surface extends beyond one Cargo subcommand. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/editions/advanced-migrations.html ; https://docs.rs/rustfix/latest/rustfix/
- `cargo fix` only sees code that is actually compiled and requires explicit feature/target selection for conditional code. That means configuration scope is part of migration truth and should be recorded, not left implicit in CI flags. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html
- Cargo can conservatively update lockfiles today, but semver-breaking dependency requirement updates remain an unstable/nightly-only lane in Cargo itself. That is concrete evidence that upgrade workflows are real and partly supported, but still fragmented. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-update.html
- `cargo-edit`, `cargo-msrv`, `cargo-public-api`, and `cargo-semver-checks` already cover manifest upgrades, MSRV discovery/verification, API diffs, and semver reasoning. The missing contribution is a shared change-intent / plan / report layer above them rather than another point checker. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-edit/latest ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-msrv/latest ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-public-api/latest ; https://github.com/obi1kenobi/cargo-semver-checks/releases
- Cargo’s `rust-version` documentation treats MSRV as a user-facing support contract and explicitly notes that selecting and verifying supported versions can get complicated in workspaces. rustup’s override and `rust-toolchain.toml` docs show toolchain pinning is already first-class input. That makes toolchain migration a real ecosystem workflow rather than a local preference. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/rust-version.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/overrides.html
- Rust’s 2024 survey results say some respondents avoid or stop using Rust because switching or introducing it would be too expensive in human effort, or because the ecosystem feels overwhelming. Better migration choreography is therefore an adoption and maintenance lever, not just maintainer neatness. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/13/2024-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add **Migration Kit** as a Tier 1/2 proposal focused on `change-intent/v0` + `change-analysis-report/v0` + `change-plan/v0` + `change-run-report/v0` + `change-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Public API Kit, Resolution Doctor Kit, Config Set Kit, and Release Pipeline Kit.

## 2026-03-06 — Macro Workflow Kit (inventory, expansion artifacts, cost/debug, migration hints)
- Rust’s accepted macro improvements goal explicitly aims to make `macro_rules!` capable enough to replace many current proc-macro use cases, and names faster builds, simpler macros, and reduced dependency supply chains as benefits. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/macro-improvements.html
- The reflection-and-comptime goal states directly that proc-macro derives have historically been hard to debug and bootstrap from scratch, which is a strong signal that “macro workflows” are an ecosystem problem in their own right rather than just a tool preference. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html
- Current practical workflow pieces remain fragmented: Cargo now marks proc-macro crates in `cargo tree`, older Cargo added `cargo tree -e no-proc-macro`, `cargo-expand` is the common expansion tool but documents itself as a lossy debugging aid, and rust-analyzer still exposes proc-macro support / ignored macros as explicit configuration. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-expand/latest ; https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration
- Design direction: add `Macro Workflow Kit` as a Tier 1/2 substrate around `cargo macro` + `macro-inventory/v0` + `macro-expansion-pack/v0` + `macro-cost-report/v0` + `macro-debug-report/v0` + `macro-migration-hints/v0` + `macro-pack/v0`.
- Boundary: keep this distinct from Compile-Time Capabilities Kit. That kit governs permissions/sandboxing/determinism for build scripts and proc macros; Macro Workflow Kit governs inventory, expansion, debugging, cost, and migration planning.

## 2026-03-06 — Sysroot Pack Kit (custom std builds + reusable sysroots)
- The build-std goal is now explicitly about an MVP that could be stabilized, and it calls out the need to make std sources available, build them without the current nightly-only assumptions, and tell the compiler to use the rebuilt libraries in a standard way: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/build-std.html
- The October 2025 program update says three build-std RFCs were posted (`context`, `always`, and `explicit dependencies`), which is a much stronger maturity signal than the old “interesting nightly experiment” framing: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/11/19/program-management-update--october-2025/
- Cargo’s current unstable docs still show why the next missing seam is packaging/reuse rather than raw build mechanics alone: `-Z build-std` remains nightly-only, requires `rust-src`, and must be passed to all cargo invocations: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Rust for Linux and adjacent low-level users still need custom std/core builds on stable foundations, and the 2025H2 compiler-features goal explicitly points back to build-std / build-core support as a related need: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/rfl.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/Rust-for-Linux-compiler.html
- Rust’s own sanitizer and mitigation docs already require or strongly recommend rebuilding std in some workflows, especially for CFI and CFG, which means the ecosystem needs a first-class way to describe *which* stdlib was actually linked: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/sanitizer.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/control_flow_guard.html
- The rustc custom-target docs still tell users to reach for build-std and explicitly warn that target JSON and compiler versions must be pinned together, reinforcing the need for honest compatibility metadata in any portable sysroot artifact: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/targets/custom.html

## 2026-03-06 — Native Dependency Kit (provider locks, link plans, native-intent substrate)
- Cargo roadmap issue `#14948`: reducing user-authored build scripts is now an explicit goal because they cost build time, bug risk, and audit scope; native dependency discovery is one of the major lingering reasons they persist. https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/14948
- RFC 2136 build systems: native dependencies are explicitly called out as a cross-cutting concern, and existing `-sys` crates are described as relying on custom build scripts that external build systems want to reroute to their own managed dependencies. https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2136-build-systems.html
- RFC 2196 metabuild: the RFC explicitly says broader build systems need structured information about native dependencies that is currently embedded inside `build.rs`, which is a direct design signal for provider-lock artifacts rather than more opaque script glue. https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2196-metabuild.html
- Sandboxed build scripts goal: Cargo users want build scripts to become more deterministic and less privileged; native probing/build logic is one of the concrete reasons this remains hard. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/sandboxed-build-script.html
- Cargo build-script docs + manifest docs: `build` and `links` are real native-dependency primitives today, but `links` still requires a build script, supports only one package per native-library identity, and passes metadata only one step down the graph. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
- Cargo FAQ: duplicate `links` values remain a concrete graph failure mode users must resolve manually, which is good evidence that native dependency identity is already a first-class problem but not yet a first-class artifact boundary. https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/cargo/faq.html
- Existing provider crates confirm the fragmentation shape: `system-deps` exposes declarative Cargo metadata for system libraries, while `pkg-config`, `vcpkg`, and `cmake` each document provider-specific build-script-centered flows. This is strong evidence for a convergence contract layer instead of another single-provider tool. https://docs.rs/system-deps/latest/system_deps/ ; https://docs.rs/pkg-config/latest/pkg_config/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/vcpkg/latest ; https://docs.rs/cmake/latest/cmake/
- RFC 3028 / artifact dependencies are an important adjacent primitive because Cargo can now provide build-time binaries or C-ABI artifacts from other Cargo packages, but that still leaves the larger system/native-provider selection story unresolved. https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3028-cargo-binary-dependencies.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/cargo/reference/unstable.html

- Cargo manifest docs: maintenance-status values still exist in `[badges]`, but crates.io no longer uses them, which leaves Rust with a vocabulary but no first-class live lifecycle channel: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html
- RFC 3537 MSRV resolver: explicitly calls out tracking version maintenance status on crates.io as useful future context for supported older versions / LTS-style policies: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3537-msrv-resolver.html
- crates.io policies: ownership of an existing crate is not transferred without explicit approval of the current owner, which makes explicit handoff consent and successor metadata more important: https://crates.io/policies
- RustSec advisory DB + cargo-deny: unmaintained advisories are already a first-class input to ecosystem policy workflows, but they are still being routed through advisory channels rather than a dedicated lifecycle substrate: https://github.com/rustsec/advisory-db ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/advisories/index.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/advisories/cfg.html

## 2026-03-06 — Repro Build Kit promotion (independent rebuild verdicts, diff reasons, attachable packs)
- Rust/Cargo now has real reproducibility-adjacent primitives: the `trim-paths` RFC exists to sanitize path leakage in binaries, diagnostics, debug info, and `file!()` expansions, which makes it an explicit source→artifact hygiene primitive rather than a cosmetic tweak. https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3127-trim-paths.html
- Cargo’s changelog shows `trim-paths` is still actively moving, including remapping all paths to `build.build-dir` and broadening Windows MSVC coverage; this is a live substrate worth building atop. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/CHANGELOG.html
- Cargo’s unstable docs now expose two especially relevant seams: `sbom` precursor files for executable/linkable outputs, and `--artifact-dir` for predictable final-artifact collection instead of fragile JSON scraping. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo 1.93’s design discussion around final-artifact uplift is another strong signal that Cargo is converging on explicit artifact boundaries rather than leaving important release subjects buried in ad hoc `target/` paths. https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- Cargo’s own fingerprinting docs are a useful reality check: more complete reproducibility would require deeper environment capture, but Cargo intentionally balances that against complexity, speed, and portability. That is exactly why the missing contribution is a report/pack layer with honest capability boundaries. https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/src/cargo/core/compiler/fingerprint/mod.rs.html
- `cargo-dist` is now strong evidence that release automation has crossed the threshold where a stricter verifier is worth standardizing: it emits machine-readable manifests and explicitly aims for rerunnable release commands, while also saying this is not trying to guarantee bit-level precision. https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/
- GitHub artifact attestations now establish build provenance, support SBOM attestations, and document offline verification flows. That makes them natural attachments or references for a Rust-native reproducibility report, but not replacements for an independent rebuild verdict. https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/use-artifact-attestations ; https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/verify-attestations-offline
- `cargo-dist`’s supply-chain docs now include CycloneDX SBOM generation, `cargo-auditable`, and OmniBOR artifact IDs, which reinforces the archive’s direction toward small composable evidence artifacts rather than giant one-off security dashboards. https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/supplychain-security/index.html
- Resulting design choice: promote the buried reproducible-build-verification thread as **Repro Build Kit** (`cargo repro` + `repro-intent/v0` + `repro-env/v0` + `repro-report/v0` + `repro-diff/v0` + `repro-pack/v0`) and keep it explicitly distinct from Release Pipeline Kit, Signed Binaries Kit, Airgap Kit, Build Extension Kit, and Cargo Report Kit.

## 2026-03-06 — Build Interop Kit promotion (workspace discovery, machine-readable build graphs, execution events)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes explicitly say Cargo should integrate into larger build systems and prototype plumbing commands, which is unusually direct evidence that interop is a roadmap concern rather than just an external-tools wish list. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The accepted 2025H1 Cargo plumbing goal is still the clearest statement of the current gap: today’s machine-facing commands are too porcelain-oriented, `cargo metadata` excludes feature resolution, and the build lifecycle needs experiment-friendly plumbing surfaces across discovery, resolution, planning, execution, and staging. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- Cargo’s external-tools docs show the present floor: stable/versioned `cargo metadata`, JSON build messages, and subcommands. That is useful, but it is not yet a complete discovery/plan/event substrate. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html
- The Cargo changelog now makes the design direction sharper by removing the old unstable `build-plan` experiment and explicitly pointing to plumbing commands, `--unit-graph`, and structured logging as the better path. https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/cargo/CHANGELOG.html
- The unstable `--unit-graph` docs are particularly important because they say this view is more complete than `cargo metadata`, especially for the newer feature resolver and intra-package dependencies like build scripts and tests. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Cargo 1.94 development notes reinforce that the machine-facing layer is actively moving: structured logging is progressing, `cargo report rebuild` and `cargo report sessions` landed, and workspace/configuration discovery is being revisited because accidental parent manifests/config files still create surprising failures. https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- rust-analyzer already documents a real discovery/event protocol for non-Cargo build systems via `workspace.discoverConfig`, but warns the JSONL output format is provisional and subject to change. https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration
- rust-analyzer’s `{label}` support in `check.overrideCommand` shows a concrete missing seam: editors already need a stable mapping from files to Cargo package IDs or external build labels. https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration
- Fuchsia is a strong concrete proof that this is not theoretical: its Rust workflow uses GN-generated `rust-project.json`, and its docs explicitly warn that the format’s instability can break rust-analyzer. https://fuchsia.dev/fuchsia-src/development/languages/rust/editors
- BSP remains relevant prior art because its whole motivation is to reduce bespoke IDE ↔ build-tool integrations; the archive uses that as a bridge target, not as a replacement for Rust-specific unit/package/feature semantics. https://build-server-protocol.github.io/docs/specification.html
- Resulting design choice: promote and merge the buried workspace-discovery, build-plan, and structured-event threads as **Build Interop Kit** (`cargo interop` + `workspace-discovery/v0` + `workspace-graph/v0` + `build-plan/v0` + `cargo-events/v0` + `interop-pack/v0`) and keep it explicitly distinct from Cargo Report Kit, Workspace Governance Kit, CompileDB Kit, and Resolution Doctor Kit.

## 2026-03-06 — Sanitizer Battery Kit promotion (runtime-checking profiles, honest capability descriptors, CI packs)
- Rust’s 2025H2 sanitizer goal is explicit: stabilize MemorySanitizer and ThreadSanitizer support, fix bugs, and provide precompiled instrumented standard libraries through rustup so the workflow is not “nightly plus rebuild std yourself” forever. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/stabilization-of-sanitizer-support.html
- The 2026 flagship slate keeps sanitizer work in the mainstream roadmap for specialized build scenarios rather than leaving it a niche side quest. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The unstable-book sanitizer docs still show why the missing seam is orchestration/evidence, not just more engines: target support is fragmented, many workflows still require `--target` and `-Zbuild-std`, and mixed-language cases may need `external-clangrt`. https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/sanitizer.html
- Rust now also has a project goal to emit retags in codegen so native instrumentation tools can find aliasing bugs; that goal explicitly frames BorrowSanitizer as an out-of-tree LLVM instrumentation tool for Tree-Borrows-style violations in large mixed-language systems. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/codegen_retags.html
- BorrowSanitizer’s February 2026 update shows enough practical momentum to matter for archive design: better error messages, active performance work, LLVM integration changes, and a proposed 2026 project goal to transition from prototype to usable tool. https://borrowsanitizer.com/status/february_2026.html
- Miri remains central, but its README also makes the limits clear: it is deterministic by default, much slower than native execution, cannot guarantee soundness from one execution, and recommends specialized tools like Loom for some concurrency questions. https://github.com/rust-lang/miri
- `cargo-careful` now fills a distinct practical lane between plain tests and Miri: it rebuilds std with debug assertions, enables extra UB checks, supports arbitrary system / C FFI calls, and can optionally use sanitizers. https://github.com/RalfJung/cargo-careful
- `nextest` already documents Miri integration and machine-readable outputs, while also noting an important capability tradeoff: process-per-test Miri runs can be 3–4× faster, but they do not detect races between tests sharing a resource. https://nexte.st/docs/integrations/miri/ ; https://nexte.st/docs/integrations/
- The rustc exploit-mitigations chapter is now a useful umbrella reference for why CFI / safe stack / shadow call stack belong in the same reviewable family of runtime-checking artifacts in the presence of Unsafe Rust. https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/exploit-mitigations.html
- Resulting design choice: promote the buried sanitizer + aliasing thread as **Sanitizer Battery Kit** (`cargo sanitize` + `sanitize-profile/v0` + `sanitize-capabilities/v0` + `sanitize-report/v0` + `sanitize-suppressions/v0` + `sanitize-pack/v0`) and keep it explicitly distinct from Safety Evidence Kit, Replay Kit, FFI Boundary Kit, and DST Kit.

- RFC 3355 says Rust still lacks an accurate specification and explicitly names unsafe-code authors, safety-critical users, language designers, and tooling maintainers as people who would benefit from one: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3355-rust-spec.html
- The accepted 2025H1 goal transferred the Ferrocene Language Specification into rust-lang infrastructure and aimed to publish a rust-lang-owned version integrated with Rust project processes and tooling: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/spec-fls-publish.html
- The proposed 2025H2 follow-on goal is explicitly about developing the capability and capacity to keep the FLS up to date sustainably, which is a strong sign that spec work is now operational rather than purely aspirational: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/FLS-up-to-date-capabilities.html
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes list **stabilizing FLS release cadence** as part of Safety-Critical Rust, which elevates this from a niche documentation concern to ecosystem strategy: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The current rust-lang-hosted FLS now includes paragraph identifiers, normative structure, and explicit “conforming tool” language, but it also says it is **not intended as a document enabling conformance between compilers**; that is the clean missing seam this promotion targets: https://rust-lang.github.io/fls/general.html
- `compiletest` remains the main harness of the Rust compiler test suite, and `ui_test` proves there is demand for reusable compile-and-compare harnesses outside rust-lang proper, but neither gives the ecosystem a versioned spec-ref/vector/capability/report bundle by default: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/tests/compiletest.html ; https://docs.rs/ui_test
- `toml-test-rs` is an adjacent proof that Rust ecosystems benefit from separating language-agnostic test data from Rust-native harness pieces; the archive takes that pattern as inspiration for `conformance-vectors/v0` rather than pretending one runner should own the whole lane: https://github.com/toml-rs/toml-test-rs
- Resulting design choice: promote the buried spec/conformance idea as **Spec Conformance Kit** (`cargo conform` + `spec-pack/v0` + `conformance-vectors/v0` + `implementation-capabilities/v0` + `conformance-report/v0` + `conformance-pack/v0`) and keep it explicitly distinct from MIR Analysis Kit, Safety Evidence Kit, and compiletest itself.

- `typify` compiles JSON Schema into Rust types and `progenitor` generates Rust clients from OpenAPI, which means both producer-side and consumer-side schema workflows are now healthy enough that the missing piece looks like shared evidence/diff tooling rather than more one-off generators: https://docs.rs/typify ; https://docs.rs/progenitor

## 2026-03-06 — Observability Kit promotion (telemetry contracts + validation vectors)
- 2025 State of Rust survey results: debugging remains one of the main productivity problems, even after slipping from 2nd to 4th place, and the compiler team immediately launched a dedicated debugging survey to learn more: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/23/rust-debugging-survey-2026/
- Cargo 1.94 development cycle: structured logging work plus `cargo report timings`, `cargo report rebuild`, and `cargo report sessions` make machine-readable diagnostics/report workflows increasingly real inside Cargo itself: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- OpenTelemetry Rust docs now present traces, metrics, and logs together, but still mark all three major signal areas as beta, which argues for a thin artifact/validation layer rather than a massive abstraction crate: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/rust/
- OpenTelemetry’s 2025 stability proposal explicitly says ecosystem complexity is creating production adoption barriers such as configuration breakage between minor versions, performance regressions at scale, and rollout complexity: https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2025/stability-proposal-announcement/
- OpenTelemetry Weaver / “observability by design” frames telemetry as something that should be versioned, validated, and treated more like a schema/API than a pile of ad hoc logs: https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2025/otel-weaver/
- OpenTelemetry Rust recommends OTLP exporters for production scenarios, SDK config docs make OTLP the default exporter class for traces / metrics / logs when auto-configured, and RustSec now flags `opentelemetry-jaeger` as unmaintained; together these support an OTLP-first reference policy with doctor warnings rather than exporter sprawl: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-rust ; https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/sdk-configuration/general/ ; https://rustsec.org/packages/opentelemetry-jaeger.html
- Tokio Console proves there is real value in Rust-specific async diagnostic streams and a wire protocol + `tracing-subscriber` layer, but it is still a specialized lane; the missing archive contribution is the shared contract tying runtime diagnostics to general telemetry and CI evidence: https://github.com/tokio-rs/console
- `tracing`, `tracing-subscriber`, `tracing-log`, `metrics`, and `metrics-util` confirm the ecosystem already has strong instrumentation and layering primitives; the design decision is to converge them with profiles/reports/vectors instead of proposing yet another logging or metrics facade: https://docs.rs/tracing ; https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber ; https://docs.rs/tracing-log ; https://docs.rs/metrics ; https://docs.rs/metrics-util/latest/metrics_util/layers/
- Priority change: promoted the buried Observability Kit idea into the concise archive as Tier 1 and explicitly bounded it against Debugger Experience Kit, Replay Kit, Perf Labs, and Cargo Report Kit.

## 2026-03-06 — Perf Labs promotion (benchmark evidence + regression review)
- 2025 State of Rust survey results: resource usage, including slow compile times and storage usage, remains a major productivity problem in Rust.
  https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- `rustc-perf` shows that benchmark-as-a-service, dashboards, and before/after comparisons are already a proven Rust pattern — but mainly for compiler work.
  https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/tests/perf.html
- Cargo 1.94 development cycle: `cargo report timings`, `cargo report rebuild`, and `cargo report sessions` make report-oriented performance workflows feel more grounded than they did previously.
  https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- `cargo bench` still rides on an unstable `#[bench]` harness foundation, which is one reason ecosystem benchmarking has grown through external tools instead of one shared Cargo-native contract.
  https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/tests/index.html
  https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-bench.html
- Existing tools are strong but fragmented: Criterion provides statistical benchmarking and historical comparison; Iai-Callgrind provides CI-friendly, low-noise counter-based benchmarking. The archive decision is to converge these into a shared evidence/gating layer rather than propose a replacement benchmark engine.
  https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/analysis.html
  https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/user_guide/command_line_output.html
  https://docs.rs/iai-callgrind
- Priority change: promoted the buried legacy “Perf Labs” idea into the concise archive as Tier 1 because it looks like a cross-cutting review/evidence substrate for real Rust teams, not just a niche benchmarking crate.

## 2026-03-06 — Async Lifecycle Kit promotion (structured concurrency + shutdown correctness)
- Rust’s async goals continue to describe async as a multi-year parity effort and explicitly call out cancellation safety, runtime choice, and cross-runtime interoperability as ecosystem pain points.

  https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/async.html

## 2026-03-06 — Resolution Doctor Kit promotion (resolution evidence as substrate)
- Cargo plumbing goal: current machine-facing surfaces are thin; `cargo metadata` includes dependency resolution but excludes feature resolution; feature resolution is a distinct build phase; `--unit-graph` is one experimental source for feature-resolution results: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- PubGrub-in-Cargo goal: standalone resolver work is explicitly meant to improve Cargo error messages, enable better MSRV / CVE-aware resolution, and support a richer ecosystem of cargo extensions: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/pubgrub-in-cargo.html
- cargo-semver-checks 2025H2 goal: precise semver reasoning now depends on witness programs, better cross-crate provenance, and richer rustdoc/Cargo coordination: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html
- July 2025 goals update: docs.rs hosting rustdoc JSON helps, but recursively determining active dependency features is still missing from lockfile/Cargo interfaces: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/
- November 2025 goals update: rustdoc JSON now includes rlib information for cross-crate work, but Cargo-side blockers remain and “getting features right in dependencies” still needs more work: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/16/Project-Goals-2025-November-Update.md/
- Cargo 1.94 development cycle: structured report UX (`cargo report timings`, `cargo report rebuild`, `cargo report sessions`) is now concrete enough that a resolution-report family feels aligned with current Cargo direction instead of speculative: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- Priority change: promoted Resolution Doctor Kit to Tier 0/1 because it looks like a missing substrate, not a niche plugin. It complements Feature Kit rather than replacing it; Feature Kit remains the policy/minimization surface while Resolution Doctor becomes the shared evidence plane.

- `ffmpeg-next` crate page: Rust still relies on broad FFmpeg integration for many real workloads, but the crate explicitly says it is a maintenance-mode fork aiming for FFmpeg compatibility across versions 3.4 through 8.0, which supports designing a portable support/evidence layer above wrappers rather than betting everything on one wrapper crate: https://docs.rs/crate/ffmpeg-next/latest
- GStreamer Rust docs + repos: the bindings explicitly target writing GStreamer applications and plugins, and `gst-plugins-rs` proves Rust media support is already plugin- and runtime-rich; that strengthens the case for explicit runtime/plugin truth in any shared media artifact: https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org/documentation/rust/stable/latest/docs/gstreamer/ ; https://github.com/GStreamer/gstreamer-rs ; https://github.com/GStreamer/gst-plugins-rs
- `mp4parse` docs: Rust already has a clear inspect/parse lane for ISO Base Media Format / MP4 streams, which supports keeping inspect-only/container-introspection support distinct from full decode/transcode claims: https://docs.rs/mp4parse
- `rav1e`: Rust already has a serious AV1 encoder project, which confirms the media conversation is not just about wrapping C decoders but about real encode/transcode surfaces too: https://github.com/xiph/rav1e

## 2026-03-07 — Lending / borrow-friendly sequence surface research
- Rust’s 2025 async goals and project-goal RFC say the next generation of async libraries has been blocked on stable solutions for async traits and streams, which makes borrow-friendly sequence interop a timely ecosystem seam rather than a speculative one: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/index.html and https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs//3764-Project-Goals-2025h1.html
- RFC 3654 exists because Rust needs a way to express bounds on returned opaque values in traits, with the Send-bound problem called out as the most acute manifestation for async fn in traits; that is direct evidence that future async sequence APIs need reviewable returned-value and runtime-posture truth: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3654-return-type-notation.html
- RFC 2996 says async iterators are a core async abstraction and explicitly frames today’s `futures` `Stream` trait as the precursor to a std `AsyncIterator`, which is strong evidence that Rust is still in a transition era for async sequence surfaces: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2996-async-iterator.html
- Nightly `std::async_iter::AsyncIterator` now exists in std but remains experimental, and its docs still distinguish the low-level `poll_next` core from a not-yet-implemented consumer `next` method; that is useful evidence that the standard surface itself is still settling: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/async_iter/trait.AsyncIterator.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/async_iter/
- Tokio’s docs still explain that `Stream` utilities were moved into `tokio-stream` because `Stream` had not reached `std` in time for Tokio 1.0, which is concrete proof that important ecosystem surfaces are still split across de facto and future-std layers: https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/stream/index.html and https://docs.rs/tokio-stream
- `streaming-iterator` exists specifically because standard iterators cannot yield items borrowing from the iterator itself, citing `std::io::Lines` as an example that must allocate a new `String` per line; this is strong evidence that borrow-friendly sequence APIs solve real allocation and reuse problems today: https://docs.rs/streaming-iterator
- `lending-iterator` and `lender` both show that stable Rust ecosystems already want generic lending patterns, with `lending-iterator` explicitly noting that this pattern used to be called streaming iteration before `Stream` changed the terminology landscape: https://docs.rs/lending-iterator/latest/lending_iterator/ and https://docs.rs/lender
- The 2025H2 Polonius goal explicitly targets accepting lending iterators, and the 2026 flagship goals place lending iterators under “unblocking dormant traits”; that is a strong roadmap signal that this seam is poised to matter more, not less: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/polonius.html and https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The reborrow-traits goal argues that user-space types still cannot achieve true reborrowing today and explicitly ties autoreborrowing to `Pin` ergonomics and Rust for Linux; that reinforces the idea that borrowing-mode truth should be treated as first-class ecosystem infrastructure: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/autoreborrow-traits.html
- RFC 3668 says async closures enable futures that borrow from captures, which matters because borrow-friendly async producers are not limited to named stream traits; the design space includes callable async producers too: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3668-async-closures.html

## 2026-03-07 — Const Surface Kit (const-evaluable APIs, cost posture, and transition bridges)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes explicitly include **Constify all the things**, with milestones to stabilize const-generics extensions and prototype reflection; that is unusually direct evidence that compile-time-evaluable library surfaces are a strategic ecosystem seam, not just local crate polish: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The reflection-and-comptime goal proposes a `const fn`-based reflection scheme and explicitly argues that today’s trait/derive-based extension model creates rollout friction for serialization, logging, and engine-style ecosystems; that is strong evidence for treating compile-time posture as a first-class migration surface: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html
- The const-traits goal says const traits are a blocker for doing more things in const contexts in general, including future heap operations; that makes trait-level const posture part of the coming public support surface for many libraries: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/const-trait.html
- The expanded-const-generics work explains that users keep hitting `min_const_generics` limitations and that `generic_const_exprs` is too broken to serve as the stabilization story, which is direct motivation for reviewable parameter-model and blocker artifacts: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/min_generic_const_arguments.html
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says `generic const expressions` are among the most-wanted stabilizations and that resource usage remains a major productivity problem, which strengthens the case for making const support and its costs legible instead of aspirational: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The 2025 compiler-performance survey says build performance still limits many users and explicitly notes that stabilizing language features could remove the need for some build scripts or proc macros, which supports designing const-surface artifacts that record compile-time alternatives and their tradeoffs: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- `generic-array` still documents that stable const generics are only the MVP and that associated-const-based sizes remain a problem; it now also documents upgrade and interoperability paths with `hybrid-array`, which is excellent evidence that the ecosystem is living in an explicit transition era rather than a finished one: https://docs.rs/generic-array
- `hybrid-array` explicitly describes itself as a hybrid const-generic / typenum array with an incremental transition path to const generics, which is almost a perfect real-world example of why the archive needs a first-class transition-bridge seam: https://docs.rs/hybrid-array
- `typenum` still provides type-level numbers and now re-exports const-generics-friendly mappings, which confirms that type-level and value-level compile-time lanes already coexist and should not be flattened into one fake model: https://docs.rs/typenum
- `heapless` shows that const construction is already operationally important for `no_std` and embedded Rust; even its queue docs emphasize `const` initialization and static placement while also documenting semantic caveats about the implementation, which is a good reminder that compile-time availability and semantic guarantees are separate truths: https://docs.rs/heapless/latest/heapless/mpmc/index.html
- `serde_arrays` exists because Serde still lacks out-of-the-box support for const-generic arrays, which is concrete evidence that ecosystem support around const surfaces remains partial and workaround-heavy: https://docs.rs/serde_arrays
- `konst` and `const_format` show active demand for compile-time parsing, iteration, assertions, and formatting, which strengthens the case that const surfaces are broader than container sizes or embedded-only APIs: https://docs.rs/konst ; https://docs.rs/const_format/

## 2026-03-07 — Initialization Surface Kit (in-place construction, staged assembly, and teardown truth)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship themes explicitly call out **immobile types and guaranteed destructors** under “Just Add Async” and **in-place initialization** under “Beyond the `&`”, which is a strong signal that construction/teardown semantics are becoming a first-class Rust frontier rather than a library-side curiosity: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H2 in-place-initialization goal says there are multiple competing proposals and that the project wants to experiment with real users like the Linux kernel and Crubit to choose a direction; that is direct evidence that the seam is real but not converged: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/in-place-initialization.html
- `MaybeUninit` explicitly documents out-pointers as a way for callers to control allocation and avoid unnecessary moves, which is concrete proof that placement and initialization phase boundaries are already part of ordinary Rust practice: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html
- `Pin` and `Box::pin` make address stability and pinned heap construction public std concepts rather than niche unsafe tricks: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/pin/index.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/pin/struct.Pin.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html
- `Rc::new_cyclic` documents a pre-fully-initialized phase where a weak handle exists before the `Rc<T>` is completed, which is exactly the sort of construction-stage truth that today mostly lives in prose: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/struct.Rc.html
- Nightly `UniqueArc` goes even further, documenting a uniquely-owned-to-shared construction lane and explicitly saying it is more flexible than `Arc::new_cyclic` for fallible or async constructors; that is strong evidence that init-surface design is evolving inside std itself: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.UniqueArc.html
- `pin-init` and `pinned-init` both expose pinned, fallible, in-place constructors, with `pin-init` also documenting unique `Rc`/`Arc` setup before conversion to shareable form; this is clear evidence that the ecosystem already wants portable vocabulary for staged pinned assembly: https://docs.rs/pin-init ; https://docs.rs/pinned-init
- `moveit` explicitly frames itself as safe, in-place construction of Rust and C++ objects and explains constructor/emplacement semantics for `!Unpin` and interop-heavy code; that shows this seam is broader than async or kernel work alone: https://docs.rs/moveit
- `pin-project` has to document `UnsafeUnpin`, `#[pinned_drop]`, and `project_replace`, which is strong evidence that pinned destruction, replacement, and teardown posture are public semantic surfaces, not mere implementation details: https://docs.rs/pin-project/latest/pin_project/attr.pin_project.html
- `self_cell` and `yoke` prove stable Rust users already need reusable self-referential and borrow-carrying assembly patterns, which means a future init-surface contract has real ecosystem consumers today: https://docs.rs/self_cell ; https://docs.rs/yoke/latest/yoke/struct.Yoke.html
