## 2026-03-07 — Vector Surface Kit (SIMD/scalable-vector surfaces, target features, and fallback truth)
- Rust’s 2026 goals explicitly include **Sized Hierarchy and Scalable Vectors**, with milestones for `const Sized`, scalable-vector RFC progress, and landing SVE types/intrinsics in `stdarch` for nightly experimentation; that is unusually direct evidence that vectorized library surfaces are active ecosystem terrain rather than a solved niche: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H1 SVE/SME goal says SVE is currently unsupported by Rust, proposes type-system changes so scalable vectors can fit into Rust, and explicitly warns against overfitting the design to one architecture; that is strong evidence that any worthwhile ecosystem layer here must stay architecture-general and future-facing: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/arm-sve-sme.html
- `std::simd` already offers a portable SIMD lane and explicitly says it compiles on every target and aims for identical behavior, but it remains nightly-only and documents at least one real semantic caveat (older architectures like `armv7` and `powerpc` may flush subnormal `f32` values to zero); that is excellent motivation for reviewable semantic/capability artifacts instead of vague “portable SIMD” claims: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/simd/index.html
- The Rust Reference states that calling a `#[target_feature]` function on unsupported hardware is UB unless the platform explicitly documents it safe, which means target-feature posture is a public safety contract, not just an optimization detail: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/codegen.html#the-target_feature-attribute
- `safe_arch` explicitly publishes the compile-time-only lane: safe wrappers around `core::arch` intrinsics via `#[cfg()]`, while also saying it is not for runtime detection and fallback; that is a concrete example of why compile-time feature selection and runtime dispatch must remain separate review objects: https://docs.rs/safe_arch
- `multiversion` explicitly publishes the runtime-dispatch lane, compiling multiple versions and selecting the best target at runtime; that is equally strong evidence that dispatch/fallback posture deserves its own artifact family rather than disappearing into benchmarks: https://docs.rs/multiversion/latest/multiversion/
- `wide` explicitly publishes a fallback-oriented lane: use explicit SIMD when possible, otherwise rely on LLVM or else become scalar while keeping the math correct; that is exactly the sort of public portability/fallback truth the archive should represent cleanly: https://docs.rs/wide
- Rust’s 2025 survey still says resource usage remains a major pain point, which supports continuing to treat performance and acceleration surfaces as first-class ecosystem design territory rather than optional polish: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/

## 2026-03-07 — Offload Surface Kit (kernel maps, device-memory truth, and accelerator evidence)
- Rust’s 2026 goals explicitly include **Finish the `std::offload` module**, which is strong evidence that heterogeneous/offload execution is no longer just an outside experiment but an active Rust project frontier: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The 2025H1 GPU-offload goal says the eventual aim is to combine batching, autodiff, and offloading cleanly and also says there is still no consensus on how or whether this functionality should be exposed on stable; that is direct evidence that the seam is real but not converged: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/GPU-Offload.html
- The October and December 2025 project-goal updates show `std::offload` becoming materially more real: offload frontend work moved to proper rustc intrinsics, the generated LLVM IR was being cleaned up, multiple kernels in one codebase were being fixed, CI work was underway to enable `std::offload` on nightly, and nightly experimentation was getting closer even though `cfg(target_os=...)` annotations and `clang-linker-wrapper`-style plumbing were still visible. That is exactly the sort of still-sharp but real substrate that benefits from reviewable artifacts: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/19/project-goals-update-october-2025/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/05/project-goals-2025-december-update/
- `wgpu` explicitly positions itself as a cross-platform, safe, pure-Rust graphics API over Vulkan, Metal, D3D12, OpenGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU, and its `Buffer` docs make host/device memory semantics very explicit: buffers are either mapped for CPU access or unmapped for GPU use, never both, with runtime checks and panic conditions around overlapping mapped views and GPU submission while mapped. That is concrete proof that transfer/mapping truth is a public contract, not an implementation detail: https://docs.rs/wgpu/latest/wgpu/ ; https://docs.rs/wgpu/latest/wgpu/struct.Buffer.html
- The Rust-GPU project already distinguishes **GPU crates** from normal CPU-side **runner** crates and already treats evidence as first-class via `cargo compiletest` and `cargo difftest`, including differential tests that compare Rust and WGSL shader outputs. That is strong evidence that kernel identity and parity evidence should be explicit archive objects: https://rust-gpu.github.io/rust-gpu/book/building-rust-gpu.html ; https://rust-gpu.github.io/rust-gpu/book/testing.html
- CubeCL already spans WebGPU, CUDA, ROCm/HIP, Metal, Vulkan, and CPU, and its docs say unsupported instructions can become runtime compilation errors while launch logic dispatches the right kernel based on device properties. That is excellent evidence that backend/device capability and fallback posture deserve their own artifact family: https://docs.rs/cubecl/latest/cubecl/
- CUDA-focused Rust remains meaningfully different rather than redundant. The Rust CUDA guide explicitly says the project aims to make Rust a tier-1 language for CUDA computing and describes separate crates for code generation, GPU-side utilities, and CPU-side launch/memory/device control; `cudarc` similarly exposes driver/runtime/library wrappers and safe abstractions like streams and device slices. That is strong evidence that a serious offload kit must preserve vendor-specific shapes rather than pretending WebGPU-style and CUDA-style ecosystems are the same thing: https://rust-gpu.github.io/rust-cuda/ ; https://docs.rs/cudarc/latest/cudarc/
- The 2025 Rust survey still says resource usage remains one of the main productivity problems, which supports continuing to treat heterogeneous execution and acceleration decisions as first-class ecosystem design terrain rather than optional polish: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/

## 2026-03-07 — Encoding Surface Kit (type-model posture, wire-format semantics, and reviewable encoding evidence)
- Serde still defines the ecosystem’s generic serialization substrate and explicitly frames itself as the layer between data structures and data formats; that is powerful, but it also means many important public encoding choices sit *above* the basic `Serialize` / `Deserialize` story rather than inside it: https://docs.rs/serde
- Rust’s reflection/comptime goal explicitly uses serialization as a motivating example for why the ecosystem gets stuck: maintainers often do not want to depend on multiple serialization stacks, so better alternatives can struggle to interoperate or spread. That is unusually direct official evidence that encoding surfaces are a strategic ecosystem seam rather than merely local crate taste: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html
- `postcard` remains a `#![no_std]`-focused Serde format aimed at constrained systems, which is a strong signal that allocation/runtime-envelope posture needs to be part of any serious encoding proposal rather than an afterthought: https://docs.rs/postcard
- `RON` remains a deliberately human-readable format that aims to support all of Serde’s data model, which is useful evidence that readability/editability is a first-class axis rather than a minor UI detail: https://docs.rs/ron
- `ciborium` centers CBOR over reader/writer-style APIs and dynamic values, which is good evidence that stream/buffer posture belongs in the public contract rather than only in examples: https://docs.rs/ciborium
- `serde_json`’s own docs make feature-sensitive semantics explicit: `Value` preserves insertion order only with `preserve_order`, and the crate also exposes `arbitrary_precision` / `raw_value` feature lanes. That is exactly the sort of public behavior that should stop disappearing into Cargo features and docs-only caveats: https://docs.rs/serde_json/latest/serde_json/enum.Value.html ; https://docs.rs/crate/serde_json/latest/source/Cargo.toml.orig
- `prost` remains a protobuf implementation built around generated Rust code from `.proto` files, using `bytes::{Buf, BufMut}` rather than generic `Read`/`Write`; this is concrete evidence that schema/codegen-first encoding lanes deserve to stay distinct from generic-data-model-first lanes: https://docs.rs/prost
- `rkyv` now documents zero-copy deserialization, `no_std` and `no_alloc` support, archived layout control, and in-place mutation; paired with `bytecheck`, this is strong evidence that borrow/zero-copy/validation posture should be first-class archive artifacts rather than hidden unsafe expectations: https://docs.rs/rkyv ; https://docs.rs/bytecheck
- `serde-reflection` explicitly says format descriptions can be stored under version control to prevent unintended modifications of binary serialization formats; that is close to the exact artifact instinct the archive should promote into a more general encoding-surface layer: https://docs.rs/serde-reflection
- `nanoserde` explicitly says it avoids Serde’s intermediate data model and cuts `syn` / `proc_macro2` / `quote` from the build tree, while `miniserde` explicitly narrows itself to JSON, structs, unit variants, and minimal customization. Those crates are valuable evidence that a serious encoding map must preserve build-cost and scope tradeoffs instead of pretending the only axis is runtime speed: https://docs.rs/nanoserde ; https://docs.rs/miniserde
- The current `bincode` crate page now states that the crate is unmaintained and directly points prospective users toward alternatives such as `postcard` and `rkyv`; regardless of the cause, this is unusually concrete evidence that migration and successor artifacts in Rust’s encoding space are a current need, not just a future nice-to-have: https://docs.rs/crate/bincode/latest
- The 2025 Rust survey says resource usage remains one of the main productivity problems, which further supports taking lighter-weight encoding stacks and build/runtime tradeoffs seriously instead of assuming one derive-heavy happy path fits the whole ecosystem: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/

## 2026-03-07 — Compile-time capabilities / sandboxing / determinism research
- The Rust Reference says procedural macros run during compilation and therefore have the same file-access posture and security concerns as Cargo build scripts; that is direct support for treating proc-macros and build scripts as one compile-time authority family even when their ergonomics differ: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html
- The Rust Reference also says `proc-macro` crates are always compiled for the host that built the compiler, even when the rest of the build targets something else; that is strong evidence that host/target lane truth belongs in first-class artifacts rather than footnotes: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html
- Cargo’s build-script docs already define several important truths that most tooling ignores: scripts receive environment-variable inputs, should write only under `OUT_DIR`, are expected to narrow reruns with `rerun-if-*`, and may in some `links` cases be overridden so they do not run at all; that means the ecosystem already has both “ambient execution” and “declared metadata override” lanes: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
- Cargo’s profile docs treat build scripts, proc-macros, and their dependencies as a distinct build-time class with dedicated `build-override` settings, which is more evidence that compile-time units deserve their own operational substrate: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html
- The sandboxed-build-scripts goal explicitly targets per-crate permissions, restriction of file/network/process access, one future interface for both build scripts and proc-macros, and even future remote-execution / hermetic-build possibilities; that is exactly the shape of a broader compile-time-capabilities substrate rather than a local sandbox experiment: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/sandboxed-build-script.html
- The compiler-team proposal for WebAssembly proc-macros argues that the current native dynamic-library model creates reproducibility and security hazards and that a wasm execution strategy could also let proc macros be built once and reused across targets; this is excellent support for making execution lane a first-class artifact instead of an implementation detail: https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-team/issues/876
- Rust’s declarative-macro-improvements goal explicitly argues that reducing proc-macro dependence would make projects build faster, simpler, and lighter-weight; this means a good compile-time-capabilities design should model reduction / replacement lanes, not only sandboxing of ambient-native execution: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/macro-improvements.html
- The 2025 compiler-performance survey says stabilizing language features could remove the need for some build scripts or proc macros and thereby improve compilation; that strengthens the case that compile-time execution authority and build-performance work should compose through shared artifacts: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/
- The user-wide build-cache goal says shared caching depends on idempotence and explicitly mentions future sandboxing work as the path to determining precise `build.rs` / proc-macro inputs; that is strong evidence that compile-time-capabilities artifacts should include explicit input-surface and determinism findings: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/user-wide-cache.html

## 2026-03-07 — Pointer Surface Kit refresh (identity / uniqueness / projection-family substrate)
- Rust’s 2025H2 flagship theme says user-defined smart pointers should become as ergonomic as built-in references and explicitly frames current custom pointer types as lacking `&` / `&mut`’s special capabilities; that is strong evidence that pointer surfaces are an ecosystem-shaping seam rather than a niche library topic: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/
- The 2026 flagships continue the same lane with field projections, reborrow traits, and in-place-initialization alignment, which strengthens the case for treating pointer semantics as a first-class substrate instead of one more isolated smart-pointer crate idea: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- RFC 3519 says custom smart pointers are still second-class citizens, motivates foreign-reference semantics that intentionally do not claim Rust-reference exclusivity, and explains that today only built-in smart pointers get certain receiver ergonomics; that directly supports modeling receiver/coercion posture as part of pointer truth: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3519-arbitrary-self-types-v2.html
- RFC 3621 exists so custom smart pointers can participate in trait objects and explicitly says the stabilized behavior depends on the `SmartPointer` derive macro rather than exposing a stable manual expansion; that is strong support for keeping dyn/coercion posture distinct from ordinary trait docs: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3621-derive-smart-pointer.html
- The reborrow-traits goal says the existing `Pin<&mut T>` compiler special-case could likely be reimagined in terms of a `Reborrow` trait, which is excellent evidence that reborrow behavior belongs in explicit artifacts instead of special-case lore: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/autoreborrow-traits.html
- The field-projections goal says the solution should be broad enough for complex projection problems such as pin projections and `RcuMutex<T>`; this supports treating “projection family” as a real design dimension instead of a detail hidden under `Deref`: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/field-projections.html
- The pin-ergonomics goal says `Pin` remains notoriously awkward even though async and generators rely on it; that is direct support for keeping pin/projection semantics reviewable rather than assuming wrappers are self-explanatory: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/pin-ergonomics.html
- Rust-for-Linux’s 2025H2 language-goals page still lists `arbitrary_self_types` and `derive_coerce_pointee` among unstable features it depends on; that is concrete evidence that real users need custom pointer semantics now, not only after the language fully settles: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/Rust-for-Linux-language.html
- `Arc`’s docs show why pointer semantics need finer-grained vocabulary: `ptr_eq` distinguishes allocation identity from value equality, `make_mut` may clone or dissociate `Weak` pointers, `get_mut` and `get_mut_unchecked` express different uniqueness stories, and nightly `is_unique` makes a temporary uniqueness witness explicit; this is exactly the kind of operational truth that should become portable artifacts: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html

## 2026-03-07 — Support Envelope Kit refresh (support-contract lanes, runtime-floor evidence, and reviewable support drift)
- The rustc platform-support page explicitly distinguishes targets from targets **with host tools**, and its target notes already include concrete runtime floors like minimum macOS, Windows, kernel, and glibc versions for major targets. That is unusually strong evidence that crate-level support claims must separate development-host support from mere target eligibility, and that runtime floors are a real public surface rather than trivia: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/rustc/platform-support.html
- The target-tier policy makes host-tool support a distinct approval surface and notes that tier guarantees differ materially; that strengthens the case that crate/workspace support claims should record what kind of support is being promised instead of pretending every target entry means the same thing: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/rustc/target-tier-policy.html
- docs.rs metadata already lets authors set `default-target`, `targets`, and `additional-targets`, and the docs.rs team changed the default target list in October 2025 to match platform reality. That is strong evidence that docs targets are ecosystem-facing support signals and that support drift is normal enough to deserve diffable artifacts: https://docs.rs/about/metadata ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/16/docsrs-changed-default-targets/
- Cargo’s active `supported-targets` RFC and the Cargo 1.86 development-cycle note show that upstream Cargo is converging on target-support declaration, but not yet on a portable evidence/diff layer; that reinforces the archive’s stance that the worthy contribution is a support-contract substrate above the manifest field, not a competing field format: https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3759 ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/02/27/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.86/
- cargo-deny already requires users to tell it what targets matter so policy checks can ignore irrelevant target-specific dependencies; that is direct evidence that target scope cannot remain folklore if other ecosystem tooling is expected to reason honestly: https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/cfg.html
- The `build-std` goal and rustc custom-target docs show why the archive’s older support-envelope shape was still too flat: some projects have real **source-build support** for targets that do not ship with a precompiled stdlib or that require custom target JSON, which is not the same thing as shipping supported release artifacts. That justified promoting the kit and rewriting it around explicit support planes: dev-host, source-build, release-artifact, and docs-surface: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/build-std.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/targets/custom.html
- `cross`, `cargo-zigbuild`, and `cargo-xwin` remain important because they prove the provisioning/toolchain problem is already partly solved, but they also expose why support contracts must not collapse into provisioning choice: `cross` provides an environment/toolchain/testing lane, `cargo-zigbuild` documents glibc-version targeting caveats, and `cargo-xwin` supports pre-caching SDK/CRT assets and running tests with Wine. Those are strong signals that provisioning backend, runtime floor, and validation strength all deserve separate artifacts: https://github.com/cross-rs/cross ; https://github.com/rust-cross/cargo-zigbuild ; https://github.com/rust-cross/cargo-xwin
- Rust release notes continue to record target promotions/demotions and host-tool changes, which is another reason the support layer should produce `support-diff-report/v0` rather than a static badge or unversioned support matrix: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/releases.html

## 2026-03-07 — MIR Analysis Kit (semantics-aware compiler analysis substrate over `rustc_public`)
- The accepted 2025H1 StableMIR goal explicitly said the point of publishing StableMIR crate(s) to crates.io was to let tool developers analyze compiled Rust crates and their dependencies without using compiler internal APIs, with reliable behavior across compiler versions. That is direct evidence that Rust wants a sustainable external-analysis substrate, not just one more internal-only compiler crate: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/stable-mir.html
- The Rustc Librarification Project page now says the effort has been renamed around **`rustc_public`** to emphasize a **SemVer compliant** public interface based on MIR for sophisticated external analyses. That is a stronger framing than the archive previously captured: the ecosystem seam is no longer merely “stable MIR someday”, but a semver-oriented public compiler interface feeding third-party tooling: https://rust-lang.github.io/project-stable-mir/ ; https://github.com/rust-lang/project-stable-mir
- The active compiler-team MCP to publish `rustc_public` v0.1 says the architecture is split between `rustc_public` and `rustc_public_bridge`, aims for multi-compiler-version support, and cites new adopters like KMIR, RBMC, os-checker distributed verification, and obol, while also mentioning ongoing migration of Kani and MiniRust. That is unusually strong evidence that downstream consumers are already arriving before a shared artifact layer exists: https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-team/issues/949
- Nightly docs still describe `rustc_public` as a WIP public interface that is “completely unstable and subject to change”, and they expose explicit `unstable` and `rustc_internal` modules. The `rustc_internal` module docs say it is outside semver and exists as a temporary bridge until the public IR is complete. That makes a huge archive-design point unavoidable: any worthy ecosystem contribution here has to make **coverage and escape-hatch use reviewable**, not pretend the public surface is already complete: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_public/index.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/rustc_public/rustc_internal/index.html
- The current `rustc_public::mir` docs already expose bodies, mono, allocations, pretty-printing, and visitors. That means the ecosystem is likely to want portable machine-facing handoff soon, because the public-ish substrate is already rich enough for multiple classes of downstream analysis: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_public/mir/index.html
- `stable-mir-json` is useful counter-evidence against naive optimism. Its architecture note says it is a **compiler driver**, not merely a library, and that it currently uses both StableMIR and rustc internals. That strongly suggests the missing contribution is not “yet another exporter” but a **capture-profile / capability-profile / observation-report boundary** that can wrap heterogeneous capture lanes honestly: https://hackmd.io/%40cds-amal/SkgYPwTOuWg
- MIR itself is not semantically frozen. The proposed 2025H2 move-elimination goal says Rust wants to change MIR move semantics so more moves can be optimized away, and then teach Miri to validate the new model. That is the strongest reason to treat **semantic epoch / comparability truth** as first-class in the archive’s MIR kit: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/mir-move-elimination.html
- The `cargo-semver-checks` roadmap now says precise semver checking still needs more compiler-backed truth, especially for cross-crate items and type-sensitive compatibility, and that witness generation via compilation is the current plan for tricky cases. Meanwhile the std-contracts goal says contract attributes should provide a compiler interface for external tools to retrieve annotated contracts. Together, those two signals make the opportunity larger than the archive previously stated: a MIR kit should not just emit snapshots, it should support **queryable derived reports** that other kits can consume: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/std-contracts.html
- Archive decision: rewrite and promote **MIR Analysis Kit** from Tier 1 to Tier 0/1, and reframe it around `mir-subject/v0` + `mir-capture-profile/v0` + `mir-capability-profile/v0` + `mir-observation-report/v0` + `mir-derived-graph/v0` + `mir-query-report/v0` + `mir-diff-report/v0` + `mir-pack/v0`. The worthy contribution here is not “stabilize MIR forever” or “write one analyzer”; it is a semantics-aware evidence and comparability layer that lets multiple compiler-aware tools compose without each inventing a custom driver format and a different unspoken notion of “same MIR”.

## 2026-03-07 — Migration Kit deepening (migration programs, config scope, destination semantics)
- The Edition Guide’s advanced migration chapter says `cargo fix --edition` works by running `cargo check` with edition-compatibility lints, may run multiple passes, only handles one configuration at a time, and may still require manual help for macros or other cases. That is direct evidence that Rust migrations are already staged, config-sensitive programs rather than one-command upgrades: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/editions/advanced-migrations.html
- The Cargo Book says `cargo fix` only touches code that is normally compiled, so inactive features and target-specific code require explicit `--features` / `--target` coverage. That makes configuration-scope truth part of any honest migration record: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html
- Rust 1.85 / Rust 2024 explicitly says automatic fixes are conservative and “should not be considered a recommendation”, which is strong evidence that migration artifacts must separate tool-produced edits from intended destination semantics: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/20/Rust-1.85.0/
- Cargo’s 1.90 development report says the current `cargo fix` architecture is slow, only applies a subset of lints, and is hard to make selective or interactive because it proxies `rustc` while holding a cross-process lock; the 2025 GSoC results repeat that diagnosis and point at an alternative architecture. That is strong evidence the ecosystem needs a durable migration-program substrate above whatever edit engine wins: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/18/gsoc-2025-results/
- Cargo’s `rust-version` docs say workspaces can support multiple policies and that verifying specific packages under specific Rust versions can get complicated; rustup’s override docs show toolchain overrides and committed `rust-toolchain.toml` files are already first-class. That makes toolchain and support-floor truth part of the migration seam, not an afterthought: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/rust-version.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/overrides.html
- Archive decision: substantially deepen the existing **Migration Kit** around `migration-subject/v0` + `migration-intent/v0` + `migration-analysis-report/v0` + `migration-plan/v0` + `migration-run-report/v0` + `migration-outcome-report/v0` + optional `migration-waiver/v0` + `migration-pack/v0`, and explicitly bound it against Edit Workflow Kit, Public API Kit, Support Envelope Kit, and Release Pipeline Kit.

I still did **not** move it into the steering shortlist: the leverage is now clearly above a speculative mid-tier workflow helper, but the shortlist remains strongest when kept even tighter around the most universal substrate bets.

## 2026-03-07 — Wasm Component Kit refresh (WIT/package identity, composition evidence, and publication truth)
- Rust’s 2026 flagships explicitly include **Wasm Components**, and the goal text says the project wants to add and stabilize three compiler targets and begin experimentation with Wasm-specific language features. That is a much stronger signal than the archive’s older framing captured: Wasm components are not just ecosystem experimentation anymore, they are part of the project’s forward language/toolchain agenda. https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Rust 1.82 made `wasm32-wasip2` Tier 2. That means direct compiler support for producing WASI 0.2 components is mainstream enough that the missing contribution is no longer “can Rust do components at all?” but “what shared artifact boundary sits above the compiler target?” https://blog.rust-lang.org/2024/11/26/wasip2-tier-2/
- The official component-model Rust guide now shows plain `cargo build --target=wasm32-wasip2` for runnable/library components. That matters because it means component emission is no longer confined to sidecar tools; plain Cargo can already produce a meaningful artifact that downstream tooling should be able to inspect and package coherently. https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org/language-support/creating-runnable-components/rust.html
- The same guide also treats unresolved imports and later composition as first-class workflow steps. That is direct evidence that a worthy contribution cannot stop at “export a component file”; it has to represent import satisfaction and composition truth explicitly. https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org/language-support/importing-and-reusing-components/rust.html
- `cargo component` remains experimental and still uses adaptation flows; its README explicitly describes adapting `wasm32-wasip1` output with an adapter and says plain upstream `wasm32-wasip2` Cargo builds do not yet replace it fully. That makes the right archive move an adapter/report substrate above heterogeneous lanes, not a premature attempt to declare one winner. https://github.com/bytecodealliance/cargo-component
- `wasm-pkg-tools` / `wkg` already support OCI and Warg registries and explicitly intend their configuration file to be reusable by other language-specific component tooling. That is unusually strong evidence that publication/package identity is already cross-language enough to deserve first-class artifacts in the archive rather than remaining hidden in Rust-only lockfiles or local scripts. https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-pkg-tools
- Warg already exists as a reference protocol/client/server for distributing components and interfaces. That strengthens the case that publication evidence belongs in the kit: package identity, digests, and registry/protocol lane are real ecosystem surfaces, not future hypotheticals. https://github.com/bytecodealliance/registry
- Archive decision: rewrite and promote **Wasm Component Kit** from Tier 1 to Tier 0/1, and reframe it around `component-subject/v0` + `wit-resolution-lock/v0` + `component-surface-report/v0` + `component-host-requirement-profile/v0` + `composition-plan/v0` + `composition-run-report/v0` + `component-compat-report/v0` + optional `component-publish-report/v0` + `component-pack/v0`, explicitly separate from Plugin Surface Kit, Runtime Capability Kit, Support Envelope Kit, and browser-focused `wasm-bindgen` UX.

- Promoted Wasm Component Kit in `PRIORITIES.md` from **Tier 1** to **Tier 0/1** and rewrote its summary so the archive now treats WIT/package identity, composition evidence, host requirements, and publication truth as separate first-class artifacts across plain `wasm32-wasip2` Cargo, `cargo-component`, `wit-bindgen`, `wkg`, `wasm-tools`, and Warg/OCI lanes.

- Strengthened the Wasm-component amnesia-resistor so future revisions keep Cargo package identity, WIT package/world identity, build-lane truth, import satisfaction/composition evidence, host requirements, and publication/package identity separate instead of flattening all component workflows into one fake universal “component build” artifact.

## 2026-03-08 — Evidence-weighted frontier refresh
- The 2025 State of Rust survey results (published 2026-03-02) continue to show compile times, storage usage, and debugging/developer-experience pain as major concerns, while also underscoring that official docs remain canonical and that editor/agentic tooling is becoming a more important part of how people navigate Rust. That strongly favors contribution seams that turn folklore into portable evidence instead of adding one more ad hoc wrapper or dashboard: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Cargo and project-goals work is currently unusually aligned around several high-leverage seams: public/private dependencies and cargo-semver-checks on the release/publish path; build-dir relayout, relink-don't-rebuild, and cargo build-analysis/reporting; sandboxed build-script exploration; Wasm Components; and supply-chain/security improvements. That means the best external contributions now are generally **companion kits** or **evidence substrates** for active motion rather than standalone replacements for it: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/pub-priv.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/build-dir-layout.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/relink-dont-rebuild.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-plumbing.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/sandboxed-build-scripts.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- crates.io is also becoming a more active governance surface: the 2026 development update adds a Security tab, expands trusted publishing, exposes `pubtime`, and continues improving source/docs discoverability, while the malicious-crate notification policy update clarifies how advisories and user notifications are handled. That strengthens the case for keeping Policy Kit, Trust Signals, Lifecycle Ledger, and SBOM Evidence tightly coupled rather than proliferating isolated “crate health” tools: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/13/crates.io-malicious-crate-notification-policy/
- Safety-critical Rust work is maturing enough that the missing layer is increasingly structured assurance rather than just another verifier or blog post: the FLS is now adopted into the project, safety-critical project goals mention MC/DC, unsafe documentation, and target-readiness, and the Inside Rust safety-critical write-up makes clear that ecosystem support thins out quickly outside narrower stacks. That keeps Safety Evidence and Support Envelope in the top band: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/03/26/adopting-the-fls/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/14/safety-critical-rust/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The Rust debugging survey makes debugger support fragmentation explicit across debugger family/version, OS, target, visualizers, async instrumentation, and expression-evaluation posture. That is strong evidence that Debugger Experience Kit should be treated as a first-class evidence problem rather than a lower-priority IDE nicety: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/23/rust-debugging-survey-2026/
- Archive decision: add `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` as the current evidence-weighted ranking of where an epic Rust ecosystem contribution is most leveraged now. Ranked frontier: Public API Kit; Build-State Evidence Stack (Build Cache + Change Impact + Build Doctor); Policy / Trust / SBOM / Lifecycle; Safety Evidence; Debugger Experience; Wasm Component; Compile-Time Capabilities; Support Envelope; Ecosystem Atlas.
- Archive decision: promote **Build Doctor Kit** and **Debugger Experience Kit** from **Tier 1** to **Tier 0/1** in `PRIORITIES.md` to reflect current user pain plus live upstream/ecosystem motion.
- Archive decision: explicitly preserve the distinction between the archive’s broad conceptual map and the current action frontier; important language-shaping seams like Pointer, Lending, Initialization, Trait, Encoding, and Validity should remain active research threads even when they are not the highest-leverage *next* external build target.


## 2026-03-08 — Semantic context / governed-edit frontier refresh
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says official online documentation remains the preferred canonical reference, while LLM tooling and agentic/editor workflows are becoming a bigger part of how people learn and navigate Rust. That combination does **not** reduce the need for better machine-facing Rust substrate; it increases it, because more consumers now sit between users and the canonical sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Cargo’s plumbing goal explicitly says the machine-facing surface is too thin and sketches phases like `resolve features` and `plan build`; the 1.93 Cargo development-cycle update says schema unification with Cargo JSON output could unblock a faster, more flexible `cargo fix` architecture. That is unusually strong evidence that **context capture** and **edit governance** are converging into a real ecosystem seam rather than two unrelated tooling curiosities: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- docs.rs now hosts rustdoc JSON and explicitly warns consumers to respect `format_version`; the July 2025 project-goals update says cross-crate semver work still needs recursively active dependency features plus `rmeta`-aware combination; the StableMIR publication goal says the compiler wants tool developers to have a reliable analysis interface. Together, these point away from “one more bespoke workspace index” and toward a missing **portable semantic context layer** with honest provenance/completeness truth: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/05/july-project-goals-update/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/stable-mir.html
- Cargo’s current direction also makes the complementary missing seam clearer on the output side: Rust already has compiler suggestions, `cargo fix`, edition migrations, and editor/refactor actions, but it still lacks one reviewable `candidate -> selection -> application -> verification` boundary that can survive attachment to issues, PRs, CI, or assistant loops. That strongly favors treating Edit Workflow Kit as the governed-execution counterpart to Semantic Context Kit rather than a standalone auto-fix gadget.
- Archive decision: refresh `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` to add **Semantic Context + Edit Workflow** as a top-band tool-facing substrate cluster, behind Public API / Build-State / Policy / Safety / Debugging but ahead of several previously stronger-looking conceptual seams because the current evidence now says this is one of the best ways to make Rust’s canonical truth usable by newer machine-facing workflows without losing reviewability.
- Archive decision: strengthen `design/semantic-context-kit.md`, `proposals/epic-semantic-context-kit.md`, `design/edit-workflow-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-edit-workflow-kit.md` around that theory-of-change, and update `PRIORITIES.md` language so the archive remembers that the broad landscape map and the current frontier are intentionally different views.
- Archive decision: add amnesia resistors requiring future tool-facing-knowledge proposals to keep canonical sources, captured semantic context, and derived assistant/editor outputs separate, and requiring edit-governance proposals to rank review boundaries above producer hype.

## 2026-03-08 — Navigation + commons refresh (starter sets, interop seams, curator overlays, plugin posture)
- Rust’s vision work is unusually explicit now: it recommends helping users navigate the crates.io ecosystem, says people need advice on a good “starter set” of crates, and says part of the answer is smoother interop through key interop traits or standard building blocks like `http`. It also notes that coherence rules make incremental ecosystem interop traits difficult. That is strong evidence that **Ecosystem Atlas** and **Interop Commons** are not side quests; together they answer one of the project’s clearest ecosystem-level asks. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/19/what-do-people-love-about-rust/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the canonical reference, while open answers suggest some learning traffic is moving toward LLM tooling; it also says resource usage remains a top pain point and concerns persist about complexity and developer/maintainer support. That is strong evidence that Rust needs bounded, freshness-aware, evidence-backed guidance artifacts rather than one more prestige ranking page or another hidden agent index. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update says crate pages now expose Security-tab advisory information, Trusted Publishing-only mode, blocked risky GitHub triggers for trusted publishing, SLOC, and `pubtime`. That is direct evidence that the registry now has materially better signals for atlas-style recommendation inputs and freshness checks than it used to. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Cargo’s 1.90 development-cycle update says Cargo cannot be everything to everyone and explicitly celebrates plugins. That is a strategic posture signal: atlas/commons work should be framed as companion ecosystem infrastructure instead of as a demand that Cargo itself absorb all recommendation and interop work. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/
- Existing ecosystem precedent remains powerful here: `http` already acts as a neutral shared vocabulary; Tower treats `Service` and `Layer` as stable integration points; `tower-http` says its middleware works across ecosystems using `http` and `http-body`; and Axum/Tonic both demonstrate real reuse from those seams. That is exactly the pattern Interop Commons should formalize instead of re-litigating by folklore. Sources: https://docs.rs/http ; https://docs.rs/tower ; https://docs.rs/tower-http ; https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/ ; https://docs.rs/tonic/latest/tonic/service/index.html ; https://docs.rs/tonic/latest/tonic/transport/server/struct.Server.html
- Archive decision: strengthen `design/ecosystem-atlas-kit.md` and `design/interop-commons-kit.md`, deepen the corresponding epic files, promote Interop Commons from Tier 1 to Tier 0/1 in `PRIORITIES.md`, and move the **Navigation + Commons Stack** into the top frontier band in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`. The intended strategic program is now: Atlas owns guidance, lanes, freshness, overlays, and derived tool-facing outputs; Commons owns neutral seams, adapter truth, conformance, readiness, and stewardship.

- Added an amnesia-resistor requiring future navigation/commons revisions to keep curator-driven atlas guidance distinct from neutral shared-building-block work, and to keep seam-readiness / common-vocabulary truth distinct from stack recommendation pressure.

## 2026-03-08 — Atlas execution refresh (pilot program, ranked opening domains, federation discipline)
- Rust’s vision work is not only saying that users need help navigating crates.io; it specifically says there is no clear place to get advice on a good ‘starter set’ of crates and that smoother interop plus standard building blocks are part of the answer. That strengthens the case for Atlas, but it also raises the execution question: how do we avoid turning the first curation pass into accidental permanent blessing? Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/19/what-do-people-love-about-rust/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online documentation remains the preferred canonical reference, hints that some questions are moving to LLM tooling, and notes a slight uptick in concern about developer and maintainer support. This argues for recommendation artifacts that are freshness-aware, tool-facing, and explicit about stewardship rather than prestige-driven. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- crates.io’s January 2026 update means Atlas now has materially better official inputs for pilot curation: Trusted Publishing posture, Security-tab advisory presence, SLOC, and `pubtime`. That makes pilot evidence budgets more realistic than they would have been a year ago. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Cargo’s 1.90 cycle explicitly says Cargo cannot be everything to everyone and that plugins play an important part of the Cargo ecosystem. That is further evidence that Atlas should be built as companion infrastructure, not framed as an attempt to turn Cargo itself into a global recommendation oracle. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/
- The C++/Rust interop problem-map goal provides a useful methodological lesson for Atlas: build a skeleton first, prioritize current pain and competing-solution zones, and do not confuse breadth mapping with solved design. Applied here, that suggests a ranked pilot program rather than universal initial coverage. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/interop-problem-map.html
- docs.rs hosting rustdoc JSON and the StableMIR/`rustc_public` push mean atlas-derived machine outputs are more plausible now — but only if they remain derived from canonical curated artifacts rather than becoming the truth source themselves. Sources: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/stable-mir.html
- Archive decision: add `design/atlas-pilot-program.md`, update the Ecosystem Atlas design/epic/frontier/priority text to treat a ranked pilot program as the next credible execution move, and add an amnesia-resistor so future revisions preserve pilot-selection logic, governance, evidence budgets, freshness, and promotion/retirement state instead of collapsing everything into one proto-blessed atlas.

## 2026-03-08 — Native-edge frontier refresh (FFI boundary, provider locks, external build handoff)
- The Rust project is explicitly treating mixed-language adoption as a first-class problem now. The 2025H1 goal **Evaluate approaches for seamless interop between C++ and Rust** says the aim is to enable Rust adoption in projects that must make use of large, rich C++ APIs, and the 2025H2 **C++/Rust Interop Problem Space Mapping** goal says the project wants a shared map of discrete interop problems to drive proposals and cooperation. That is much stronger evidence than the archive previously captured for promoting the native edge from “important niche” to “strategic frontier.” Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/seamless-rust-cpp.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/interop-problem-map.html
- Cargo is also moving in a direction that makes a native-edge evidence layer more timely. The Cargo plumbing goal explicitly argues that larger applications need programmatic seams beyond porcelain commands; the 2025 GSoC build-script delegation work says the long-term direction is passing parameters through `Cargo.toml` metadata and delegating build scripts through artifact dependencies; Cargo 1.90 discusses build-script delegation and artifact dependencies; Cargo 1.93 discusses custom final artifacts and how Cargo-managed uplift / collision handling should work. Together, that is strong evidence that boundary artifacts and native-provider/link-plan artifacts can now compose with real upstream motion instead of floating as isolated tooling dreams. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/18/gsoc-2025-results/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- The sandboxed-build-script goal is especially clarifying here. It says unsandboxed build scripts are effectively enormous `unsafe` blocks from a review perspective and explicitly names `-sys` crates / system-library probing as a first-class use case the sandbox story must support. That makes it harder to justify leaving native provider truth buried in opaque probes and stdout logs. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/sandboxed-build-script.html
- The Rust Foundation's 2026–2028 strategy emphasizes **responsible growth in adoption** and **meaningful engagement from organizations that rely on Rust**, while the 2025 State of Rust survey says hiring is continuing and codebases are consolidating. That combination points toward mixed-language adoption infrastructure as a leverage-heavy seam: many organizations will not start from a greenfield Rust-only world. Sources: https://rustfoundation.org/strategic-plan/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Existing tools are already good enough that the archive should not propose one more generator or one more provider-specific helper crate as the “epic” answer. `bindgen`, `cbindgen`, `cxx`, `autocxx`, `system-deps`, `pkg-config`, `vcpkg`, and `cmake` demonstrate that the ecosystem already has strong point tools; the missing contribution is the shared contract / diff / handoff layer across them. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-bindgen/ ; https://github.com/mozilla/cbindgen ; https://cxx.rs ; https://google.github.io/autocxx/ ; https://docs.rs/system-deps/latest/system_deps/ ; https://docs.rs/pkg-config/latest/pkg_config/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/vcpkg/latest ; https://docs.rs/cmake/latest/cmake/
- Archive decision: add `design/native-edge-pilot-program.md`, strengthen the FFI Boundary and Native Dependency design/epic files, promote **Native Dependency Kit** from Tier 1 to Tier 0/1, and add a new **Native Edge Stack** to `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`. The execution posture is now explicit: ranked pilots first (C ABI export → system-library consumers → C++ bridges → external build handoff → audited/safety-oriented compositions), companion substrate posture second, and no fake universal native package manager.

## 2026-03-08 — Compatibility-claims frontier refresh (support-envelope + acceptance-surface convergence)
- The safety-critical adoption writeup makes a sharper version of the support problem explicit: Rust target tiers are useful, but teams still need to map those tiers and upgrade drift to what they can responsibly bet on for a given platform and product lifetime. That is strong evidence that the missing ecosystem contribution is not another cross-build wrapper; it is a better support-claims substrate. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/14/what-does-it-take-to-ship-rust-in-safety-critical/
- Rust 1.91 promoted `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` to Tier 1. That is a concrete reminder that target support is not static and that support-diff artifacts matter in practice. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/30/Rust-1.91.0/
- The Rust debugging survey says debugging support varies across debugger families, versions, and operating systems, and explicitly calls out visualizers, async debugging, and expression evaluation as the shape of a good future. That means “support” is already broader than target triples and binary artifacts; a compatibility-claims story should be able to express debugger-capability lanes too. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/23/rust-debugging-survey-2026/
- The 2026 flagships plus the 2025H2 next-solver / Polonius / evolving-traits goals make advanced-pattern acceptance a live transition zone, not a theoretical one. The ecosystem needs a portable way to publish which patterns are supported on stable vs nightly vs experimental lanes, with which workarounds, and how that changed. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/next-solver.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/polonius.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/evolving-traits.html
- Cargo’s machine-facing direction (plumbing commands, structured `cargo report` work, and JSON-schema work) makes a compatibility-claims layer more plausible now than it would have been when Cargo outputs were mostly porcelain-oriented. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2024/12/13/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.84/
- Archive decision: add `design/compatibility-claims-pilot-program.md`, strengthen Support Envelope and Acceptance Surface as a shared **Compatibility Claims Stack** in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, clarify the same framing in `PRIORITIES.md`, and strengthen the two epic files so future work knows the next credible execution move is a ranked pilot program rather than another wrapper, badge, or local test harness empire.
