## 2026-03-08 — Compile-Time Surface frontier deepening (authority + replacement + workflow + transition)
- Rust now has enough converging official motion on compile-time surfaces that the archive should stop treating them as one isolated sandbox/security concern. The sandboxed-build-scripts goal explicitly explores per-crate permissions and a common interface with proc-macro concerns; the macro-improvements goal explicitly aims to make `macro_rules!` capable enough to replace many proc-macro use cases, with faster builds and smaller supply chains as stated benefits; the compiler-performance survey names understanding build slowness as an explicit need; and the user-wide-cache work says better sandboxing/input truth can help infer or verify idempotence for `build.rs` and proc-macros. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/sandboxed-build-script.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/macro-improvements.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/10/rust-compiler-performance-survey-2025-results/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/user-wide-cache.html
- Two more signals make this broader than “just sandboxing”: `cargo-script` remains a 2026 flagship and had concrete progress in the December 2025 goals update, while reflection-and-comptime also had concrete compiler progress plus clearly stated blockers in that same update. That means ideal Rust is opening more first-class compile-time or compile-time-adjacent lanes, which increases the value of a shared evidence substrate and explicit migration story instead of more folklore. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/05/project-goals-2025-december-update/
- Archive decision: add [`design/compile-time-surface-pilot-program.md`](./design/compile-time-surface-pilot-program.md) and treat **Compile-Time Capabilities Kit + Build Extension Kit + Macro Workflow Kit** as a shared **Compile-Time Surface Stack**, with ScriptKit as an adjacent share/repro lane. The execution posture should be a ranked pilot program: strict build-script authority lane → proc-macro-heavy workflow lane → structured replacement lane (`links` override / metabuild / delegation) → shareable single-file repro lane → future-facing transition lane.

## 2026-03-08 — Priority update
- Promoted **Build Extension Kit** from **Tier 1** to **Tier 0/1** and **Macro Workflow Kit** from **Tier 1/2** to **Tier 1** in `PRIORITIES.md`. The key reason is not that either tool became independently glamorous, but that together with Compile-Time Capabilities they now form a more credible top-band strategic stack.
- Updated `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` so the frontier now names **Compile-Time Surface Stack** directly and ranks it above Native Edge / Wasm / Compatibility Claims, while keeping those bands important.

## 2026-03-08 — Hygiene update
- Strengthened `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future compile-time revisions keep authority, declarative replacement, workflow/debug/cost artifacts, single-file share/repro ergonomics, and future transition lanes distinct instead of collapsing them into one compile-time mega-kit or one fake “safe build” story.

## 2026-03-08 — Compile-time governance-profile refresh (named ladders, stage gates, profile-fit reports)
- The compile-time frontier now looks mature enough that the archive should stop talking only in terms of “sandboxing” and start talking in terms of named governance profiles. The sandboxed-build-scripts goal explicitly wants per-crate permissions, a shared configuration surface with proc-macro concerns, support for `-sys` crates, and an eventual path where sandboxed build scripts can become the default. That is a strong sign that ideal Rust needs a profile ladder, not just one yes/no sandbox switch. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/sandboxed-build-script.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html
- Cargo’s 1.94 development-cycle update makes the operational side clearer: proc-macros and build scripts are still special enough to complicate target-dir locking and concurrent workflows, and Cargo is simultaneously adding `cargo report rebuild` plus session/timing/report plumbing. That suggests compile-time surfaces should be legible enough for rebuild, cache, and workflow consumers — another reason to add named profiles and fit reports instead of leaving each tool to invent its own maturity language. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The language-side pressure is also stronger than the archive previously encoded. The macro-improvements goal explicitly argues that reducing proc-macro demand can make projects build substantially faster and shrink dependency chains; the reflection-and-comptime goal explicitly frames compile-time reflection as a way to avoid derive lock-in for crates like serializers, logging stacks, and Bevy-style ecosystems; and the const-traits goal says people write a lot of compile-time code today and sometimes move logic into build scripts because `const fn` is not expressive enough. Together, that means the transition targets are not all the same: some code should be narrowed, some should be replaced, and some should migrate into more language-shaped compile-time lanes. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/macro-improvements.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/reflection-and-comptime.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/const-trait.html
- `cargo-script` remaining a 2026 flagship matters here too. It is a reminder that small single-file packages are becoming more first-class and should not live outside the compile-time governance story; they need lightweight packs plus an answer to which compile-time profile they actually satisfy. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Archive decision: add `design/compile-time-profile-ladder.md`, extend Compile-Time Capabilities with `ct-profile-catalog/v0` and `ct-profile-fit-report/v0`, update the compile-time pilot program so every lane has an explicit graduation target, and refresh the frontier/priorities/amnesia resistors around the idea that the real missing contribution is a named governance ladder, not one more compile-time gadget.

## 2026-03-08 — Perf-labs frontier refresh (collector profiles, baseline hygiene, ranked pilots)
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still says resource usage — especially slow compile times and storage usage — remains one of the biggest productivity problems. That keeps performance work squarely in the “ecosystem-wide pain” category rather than a specialist concern. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The 2025H2 goals program puts **Flexible, fast(er) compilation** in the flagship themes and explicitly frames it as improving both specialized build scenarios and everyday development workflows. That matters for the archive because it means performance evidence is not just compiler-team housekeeping; it is part of Rust’s declared near-term direction. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/28/project-goals-2025h2/
- Cargo’s build-analysis goal and the 1.93/1.94 development-cycle updates make the machine-facing angle much sharper than before. Cargo is recording build metadata across invocations, adding `cargo report timings`, `cargo report rebuild`, and `cargo report sessions`, and explicitly discussing schema work that could also help other machine consumers. That creates a better landing zone for an external performance-evidence substrate than the archive had previously captured. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-build-analysis.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- The `rustc-perf` improvements goal is especially clarifying: it is explicitly about distributed benchmarking across multiple platforms and configurations, and it notes that current regression-handling policy does not yet consider conflicting benchmarking results. That is strong evidence that collector identity and comparability need first-class treatment instead of being hidden in implementation lore. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/rustc-perf-improvements.html
- The rustc dev guide says a perf run compares compiler versions across concrete configurations like fresh and incremental builds, and today only `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` builds are tracked on the hosted service. That reinforces the archive’s decision to treat performance lanes and collector profiles as explicit artifacts, not footnotes. Source: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/tests/perf.html
- `cargo bench` still centers a fragmented story: libtest-style `#[bench]` is unstable/nightly-only and stable benchmarking commonly relies on custom harnesses or ecosystem tools. That is another reason the archive should stop looking for one universal benchmark runner and instead emphasize shared evidence, comparison, and gating artifacts. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-bench.html
- The compiler-facing performance goals also sharpen the pilot order. Cranelift is being pushed toward recommendation for local development, with measured wins in codegen and total clean-build time on some projects, while the parallel front end continues working toward stabilization and more benchmarks. That makes compile-workflow evidence the right first pilot instead of an afterthought. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/production-ready-cranelift.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/parallel-front-end.html
- Archive decision: add `design/perf-pilot-program.md`, strengthen `design/perf-labs.md` and `proposals/epic-perf-labs.md`, promote **Perf Labs** into the strategic frontier, refresh the broad priority note so future revisions prefer baseline hygiene and ranked pilots over benchmark-dashboard work, and add an amnesia resistor requiring subject / lane / collector / baseline / verdict separation.

## 2026-03-08 — Toolchain productization refresh (sysroot identity, instrumented std, ranked pilots)
- The sysroot/build-std thread now deserves promotion from buried Tier-1 idea to active frontier. The `build-std` goal is explicitly about a stabilizable MVP, the October 2025 program update says build-std RFCs were posted, and the 2026 flagships page keeps build-std in the active “Building blocks” direction. That means the archive should stop treating rebuilt std as a speculative niche and start treating it as an ecosystem seam with a real upstream landing zone. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/build-std.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/11/19/program-management-update--october-2025/ ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The strongest additional signal is sanitizer support. The sanitizer-support goal explicitly says MemorySanitizer and ThreadSanitizer need infrastructure to provide **precompiled and instrumented standard libraries**, while the unstable-book sanitizer docs still recommend rebuilding and instrumenting std for sanitizer workflows. That makes sysroot identity, activation, and reuse a first-class ecosystem problem rather than hidden local build state. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/stabilization-of-sanitizer-support.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/sanitizer.html
- Rust-for-Linux also sharpens the practical requirements: the tooling goal explicitly calls out a blessed way to rebuild std and ABI-affecting / hardening-related flags, and the end-of-2025 program update says other adopters like CPython are surfacing a similar cluster of needs (`build-std`, platform support, sanitizer support). That means the archive should think in terms of **toolchain productization** rather than just “custom std builds”. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/rfl.html ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/12/19/program-management-update--end-of-2025/
- Archive decision: add [`design/toolchain-productization-pilot-program.md`](./design/toolchain-productization-pilot-program.md), strengthen [`design/sysroot-pack-kit.md`](./design/sysroot-pack-kit.md) and [`proposals/epic-sysroot-pack-kit.md`](./proposals/epic-sysroot-pack-kit.md), promote **Sysroot Pack Kit** from **Tier 1** to **Tier 0/1**, and treat **Sysroot Pack Kit + Cross Toolchain Kit + Sanitizer Battery Kit** as a shared **Toolchain Productization Stack** in the strategic frontier. The ranked pilot order should be instrumented stdlib → hardened / ABI-modifying → custom target / tier-3 → shared cache / CI → external build handoff.

## 2026-03-08 — Async lifecycle frontier refresh (pilot lanes, shutdown policy, runtime capability profiles)
- The archive had Async Lifecycle Kit in the broad map, but it was under-specified relative to current official Rust direction. The 2025H1 async flagship is explicit that async should feel as expressive, reliable, and productive as sync Rust, and it calls out runtime choice, runtime interoperability, cancellation sharp edges, and reliability as active ecosystem pain. That makes lifecycle structure a worthy substrate problem, not just a Tokio convenience niche. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/async.html
- The May 2025 project-goals update is a good maturity signal: the official Async Book gained chapters on concurrency primitives, structured concurrency, and pinning. That suggests the problem is moving from scattered community lore toward something the ecosystem can standardize around with portable artifacts and review surfaces. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/06/20/may-project-goals-update/
- The 2026 flagship themes keep **Just Add Async** alive, with milestones including return type notation, `async fn` in `dyn Trait`, immobile types / guaranteed destructors, and ergonomic ref-counting. Those language improvements matter, but they do not eliminate the present need for task ownership, shutdown policy, and runtime-capability truth; if anything, they make a convergence layer more useful because more libraries and patterns will be viable. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- Pin ergonomics and ergonomic ref-counting sharpen the same conclusion from two angles: `Pin` remains awkward enough to block async/generator ergonomics, while async programs frequently share state across tasks via `Arc`-like patterns. Together they suggest that “ideal Rust async” is not just syntax; it is lifecycle structure with explicit ownership and less incidental friction. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/pin-ergonomics.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/ergonomic-rc.html
- Tokio’s graceful-shutdown guidance shows the ecosystem already has real primitives (`CancellationToken`, task tracking, join/drain phases), but today they remain runtime-shaped building blocks rather than a portable review boundary. That is exactly the kind of seam this archive should prioritize: not replacing the runtime, but exporting attachable lifecycle truth that CI, triage, replay, and debugger consumers can reuse. Source: https://tokio.rs/tokio/topics/shutdown
- Archive decision: add [`design/async-lifecycle-pilot-program.md`](./design/async-lifecycle-pilot-program.md), refresh the gap/design/epic docs around `runtime-capability-profile/v0`, `shutdown-policy/v0`, `async-lifecycle-report/v0`, and `async-pack/v0`, promote **Async Lifecycle Kit** from **Tier 1** to **Tier 0/1**, and add an async-specific amnesia resistor so future revisions keep runtime capability, ownership policy, cancellation/shutdown evidence, and replay/debugger consumer lanes distinct.


## 2026-03-08 — Release-truth frontier refresh (release subject, signed-install attachments, rebuild attachments)
- The release/distribution seam now deserves promotion from buried Tier-1 idea to a real frontier band. Cargo’s official publishing model is already a permanent act based on a concrete `.crate` package boundary, which means release evidence matters at least as much as build/test evidence. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-publish.html
- crates.io’s January 2026 update is a strong signal that release identity and policy are becoming more security-sensitive: Trusted Publishing now supports GitLab CI/CD as well as GitHub Actions, crate owners can enforce Trusted-Publishing-only mode, and risky GitHub triggers (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run`) are blocked. That means a worthy ecosystem contribution should assume release policy is about explicit issuer/CI identity, not just possession of a token. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Cargo’s 1.93 development-cycle update strengthens the “release boundary” case from another angle: Cargo is explicitly exploring **custom final artifacts** for build scripts with controlled uplift into the artifact directory, and it continues pushing structured reporting / artifact collection rather than forcing tools to scrape target-dir folklore. That makes a release-pack layer look aligned with Cargo’s direction instead of bolted on. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- Cargo’s unstable `sbom` support also matters more than the archive had previously captured. SBOM precursor files are generated beside executable and linkable outputs uplifted into the target/artifact directories, which is exactly the sort of native attachment seam a release-boundary kit should import rather than reinvent. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- The ecosystem already has credible machine-readable and operational building blocks. `cargo-dist-schema` publishes a schema for `dist-manifest.json`; `release-plz` already automates release PRs, changelogs, publishing, and release creation; `cargo-binstall` already supports signature verification with explicit metadata; and `cargo-dist` has grown security-adjacent outputs such as SBOM support and OmniBOR artifact IDs. That combination argues for a shared contract layer rather than another bespoke release tool. Sources: https://docs.rs/cargo-dist-schema/latest/cargo_dist_schema/ ; https://github.com/release-plz/release-plz ; https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall/blob/main/SIGNING.md ; https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md
- The Jan David Nose interview is the key “outside the box” signal: the infrastructure side explicitly says Rust likely has not reached the final state of what the crates.io package format should look like, especially for use cases that may want precompiled material. That is strong evidence that the release/distribution story still needs intentional ecosystem design instead of assuming the current upload/install surface is the last word. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/25/interview-with-jan-david-nose/
- Archive decision: add `design/release-pipeline-pilot-program.md`, strengthen `design/release-pipeline-kit.md`, `design/signed-binaries-kit.md`, `design/repro-build-kit.md`, and `proposals/epic-release-pipeline-kit.md`, introduce a shared **Release Truth Stack** in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, promote **Release Pipeline Kit** from **Tier 1** to **Tier 0/1**, and add a release-specific amnesia resistor so future revisions keep source publish, built-artifact inventory, signatures, provenance, and rebuild verdicts separate instead of collapsing them into one fake “secure release” status.


## 2026-03-08 — Policy frontier refresh (decision points, waiver budgets, ranked pilots)
- The current Rust direction keeps strengthening the policy seam rather than replacing it. The 2026 flagships explicitly put supply-chain work on the board through public/private dependencies, breaking-change detection, and SBOM generation, which means release- and dependency-governance decisions are increasingly core Rust workflow rather than optional enterprise garnish. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update adds a Security tab, expands Trusted Publishing, exposes `pubtime`, and improves source/docs discoverability. Combined with Cargo’s permanent-publish model, that means the ecosystem now has richer governance inputs and stronger reasons to make release-admission decisions reviewable and diffable. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html
- The February 2026 malicious-crate notification-policy update is strategically important: the crates.io team is intentionally reducing incident-blog noise, which makes local, attachable policy artifacts more valuable because teams cannot rely on public posts as the main governance interface. The September 2025 `faster_log` / `async_println` incident remains a concrete reminder that registry-risk handling is not hypothetical. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/13/crates.io-malicious-crate-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/24/crates.io-malicious-crates-fasterlog-and-asyncprintln/
- The ecosystem already has serious policy ingredients, but they are split across tools. `cargo vet` already models built-in criteria, subtree-sensitive policies, trusted entries, and audit/diff workflows; `cargo-deny` already models advisories, bans, licenses, sources, and machine-readable exit classes. That strengthens the archive’s existing view that the missing contribution is an explainable decision layer and rollout plan, not another scanner. Sources: https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/audit-criteria.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/specifying-policies.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/trusted-entries.html ; https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/performing-audits.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/cfg.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/advisories/cfg.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/bans/index.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/licenses/index.html ; https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/cli/check.html
- Archive decision: add [`design/policy-pilot-program.md`](./design/policy-pilot-program.md), refresh [`design/policy-kit.md`](./design/policy-kit.md) and [`proposals/epic-policy-kit.md`](./proposals/epic-policy-kit.md), and tighten [`STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`](./STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md) / [`PRIORITIES.md`](./PRIORITIES.md) so **Policy Kit** is now explicitly a ranked rollout (package release gate → workspace split-scope → proc-macro/build-lane cooldown → artifact-linked release candidate → migration diff lane) instead of a generic future compliance substrate.


## 2026-03-08 — Support-envelope pilot refresh (explicit support lanes, evidence policy, docs truth)
- The rustc platform-support book keeps the target-tier story explicit: Tier 1 means guaranteed to work with tests, Tier 2 means guaranteed to build, and several mainstream targets publish minimum kernel/libc floors. That is strong evidence that support claims are already lane-shaped and floor-shaped upstream, even if crate-level tooling rarely preserves that shape. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/rustc/platform-support.html
- Rust 1.91 promoted `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` to Tier 1 and re-explained the tier system in the release notes. This is a concrete reminder that target support changes over time and that support-diff artifacts should be treated as first-class release information rather than optional nice-to-have metadata. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/30/Rust-1.91.0/
- docs.rs target metadata plus the October 2025 default-target change make docs support impossible to treat as a side detail. Crate authors can already control `default-target`, `targets`, and `additional-targets`, and the Rust project itself changed the defaults to reflect ecosystem reality. That means docs surfaces are part of the public support contract. Sources: https://docs.rs/about/metadata ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/10/16/docsrs-changed-default-targets/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the canonical reference while editor/agentic tooling rises. That strengthens the case for explicit docs-surface truth: hidden docs-target choices now shape both human reading and machine-assisted consumption. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- RFC 3477 is the operationally important missing ingredient the archive had underweighted: Rust’s standard stability guarantee attaches to `cargo build`, not `cargo check`. For support-envelope work, that means released-artifact or runtime claims cannot be honestly grounded in check-only evidence, and pilot programs need explicit evidence-policy artifacts instead of inheriting whatever CI happened to run. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3477-cargo-check-lang-policy.html
- Cargo’s 1.94 development-cycle update reiterates that Cargo plugins matter because Cargo cannot be everything to everyone. That is a good fit for `cargo support`: the ecosystem does not need to wait for one giant built-in Cargo feature before support contracts become reviewable. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/02/18/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.94/
- Archive decision: add [`design/support-envelope-pilot-program.md`](./design/support-envelope-pilot-program.md), refresh [`design/support-envelope-kit.md`](./design/support-envelope-kit.md) and [`proposals/epic-support-envelope-kit.md`](./proposals/epic-support-envelope-kit.md), and tighten [`STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`](./STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md) / [`PRIORITIES.md`](./PRIORITIES.md) so the **Support Envelope** half of the broader Compatibility Claims stack now has its own ranked pilot program and explicit evidence-policy posture.

## 2026-03-08 — Canonical learning stack refresh (docs remain canon, crate guidance rises, tools must import rather than overwrite)
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the preferred canonical reference, while some learning traffic appears to be shifting toward LLM tooling and agentic editors. That is a strong signal that the ecosystem needs clearer maintainer-authored learning artifacts, not fewer. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Rust’s recent vision work explicitly recommends expanding extensibility to include **better diagnostics and guidance from crates**. That strengthens the case that crate-authored compile guidance is not just UX polish; it is part of how Rust should scale across domains and skill levels. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/19/what-do-people-love-about-rust/
- docs.rs metadata already exposes public knobs that shape the published docs surface (`default-target`, `targets`, `additional-targets`, features, rustdoc args), rustdoc already executes documentation examples, mdBook already tests book examples, and `trybuild` already treats compile-fail output as a user-facing teaching surface. That means the missing contribution is increasingly the canonical artifact layer and rollout discipline above these primitives. Sources: https://docs.rs/about/metadata ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/documentation-tests.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/mdBook/cli/test.html ; https://docs.rs/trybuild
- Archive decision: add `design/docproof-pilot-program.md` to make DocProof executable, add `design/canonical-learning-stack.md` to synthesize **DocProof Kit + Compile Guidance Kit**, promote DocProof in `PRIORITIES.md`, and replace the standalone frontier-edge Compile Guidance framing with a broader **Canonical Learning Stack** framing in `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`. The strategic theory is now explicit: maintainers publish canonical learning truth first, and semantic/editor/assistant/release/support/atlas consumers import it second.

## 2026-03-08 — Canonical-learning consumer pilot refresh (import discipline for docs hosts, CI, editors, assistants)
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the preferred canonical reference while editor/agentic use is rising. That makes a missing boundary sharper: Rust needs more than structured outputs; it needs consumer lanes that can import canonical learning truth without replacing it. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Rust’s recent vision work explicitly recommends better diagnostics and guidance from crates plus deeper compilation-workflow extensibility. That suggests crate-authored learning/guidance surfaces should have downstream consumers, but it does **not** imply those consumers should become the authority source. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/12/19/what-do-people-love-about-rust/
- docs.rs already hosts rustdoc JSON, which means hosted docs now have a real structured import surface. Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json
- `rustc` JSON diagnostics and Cargo’s JSON diagnostic modes mean compile-time guidance is already structurally consumable, while `cargo fix` proves some downstream consumers can apply suggestions. That increases the need for explicit derivation/mutation boundaries rather than ambient scraping. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/rustc/json.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-build.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html
- Stable diagnostic attributes strengthen the case that crates can intentionally publish compile-time guidance surfaces. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html
- Archive decision: add `design/canonical-learning-consumer-pilot-program.md`, refresh the canonical-learning/docproof/compile-guidance design text, and tighten `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md` / `PRIORITIES.md` so the next credible move is no longer only “run docproof and compile-guidance pilots”, but also “run an explicit shared consumer-import pilot” with a ranked order: docs host → CI/release review → editor overlay → assistant slice → atlas/support/release import.


## 2026-03-08 — Airgap pilot refresh (restricted-network truth needs ranked lanes, not one “offline Rust” claim)
- The Rust project’s accepted mirroring goal is explicit that Rust needs cryptographic verification and secure mirroring for crates.io and Rust releases, motivated by restrictive firewalls, unreliable internet, CI mirrors, and stronger supply-chain assurances. That makes this seam strategically real rather than enterprise-local folklore. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/verification-and-mirroring.html
- Cargo’s source-replacement docs say replacement sources are for mirrors or exact local copies, and they rely on a core assumption that the source code is **exactly the same** in both sources. That is stronger and more useful than a generic “offline support exists” claim: it means mirror topology and exact-copy posture are already reviewable semantics upstream. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/source-replacement.html
- Cargo’s own install story makes the three-plane separation unavoidable. `cargo install` is system/user-level, starts config discovery at `$CARGO_HOME/config.toml`, and by default ignores the packaged `Cargo.lock` unless `--locked` is passed. The FAQ also warns that `Cargo.lock` does not protect consumers like `cargo install` automatically. That means workspace-build success, developer-tool-install success, and toolchain bootstrap success are distinct restricted-network lanes. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/faq.html
- rustup’s documented mirror variables (`RUSTUP_DIST_SERVER`, `RUSTUP_UPDATE_ROOT`) mean toolchain mirroring is a supported path, not a hack. This strengthens the archive’s earlier Airgap Kit thesis that rustup distribution must remain a separate plane from Cargo registry/build behavior. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/environment-variables.html
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update adds Trusted Publishing Only Mode and other publish-side hardening, but that still does not answer consumer-side restricted-network truth. In other words: upstream publishing security is improving, but install/mirror/bootstrap validation is still a missing shared contract. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/
- Archive decision: add [`design/airgap-pilot-program.md`](./design/airgap-pilot-program.md), refresh [`design/airgap-kit.md`](./design/airgap-kit.md) and [`proposals/epic-airgap-kit.md`](./proposals/epic-airgap-kit.md), promote **Airgap Kit** in [`PRIORITIES.md`](./PRIORITIES.md), and add a first-class restricted-network seam to [`STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`](./STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md). The archive now treats restricted-network Rust as a ranked rollout: workspace dependency/build lane → developer-tool install lane → rustup/toolchain mirror lane → secure mirror verification lane → integrated CI/bootstrap lane.

## 2026-03-16 — Web productization stack refresh (browser Wasm and full-stack web need a boundary above frameworks)
- The 2024 State of Rust survey says WebAssembly use is mostly in the **browser** (23%) rather than other Wasm contexts (7%), and the same survey says Rust remains especially popular for server backends plus web/networking services. That makes browser-facing and mixed client/server web work a mainstream Rust product lane rather than a niche experiment. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/13/2024-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- `wasm-bindgen` remains the center of Rust↔JavaScript interop, `web-sys` exposes browser APIs behind cargo features, and unstable browser APIs are explicitly treated as a separate unstable lane. That strengthens the case that browser capability truth should be reviewable instead of hidden in crate feature sets and generated glue. Sources: https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-bindgen/ ; https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-bindgen/web-sys/index.html ; https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-bindgen/web-sys/using-web-sys.html ; https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-bindgen/web-sys/unstable-apis.html
- `wasm-pack` already makes JS/Wasm package identity real by generating a Wasm binary, JS wrapper, README, and `package.json`, while Trunk treats Wasm, JS snippets, and static assets as one bundling lane from an HTML entrypoint. That is a strong signal that package/bundle/base-path truth is already a product concern above raw compilation. Sources: https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-pack/introduction.html ; https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-pack/commands/build.html ; https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-pack/tutorials/npm-browser-packages/packaging-and-publishing.html ; https://trunkrs.dev/
- The framework layer is now openly plural and operationally sharp-edged: Leptos explicitly splits CSR with Trunk from SSR/hydration with `cargo-leptos`, documents hydration mechanics and bugs, and treats Wasm binary size and path deployment as real concerns; Dioxus explicitly treats SSG, route bundle splitting, CDN assets, Wasm-provider deployment, and server-only dependency leakage as part of its full-stack story; Yew’s SSR docs explicitly warn that `web_sys` APIs are unavailable during server rendering and can panic if used there. Sources: https://book.leptos.dev/getting_started/index.html ; https://book.leptos.dev/ssr/22_life_cycle.html ; https://book.leptos.dev/ssr/24_hydration_bugs.html ; https://book.leptos.dev/deployment/binary_size.html ; https://book.leptos.dev/islands.html ; https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-leptos/latest ; https://dioxuslabs.com/learn/0.7/essentials/fullstack/ ; https://dioxuslabs.com/learn/0.7/essentials/fullstack/project_setup/ ; https://dioxuslabs.com/learn/0.7/guides/deploy/ ; https://yew.rs/docs/0.21/advanced-topics/server-side-rendering
- The 2025 State of Rust survey says online docs remain the canonical reference while editor/agentic consumption rises. That makes browser/runtime/deploy/support truth more important, because generated web output is increasingly consumed by both humans and machine tooling. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/web-apps-browser-wasm-and-fullstack-productization-contracts.md`, `design/web-productization-stack.md`, `design/web-productization-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-web-productization-stack.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and promote an explicit **Web Productization Stack** so the archive treats **render mode + browser capability + bundle/deploy + server/client split + support truth** as a ranked seam instead of leaving Rust web work fragmented across frameworks and bundlers.

## 2026-03-16 — Media productization stack refresh (transcoding, playback, streaming, and support need a boundary above crates)
- `image` is now more than a basic image decode/encode lane: the main docs emphasize a stable common-operations surface plus low-level decoder/encoder control and format hooks, while the recent changelog records new XMP/IPTC/ICC metadata handling and broader TIFF/color behavior. That sharpens the need to keep format recognition, metadata behavior, and processing posture explicit instead of flattening them into “supports PNG/JPEG/etc.” Sources: https://docs.rs/image/latest/image/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/image/latest/source/CHANGES.md
- Symphonia is explicit about being a **100% pure Rust** audio decoding and multimedia format demuxing framework, and it keeps default-vs-feature-gated format/codec support visible. That is exactly the kind of support truth a productization layer should preserve rather than hide behind feature defaults. Source: https://docs.rs/symphonia/latest/symphonia/
- `ffmpeg-next` remains strategically important precisely because it is honest about its limits: the crate says it is in maintenance mode and aims for compatibility across FFmpeg 3.4 through 8.0. That makes native-version/runtime posture first-class product truth for real Rust media products, not just build setup trivia. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ffmpeg-next/latest
- GStreamer Rust explicitly targets writing GStreamer-based applications and plugins, which means Rust media products already have a serious plugin/runtime lane; `tracing-gstreamer` makes the observability side explicit by bridging GStreamer logging/tracing into Rust `tracing`. That strengthens the archive’s conclusion that runtime evidence belongs inside the shared boundary. Sources: https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org/documentation/rust/stable/latest/docs/gstreamer/ ; https://docs.rs/tracing-gstreamer/latest/tracing_gstreamer/
- `video-rs` is a useful “state of the seam” signal: it aims to provide a stable and Rusty interface to reading, writing, muxing, encoding, and decoding on top of FFmpeg/libav, while also warning that it is still work-in-progress and depends on FFmpeg libraries. That is strong evidence that Rust needs a product boundary above the runtime lane rather than one more runtime-local abstraction. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/video-rs/latest
- `rav1e` and `mp4parse` push the same conclusion from opposite ends: Rust media can be encode-heavy (`rav1e`) or inspect/container-focused (`mp4parse`) without those lanes being interchangeable. Source: https://github.com/xiph/rav1e ; https://docs.rs/mp4parse/latest/mp4parse/
- Archive decision: add `gaps/media-products-transcoding-streaming-playback-and-support-contracts.md`, `design/media-productization-stack.md`, `design/media-productization-pilot-program.md`, and `proposals/epic-media-productization-stack.md`; refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`; and promote an explicit **Media Productization Stack** so the archive treats **operation/format/processing truth + runtime/plugin/backend activation + service/client attachments + observability/fidelity evidence + shipped/support truth** as a ranked seam instead of leaving Rust media products fragmented across crate docs and setup lore.

## 2026-03-16 — Cryptography productization refresh (provider truth, runtime validation, secret posture, support imports)
- The archive already had a strong **Cryptography Surface Kit**, but the current ecosystem signals say the missing seam is now higher-level and product-facing. `rustls` has a first-class `CryptoProvider` seam with two built-in provider lanes, process-default installation, explicit custom-provider hooks, and even an HSM-style key-loading example. That means provider selection and key-source posture are already part of the public product boundary, not private implementation detail. Sources: https://docs.rs/rustls/latest/rustls/crypto/struct.CryptoProvider.html ; https://docs.rs/rustls/latest/rustls/manual/_03_howto/index.html
- The compliance story is also much sharper than the archive’s older kit-level framing. `rustls`’s FIPS guide explicitly requires the `fips` feature, the FIPS provider, and runtime validation of `ClientConfig`/`ServerConfig`; `aws-lc-rs` is explicit that FIPS and non-FIPS builds differ materially in build requirements, and its docs tell users who need an older validated module to pin `aws-lc-rs` to a specific version. That is strong evidence that “supports FIPS” is not one boolean and should not remain README prose. Sources: https://docs.rs/rustls/latest/rustls/manual/_06_fips/index.html ; https://docs.rs/aws-lc-rs/latest/aws_lc_rs/ ; https://docs.rs/crate/aws-lc-rs/latest
- The trait/generic and secret-handling side is also more clearly a product seam now. RustCrypto’s `crypto` facade crate exists to keep independently versioned trait crates compatible; `secrecy` and `zeroize` describe wrapper and wipe behavior rather than full memory protection; `subtle` is explicit that its constant-time story is best-effort and release-build-sensitive; `signature::Error` is deliberately opaque to avoid side-channel leakage while still allowing source errors for remote signers like HSM/KMS integrations; and `password-hash` gives Rust a real PHC-string interchange lane. Those are exactly the kinds of truths a productization layer should keep separate but composable. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/crypto/latest ; https://docs.rs/secrecy/latest/secrecy/ ; https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/ ; https://docs.rs/subtle/latest/subtle/ ; https://docs.rs/signature/latest/signature/struct.Error.html ; https://docs.rs/password-hash/latest/password_hash/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still says online documentation is the preferred canonical reference while LLM/editor workflows are rising, and it also shows support/maintenance concerns staying visible. That means crypto-facing support claims need better portable artifacts than issue-thread memory and framework examples. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- Archive decision: promote an explicit **Cryptography Productization Stack** above the earlier Cryptography Surface Kit, add `design/cryptography-productization-stack.md`, `design/cryptography-productization-pilot-program.md`, `proposals/epic-cryptography-productization-stack.md`, and `gaps/crypto-products-keys-providers-compliance-and-support-contracts.md`, update the frontier/priorities so future work prefers **provider/compliance truth + randomness posture + runtime/key-source activation + support/docs truth** over another primitive/provider bake-off, and add an amnesia resistor to stop future revisions from collapsing crypto products into a single fake “secure” verdict.

- The Rust Foundation’s 2026–2028 strategy now names **Sustainable Maintenance** as a core pillar, which is strong evidence that maintenance is upstream ecosystem infrastructure rather than just community sentiment. Source: https://rustfoundation.org/strategic-plan/

That is direct evidence that maintenance observation, support-routing, and funding posture are related but distinct lanes. That makes maintenance-support reality more concrete than older archive language implied. Source: https://rustfoundation.org/media/annual-report-strategy-2025/
- The maintainer-fund design note says maintenance success often looks like “things still work as they used to”, which is strong evidence that raw operational observations and derived maintenance-value conclusions must stay separate. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/12/what-is-maintenance-anyway/
- Forge’s issue-triaging and triage-procedure docs already encode queue states, reproduction/minimization routing, and 15-day PR aging thresholds, which is direct evidence that **workflow policy** is already a first-class maintenance lane rather than project-local folklore. Sources: https://forge.rust-lang.org/release/issue-triaging.html ; https://forge.rust-lang.org/release/triage-procedure.html ; https://forge.rust-lang.org/compiler/prioritization.html

Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/06/05/a-glance-at-the-team-compiler-operations/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/13/infrastructure-team-q4-2025-recap-and-q1-2026-plan/
- The 2025 State of Rust survey still shows concern around developer and maintainer support and asks companies to support contributors and crate authors, while also saying online docs remain canonical as LLM/editor use rises. That increases the value of portable maintenance artifacts that both humans and bounded assistants can import. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/02/2025-State-Of-Rust-Survey-results/
- The March 2026 challenges writeup says experienced users increasingly hit domain-specific ecosystem-maturity issues, which strengthens the case for honest stewardship handoffs in adoption and keystone work. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/20/rust-challenges/
- Archive decision: add `design/maintenance-reality-lane-map.md`, refresh `design/maintenance-reality-stack.md`, `design/stewardship-pilot-program.md`, `gaps/maintenance-operations-and-stewardship-queues.md`, and `proposals/epic-maintenance-reality-stack.md`, then update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future maintenance/lifecycle/keystone/support revisions keep lifecycle intent, workflow policy, observed state, derived pressure findings, help-routing, mentoring capacity, visibility posture, and consumer handoffs distinct instead of flattening them into one fake health verdict.

## 2026-03-17 — Package admission stack refresh (publish review needs a boundary above graph, API, inventory, trust, and policy)
- Rust’s 2026 flagship roadmap keeps **Secure your supply chain** active and explicitly names **public/private dependencies** and **SBOM generation** as milestones. That means package publication is upstream strategic terrain, not just downstream compliance glue. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The public/private dependencies goal exists specifically to help users catch accidental implementation-detail exposure and help tooling identify what constitutes an API, while Cargo’s unstable feature docs show `public-dependency` as a real machine-facing seam. That strengthens the archive’s view that public-contract review belongs inside package admission rather than living only in semver folklore. Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/pub-priv.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- The `cargo-semver-checks` goal text still frames publish-time SemVer checking as part of the long-term `cargo publish` direction. That makes the missing layer less “yet another API diff tool” and more “a reviewable publish bundle that can import API evidence honestly.” Sources: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/cargo-semver-checks.html ; https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2024h2/cargo-semver-checks.html
- Cargo’s package/install docs sharpen the package boundary in a useful way: `cargo package` says `Cargo.lock` is always included unless excluded, while `cargo install --locked` uses the packaged lockfile when available. Together they show that publication already carries durable graph intent, but consumer installation can still diverge unless that intent is preserved explicitly. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-package.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html
- Cargo’s features reference says new crates or versions published on crates.io are limited to **300 features** unless an exception is granted. That is a strong reminder that feature posture is not just local manifest trivia; it already affects publication reality. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
- The Cargo publishing reference says crates.io is intended as a permanent archive and that yanking, not deletion, is the mechanism for later correction. That reinforces the archive’s claim that publication is durable enough to deserve explainable admission evidence and visible waivers. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html
- crates.io’s January 2026 development update added Trusted Publishing Only Mode, blocked risky GitHub triggers for Trusted Publishing, and added the `pubtime` field to the index. The February 2026 malicious-crate policy update says routine malware removals will always receive a RustSec advisory. Those changes strengthen the package-admission seam because registry-side publish identity, freshness, and advisory imports are becoming more regular and more structured. Sources: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/01/21/crates-io-development-update/ ; https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/02/13/crates.io-malicious-crate-update/
- Archive decision: add `proposals/epic-package-admission-stack.md`, deepen `design/package-admission-stack.md` and `design/package-admission-pilot-program.md`, refresh `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, and `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, and treat **Package Admission Stack** as an explicit epic candidate centered on **graph truth + exposure truth + inventory/trust imports + policy decision + bounded package-to-release handoff** rather than a loose bundle of adjacent kits.

## 2026-03-22 — rev0398: Cargo artifact contract / artifact-surface promotion
- Rust's 2026 flagship “Building blocks” roadmap explicitly includes **prototype cargo plumbing commands**, which is strong evidence that build-system integration and reusable Cargo internals remain official strategic terrain rather than downstream niche glue. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/flagships.html
- The accepted Cargo plumbing goal already decomposes a build into locate/read/lock/resolve/plan/execute/**stage final artifacts**, and says later commands should accept the outputs of earlier commands. That makes final-artifact staging an explicit seam in Cargo's own mental model. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h1/cargo-plumbing.html
- The 2025 GSoC plumbing prototype implemented seven subcommands through `plan-build`, but not final-artifact staging, and documented blockers in current Cargo APIs. That is good evidence that the missing contribution is now less “invent plumbing” and more “close the reusable handoff boundary above it.” Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/11/18/gsoc-2025-results/
- Cargo's external-tools docs still present the main stable integration surfaces as `cargo metadata`, `--message-format=json`, and custom subcommands. Those are useful primitives, but they still leave downstream tools stitching together final-artifact truth for themselves. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html
- Cargo 1.93's custom-final-artifacts discussion makes explicit that Cargo is reasoning about artifact staging directories, collision checks, selected-package rules, and Cargo-mediated uplift rather than treating final outputs as a purely private implementation detail. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/07/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.93/
- The March 13, 2026 build-dir-layout-v2 testing call says many projects still rely on unspecified build-dir details due to missing features, names artifact/path lookup failure modes directly, and simultaneously says final-artifact layout inside `target-dir` is not what is changing. That sharpens the need for a real Cargo-facing artifact boundary. Source: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/03/13/call-for-testing-build-dir-layout-v2/
- Cargo's build-cache and layout docs now draw a clearer line between internal `build-dir` state and public-facing final-artifact surfaces, and nightly rustc's Cargo layout docs say `artifact-dir` is considered part of the public API. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html ; https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/cargo/core/compiler/layout/index.html
- Cargo's unstable docs say `--artifact-dir` exists because exact artifact filenames are otherwise awkward to determine, and they now tie SBOM precursor files to executable/linkable outputs uplifted into target or artifact directories. That is strong evidence that artifact-sidecars and final-output access are now part of the upstream surface area. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html
- Archive decision: add `design/cargo-artifact-contract-2026Q1.md`, refresh `design/artifact-surface-kit.md`, `gaps/final-artifact-surface-identity-selection-outputs-and-handoffs.md`, `proposals/epic-artifact-surface-kit.md`, and update `INDEX.md`, `PRIORITIES.md`, `STRATEGIC_FRONTIER.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `meta/ACTIVE_FRONTIER.md`, `meta/CANONICAL_WORKING_SET.md`, `meta/REVISION_OPERATING_PROTOCOL.md`, and `meta/AMNESIA_RESISTORS.md` so future revisions treat **build subject truth + phase/evidence-path truth + final artifact identity + origin/staging/copy truth + sidecar truth + downstream handoff truth** as the portable missing boundary instead of flattening Cargo outputs into target-dir archaeology or release-tool lore.
